Chapter 1 · Step-by-step

The Living World

What makes something alive, why biodiversity needs naming, and how taxonomy organises 1.7 million known species.

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

A. What is Living?
1. Characteristics of living organisms2. Growth3. Reproduction4. Metabolism5. Cellular organisation6. Consciousness7. Response to stimuli8. Adaptation
B. Biodiversity
9. Meaning of biodiversity10. Need for classification11. Diversity of living organisms
C. Taxonomy
12. Identification13. Nomenclature14. Classification15. Taxonomy16. Systematics
D. Taxonomic Categories
17. Species18. Genus19. Family20. Order21. Class22. Phylum/Division23. Kingdom
E. Nomenclature
24. Binomial nomenclature25. Scientific names26. Rules of nomenclature27. International codes
F. Taxonomic Aids
28. Herbarium29. Botanical gardens30. Museum31. Zoological parks32. Key33. Flora34. Manuals35. Monographs

Deep Dive · From traits to names

Biology begins by defining life (growth, reproduction, metabolism, consciousness) and immediately faces millions of diverse species needing order - so biodiversity description flows into classification need, taxonomy machinery (identification, nomenclature, ranks) organises it, and taxonomic aids (herbaria to keys) make the system usable daily. Living-versus-nonliving borderlines (viruses) plus rank logic (species to kingdom) plus naming rules (binomial codes) form one connected story examiners love testing end-to-end.
NEET facts:
  • Growth and reproduction are characteristic but not defining (crystals grow; mules are sterile); metabolism plus consciousness define.
  • Species is the basic unit; kingdom the highest rank; genus plus species names every organism.
Fig: Hierarchy widens upward from species to kingdom - humans trace all seven ranks.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Which pair lists defining (not merely characteristic) traits of life?

Solution: Only metabolism plus consciousness lack non-living parallels; growth and reproduction have exceptions on both sides.

Chapter 1 · Topic 1

Characteristics of living organisms

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Living organisms share defining traits no non-living object shows together: growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation, consciousness (sensing plus responding), and adaptation through evolution. Viruses sit on the borderline - they reproduce and evolve but show no metabolism outside hosts. This chapter builds the logic from traits to biodiversity to naming - the foundation of all biology classification.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Growth plus reproduction plus metabolism plus consciousness define life.
  • Viruses are borderline - link between living and non-living.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Which is NOT a defining characteristic of living organisms?

Solution: Growth, reproduction and metabolism define life; sound-making is incidental.

Related Diagram · Living versus non-living traits

Fig: Defining traits have no non-living parallel; shared traits do; viruses sit between.

Chapter 1 · Topic 2

Growth

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Growth in living things means irreversible mass increase by cell division plus enlargement - plants grow lifelong through meristems (indeterminate, open growth), animals stop at maturity (determinate). Non-living things also grow (mountains by accretion, crystals), so growth alone never defines life - only living growth is internal and regulated. Measurement differs: plants by length/area, animals by weight, microbes by cell counts.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living growth is internal (cell division); non-living grows by surface accretion.
  • Plants: indeterminate lifelong growth. Animals: determinate, stops at maturity.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Growth is NOT a defining trait of life because

Solution: Crystal and mountain growth by external accretion mimics size increase without life.

Related Diagram · Growth types

Fig: Living growth builds from inside; crystals accrete outside - only one defines life.

Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 3

Reproduction

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Reproduction makes offspring resembling parents - sexual (two parents, variation via meiosis plus fusion) or asexual (one parent, clones via mitosis: fission, budding, fragmentation, spores, vegetative propagation). Fungi multiply by millions of asexual spores; Planaria regenerates from fragments; mules are sterile despite being alive - so reproduction, though characteristic, is not defining either (like growth). No non-living object reproduces itself.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sexual gives variation; asexual gives speed and clones.
  • Mules are alive but sterile - reproduction is characteristic, not defining.
Remember
  • No non-living object reproduces - reproduction is life-exclusive but not universal.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Mules prove that reproduction is

Solution: Sterile yet living mules show reproduction, like growth, is not universal to life.

Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 4

Metabolism

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in the body - anabolism builds (photosynthesis, protein synthesis) plus catabolism breaks (respiration, digestion) - running every moment in every cell. Isolated single-cell reactions in test tubes count as metabolism performed outside organisms, unlike growth or reproduction. Because no non-living object metabolises, metabolism is the scharfest defining feature - all living things metabolise without exception.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Anabolism builds up; catabolism breaks down; sum is metabolism.
  • Metabolism has no non-living parallel - the most defining trait.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Metabolism can be best defined as

Solution: Every cellular reaction, constructive plus destructive, constitutes metabolism.

Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 5

Cellular organisation

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cellular organisation means all life is built of cells - unicellular (bacteria, Amoeba, Chlamydomonas) or multicellular (fungi, plants, animals) - each cell carrying protoplasm with organelles performing divided labour. Cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann; Virchow adding omnis cellulae e cellula) formalised this. Organisation scales cells to tissues to organs to systems - complexity rising with division of labour, all traceable to cellular units.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Unicellular or multicellular - all life is cellular.
  • Cell theory: all organisms of cells; new cells from pre-existing cells.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Cell theory was proposed by

Solution: Schleiden (plants) plus Schwann (animals) stated cellular composition; Virchow added cell lineage.

Related Diagram · Cell organisation levels

Fig: Cells to tissues to organs to systems - hierarchy of complexity.

Chapter 1 · Topic 6

Consciousness

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Consciousness is sensing the environment plus responding - the most obvious yet technically trickiest trait: humans sense light, microbes swim toward food, plants bend toward light. Self-consciousness (awareness of self) belongs to humans alone, but basic consciousness spans all life. Patient-coma debates and plant-response experiments (Bose crescograph) keep the definition evolving - NCERT treats sensing-plus-response as the working criterion.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Consciousness = sensing plus responding to surroundings.
  • Self-consciousness is human-only; basic consciousness is universal.
Remember
  • Plants sense light, gravity, touch - consciousness without a brain.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Consciousness as a defining trait means

Solution: Microbes to plants sense and respond; only self-awareness is human-exclusive.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 7

Response to stimuli

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Response to stimuli (irritability) is protoplasm fundamental property: phototropism bends shoots to light, roots flee it; touch closes Mimosa leaflets; chemicals attract bacteria (chemotaxis); temperature shifts trigger flowering. Responses range from millisecond electrical signals (Venus flytrap snap) to seasonal developmental switches (photoperiodism). Hormones (auxin redistributing in bending) plus electrical signals mediate plant responses without nerves.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Irritability is protoplasm property - all living cells respond.
  • Tropisms (directional) differ from nastic movements (non-directional).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Mimosa leaf folding on touch is an example of

Solution: Touch-triggered folding is nastic (direction-independent), not tropic.

Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 8

Adaptation

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldA. What is Living?Step-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Adaptation is heritable adjustment to environment built over generations by natural selection: desert succulents store water (reduced leaves, CAM photosynthesis), Arctic mammals grow thick fur plus small extremities (Bergmann/Allen rules), deep-sea fish carry pressure-resistant enzymes. Acclimatisation (one lifetime adjustment, e.g. altitude RBC rise) differs - reversible, non-heritable. Adaptations prove evolution ongoing signature on every lineage.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Adaptations are heritable; acclimatisation is temporary lifetime adjustment.
  • Form follows habitat pressure - succulents, fur, enzymes each solve local problems.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Adaptation differs from acclimatisation in being

Solution: Adaptations evolve genetically; acclimatisation adjusts physiology temporarily.

Chapter 1 · Topic 9

Meaning of biodiversity

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldB. BiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Biodiversity is variety of life at three levels: genetic (gene variants within species - basmati versus IR36 rice), species (counts per area - Western Ghats richness), ecosystem (forests, deserts, reefs variety). India holds ~8 percent of global species on 2.4 percent land - mega-diversity from Himalayan to marine zones. Described species (~1.7 million) likely undercount real diversity (5-30 million estimated) - most undiscovered life is microbial and insect.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Genetic, species, ecosystem - three biodiversity levels.
  • India: mega-diverse (~8 percent species, 2.4 percent land).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Biodiversity includes diversity at levels of

Solution: All three tiers together constitute biodiversity - genes within, species among, systems above.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 10

Need for classification

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldB. BiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Classification became necessary because millions of species overwhelm memory: grouping by similarities lets one description cover thousands (study Poaceae once, know all grasses). It reveals relationships (whale-hippo kinship), predicts properties (close relatives share chemistry), stabilises communication (one scientific name worldwide), and organises conservation priorities. Without classification biology would be an unindexed warehouse of specimens.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Classification enables memory, relationships, prediction, communication.
  • One family description replaces thousands of species accounts.
Remember
  • Classify to remember, relate, predict and communicate - four needs.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

The need for classification arose mainly because

Solution: Millions of species demand grouped, retrievable, relationship-revealing order.

Related Diagram · Why classify

Fig: Remember millions, relate kinship, predict traits, communicate worldwide.

Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 11

Diversity of living organisms

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldB. BiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Living diversity spans Monera to mammals: prokaryotes (oldest, most metabolically inventive - photosynthesis, nitrogen fixation, extremophiles), protists (eukaryotic experiments), fungi (decomposer absorbers), plants (photosynthetic producers from algae to angiosperms), animals (consumers from sponges to humans). Each kingdom solved survival differently - walls versus movement, spores versus seeds, gills versus lungs. Extremophiles (hot springs, salt pans, deep vents) prove life toughest margins.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Five kingdoms span prokaryote to mammal diversity.
  • Extremophiles prove life survives boiling, salt and pressure extremes.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most metabolically diverse organisms are

Solution: Bacteria photosynthesise, fix nitrogen and thrive in extremes - unmatched metabolic range.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 12

Identification

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldC. TaxonomyStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Identification assigns an observed specimen to its correct taxon using diagnostic characters - comparing collected material with preserved references, descriptions and keys. Field botanists press plants, note habitat plus flowering time, then match herbarium sheets and floras; zoologists compare morphology plus anatomy with museum specimens. Correct identification precedes naming and classification - a wrong ID cascades into wrong name, wrong relationships and wrong conservation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Identification = matching specimen to known taxon via characters.
  • Herbarium sheets, museum specimens and keys are comparison tools.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

First step in taxonomy for a collected specimen is

Solution: Match before naming - identification anchors all later taxonomic acts.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 1 · Topic 13

Nomenclature

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldC. TaxonomyStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nomenclature gives each taxon one universal scientific name following agreed rules - eliminating vernacular chaos (one plant, dozens of local names). Binomial names (Genus species) identify species globally; higher taxa get single names (Familia -aceae, Order -ales). Names carry authority citations (who described it) and type specimens anchor them physically. Stability matters - renamed taxa confuse literature, so codes strictly govern changes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One taxon, one universal name - ending vernacular confusion.
  • Species binomial; higher taxa single names with standard endings.
Remember
  • Name once, use worldwide - nomenclature is biology passport system.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Nomenclature chiefly solves the problem of

Solution: Universal scientific names replace conflicting vernacular names across languages.

Chapter 1 · Topic 14

Classification

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldC. TaxonomyStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Classification arranges taxa into hierarchical groups by shared characters - classical (morphology-based, Bentham-Hooker, Linnaean ranks), phylogenetic (evolutionary relationships, Engler-Prantl to APG DNA systems), and numerical/phenetic (overall similarity scores). Modern systems converge on phylogeny (DNA evidence reshuffling families), but herbaria still file Bentham-Hooker style for practicality. Good classification is predictive - family placement forecasts chemistry and traits.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Classical (form), phylogenetic (evolution), numerical (overall similarity).
  • Modern trend: DNA-based APG phylogenetic systems.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Phylogenetic classification is based on

Solution: Shared ancestry grouping reflects true relationships, increasingly DNA-decoded.
Back to Index

Chapter 1 · Topic 15

Taxonomy

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldC. TaxonomyStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Taxonomy is the science of identification, nomenclature and classification - the rules-plus-practice of ordering life (coined by de Candolle). It provides ranks, names, keys and systems; taxonomists describe ~15,000 new species yearly, mostly insects and microbes. Alpha taxonomy (describing species), beta (arranging ranks), gamma (evolutionary patterns) layer the discipline from naming to synthesising. Every biology textbook chapter order is applied taxonomy.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Taxonomy = identification plus nomenclature plus classification.
  • New species described yearly (~15,000, mostly small organisms).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

The term taxonomy was coined by

Solution: de Candolle named the science; Linnaeus built its binomial-rank machinery.

Chapter 1 · Topic 16

Systematics

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldC. TaxonomyStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Systematics is taxonomy plus evolutionary relationships - the broader science placing diversity in phylogenetic context (Simpson: scientific study of kinds plus diversity plus all relationships). While taxonomy names and files, systematics asks why groups exist - reconstructing trees from fossils, anatomy, embryos and molecules. Cladistics (shared derived characters) now dominates, redrawing classic groups (birds inside reptiles, whales inside hoofed mammals).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Systematics = taxonomy plus evolutionary relationships.
  • Cladistics groups by shared derived traits, redrawing old trees.
Remember
  • Taxonomy files; systematics explains the filing order evolutionarily.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Systematics differs from taxonomy in including

Solution: Systematics adds phylogeny to taxonomy naming-filing core.

Chapter 1 · Topic 17

Species

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldD. Taxonomic CategoriesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Species is the basic taxonomic unit - groups of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations reproductively isolated from others (Mayr biological concept). Practical proxies apply where breeding tests fail: morphological (museum specimens), ecological (niche), phylogenetic (DNA clusters) species concepts. Subspecies, varieties and forms rank below. Speciation (isolation plus divergence) manufactures new species - the units taxonomy counts.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Species: interbreeding populations isolated reproductively.
  • Lowest standard rank; subspecies and varieties sit below.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Biological species concept emphasises

Solution: Mayr: interbreeding populations separated reproductively from others.

Chapter 1 · Topic 18

Genus

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldD. Taxonomic CategoriesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Genus groups closely related species sharing a recent ancestor plus major characters - Panthera (lion, tiger, leopard: roaring cats), Solanum (potato, tomato, brinjal: nightshades), Homo (humans plus extinct kin). Monotypic genera hold one species; large genera (Astragalus, 2000+ species) hold thousands. Genus plus species forms the binomial every organism carries - the rank citizens actually use in names.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Genus = related species sharing recent ancestry.
  • First word of every binomial name (capitalised).
Remember
  • Panthera roars, Solanum nightshades - genus groups by kinship.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

In Mangifera indica, Mangifera denotes the

Solution: First binomial word (capitalised) is always the genus.

Family

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldD. Taxonomic CategoriesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Family gathers related genera: Poaceae (grasses - cereals, bamboo), Fabaceae (legumes - pulses, nitrogen fixers), Solanaceae (potato family - alkaloids), Felidae (cats), Hominidae (great apes plus humans). Plant families end -aceae, orders -ales - suffix discipline aids memory. Family-level traits predict chemistry (Fabaceae fix nitrogen, Solanaceae make alkaloids) guiding agriculture and drug prospecting.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Family = related genera; plant suffix -aceae.
  • Family traits predict uses - pulses fix N2, nightshades make drugs.
NEET Practice MCQ

Poaceae is the family of

Solution: Grass family feeds humanity - rice, wheat, maize, bamboo all Poaceae.

Chapter 1 · Topic 20

Order

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldD. Taxonomic CategoriesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Order assembles related families: Poales (grasses plus sedges), Carnivora (cats, dogs, bears - flesh-eaters), Primates (monkeys, apes, humans - grasping hands, big brains). Plant orders end -ales (Liliales, Poales); animal orders lack fixed suffixes. Orders reveal adaptive radiations - Carnivora shearing teeth across continents, Primates arboreal hands freeing for tools - rank where lifestyles diversify visibly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Order = related families; plant suffix -ales.
  • Carnivora teeth, Primate hands show order-level adaptive themes.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Primates as an order includes

Solution: Grasping hands plus forward eyes plus big brains unite the order.

Chapter 1 · Topic 21

Class

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldD. Taxonomic CategoriesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Class unites related orders: Monocotyledonae/Dicotyledonae (flowering plants split by seed leaves), Mammalia (hair, mammary glands, diaphragm), Aves (feathers, flight), Reptilia, Amphibia. Class characters are body-plan fundamentals - mammary glands define mammals more than any single order trait. Angiosperm APG systems now reorganise classes by DNA, but monocot-dicot classroom split persists for teaching.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Class = related orders sharing body-plan fundamentals.
  • Mammalia (hair, milk), Aves (feathers) are class-defining traits.
Remember
  • Class traits are constitutive - feathers make birds, milk makes mammals.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Mammalia as a class is defined by

Solution: Hair plus milk plus diaphragm diagnose mammals - heart chambers shared with birds.

Chapter 1 · Topic 22

Phylum/Division

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldD. Taxonomic CategoriesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phylum (animals) or Division (plants) groups related classes by fundamental body plan: Chordata (notochord, nerve cord, gill slits - all vertebrates plus kin), Arthropoda (jointed legs, chitin - insects, crabs), Bryophyta and Pteridophyta (plant divisions by vascular tissue). Phylum-level traits rarely vary - every chordate keeps dorsal nerve cord position; every arthropod moults chitin. Kingdom-to-phylum is the steepest rank jump in shared traits.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Phylum (animals) = Division (plants); body-plan rank.
  • Chordata nerve cord, Arthropoda chitin - phylum badges.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

In plants, the rank equivalent to animal phylum is

Solution: Botanists say Division (Bryophyta) where zoologists say Phylum (Chordata).

Chapter 1 · Topic 23

Kingdom

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldD. Taxonomic CategoriesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Kingdom is the highest standard rank partitioning all life: Whittaker five (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) by cell type, walls, nutrition and organisation; newer three-domain systems (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) split Monera by molecular depth. Kingdoms reflect life deepest divides - prokaryote versus eukaryote, producer versus consumer versus decomposer. Viruses fit no kingdom (acellular) - taxonomy borderline cases.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Kingdom = highest rank; five (Whittaker) or three domains (Woese).
  • Viruses belong to no kingdom - acellular outsiders.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Five-kingdom system was proposed by

Solution: Whittaker (1969) split life by cell type, walls, nutrition and organisation.

Binomial nomenclature

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldE. NomenclatureStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus, Systema Naturae 1758) names every species Genus species - Mangifera indica (mango), Homo sapiens (humans), Panthera tigris (tiger) - unique worldwide, ending vernacular chaos. Genus capitalised, species lowercase, both italicised in print (underlined separately when handwritten). Authority may follow (Mangifera indica Linn.) crediting the describer. Two words carry global identity - biology universal language.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Genus (capital) + species (lowercase), italicised together.
  • Linnaeus 1758 system still names every new species.
Remember
  • Underline genus and species separately when handwriting - italic substitute.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Correctly written scientific name is

Solution: Capital genus, lowercase species, both italicised - format is testable.

Scientific names

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldE. NomenclatureStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Scientific names follow Latin or latinised form regardless of origin - honouring people (Wolffia johndalensis), places (indica), or traits (alba = white). Generic names are nouns, specific epithets often adjectives agreeing in gender. Once validly published with type specimen and description, names gain priority - oldest valid name wins disputes. Renaming follows strict code rules, keeping literature stable across centuries and languages.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Latinised form; genus noun plus descriptive epithet.
  • Priority rule: oldest validly published name wins.

Chapter 1 · Topic 26

Rules of nomenclature

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldE. NomenclatureStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nomenclature rules enforce stability: valid publication (printed description plus type specimen in recognised journal), priority (oldest valid name stands), tautonym bans in botany (no Tautonyms like Malus malus, allowed in zoology - Gorilla gorilla), Latin form, and author citation. Type specimens anchor names physically - disputes resolve by examining the type. Codes update via international congresses, conserving well-known names against obscure older ones where stability demands.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Valid publication plus type plus priority anchor every name.
  • Botany bans tautonyms; zoology allows them.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Principle of priority in nomenclature means

Solution: Priority stabilises names - first valid publication claims the taxon.

International codes

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldE. NomenclatureStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

International codes govern each kingdom group: ICN (algae, fungi, plants - Vienna Code updates), ICZN (animals), ICNB (bacteria), ICTV (viruses). Each sets valid-publication rules, ranks, name endings and dispute resolution for its domain. Congresses revise codes periodically (algae-fungi-plant code renamed from ICBN). One organism follows one code - no cross-kingdom name clashes allowed within each system.
NEET Snapshot:
  • ICN plants, ICZN animals, ICNB bacteria, ICTV viruses.
  • Codes update at congresses; stability guides every revision.

Herbarium

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldF. Taxonomic AidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Herbarium sheets preserve pressed, dried, poisoned-mounted plants with labels (collector, date, locality, habitat, flower state) - permanent reference vouchers for identification, types and floristic records. Kew (UK, 7M+ sheets) and CAL (Kolkata, India largest) anchor world and national collections. Proper pressing (newspaper changes, no overlap), poisoning (mercuric chloride alternatives now), stitching and fumigation keep sheets centuries-usable. Digital herbaria now image types globally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Pressed, dried, labelled, mounted plants = permanent vouchers.
  • Labels carry collector, date, locality, habitat - data with specimen.

Herbarium sheets mainly serve as

Botanical gardens

Botanical gardens grow living collections for research, conservation, education and reference: Kew (London, world reference), Indian Botanic Garden Howrah (Great Banyan - 250-year-old, 4-acre canopy), Lloyd Darjeeling, Ooty. Gardens maintain seed banks, propagate rarities, display economic plants and train taxonomists. Ex-situ conservation in gardens backs wild reserves - living backup for endangered flora.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living plant museums for research plus conservation plus teaching.
  • Howrah Great Banyan: world largest canopy single tree.
Remember
  • Gardens conserve ex-situ; herbaria record; both serve taxonomy.

Museum

Topic in Depth

Museums preserve animal specimens (stuffed, skeletons, jars in preservatives) plus plant products (woods, fruits, fibres) with collection data - identification references and public education combined. Insect boxes (pinned, labelled, naphthalene-guarded), skeletons showing comparative anatomy, and type specimens anchor taxonomy physically. Natural History Museum London and Indian Museum Kolkata rank among historic giants - research wings describe new species from stored material.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Stuffed, skeletonised and fluid-preserved animals plus data.
  • Insect boxes need naphthalene guarding against pests.

Zoological parks

Topic in Depth

Zoological parks keep live wild animals for conservation breeding, research, education and recreation - ex-situ complements to sanctuaries: breeding endangered species (rhino, lion-tailed macaque programmes), studbooks managing genetics, public awareness funding protection. Modern zoos prioritise spacious naturalistic enclosures plus enrichment over barred cages. Rescue centres rehabilitate injured wildlife for release - parks as ark plus hospital.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Live-animal conservation breeding plus education plus research.
  • Studbooks manage captive genetics against inbreeding.

Zoological parks mainly contribute to

Key

The Living WorldDiversity in the Living WorldF. Taxonomic AidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Taxonomic keys are paired-contrasting identification tools: each couplet offers two opposite leads (flowers red vs not-red), choosing one jumps to the next couplet until the taxon keys out. Indented (yoked) and bracketed formats present the same logic differently. Keys exist for every rank - family keys separate grasses from lilies, species keys separate rice from wheat. Good keys use stable, observable, non-overlapping characters; field botanists carry regional keys routinely.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Couplets of opposite leads narrow down stepwise to taxon.
  • Keys use stable visible characters; exist per rank and region.

A taxonomic key works through

Topic in Depth

Floras are systematic accounts of plants of a defined area - Flora of British India (Hooker), Flora of Madras Presidency, district floras - listing every species with descriptions, keys, flowering times and distributions. Botanists identify unknowns by matching regional floras before monographs; conservation planners mine floras for rarity and endemism data. Writing a flora demands years of herbarium plus field work - the regional taxonomy bible.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Flora = complete plant account of a geographic area.
  • Hooker Flora of British India is the subcontinental classic.
Remember

Manuals

Topic in Depth

Manuals are portable field identification guides - compact keys, spot characters, flowering calendars and illustrations for on-site naming without herbarium access. Forest officers, students and survey teams carry regional manuals (e.g.manuals of Delhi, Madras trees) for quick field decisions. Manuals sacrifice monographic depth for speed and portability - identify now, verify later against floras and sheets.

Topic in Depth

Monographs are exhaustive single-taxon treatises - one family, genus or species group covered completely: taxonomy, anatomy, cytology, chemistry, distribution, phylogeny, keys and revisions. Writing one takes years of global specimen study; using one settles any dispute about that group. Flora chapters often condense monographic research - monographs are taxonomy primary literature, floras its regional application.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Monograph = complete account of one taxon from all angles.
  • Primary research source; floras apply its conclusions regionally.

Biological Classification

Five kingdoms from bacteria to fungi, plus the acellular rebels - viruses, viroids and prions.

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

B. Kingdom Monera
7. Archaebacteria8. Halophiles9. Thermoacidophiles10. Methanogens11. Eubacteria12. Cyanobacteria13. Nitrogen fixation14. Mycoplasma
C. Kingdom Protista

D. Kingdom Fungi

E. Lichens

F. Viruses

39. Structure40. Difference from viruses

Deep Dive · Five kingdoms plus three rebels

Whittaker kingdoms sort life by cell type, walls, organisation, nutrition and phylogeny - Monera (prokaryote generalists plus archaeal extremophiles), Protista (eukaryotic experiments from diatoms to Plasmodium), Fungi (absorptive spore-masters in four classes), Plantae and Animalia (covered in their own chapters). Then the acellular rebels break every rule: viruses (nucleoprotein parcels), viroids (naked RNA), prions (naked protein) - infectivity stripped to smaller packages, each demanding its own code and concept.
NEET facts:
  • Archaea look bacterial but transcribe eukaryotic-like; fungi absorb while plants photosynthesise; Euglena forced Protista creation.
  • Virus (DNA/RNA + protein), viroid (RNA only), prion (protein only) - three minimal rungs.
Fig: Five kingdoms by cell type, walls, organisation and nutrition - plus acellular rebels outside all five.

Which set is correctly matched?

Solution: Euglena photosynthesises plus engulfs; Mycoplasma lacks walls, Penicillium is ascomycete, TMV is RNA virus.

Chapter 2 · Topic 1

Basis of classification

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldA. Five Kingdom ClassificationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Whittaker five kingdoms rest on five bases: cell type (prokaryotic Monera versus eukaryotic rest), cell wall (present in Monera, Protista-some, Fungi, Plantae; absent in Animalia), body organisation (unicellular to complex multicellular), mode of nutrition (photosynthetic, absorptive, ingestive) and reproduction plus phylogenetic relationships. Earlier two-kingdom (Plantae-Animalia) failed - bacteria, fungi and Euglena fit neither - and three-domain (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) later split Monera by molecular depth.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cell type, walls, organisation, nutrition, reproduction plus phylogeny.
  • Two kingdoms failed on bacteria, fungi and Euglena.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Five-kingdom classification is mainly based on

Solution: Whittaker combined structural, nutritional and evolutionary criteria.

Fig: Cell type, walls, organisation, nutrition, phylogeny - five sorting bases.

Chapter 2 · Topic 2

Cell type

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldA. Five Kingdom ClassificationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cell type divides life deepest: prokaryotic cells (Monera - no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA) versus eukaryotic cells (membrane nucleus, organelles, 80S ribosomes). Archaebacteria look prokaryotic but run eukaryotic-like transcription machinery - molecular proof they deserve their own domain. Every kingdom above Monera is eukaryotic; every complexity leap (multicellularity, sex, tissues) happened in eukaryotes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Prokaryotic (Monera) versus eukaryotic (all other kingdoms).
  • Archaea look bacterial but work eukaryotic-like inside.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Prokaryotic cells lack

Solution: Naked nucleoid plus 70S ribosomes define prokaryotes - no membrane partitions.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 2 · Topic 3

Cell wall

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldA. Five Kingdom ClassificationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cell walls mark kingdoms chemically: bacterial peptidoglycan (Gram-positive thick, Gram-negative thin plus outer membrane), fungal chitin, plant cellulose (plus lignin, pectin), algal cellulose variants - while animal cells and most protists go naked. Wall chemistry decides antibiotics (penicillin blocks peptidoglycan, harmless to humans), staining (Gram sorts bacteria), and digestion (cellulase unlocks plant fibre for herbivores). Presence plus composition together classify.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Bacteria peptidoglycan, fungi chitin, plants cellulose.
  • Wall chemistry decides drugs, stains and digestion.
Remember
  • Penicillin targets peptidoglycan - safe for wall-less human cells.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Fungal cell walls are made of

Solution: Chitin (also insect armour) walls fungi; cellulose walls plants.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 2 · Topic 4

Mode of nutrition

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldA. Five Kingdom ClassificationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nutrition modes sort kingdoms functionally: photosynthetic autotrophs (plants, algae, cyanobacteria - chlorophyll carbon-fixers), chemosynthetic autotrophs (iron-sulphur bacteria oxidising minerals), absorptive heterotrophs (fungi digesting outside, absorbing inside), ingestive heterotrophs (animals eating plus internal digestion), plus parasitic and saprophytic variants everywhere. Mixotrophs (Euglena photosynthesises yet engulfs, insectivorous plants supplement poor soils) prove modes blend at borders.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Photo- and chemo-autotrophs make; absorptive and ingestive heterotrophs take.
  • Euglena does both - the two-kingdom breaker.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Fungi obtain nutrition mainly by

Solution: Hyphae secrete enzymes outward and absorb digested nutrients inward.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 2 · Topic 5

Reproduction

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldA. Five Kingdom ClassificationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Reproduction complexity climbs kingdoms: binary fission plus conjugation (bacteria - no true sex, but gene exchange via transformation, transduction, conjugation), protists (binary fission, cysts, plus sexual syngamy in some), fungi (asexual spores by the million plus sexual plasmogamy-karyogamy-meiosis, often delayed), plants and animals (alternating sporic-meiotic cycles with embryo protection). Asexual speed versus sexual variation trades off everywhere - fungi run both simultaneously at industrial spore volumes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Bacteria: fission plus gene-exchange tricks. Fungi: spore millions plus delayed sex.
  • Higher kingdoms add protected embryos and alternation cycles.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Bacterial gene exchange does NOT include

Solution: Bacteria swap DNA three ways but never run true meiotic sex.
Back to Index

Chapter 2 · Topic 6

Phylogenetic relationships

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldA. Five Kingdom ClassificationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phylogenetic relationships (evolutionary kinship) increasingly decide placement: DNA-rRNA sequencing split Archaea from Bacteria, merged birds into reptiles (cladistics), and reshuffles plant families (APG system). Fossils calibrate molecular clocks timing splits; shared derived characters (mammary glands, flowers, feathers) define clades. Modern classification converges on monophyletic groups (ancestor plus all descendants) - paraphyletic leftovers like classic Reptilia get corrected.
NEET Snapshot:
  • DNA plus fossils plus shared derived traits redraw trees.
  • Monophyletic groups (ancestor plus all descendants) are the goal.
Remember
  • Birds nest inside reptiles cladistically - feathers are modified scales.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Three-domain system (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) is based mainly on

Solution: Woese rRNA work split prokaryotes into two domains rivalling Eukarya.

Chapter 2 · Topic 7

Archaebacteria

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldB. Kingdom MoneraStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Archaebacteria are ancient extremophiles with mosaic biology: bacterial looks (no nucleus, circular DNA) but eukaryotic-like transcription plus unique ether-linked membrane lipids surviving boiling acid, saturated salt and gut anoxia. Three flagship groups - halophiles (salt pans), thermoacidophiles (hot sulphur springs), methanogens (marshes, guts making biogas) - prove life toughest margins. Their enzymes (Taq polymerase from hot-spring bacteria) run PCR worldwide.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Prokaryotic outside, eukaryotic-like inside, extremophile lifestyle.
  • Ether lipids plus unique transcription mark the domain.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Archaebacteria differ from eubacteria mainly in

Solution: Ether-linked lipids plus eukaryotic-like RNA machinery define Archaea molecularly.

Halophiles

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldB. Kingdom MoneraStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Halophiles thrive in saturated salt (salt pans, Dead Sea) where ordinary cells shrivel: they pump potassium inward to balance external sodium, run salt-stable enzymes, and often carry red carotenoid pigments (pink salt ponds are halophile blooms). Facultative types tolerate wide ranges; extreme types require salt absolutely. Their enzymes inspire salt-tolerant industrial biocatalysts - biotechnology mines extremophile chemistry routinely.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Balance salt with internal potassium plus salt-proof enzymes.
  • Pink salt ponds are halophile carotenoid blooms.

1

Solution: Osmotic matching plus adapted proteins beat desiccation chemically.

Thermoacidophiles

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldB. Kingdom MoneraStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Thermoacidophiles inhabit boiling sulphur springs (Yellowstone, hot vents) at 80C-plus and pH near 2: ether-lipid membranes stay intact where normal lipids melt, DNA-binding proteins brace genomes, and sulphur replaces oxygen in respiration (oxidising H2S to sulphuric acid). Taq polymerase (PCR engine) comes from Thermus aquaticus of hot springs - their heat-proof enzymes run global biotechnology. Life upper temperature limit keeps rising with each discovery.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Boiling acid survivors via ether membranes plus braced DNA.
  • Taq polymerase gifts PCR from hot-spring bacteria.
Remember
  • Sulphur breathers turn hot-spring chemistry into energy.

Solution: Hot-spring heat-stable polymerase survives PCR denaturation cycles.

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldB. Kingdom MoneraStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Methanogens (anaerobic archaea) make methane converting CO2 plus hydrogen or acetate - in marshes (marsh gas), cattle rumens (belches), sewage digesters and biogas plants. Strict anaerobes poisoned by oxygen, they run unique coenzyme biochemistry (F420, methanopterin). Gobar-gas plants farm them in dung slurry for cooking fuel plus fertiliser - ancient metabolism powering rural energy plus sanitation together.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Anaerobic methane-makers of marshes, rumens and digesters.
  • Strictly oxygen-poisoned; unique coenzyme chemistry.

Topic in Depth

Eubacteria (true bacteria) are the metabolic generalists: photosynthetic cyanobacteria, chemosynthetic iron-sulphur oxidisers, heterotrophic decomposers and pathogens - rod (bacilli), spherical (cocci), spiral (spirilla, vibrios) shapes with flagella, pili and capsules. Gram stain sorts them (thick peptidoglycan purple-positive versus thin plus outer-membrane pink-negative), deciding antibiotics. Lactobacillus curdles milk; Rhizobium fixes nitrogen; Streptomyces gifts most antibiotics.

  • Shapes bacilli-cocci-spirilla; Gram sorts walls; metabolisms span all modes.

Cyanobacteria

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldB. Kingdom MoneraStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae, actually bacteria) invented oxygenic photosynthesis - chlorophyll-a plus phycobilins splitting water, oxygenating Earth air ~2.5 billion years ago. Some (Anabaena, Nostoc) fix nitrogen in heterocysts (thick-walled, oxygen-free cells protecting nitrogenase), fertilising paddy fields free. Blooms colour ponds green; Spirulina packs protein as superfood. Chloroplasts descend from engulfed cyanobacteria (endosymbiosis) - plant photosynthesis is rented bacterial machinery.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Oxygenic photosynthesis inventors; heterocysts fix nitrogen.
  • Chloroplasts are domesticated cyanobacteria (endosymbiosis).
Remember
  • Heterocyst = thick-walled nitrogen-fixing cell excluding oxygen.

Nitrogen fixation

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldB. Kingdom MoneraStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nitrogen fixation converts inert N2 to usable ammonia via nitrogenase (oxygen-poisoned, ATP-hungry): symbiotic Rhizobium in legume nodules (plant feeds sugars, bacteria return ammonia), free-living Azotobacter plus Azospirillum, cyanobacterial Anabaena in paddy plus Azolla fern partnership. Lightning fixes some abiotically; Haber-Bosch factories fix industrially. Nitrification (ammonia to nitrate) then denitrification (nitrate to N2) complete the cycle bacteria drive.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Nitrogenase needs anoxia plus ATP - symbiosis provides both.
  • Rhizobium nodules, Azolla paddies, lightning, factories - four fixers.

1

Legume root-nodule nitrogen is fixed by

Solution: Root-nodule symbiosis trades plant sugars for bacterial ammonia.

Mycoplasma

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldB. Kingdom MoneraStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mycoplasma are the smallest living cells (~0.3 micrometre) - wall-less bacteria bounded only by plasma membrane, pleomorphic (shape-shifting), filter-passing. Wall-lessness makes them penicillin-proof (no peptidoglycan target) but osmotically fragile; many parasitize animals and plants (pleuropneumonia in cattle, little-leaf in brinjal). Cell cultures fear them as invisible contaminants. PPLO (pleuropneumonia-like organisms) was their original name.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Smallest cells, no wall, pleomorphic - penicillin-proof by design.
  • Cattle pleuropneumonia plus plant little-leaf diseases.
Remember
  • No wall means no Gram stain and no penicillin effect.

Topic in Depth

Chrysophytes (diatoms, golden algae) armour themselves in silica frustules - two overlapping glass halves (epitheca plus hypotheca) etched with species-specific patterns. Photosynthetic in sunlit waters, they dominate phytoplankton and power marine food webs; dead frustules accumulate as diatomaceous earth (filters, polishes, insulation). Their oils (not starch) store energy; sexual auxospores restore shrinking cell size after divisions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Silica glass houses with overlapping halves.
  • Diatomaceous earth: filters, abrasives from dead frustules.

Dinoflagellates swim with two perpendicular flagella (one transverse in a groove, one trailing) spinning them through seas - photosynthetic Zooxanthellae feeding corals, plus armoured Gonyaulax causing red tides. Red-tide blooms poison shellfish (saxitoxin, PSP) and paint seas rust-red; nocturnal species bioluminesce in breaking waves. Their cellulose plates plus dual flagella make them unmistakable plankton under microscopes.

  • Red tides poison shellfish; Zooxanthellae feed corals.

Euglenoids

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldC. Kingdom ProtistaStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Euglena mixes kingdoms: chlorophyll photosynthesis in sunlight plus phagocytic engulfing in darkness (mixotrophy), swimming by anterior flagella with eyespot-guided phototaxis, storing paramylon (not starch), wrapped in flexible protein pellicle instead of walls. Two-kingdom systems stranded it homeless - plant or animal? - which is exactly why five kingdoms created Protista. Pond-green scums often signal Euglena blooms.

  • Photosynthesis plus engulfing; pellicle not wall; paramylon storage.
  • Kingdom-breaker that forced Protista creation.

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldC. Kingdom ProtistaStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Slime moulds (Myxomycetes) live double lives: free-living amoeboid plasmodium (giant multinucleate streaming mass eating decay) transforms under starvation into stalked fruiting bodies releasing spores - fungus-like fruiting from animal-like feeding. Dictyostelium (cellular slime mould) aggregates individual amoebae via cAMP signals into slugs - development biology model for signalling and differentiation. Neither true fungi nor animals, they bridge kingdoms.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Feeding plasmodium plus fruiting spores - animal life, fungal reproduction.
  • Dictyostelium cAMP aggregation models cell signalling.

Protozoans

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldC. Kingdom ProtistaStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Protozoans are animal-like unicellular protists in four locomotor groups: amoeboids (Amoeba, Entamoeba - pseudopodia, some parasitic dysentery), flagellates (Trypanosoma sleeping sickness via tsetse, Giardia), ciliates (Paramecium - rows of cilia plus dual nuclei: macro for daily life, micro for sex), sporozoans (Plasmodium - no locomotion, parasitic life cycles). They preview animal innovations - mouth-like cytostomes, contractile vacuole kidneys, even primitive sex (conjugation).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Amoeboid, flagellate, ciliate, sporozoan - movement defines groups.
  • Paramecium dual nuclei; Plasmodium parasitic cycles.

Chapter 2 · Topic 20

General characteristics

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldD. Kingdom FungiStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fungi are absorptive heterotrophs built of hyphal networks (mycelium) with chitin walls - digesting outside via secreted enzymes, absorbing inside. Body plans span unicellular yeasts to kilometre-wide Armillaria individuals; reproduction fires millions of asexual spores (conidia, sporangiospores) plus sexual plasmogamy-karyogamy-meiosis (often separated in time and space). Decomposer keystone role recycles forests; partnerships (mycorrhiza, lichens) feed plants.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hyphal mycelium, chitin walls, external digestion, spore millions.
  • Decomposer keystone plus mycorrhizal partner plus food/medicine source.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Fungi differ from plants mainly in

Solution: No photosynthesis - fungi digest externally and absorb, plants fix carbon.

Chapter 2 · Topic 21

Nutrition

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldD. Kingdom FungiStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fungal nutrition is absorptive at hyphal tips: saprophytes digest dead matter (forest recyclers), parasites tap living hosts (rusts, smuts, mildews safe from host defences via haustoria), symbionts trade (mycorrhiza phosphorus for plant sugars; lichens sheltered algae), predators trap nematodes with constricting rings. Enzymes (cellulases, ligninases) crack the toughest plant polymers - white-rot fungi digest wood lignin completely, enabling forest turnover.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Saprophytic recyclers, parasitic drainers, symbiotic traders, predatory trappers.
  • External enzymes crack lignin and cellulose others cannot.
Remember
  • Haustoria tap hosts; rings trap worms - fungal feeding ingenuity.

Reproduction

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldD. Kingdom FungiStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fungal reproduction pairs spore profusion with flexible sex: asexual conidia (exposed chains), sporangiospores (sacs), budding (yeasts), fragmentation - millions airborne daily; sexual plasmogamy (cytoplasm fusion) often long precedes karyogamy plus meiosis (delayed in dikaryotic secondary mycelium), yielding zygospores, asci or basidia by class. Parasexual cycles plus heterokaryosis shuffle genes without full sex - industrial strain improvement exploits it.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Asexual millions plus delayed sexual fusion (plasmogamy then karyogamy).
  • Dikaryotic phase stretches between fusions uniquely.

Phycomycetes (lower/algal fungi: Rhizopus bread mould, Albugo white rust, Saprolegnia water mould) run coenocytic (multinucleate, unseptated) hyphae - one continuous cytoplasmic tube. Asexual sporangiospores burst from sacs; sexual gametangial copulation makes thick-walled oospores (oogamous) or zygospores. Aquatic ancestry shows in flagellated zoospores; terrestrial members attack crops (white rust crucifers, downy mildews) and stored bread alike.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Coenocytic aseptate hyphae; oospores/zygospores sexually.
  • Rhizopus (bread), Albugo (white rust) are textbook examples.

Ascomycetes (sac fungi: yeasts, Penicillium, Aspergillus, morels, truffles, Neurospora) pack sexual meiospores as eight ascospores inside sac-like asci (often in fruiting ascocarps), with septate hyphae plus vast conidial asexual output. Gifts span bread-beer-yeast fermentation, penicillin antibiotics, citric-acid industry, plus prized morel-truffle foods; Claviceps ergot poisons grain (historic dancing mania). Neurospora (pink bread mould) founded biochemical genetics (one-gene-one-enzyme).
NEET Snapshot:

  • Yeast ferments, Penicillium heals, Neurospora taught genetics.

Basidiomycetes (club fungi: mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs, rusts, smuts) bear sexual meiospores as four basidiospores on club-shaped basidia lining gills, with long-lived dikaryotic secondary mycelium (clamp connections marking it). Edibles (Agaricus button, oyster) plus killers (Amanita death cap) share the plan; rusts (wheat stem rust, heteroecious Puccinia shuttling wheat-barberry) and smuts (covered grain kernels) devastate crops. Fairy rings trace giant underground mycelia fruiting in circles.

Deuteromycetes (fungi imperfecti: Alternaria leaf spots, Colletotrichum anthracnose, Trichoderma biocontrol) are the waiting room for fungi whose sexual stage is unknown or lost - classified by asexual conidia plus mycelium alone. Molecular sequencing keeps promoting members into Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes once sex (or genes) reveals kinship - the group shrinks yearly. Athlete foot and ringworm agents sit here; so do antibiotic and biocontrol workhorses. Imperfect knowledge, not imperfect fungi.
NEET Snapshot:

  • DNA keeps graduating members to sac or club fungi.

Economic importance

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldD. Kingdom FungiStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fungal economics spans kitchen to clinic: foods (mushrooms, morels, truffles, yeast bread-beer, Roquefort-Camembert cheeses), industry (citric acid, enzymes, statins, cyclosporin), agriculture (mycorrhiza boosters, Trichoderma biocontrol, Beuveria insect killers), medicine (penicillin plus descendants, ergot drugs) - against costs (crop rusts-smuts-mildews, food spoilage, human mycoses like ringworm, aflatoxin poisoning). Managed fungi feed and heal; unmanaged ones rot and kill.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Food, drugs, industry, biocontrol versus rot, blight and mycoses.
  • Penicillin plus mycorrhiza headline the benefit ledger.

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldE. LichensStep-by-step Topic

Lichens pioneer bare rock (secreting acids that etch stone into soil), feed Arctic food webs (reindeer moss), fix nitrogen (cyanolichens), and supply dyes (litmus from Roccella), perfumes and traditional medicines. Succession starts with crustose rock-etchers, proceeds through foliose to mosses - lichens literally manufacture soil from stone. Their slowness (millimetres yearly) records centuries of undisturbed ecology.

Topic in Depth

Lichens breathe air directly (no roots, no cuticle filters), so sulphur dioxide kills sensitive species first - lichen diversity maps air quality street by street (luxuriant countryside, barren industrial cores). Usnea (old-man beard) vanishes first; hardy crusts persist longest. Monitoring programmes transplant lichen bags into cities and score damage - cheaper than sensor networks, biologically integrated over months. SO2 scrubbing visibly returns lichens within years.

Structure

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldF. VirusesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Viruses are nucleoprotein parcels: nucleic-acid core (DNA or RNA, never both) wrapped in protein capsid of capsomeres, sometimes plus lipid envelope stolen from host membranes (flu, HIV) with spike glycoproteins for docking. Shapes span helical rods (TMV), icosahedral spheres (polio), tadpole phages (head-tail-fibres), and filamentous threads. No cells, no metabolism, no growth - crystallisable yet infectious (Stanley TMV crystals proved it).

  • Crystallisable chemicals that replicate only inside hosts.

Chapter 2 · Topic 34

Genetic material

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldF. VirusesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Viral genomes break cellular rules freely: double- or single-stranded DNA (phages, smallpox, herpes), double- or single-stranded RNA (flu, corona, HIV retroviruses with reverse transcriptase writing DNA from RNA). Baltimore classes I-VII organise them by expression route to mRNA. RNA viruses mutate fastest (no proofreading) - flu needs yearly vaccines, HIV escapes immunity continuously. Genome type predicts drugs (reverse-transcriptase inhibitors hit retroviruses only).
NEET Snapshot:
  • dsDNA, ssDNA, dsRNA, ssRNA (+/-) - all genome chemistries occur.
  • RNA viruses mutate fastest - flu and HIV escape repeatedly.
Remember
  • Reverse transcriptase copies RNA to DNA - retrovirus signature enzyme.

Chapter 2 · Topic 35

Viral reproduction

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldF. VirusesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Viral replication hijacks in five acts: attachment (spikes dock receptors), penetration (injection, endocytosis or fusion), uncoating (capsid stripped), biosynthesis (host ribosomes plus polymerases mass-produce viral parts - eclipse phase with no visible virions), maturation plus release (lysis bursting cells, or budding wrapping envelope). Lytic cycles kill fast; lysogenic phages (lambda) integrate silently as prophages, awakening under stress. One virion becomes hundreds per cell per cycle.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Attach, enter, uncoat, replicate (eclipse), release by lysis or budding.
  • Lytic kills now; lysogenic hides as prophage till stress.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Disassembled replication hides virions until assembly completes.

Bacteriophages

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldF. VirusesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bacteriophages (T2, T4, lambda) are tadpole viruses hunting bacteria: icosahedral heads packing DNA, contractile tail sheaths, base plates with tail fibres sensing wall receptors. T-even phages follow lytic cycles (Hershey-Chase 32P-DNA-entry proof using them); lambda chooses lytic or lysogenic integration. Phage therapy (treating bacterial infections with viruses) revives against antibiotic resistance; phage display engineers antibodies. Most abundant biological entities on Earth - oceans hold 10^30+.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Head-tail-fibre tadpoles injecting DNA into bacteria.
  • Hershey-Chase proved DNA heredity using phages.

Plant viruses

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldF. VirusesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Plant viruses (TMV first discovered, Stanley crystallised it) spread without vectors flying themselves - sap-sucking insects (aphids, whiteflies), nematodes, grafting, seeds and farm tools carry them; wind and water rarely do. Symptoms mosaic (mottled leaves), stunt, curl and necrosis diagnose fields; no cures exist - control means vector control, certified seeds, resistant varieties and roguing infected plants. CaMV 35S promoter from cauliflower mosaic virus now drives transgenes worldwide - pathogen turned biotechnology tool.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Spread by insects, grafts, seeds, tools - never cures, only prevention.
  • Mosaic, stunt, curl symptoms; CaMV promoter drives GM crops.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

TMV is significant historically as the

Solution: Ivanovsky-Beijerinck discovery plus Stanley crystals founded virology.

Chapter 2 · Topic 38

Diseases

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldF. VirusesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Viral diseases span kingdoms: human (cold, flu, dengue, hepatitis, rabies, AIDS, COVID), animal (foot-and-mouth, bird flu), plant (TMV mosaic, bunchy top banana, leaf curl). Antibiotics never work (no bacterial targets); antivirals block specific steps (reverse transcriptase, protease, neuraminidase); vaccines prevent most childhood killers. Diagnosis by ELISA, PCR and rapid antigens; control by vaccination, vectors and quarantine - treatment largely supportive.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Antibiotics useless; antivirals step-specific; vaccines preventive.
  • ELISA plus PCR diagnose; quarantine plus vectors contain.
Remember
  • Supportive care plus prevention beats cure for most viral diseases.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Antibiotics fail against viruses because viruses

Solution: No peptidoglycan or bacterial ribosomes means no drug foothold.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 2 · Topic 39

Structure

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldG. ViroidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Viroids (Diener, potato spindle tuber) are naked infectious RNA circles - no capsid, no proteins - hundreds of nucleotides folding into rods that hijack host RNA polymerase for rolling-circle replication. Smaller than any virus, they stunt plants (spindle tubers, chrysanthemum stunt) via RNA-silencing interference. Strictly plant pathogens so far; no animal viroids confirmed. Pure minimalism: infectivity from RNA structure alone.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Naked circular RNA, no capsid, no proteins - smallest pathogens.
  • Plants only; replicate via host polymerase rolling circles.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Viroids consist of

Solution: Free RNA circles folding into infectious rods - below-virus minimalism.

Chapter 2 · Topic 40

Difference from viruses

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldG. ViroidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Viroids differ from viruses in lacking capsids and proteins entirely (pure RNA vs nucleoprotein), smaller genomes (hundreds vs thousands of bases), plant-only hosts (vs all kingdoms), and host-polymerase dependence (vs virus-encoded enzymes). Prions step further down - protein without any nucleic acid. The sequence virus-viroid-prion strips infectivity to smaller packages: nucleic acid plus protein, then nucleic acid alone, then protein alone - three rungs of minimal life-borderline agents.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Virus: RNA/DNA plus protein. Viroid: RNA only. Prion: protein only.
  • Hosts narrow similarly: all kingdoms, plants only, animals mostly.
Minimal agents
PointDetail
VirusNucleic acid + capsid
ViroidNaked RNA circle
PrionMisfolded protein, no nucleic acid

Prions differ from viroids in

Solution: Prions flip viroids: infectious protein with zero nucleic acid.

Chapter 2 · Topic 41

Basic concept

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldH. PrionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Prions (Prusiner, Nobel) are misfolded proteins that corrupt normal counterparts into clones - infectious conformation without any nucleic acid, defying the central dogma template logic. Normal PrP cellular protein flips to scrapie form, aggregating into brain plaques. Heat, radiation and enzymes that kill viruses fail - only harsh incineration or strong alkali inactivate prions. Yeast and fungal prions (non-pathogenic) prove the mechanism spans kingdoms.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Infectious misfolded protein; no nucleic acid; template-free corruption.
  • Resists heat, radiation, enzymes - sterilisation nightmare.
Remember
  • Mad-cow, Creutzfeldt-Jakob, scrapie - same prion logic, different hosts.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Prion diseases are caused by

Solution: Protein-only infectivity without DNA or RNA - dogma-defying agents.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 2 · Topic 42

Infectious proteins

Biological ClassificationDiversity in the Living WorldH. PrionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Infectious proteins spread by seeded corruption: ingested or inherited misfolded PrP contacts normal PrP and refolds it - chain reaction templated by shape, not sequence. Routes include contaminated meat (BSE mad-cow), medical grafts and instruments, plus inherited PRNP mutations (familial CJD) and rare spontaneous flips (sporadic CJD, commonest form). Incubation spans years to decades; symptoms (dementia, ataxia) progress fatally within months once started - no treatment yet.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Shape-templated corruption spreads without replication machinery.
  • Acquired (meat, grafts), inherited (PRNP), sporadic (random flip).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Commonest human prion disease form is

Solution: Most CJD arises from chance PrP misfolding, not infection or inheritance.

Plant Kingdom

Algae to angiosperms - the plant conquest of land told group by group.

36. General characteristics37. Roots38. Stem39. Leaves40. Cones41. Reproduction42. Seeds43. Examples

Deep Dive · Conquest of land in four leaps

Plant evolution climbs four innovations: algae master photosynthesis without land protection; bryophytes add cuticle, stomata and jacketed sex organs but keep swimming sperm (amphibian compromise); pteridophytes add vascular plumbing plus dominant sporophytes yet still need water for fertilisation; gymnosperms break water dependence with pollen plus seeds (siphonogamy); angiosperms perfect it with flowers, fruits and double fertilisation. Each leap solves one constraint - drying, support, transport, then reproduction.
NEET facts:
  • Dominance flips: gametophyte (bryophytes) to sporophyte (all vascular plants).
  • Heterospory previews seeds; pollen plus seed frees sex from water.
Fig: Algae to angiosperms: protection, plumbing, pollen and flowers in sequence.

Solution: Moss plants and liverwort thalli are gametophytes; all vascular plants flip dominance.

Chapter 3 · Topic 1

General characteristics

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldA. AlgaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Algae are simple photosynthetic eukaryotes (plus cyanobacterial blue-greens) lacking true roots, stems, leaves and embryo protection - thallus bodies in unicellular (Chlamydomonas), colonial (Volvox), filamentous (Spirogyra), massive parenchymatous (kelps) grades. Chlorophyll plus accessory pigments (phycoerythrin red, fucoxanthin brown) harvest light at different depths. Three classes - green, brown, red - split by pigments, storage food and flagellation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Thallus organisation, no embryo protection, pigment-based classes.
  • Unicellular to kelp grades; chlorophyll plus accessory pigments.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Algae differ from bryophytes mainly in

Solution: Algal zygotes never develop protected embryos - the land-plant innovation.

Chapter 3 · Topic 2

Habitat

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldA. AlgaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Algae inhabit waters fresh and marine plus every damp surface - tree bark, moist soil, snow (red snow Haematococcus), hot springs, inside animals (Zooxanthellae in corals) and even fur (sloth algae). Marine zonation follows light: greens near surface, browns mid-depth, reds deepest (phycoerythrin harvests blue-green light penetrating far). Terrestrial algae survive desiccation as mucilage-coated resting stages - moisture, not taxonomy, decides address.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Water plus damp everything - bark, snow, fur, coral tissues.
  • Pigments zone by depth: green shallow, red deepest.
Remember
  • Red snow is Haematococcus bloom; coral colour is Zooxanthellae symbionts.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Red algae dominate deep waters because phycoerythrin absorbs

Solution: Blue-green wavelengths reach deepest; red pigment harvests exactly them.

Chapter 3 · Topic 3

Body organisation

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldA. AlgaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Algal bodies scale four grades: unicellular flagellates (Chlamydomonas) and non-motile (Chlorella), colonial motile spheres (Volvox with cytoplasmic bridges plus division of labour) and non-motile clusters, unbranched filaments (Spirogyra, Ulothrix), and parenchymatous sheets plus giant kelps (Macrocystis 60-metre stipes with holdfasts and blades). Complexity rises without true tissues - even kelps lack vascular plumbing, transporting by diffusion and active cells.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Unicellular, colonial, filamentous, parenchymatous - four grades.
  • Volvox shows early division of labour; kelps mimic trees without vessels.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Volvox colonies are significant as showing

Solution: Somatic beaters plus reproductive gonidia preview multicellular organisation.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 3 · Topic 4

Reproduction

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldA. AlgaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Algal reproduction spans all three modes: vegetative fragmentation (Spirogyra pieces), asexual zoospores (flagellated) plus aplanospores/aplanospores, and sexual isogamy (equal gametes, Chlamydomonas), anisogamy (unequal, Chlamydomonas some), oogamy (large egg plus small sperm - Volvox, Fucus). Oogamy advances with complexity - green-to-red progression mirrors land-plant evolution toward protected large eggs. Cysts and akinetes overwinter harsh seasons.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fragmentation, zoospores, isogamy to oogamy - complexity ladder.
  • Oogamy (big egg, small sperm) is the advanced state.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Oogamous reproduction in algae involves

Solution: Volvox and Fucus run large-egg-small-sperm oogamy like land plants.
Back to Index

Chapter 3 · Topic 5

Economic importance

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldA. AlgaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Algal economics feed industries: food (kombu, nori/Porphyra sushi sheets, Chlorella protein), agar (Gracilaria/Gelidium culture medium plus desserts), carrageenan (Chondrus thickener), alginates (Laminaria wound dressings, ice-cream stabiliser), iodine and potash (kelp ash), fertilisers (seaweed meal), plus CO2-fixing oxygen production (half of Earth photosynthesis). Single-cell protein projects farm Spirulina/Chlorella for malnutrition - ponds as protein factories.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Agar, carrageenan, algin, iodine, food, fertiliser, oxygen.
  • Half of global photosynthesis is algal - planetary lungs.

Chapter 3 · Topic 6

Green algae

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldB. ChlorophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Chlorophyceae (green algae: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Spirogyra, Chara) are the land-plant ancestors - chlorophyll a/b in true chloroplasts, starch storage, cellulose walls, flagellated stages. Habitats span freshwater (majority), damp soil, bark and snow; marine greens are fewer. Their biochemistry (pigments, storage, walls) matches land plants exactly - molecular clocks confirm the ancestry green algae claim.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Grass-green from chlorophyll a/b; starch storage; cellulose walls.
  • Land plants evolved from charophyte green ancestors.
Remember
  • Green chemistry (chlorophyll b, starch, cellulose) equals land-plant chemistry.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Land plants most likely evolved from

Solution: Stoneworts share pigments, storage, walls and division chemistry with land plants.

Chapter 3 · Topic 7

Characteristics

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldB. ChlorophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Green-algal hallmarks: grass-green chloroplasts (chlorophyll a/b plus carotenoids), pyrenoids (protein bodies storing starch), cellulose walls (plus pectin), starch reserve, and flagellated motile stages (2, 4 or many equal apical flagella). Contractile vacuoles osmoregulate freshwater forms; eyespots steer phototaxis. Chara (stonewort) adds plant-like nodes-internodes plus male globules and female nucules - advanced oogamy previewing land-plant sex organs.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Pyrenoids store starch; flagella swim; Chara mimics plant organs.
  • Chlorophyll b plus starch plus cellulose - land-plant signature trio.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Pyrenoids in green algae store

Solution: Protein-cored pyrenoids accumulate starch reserves in chloroplasts.

Examples

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldB. ChlorophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Green-algal examples map the grades: Chlamydomonas (unicellular flagellate lab model), Volvox (colonial sphere), Spirogyra (unbranched filament, spiral chloroplasts, ladder conjugation), Ulothrix (attached filament), Chara (stonewort macroalga with plant-like organs), Chlorella (non-motile protein-rich single cells). Each illustrates one organisation step - textbooks sequence them unicell to colony to filament to parenchyma deliberately.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Chara, Chlorella.
  • Sequence maps organisation grades in order.

Chapter 3 · Topic 9

Reproduction

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldB. ChlorophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Green algae reproduce vegetatively (fragmentation, akinetes), asexually (biflagellate zoospores, aplanospores) and sexually across the full ladder - isogamy (Chlamydomonas equal gametes), anisogamy (unequal), oogamy (Chara globule-to-nucule sperm-egg). Chlamydomonas even switches mating types (plus/minus strains) previewing sexes. Environmental stress triggers sex; favourable water favours cloning - strategy follows season.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fragmentation, zoospores, isogamy to oogamy full ladder.
  • Stress induces sex; good times clone - strategy follows season.
Remember
  • Chara globule (male) plus nucule (female) is advanced oogamy.

Brown algae

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldC. PhaeophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phaeophyceae (brown algae: Laminaria, Fucus, Sargassum, Macrocystis) are the seaweed giants - fucoxanthin masking chlorophyll into olive-brown, laminarin plus mannitol storage, cellulose-plus-algin walls, exclusively marine (cold coasts). Kelp forests (Macrocystis 60 m) shelter whole ecosystems; Sargasso Sea floats Sargassum islands mid-Atlantic. No freshwater browns of note - cold marine monopoly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fucoxanthin brown; laminarin storage; algin walls; marine giants.
  • Kelp forests are underwater rainforests sheltering ecosystems.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Fucoxanthin pigment occurs in

Solution: Brown accessory pigment masks chlorophyll into olive-brown kelps.

Chapter 3 · Topic 11

Characteristics

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldC. PhaeophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Brown-algal construction: holdfast (anchoring, not absorbing), stipe (stem-like, sometimes gas-bladdered for buoyancy), blades/fronds (photosynthetic, often serrated), with no true vascular tissue - trumpet hyphae translocate in kelps instead. Algin (wall) plus laminarin/mannitol (storage) chemistry differs from greens; biflagellate zoospores (unequal lateral flagella) swim. Air bladders (Fucus, Sargassum) float blades to light.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Holdfast-stipe-blade mimicry without true organs or vessels.
  • Algin walls, laminarin storage, unequal-flagella zoospores.
Remember
  • Trumpet hyphae translocate like phloem without being vascular tissue.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Holdfast in brown algae functions in

Solution: Holdfasts grip; absorption happens across all surfaces.

Examples

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldC. PhaeophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Brown-algal examples: Laminaria (kombu food, algin source), Fucus (rockweed with air bladders and receptacles), Sargassum (floating Gulf weed forming the Sargasso Sea), Macrocystis (giant kelp forests), Ectocarpus (filamentous lab model for brown-algal genetics). Each shows one habit - attached rockweeds, drifting Sargassum, towering kelps - mapping brown-algal ecological range from intertidal to open ocean.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Laminaria, Fucus, Sargassum, Macrocystis, Ectocarpus.
  • Rockweeds anchor, Sargassum drifts, kelps tower.

Chapter 3 · Topic 13

Reproduction

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldC. PhaeophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Brown algae reproduce vegetatively (fragmentation, Sargassum drift pieces), asexually (biflagellate zoospores with unequal flagella), and sexually isogamous to oogamous - Fucus oogamy uses conceptacles (flask cavities) releasing eggs plus sperm into seawater. Alternation varies: isomorphic (Ectocarpus equal phases) to heteromorphic (Laminaria giant sporophyte, microscopic gametophyte). Fucus skips alternation entirely (diplontic like animals) - brown diversity previews all life-cycle types.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Conceptacle oogamy; isomorphic to heteromorphic alternations.
  • Fucus is diplontic - no alternation, like animals.

1

Conceptacles (reproductive flasks) occur in

Solution: Brown-algal conceptacles house oogamous organs opening to seawater.

Economic importance

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldC. PhaeophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Brown-algal economics: alginates (Laminaria - wound dressings, ice-cream and paint stabilisers, dental moulds), food (kombu, wakame - iodine-rich), fertiliser (seaweed meal potash), iodine and bromine extraction (kelp ash), plus kelp-forest fisheries nursing commercial fish. Sargassum drifts shelter turtles and eels mid-ocean. Cold-water farming (China, Korea) scales kombu harvests - seaweed aquaculture feeding millions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Alginates stabilise foods, paints and dressings.
  • Kombu food plus potash fertiliser plus fishery nurseries.

Chapter 3 · Topic 15

Red algae

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldD. RhodophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Rhodophyceae (red algae: Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium, Chondrus) colour from phycoerythrin masking chlorophyll - harvesting blue-green light at depths greens and browns cannot reach. Floridean starch storage, cellulose-plus-agar/carrageenan walls, complete absence of flagellated stages (even gametes crawl or drift), and complex triphasic life cycles (gametophyte-carposporophyte-tetrasporophyte) mark the group. Mostly marine warm coasts; few freshwater Batrachospermum.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Phycoerythrin red; floridean starch; agar walls; no flagella ever.
  • Triphasic cycles; deepest-living photosynthetic eukaryotes.
Remember
  • No swimming stages at all - red algae drift or creep to reproduce.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Red algae lack

Solution: No motile cells at any stage - unique among algal classes.

Characteristics

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldD. RhodophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Red-algal construction: pit connections (cytoplasmic links between cells, unique), diffuse growth (not apical), calcified crusts in corallines (Corallina reef-builders rivalling corals), and polysaccharide walls (agar, carrageenan, funoran) harvested industrially. Phycoerythrin-phycocyanin antennae tune to depth light; floridean starch stores in cytoplasm (not plastids). Coralline crusts cement reefs - algae building rock.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Pit connections plus diffuse growth plus calcified crusts.
  • Agar/carrageenan walls; floridean starch outside plastids.

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldD. RhodophyceaeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Red algae reproduce vegetatively (fragments), asexually (non-motile tetraspores/monospores) and oogamously without any swimming gametes - spermatia drift to carpogonia (tricoblast-fruited), fertilisation grows carposporophyte on the female, releasing carpospores that become tetrasporophytes cycling tetraspores back. Polysiphonia triphasic cycle (gametophyte-carposporophyte-tetrasporophyte) is the textbook most complex plant life cycle - three multicellular phases alternating.
