Chapter 3 · Topic 20

General characteristics

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) are land-plant pioneers stuck between worlds: true land adaptations (cuticle, stomata, jacketed sex organs - antheridia, archegonia) but sperm still swimming through water films, restricting them to damp habitats - amphibians of the plant kingdom. Dominant free-living gametophyte with dependent sporophyte (reversed from vascular plants); root-like rhizoids (not true roots); no true vascular tissue. Peat moss (Sphagnum) built fuel bogs across northern lands.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Land adaptations plus swimming sperm - amphibian strategy.
  • Gametophyte dominant; sporophyte dependent; no vessels.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because

Solution: Motile sperm swim through external water - land life, aquatic sex.
Back to Index
Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 3 · Topic 21

Habitat

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bryophytes carpet every damp surface - moist soil, rocks, tree bark, rotting logs, stream banks, tundra - from Himalayan slopes to Antarctic fringes, wherever films of water persist for sperm swimming. Sphagnum bogs engineer whole wetlands (acidic, waterlogged, carbon-storing peat); desert mosses revive after years dry (poikilohydry - equilibrating with air moisture). They colonise bare rock after lichens, paving succession toward forests.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Damp surfaces worldwide; Sphagnum bogs engineer wetlands.
  • Poikilohydry lets desert mosses resurrect after drought.
Remember
  • After lichens etch rock, mosses build the first soil mats.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Sphagnum is ecologically important as

Solution: Peat moss bogs accumulate fuel peat and lock carbon for millennia.

Plant body

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bryophyte bodies stay small (no vessels limits height): leafy or thalloid gametophytes with rhizoids anchoring (absorbing across surfaces, not roots), simple conducting strands in mosses (hydroids-leptoids previewing xylem-phloem), cuticle plus stomata on capsules regulating water. Liverwort thalli (Marchantia) versus moss leafy shoots (Funaria) show two architectures; hornworts (Anthoceros) add symbiotic Nostoc colonies fixing nitrogen inside.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Rhizoids anchor; cuticle slows drying; strands preview vessels.
  • Liverwort thallus vs moss leafy shoot - two body plans.

1

Rhizoids in bryophytes function in

Solution: Hair-like rhizoids grip and absorb; true roots with vessels come later.

Chapter 3 · Topic 23

Reproduction

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bryophyte reproduction runs water-dependent sex plus rugged asexuals: antheridia release biflagellate sperms swimming through rain films to archegonia (flask: neck canal plus venter holding one egg); fertilisation grows the dependent sporophyte (foot-seta-capsule) on the mother gametophyte. Asexual gemmae cups (Marchantia), fragmentation and tubers spread clones faster than sex. One egg per archegonium, millions of spores per capsule - investment split between care and numbers.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Swimming sperm to single archegonial egg; sporophyte grows dependent.
  • Gemmae cups plus fragments clone faster than sex.
Remember
  • One egg per archegonium; millions of spores per capsule.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Bryophyte sex organs are

Solution: Sterile jackets protecting gametes define land-plant sex organs.

Chapter 3 · Topic 24

Gametophyte

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bryophyte gametophyte is the dominant free-living phase - photosynthetic, independent, haploid (n) - leafy moss shoots or liverwort thalli carrying sex organs. Antheridia (club-shaped, sperm mother cells) and archegonia (flask: neck, venter, egg) may share plants (monoicous) or split sexes (dioicous). Sperm release needs liquid water films; fertilisation success caps bryophyte range to damp habitats - dominance with aquatic strings attached.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Haploid, photosynthetic, independent - the main plant you see.
  • Monoicous (both sexes) or dioicous (separate) arrangements.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Dominant phase in bryophyte life cycle is the

Solution: Moss plants and liverwort thalli are gametophytes; sporophytes depend on them.

Chapter 3 · Topic 25

Sporophyte

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bryophyte sporophyte (diploid, foot-seta-capsule) grows attached to and nourished by the mother gametophyte - partial dependence (moss capsules photosynthesise somewhat) to full dependence (liverworts). Capsules manufacture millions of meiospores (haploid via meiosis) released through peristome teeth (mosses, hygroscopic openers) or simple splitting. Spore germination grows protonema (moss buds) or direct thalli - the dependent diploid serving the dominant haploid generation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Diploid, attached, nutritionally dependent on gametophyte.
  • Capsules release meiospores; peristome teeth regulate moss dispersal.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Bryophyte sporophyte is

Solution: Foot embedded in gametophyte tissue feeds the capsule generation.

Chapter 3 · Topic 26

Life cycle

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bryophyte life cycle is haplontic with reversed dominance: haploid gametophyte (main plant) makes gametes by mitosis, fertilisation yields diploid zygote retained in archegonium, zygote divides into dependent sporophyte, capsule meiosis releases haploid spores growing new gametophytes. Gametophytic (n) dominance distinguishes bryophytes from all vascular plants (sporophytic 2n dominance) - the great generation flip in land-plant evolution.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Haploid-dominant haplontic cycle with dependent diploid interlude.
  • Gametes by mitosis (already haploid); spores by meiosis.
Fig: Big gametophyte makes gametes; small dependent sporophyte makes spores - haploid dominance.

1

In bryophytes, meiosis occurs in the

Solution: Sporophyte capsule meiosis yields the haploid spores starting gametophytes.

Chapter 3 · Topic 27

Mosses

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mosses (Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum) run leafy gametophytes: protonema buds grow erect shoots with spirally arranged leaves, antheridial and archegonial clusters capping stems, sporophytes with long setae plus operculate capsules bearing peristome teeth that open in dry air. Sphagnum (peat moss) lacks rhizoids, absorbs water like sponge (antiseptic dressings historically), and builds peat bogs. Polytrichum (haircap) reaches 40 cm - moss giant via conducting strands.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Leafy shoots, peristome capsules, protonema stage.
  • Sphagnum: peat, sponge-water, antiseptic history.
Remember
  • Peristome teeth open capsules in dry air - humidity-gated dispersal.

Peristome teeth regulating spore release occur in

Chapter 3 · Topic 28

Liverworts

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldE. BryophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Liverworts (Marchantia, Riccia) grow dorsiventral thalli - dichotomously lobed ribbons (liver-shaped, hence name) with dorsal gemmae cups cloning plus ventral rhizoids and scales. Marchantia is dioicous with umbrella-like antheridiophores and archegoniophores lifting sex organs for wind plus rain-splash fertilisation; sporophytes lack setae elongation (elaters scatter spores instead). Asexual gemmae outpace sex in spreading clones.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Thalloid ribbons; gemmae cups clone; umbrella sex branches.
  • Elaters (not peristome) scatter liverwort spores.

General characteristics

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldF. PteridophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pteridophytes (ferns, horsetails, clubmosses: Dryopteris, Equisetum, Selaginella) are the first vascular land plants - true roots, stems, leaves with xylem-phloem - yet still need water for swimming sperm, restricting them to damp shade. Dominant independent sporophyte with small free-living prothallus gametophyte flips bryophyte dominance. Horsetails (Equisetum, silica-rich scouring rushes) and whisk ferns (Psilotum, rootless) preserve ancient body plans.
NEET Snapshot:
  • First vascular plants; sporophyte dominant; sperm still swim.
  • True organs plus vessels, but aquatic fertilisation persists.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Ferns add xylem-phloem plumbing while keeping swimming sperm.

Chapter 3 · Topic 30

Vascular tissue

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldF. PteridophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pteridophyte vascular tissue runs protosteles (solid xylem core - most primitive) to siphonosteles (pith-centred) to dictyosteles (overlapping leaf gaps) - stele evolution visible across groups. Xylem lacks vessels (tracheids only, like gymnosperms); phloem lacks companion cells (sieve cells instead). Leaves split microphylls (single vein: Selaginella, Equisetum) versus megaphylls (branched veins: ferns) - two independent leaf inventions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Tracheids without vessels; sieve cells without companions.
  • Microphylls (one vein) versus megaphylls (branched) - separate origins.
Remember
  • Stele rings record vascular evolution: solid to pith to gaps.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Vessels evolve later in angiosperms (plus Gnetum) - ferns pipe via tracheids.

Sporophyte

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldF. PteridophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pteridophyte sporophyte is the familiar fern plant - rhizome (underground stem), adventitious roots, fronds (large divided leaves) unrolling as circinate fiddleheads, sporangia clustered in sori (often indusium-covered) on frond undersides. Sporophylls may specialise into cones (Selaginella, Equisetum strobili). Dominant, photosynthetic, independent - the generation that conquered land with plumbing while gametes stayed aquatic.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Rhizome, fronds, sori - the dominant diploid plant.
  • Circinate vernation unrolls fiddleheads distinctively.

Gametophyte

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldF. PteridophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pteridophyte gametophyte (prothallus) is a tiny heart-shaped free-living haploid - photosynthetic, rhizoid-anchored, bearing antheridia (multiflagellate sperms) and archegonia (single eggs) on its underside, needing water films for fertilisation. Small, short-lived and independent (unlike bryophyte dominance or seed-plant dependence) - the middle step in gametophyte reduction: big (bryophytes) to small-free (ferns) to microscopic-dependent (seed plants).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Small heart-shaped prothallus, free-living, water-dependent sex.
  • Multiflagellate sperms need films to reach archegonia.
Remember
  • Prothallus size marks evolution midpoint: shrinking toward seeds.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Fern prothallus is

Solution: Independent haploid heart produces both gametes then dies after fertilisation.

Chapter 3 · Topic 33

Reproduction

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldF. PteridophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pteridophyte reproduction: sporangia (leptosporangiate single-cell-origin in ferns, eusporangiate massive in horsetails) release homosporous meiospores growing prothalli; antheridia release coiled multiflagellate sperms swimming to archegonial eggs; zygotes grow foot-first into new sporophytes on dying prothalli. No seeds, no pollen - every step except spore dispersal needs external water, chaining ferns to damp habitats despite vascular independence.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Homosporous spores, swimming multiflagellate sperm, no seeds.
  • Sporangia type (lepto vs eu) classifies fern groups.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Pteridophyte sperms are

Solution: Coiled multiflagellate sperms swim through water films to archegonia.

Chapter 3 · Topic 34

Heterospory

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldF. PteridophytesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Heterospory (Selaginella, Salvinia: microspores plus megaspores from separate micro- and megasporangia) is the seed habit precursor - small male spores make male gametophytes, large female spores provision single embryos, both retained toward protection. Homosporous ferns gamble millions of identical spores; heterosporous plants invest in few provisioned daughters. Endosporic gametophytes (developing inside spore walls) plus retained megaspores logically extend to seeds - heterospory predicts gymnosperms.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Microspores (male) plus megaspores (female) - unequal investment.
  • Retained provisioned megaspore logically becomes seed.
Remember
  • Heterospory is called the precursor of seed habit - reasoning favourite.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Two spore types with female provisioning preview seed protection.

Topic in Depth

Pteridophyte examples map groups: Dryopteris (male fern, medicinal rhizome), Pteris, Adiantum (maidenhair, walking fern), Equisetum (horsetail scouring rush, silica stems, cone strobili), Selaginella (spike moss, heterosporous, resurrection species), Lycopodium (clubmoss), Psilotum (whisk fern, rootless dichotomous axes), Salvinia-Azolla (floating heterosporous ferns; Azolla-Anabaena fixes paddy nitrogen). Each illustrates stele, spore or habitat speciality.

General characteristics

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperms (Cycas, Pinus, Ginkgo, Ephedra) are naked-seed plants - ovules exposed on cone scales, never enclosed in ovaries - with reduced dependent gametophytes, wind pollination and siphonogamy (pollen tubes delivering non-swimming sperm). Woody trees or shrubs with sunken stomata plus thick cuticle surviving cold and drought; living fossils (Ginkgo) preserve Mesozoic body plans. Seeds with wings (Pinus) or flesh (Cycas) disperse without fruits.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Naked ovules on cones; no flowers, fruits or vessels (mostly).
  • Pollen plus seed frees sex from water - gymnosperm breakthrough.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Cone-scale ovules never enclosed - gymnosperm defining trait.

Roots

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperm roots specialise by partnership: Cycas coralloid roots (bark-surface clusters) house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria (Anabaena), greening nitrogen supply; Pinus roots wrap ectomycorrhizal fungi trading phosphorus for sugars; taproots anchor massive trunks. Coralloid + mycorrhizal dual strategy feeds nutrient-poor soils where gymnosperms dominate (boreal sands, mountain slopes).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cycas coralloid roots fix N2 via cyanobacteria.
  • Pinus mycorrhiza trades sugars for phosphorus.
Remember
  • Coralloid = cyanobacteria; mycorrhiza = fungi - both feed gymnosperm roots.
NEET Practice MCQ

Chapter 3 · Topic 38

Stem

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperm stems run woody monopodial trunks (Pinus excurrent conical form shedding snow) or stout pachycaul trunks (Cycas with persistent leaf bases plus bulbils for vegetative spread). Wood is manoxylic (soft, parenchyma-rich: Cycas) or pycnoxylic (dense tracheid-packed: Pinus timber) - anatomy recording growth strategy. Resin canals waterproof wounds and deter borers; bark thickens against fire and frost.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Monopodial trunks; resin canals defend wounds.
  • Manoxylic (Cycas, soft) versus pycnoxylic (Pinus, timber) wood.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Resin canals in Pinus stem function in

Solution: Resin waterproofs injuries and poisons boring insects.

Leaves

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperm leaves endure cold-drought: Pinus needles (reduced surface, sunken stomata, thick cuticle, sclerenchyma) persist years; Cycas pinnate fronds flush in crowns; scale leaves protect buds. Xerophytic anatomy (rolled, hairy, sunken-stomata) cuts transpiration where water freezes unavailable half the year. Dimorphic foliage (foliage plus scale leaves on long-short shoots in Pinus) organises growth rhythmically.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Needles persist years; sunken stomata plus cuticle save water.
  • Dimorphic shoots (long + dwarf) organise pine growth.
Remember
  • Needle longevity (years) beats deciduous replacement costs in cold zones.

Cones

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperm cones are unisexual strobili: male (microsporophylls shedding winged pollen in clouds), female (megasporophylls bearing naked ovules - woody Pinus cones scaling shut, fleshy Cycas megasporophylls). Monoecious pines carry both on one tree; dioecious Cycas splits sexes across trees. Cone scales open dry (release) and close wet - hygroscopic dispersal timing. Seed wings (Pinus) versus fleshy coats (Cycas, Ginkgo) split wind-animal dispersal.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Male sheds pollen; female bears naked ovules; unisexual always.
  • Monoecious Pinus versus dioecious Cycas - both strategies occur.

1

Chapter 3 · Topic 41

Reproduction

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperm reproduction runs wind plus tubes: massive pollen clouds (pines shed kilograms), siphonogamy (pollen tubes grow to archegonia, delivering sperm - swimming only in Cycas-Ginkgo relics with thousand-flagella sperms), fertilisation fusing one male nucleus with egg (second degenerates), zygote growing perisperm-nourished embryo. Pollination-to-fertilisation delays span months (pines take a year) - slow sex for long-lived trees.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Wind pollen, tube delivery, single fusion, delayed schedules.
  • Cycas-Ginkgo keep swimming sperm - living reproductive fossils.
Remember
  • Siphonogamy (tube delivery) replaces swimming except in Cycas-Ginkgo.
NEET Practice MCQ

Seeds

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperm seeds pack embryo plus haploid female-gametophyte food (perisperm in some, not triploid endosperm - single fusion makes no endosperm) inside protective coats, winged (Pinus autorotation) or fleshy (Cycas red, Ginkgo foul-smelling sarcotesta). Seeds wait out cold-drought seasons dormant, germinating when warmth plus moisture return. Naked yet complete - protection without fruit flesh defines the grade.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Haploid female-gametophyte food (not triploid endosperm).
  • Wings (wind) or flesh (animals) disperse naked seeds.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Gymnosperm seed food tissue is mainly

Solution: Single fusion yields no endosperm; gametophyte tissue feeds embryos.

Examples

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldG. GymnospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gymnosperm examples anchor groups: Cycas (sago palm, coralloid roots, dioecious crowns, swimming sperm), Pinus (pines - needles, winged seeds, resin, monoecious cones), Ginkgo (maidenhair living fossil, foul fleshy seeds, swimming sperm), Ephedra-Gnetum-Welwitschia (gnetophytes with vessels plus angiosperm-like traits), Sequoia (redwood giants, tallest organisms). Each illustrates seed-plant experiments - relic swimmers, vessel pioneers, timber giants.

Monocots

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldH. AngiospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Monocots (grasses, lilies, palms, orchids) run one cotyledon plus parallel venation, fibrous roots, scattered vascular bundles (no cambium, no secondary growth), trimerous flowers and single-pored pollen. Economically dominant (rice, wheat, maize, sugarcane, bamboo) despite anatomically simpler stems - herbaceous speed beats woody persistence in disturbed habitats. Palms secondarily thicken without true cambium.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots, scattered bundles, trimerous flowers.
  • No cambium means no true wood - herbs and palms instead.
Remember
  • Scattered bundles plus no cambium diagnose monocot stems instantly.

Dicots

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldH. AngiospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dicots (mango, pea, rose, oaks) run two cotyledons plus reticulate venation, taproots, ringed vascular bundles with cambium (secondary growth into wood), tetramerous-pentamerous flowers and three-pored pollen. Woody trees, shrubs and diverse herbs dominate stable habitats; cambium-driven wood, bark and annual rings record years. APG DNA reshuffles classic dicots (eudicots refined), but classroom monocot-dicot split persists for teaching.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Two cotyledons, net veins, taproot, ringed bundles with cambium.
  • Cambium wood plus bark enables tree longevity.

Chapter 3 · Topic 46

Flower

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldH. AngiospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Flowers are compressed reproductive shoots: pedicel stalk, thalamus/receptacle base, four whorls - calyx (sepals, protection), corolla (petals, advertisement), androecium (stamens, male), gynoecium (carpels, female). Symmetry (actinomorphic radial, zygomorphic bilateral), sexuality (bisexual, unisexual monoecious/dioecious) and completeness (all whorls or missing) classify every bloom. Position (hypogynous superior ovary, perigynous, epigynous inferior) records floral evolution.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Four whorls on thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium.
  • Symmetry plus sexuality plus ovary position classify flowers.

Fruit

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldH. AngiospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fruits are ripened ovaries (true) sometimes plus thalamus (false apple, strawberry): simple (one ovary - berry tomato, drupe mango, legume pea), aggregate (many carpels one flower - raspberry), multiple (whole inflorescence - jackfruit, pineapple). Pericarp layers (exo-meso-endocarp) specialise - fleshy mesocarp rewards dispersers, stony endocarp shields seeds. Parthenocarpy (seedless banana, grapes) skips fertilisation via hormones.
NEET Snapshot:
  • True (ovary) vs false (plus thalamus); simple vs aggregate vs multiple.
  • Flesh rewards dispersers; stones shield seeds.
Remember
  • Mango drupe: skin, flesh, stone - pericarp triple demo.

Seed

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldH. AngiospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Seeds pack embryo (plumule shoot, radicle root, cotyledons) plus food (endosperm albuminous like cereals, or consumed non-endospermic like pea) inside protective coats (testa plus tegmen). Monocot grains (single cotyledon scutellum, aleurone layer, coleoptile-coleorhiza sheaths) differ structurally from dicot seeds (two fleshy cotyledons). Dormancy (hard coats, inhibitors, immature embryos) times germination; viability spans days (willow) to millennia (date palm).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Embryo plus food plus coat - dormancy times awakening.
  • Albuminous (endosperm persists) vs non-endospermic (cotyledons store).

Chapter 3 · Topic 49

Double fertilisation

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldH. AngiospermsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Double fertilisation (angiosperm signature): pollen tube releases two male gametes - one fuses egg (syngamy, diploid zygote) plus one fuses two polar nuclei (triple fusion, triploid endosperm) - so embryo plus food form together, no wasted provisioning of unfertilised ovules. Endosperm may persist (cereals) or be consumed (pea); helobial and nuclear types vary. Apomixis (seed without fertilisation) and polyembryony (multiple embryos - citrus adventive) bend the rules agriculturally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Syngamy (embryo) plus triple fusion (endosperm) - twin fusions.
  • Food forms only when embryos do - angiosperm efficiency.
Double fusion
PointDetail
SyngamyMale gamete + egg = diploid zygote
Triple fusionMale gamete + 2 polar nuclei = triploid endosperm
ResultEmbryo plus matched food supply

Chapter 3 · Topic 50

Haplontic

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldI. Plant Life CyclesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Haplontic cycles run haploid-dominant: free-living gametophyte (n) makes gametes by mitosis, zygote (2n) immediately meioses into spores - diploid exists only as single-celled zygote (Volvox, Spirogyra, Chlamydomonas, many algae). No multicellular diploid body at all. Land-plant bryophytes extend haplontic logic with multicellular dependent sporophytes, but the pattern (dominant n, fleeting 2n) stays recognisably algal.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Gametophyte dominant; zygote alone represents diploidy.
  • Algae plus bryophytes share haploid dominance.

Solution: Free-living n generation with single-celled 2n zygote defines haplontic.

Chapter 3 · Topic 51

Diplontic

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldI. Plant Life CyclesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Diplontic cycles run diploid-dominant: free-living sporophyte (2n) makes spores by meiosis, gametophytes reduced (Fucus conceptacles, animal bodies) - diploid is the plant you see. Seed plants extend diplontic logic with microscopic dependent gametophytes (pollen, embryo sacs); animals run pure diplontic cycles (gametes by meiosis, no multicellular haploid at all). Dominance flipped from haplontic algae toward protected diploid complexity.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sporophyte dominant; gametophyte reduced or microscopic.
  • Fucus, seed plants and animals share diploid dominance.
Remember
  • Animals are diplontic without alternation - gametes straight from body.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Diplontic life cycle occurs in

Solution: Dominant diploid bodies with reduced haploid phases define diplontic.

Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 3 · Topic 52

Haplo-diplontic

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldI. Plant Life CyclesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Haplo-diplontic cycles alternate multicellular haploid and diploid bodies: isomorphic (Ectocarpus equal phases) or heteromorphic (Laminaria giant sporophyte, moss dominant gametophyte). Bryophytes (n-dominant) and pteridophytes (2n-dominant) both alternate substantially free-living phases - the middle ground between algal haplontic and seed-plant diplontic extremes. Which generation dominates marks evolutionary position precisely.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Both phases multicellular; dominance decides the group.
  • Isomorphic equal vs heteromorphic unequal alternation.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Heteromorphic alternation with dominant sporophyte occurs in

Solution: Big fern sporophytes alternate tiny prothallus gametophytes.

Index / Diversity in the Living World
Chapter 3 · Topic 53

Alternation of generations

Plant KingdomDiversity in the Living WorldI. Plant Life CyclesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alternation of generations is the universal plant rhythm - haploid gametophyte (mitotic gametes) alternating diploid sporophyte (meiotic spores) - tuned from haplontic (algae, bryophytes) through haplo-diplontic (pteridophytes) to diplontic (seed plants). Evolution progressively reduced and protected the gametophyte (free prothallus to pollen-embryo-sac dependence) while elaborating sporophytes (mats to trees). Haplontic-diplontic is a spectrum, not a switch.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Gametophyte (mitosis gametes) alternates sporophyte (meiosis spores).
  • Trend: gametophyte shrinks and hides; sporophyte grows and dominates.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

In alternation of generations, spores are always produced by

Solution: Meiotic spores from diploid bodies start each haploid generation.

Deep Dive · Form follows function outdoors

Morphology reads plant bodies as engineering: roots anchor-absorb-store (tap, fibrous, modified knees and props), stems position-conduct-support (nodes, buds, tubers, thorns), leaves capture light (venation, phyllotaxy, traps), inflorescences schedule blooms (racemose endless, cymose ending), flowers package sex (whorls, symmetry, unions), fruits package dispersal (true-false, simple-multiple). Three families - Fabaceae (pea mechanics), Solanaceae (potato poisons), Liliaceae (lily regularity) - convert theory into identification practice.
NEET facts:
  • Potato is stem tuber (eyes); sweet potato is root tuber (no eyes).
  • Pea: zygomorphic, diadelphous 9+1, vexillary, marginal placentation - one flower teaches five concepts.

Chapter 4 · Topic 1

Types of roots

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Roots anchor, absorb and store - three origin types: tap (primary radicle persists, dicots), fibrous (cluster replacing radicle, monocots/grasses), adventitious (any non-radicle part - stems, leaves: banyan props, maize stilts, money-plant cuttings). Root hairs (tubular extensions) multiply absorption area; root caps (plus quiescent centre) protect growing tips boring through soil. No nodes, internodes, buds or green colour - root badges versus stems.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Tap (dicot radicle), fibrous (monocot cluster), adventitious (stem/leaf origin).
  • Root hairs absorb; root caps protect; no nodes or buds ever.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Adventitious roots arise from

Solution: Banyan props, maize stilts and cutting roots all start non-radicle.

Related Diagram · Root systems

Fig: One dominant tap, clustered fibrous mat, or stem-born adventitious roots.

Chapter 4 · Topic 2

Primary root

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Primary root is the radicle grown direct - first organ out of germinating seeds, diving geotropically down while shoots rise. It establishes the seedling (anchorage plus first water) before laterals branch. In dicots it persists as the tap system lifelong; in monocots it aborts early, replaced by fibrous clusters. Positive geotropism plus positive hydrotropism steer it - gravity and moisture compasses in the cap.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Radicle elongation forms the seedling first anchor and straw.
  • Persists in dicots; aborts in monocots.
Remember
  • Radicle first out, geotropic down - germination polarity.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Primary root develops directly from the

Solution: Embryonic radicle elongates into the primary root on germination.

Chapter 4 · Topic 3

Lateral roots

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Lateral roots branch endogenously - arising from deep pericycle tissue and pushing outward through cortex and epidermis (unlike stems branching exogenously from surface buds). This inside-out origin strengthens junctions against pull-out forces. Order follows acropetal sequence (youngest near tips); root hairs zone sits just behind elongation zones. Mycorrhizal fungi plus nodule bacteria colonise laterals - absorption partnerships cluster here.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Endogenous pericycle origin pushes through outer layers.
  • Acropetal order; hairs behind tips; symbionts colonise laterals.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Lateral roots originate from the

Solution: Deep pericycle branching bursts outward - inside-out junctions resist pulling.

Index / Plant Structure
Chapter 4 · Topic 4

Tap root

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Taproot systems (dicots: mango, pea, mustard) run one dominant primary root with ordered laterals - deep penetration reaching water tables, strong anchorage against storms, plus storage swelling in carrot, radish, turnip (hypocotyl joins), and respiratory knees in mangroves. Conical (carrot), fusiform (radish), napiform (turnip) shapes classify storage taps. Deep plus strong plus storable - dicot root strategy.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One dominant radicle root with ordered laterals (dicots).
  • Storage shapes: conical carrot, fusiform radish, napiform turnip.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Napiform storage root is seen in

Solution: Top-heavy turnip/beet napiform contrasts tapering carrot conical.

Chapter 4 · Topic 5

Fibrous root

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fibrous systems (monocots: wheat, rice, maize, onion) replace the short-lived radicle with dense adventitious clusters from stem bases - shallow, spreading mats superb at topsoil exploitation and erosion control (grasses bind dunes and bunds). No dominant root; hundreds of equals. Shallow reach limits drought tolerance versus taps - irrigation dependence follows. Fibrous mats plus tillers make grasses supreme colonisers.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dense stem-base clusters replacing radicle (monocots).
  • Shallow mats excel at topsoil mining and erosion binding.
Remember
  • Grasses bind soil; taproots mine depth - strategy matches habitat.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Fibrous root system is characteristic of

Solution: Monocot radicles abort; stem-base adventitious clusters take over.

Chapter 4 · Topic 6

Adventitious roots

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Adventitious roots prove roots can start anywhere: stem nodes (maize stilt props, sugarcane), branches (banyan pillar props), leaves (Bryophyllum plantlets, money plant), cuttings (horticultural propagation). Functions diversify - props and stilts support, climbers (money plant) grip, floaters (Pistia) balance, parasites (Cuscuta haustoria) steal. Gardeners root cuttings exploiting this totipotency - stems remembering root programmes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Any non-radicle origin - stems, leaves, cuttings.
  • Props, stilts, climbers, haustoria - jobs beyond absorption.

Banyan propsPillar support
Maize stiltsLodging resistance
Cuscuta haustoriaParasitic theft

Chapter 4 · Topic 7

Root modifications

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Root modifications rewrite root jobs: storage (carrot, sweet potato), support (banyan props, maize stilts, betel climbers), respiration (mangrove pneumatophores with lenticel breathing knees), photosynthesis (Tinospora green aerial roots, Trapa), parasitism (Cuscuta haustoria tapping host xylem-phloem), nitrogen fixation (legume nodules housing Rhizobium), reproduction (sweet potato buds sprouting). Same organ, many careers - modification patterns are pure NEET matching material.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Storage, support, breathing, photosynthesis, parasitism, fixation.
  • Form matches new job; origin stays root.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Pneumatophores (respiratory roots) occur in

Solution: Mud-buried roots send breathing knees up for air exchange.

Chapter 4 · Topic 8

Storage roots

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Storage roots stockpile starch and sugars: tap-derived (carrot conical, radish fusiform, turnip napiform - plus hypocotyl contributions) and adventitious (sweet potato tuberous clusters, Dahlia, Asparagus). Biennials store in year one, flower in year two on reserves - vernalisation plus size thresholds gate bolting. Humans harvest the savings: roots and tubers feed billions (potato is stem, sweet potato is root - classic distinction).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Tap shapes plus adventitious tubers stock biennial reserves.
  • Sweet potato is root; potato is stem - examiner favourite.
Remember
  • Potato (stem tuber, eyes) vs sweet potato (root, no eyes).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Sweet potato storage roots are

Solution: Clustered adventitious roots swell; stem-tuber potato differs (eyes present).

Chapter 4 · Topic 9

Support roots

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Support roots brace plants mechanically: banyan pillar props (branch-born, becoming trunks), maize/sugarcane stilt roots (nodal, lodging resistance), betel and money-plant climbing roots (grip bark), Pandanus screw-pine stilts (coastal anchorage). All adventitious, all lignified with age, all converting absorption organs into structural cables. Lodging-resistant cereals owe standing harvests to stilt whorls.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Props, stilts, climbers - adventitious roots as cables.
  • Lignify with age; brace against wind and weight.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Prop roots of banyan arise from

Solution: Branch-born pillars descend and thicken into trunk-like supports.

Chapter 4 · Topic 10

Respiratory roots

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Respiratory roots (pneumatophores) breathe for drowned systems: mangrove (Rhizophora, Avicennia) mud buries roots in anoxic slush, so sub-aerial knees rise with lenticel pores piping air down aerenchyma to submerged parts. Negatively geotropic (grow upward against gravity), spongy, pore-studded - every trait serves gas exchange. Pneumatophore density maps tidal flooding tolerance across mangrove zones.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Upward knees with lenticels pipe air to buried roots.
  • Negatively geotropic; aerenchyma conducts gases down.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Pneumatophores are negatively

Solution: Upward growth against gravity lifts breathing pores above mud.

Chapter 4 · Topic 11

Characteristics

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Stems are plant axes bearing nodes (leaf/branch/bud junctions), internodes (elongating spans), buds (dormant shoot tips - terminal plus axillary) and green youth (photosynthetic before barking). Unlike roots they grow negatively geotropic (up), positively phototropic, bear leaves/flowers/fruits, and branch exogenously. Conducting (xylem-phloem highways), supporting (wood/sclerenchyma), storing (pith, tubers) and propagating (runners, cuttings) - axis multitasker.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Nodes, internodes, buds, exogenous branches - stem badges.
  • Up-growing, leaf-bearing, conducting axis.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Stems differ from roots in bearing

Solution: Nodal architecture with buds and leaves diagnoses stems instantly.

Chapter 4 · Topic 12

Nodes

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nodes are stem junctions where leaves, branches and buds attach - vascular traces diverge into appendages here, making nodes nutrient crossroads. Compressed nodes stack leaves into rosettes (cabbage) or whorls; elongated internodes space them for light (etiolated shade stems stretch). Buds nestle in leaf axils at nodes - pruning above nodes preserves regrowth points. Sugarcane nodes root cuttings; mint nodes strike runners.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Leaf-branch-bud junction crossroads with vascular traces.
  • Axillary buds at nodes drive branching and regrowth.
Remember
  • Cut above a node - buds below resprout the shoot.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Axillary buds occur

Solution: Node-axil buds branch shoots and rescue pruned plants.

Index / Plant Structure
Chapter 4 · Topic 13

Internodes

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Internodes are stem spans between nodes that elongate (intercalary meristems in grasses/bamboo - metres per day), spacing leaves for light and lifting flowers to pollinators. Short internodes compress rosettes (radish) and bulbs; long ones climb (vines) or race upward in shade (etiolation). Sugarcane stores sugar in parenchymatous internodes - harvest targets the spans, not the nodes. Gibberellins stretch internodes (bolting); dwarf mutants lack the signal.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Elongating spans spacing leaves and lifting flowers.
  • Intercalary meristems power grass-bamboo sprint growth.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Intercalary meristem elongating grass internodes sits

Solution: Basal intercalary growth pushes grass blades up after grazing.

Chapter 4 · Topic 14

Buds

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Buds are dormant shoot tips - terminal (apical dominance via auxin suppressing laterals), axillary (branching reserve), accessory and adventitious backups. Dormancy (bud scales, inhibitors) times spring flush; chilling (vernalisation) or pruning breaks it.，吃 buds feed us (cabbage heads, Brussels sprouts); floral buds become blooms. Apical dominance shapes trees (excurrent pines) versus bushes (decapitated hedges bush out).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Terminal leads (auxin suppresses laterals); axillaries wait.
  • Cabbage and sprouts are giant edible buds.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Apical dominance (terminal bud suppressing laterals) is maintained by

Solution: Tip-made auxin inhibits axillary buds; decapitation releases branching.

Index / Plant Structure
Chapter 4 · Topic 15

Branching

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Branching patterns shape canopies: racemose monopodial (single leader - pines excurrent), cymose sympodial (leader aborts, laterals take over - dichasial/dendritic crowns), dichotomous (equal forks - ferns, Palmyra). Auxin-cytokinin balance decides - auxin preserves leaders, cytokinin releases laterals. Orchardists prune to programme shapes (open centres, espaliers); foresters protect leaders for timber poles.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Monopodial leader vs sympodial takeovers vs dichotomous forks.
  • Pruning rewires auxin-cytokinin branching decisions.
Remember
  • Leader versus lateral struggle shapes every tree crown.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Sympodial branching means

Solution: Successive lateral takeovers build forked sympodial crowns.
Back to Index
Index / Plant Structure
Chapter 4 · Topic 16

Stem modifications

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Stem modifications repurpose axes: storage (potato tuber eyes, ginger rhizome, onion bulb scales, Colocasia corm), support/climbing (pea tendrils, grape tendrils, thorn Citrus/Bougainvillea defence, prickles), photosynthesis (Opuntia phylloclades, Euphorbia, Ruscus cladodes), protection (thorns), propagation (runners, stolons, offsets, suckers). Same nodal-bud anatomy proves stem origin despite wild shapes - eyes, scales and buds betray tubers and bulbs.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Tubers store, tendrils climb, thorns defend, phylloclades photosynthesise.
  • Eyes/scales/buds prove stem origin of odd shapes.

Chapter 4 · Topic 17

Underground stems

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Underground stems survive bad seasons buried: rhizomes (ginger - horizontal, nodes, scale leaves, buds), tubers (potato - swollen tips), bulbs (onion - disc stem plus fleshy scales), corms (Colocasia - solid swollen base). Stored starch plus dormant buds resprout yearly - perennation strategy beating annual reseeding. Humans propagate them vegetatively (seed potatoes, ginger hands, onion sets) - clones farming itself.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Rhizome, tuber, bulb, corm - buried buds plus starch banks.
  • Perennate underground, resprout aerially each season.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Onion bulb stores food mainly in

Solution: Concentric scale leaves swell; disc stem stays tiny at base.

Chapter 4 · Topic 18

Sub-aerial stems

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sub-aerial stems spread horizontally at ground level for vegetative conquest: runners (grass, strawberry - long internodes rooting nodes), stolons (arched runners rooting tips), offsets (water hyacinth short thick runners), suckers (banana, mint - underground-born aerial shoots). Each node roots and shoots - fragment nettles a clone army. Lawns, strawberry beds and water-hyacinth mats all run sub-aerial colonisation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Runners, stolons, offsets, suckers - horizontal clone spreaders.
  • Every rooted node becomes an independent plant.
Remember
  • Node-rooting defines sub-aerial spreaders - check nodes.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Strawberry spreads vegetatively by

Solution: Surface runners root nodes into daughter plants serially.

Index / Plant Structure
Chapter 4 · Topic 19

Aerial modifications

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Aerial stem modifications work above ground: tendrils (pea leaflets, grape stems - coiling climbers), thorns (Citrus axillary, Bougainvillea - defence plus climbing), phylloclades (Opuntia pads - photosynthesis after leaf loss), cladodes (Asparagus needles - one-internode photosynthesizers), hooks and spines. Climbing without wood (tendrils), defending without poison (thorns), feeding without leaves (phylloclades) - aerial innovation triple.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Tendrils climb, thorns defend, phylloclades feed.
  • Pea tendrils are leaflets; grape tendrils are stems - homology differs.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Opuntia flattened green pads (phylloclades) perform

Solution: Spines are leaves; pads are photosynthetic stems - desert swap.

Chapter 4 · Topic 20

Leaf structure

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Leaves are photosynthetic factories on petiole stalks: leaf base (sheathing in grasses/legumes, pulvinus swollen in legumes for sleep movements), petiole (positioning blade, pulvinus articulation), lamina/blade (expanded green surface with veins, midrib, margins). Stipules (basal appendages - free, adnate, spiny, tendrillar) aid identification. Blade plus stalk plus base - three parts, endless modification for light capture.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Base (sheath/pulvinus), petiole (stalk), lamina (blade).
  • Stipule forms aid family identification.

Chapter 4 · Topic 21

Leaf base

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Leaf bases attach blades to stems: sheathing bases wrap stems (grasses, banana - strength plus protection), pulvinus swellings articulate legume leaflets (potassium-driven sleep/nastic movements), decurrent wings extend down stems (Laggera). Onion scales are whole swollen bases storing food. Base form predicts family (sheaths scream Poaceae) and function (pulvini move, sheaths brace).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sheathing (grasses), pulvinus (legumes), decurrent wings.
  • Sheaths brace; pulvini articulate; scales store.
Remember
  • Touch-me-not folds via pulvinus turgor shifts.

Sheathing leaf bases are characteristic of

Chapter 4 · Topic 22

Petiole

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Petioles position blades to light - twisting, lengthening (shade leaves grow longer stalks), sometimes flattening, winging (Citrus) or swelling (water-hyacinth floats). Sessile leaves skip stalks (wheat, Calotropis); petiolate leaves articulate via pulvini in legumes. Petiole vascular traces prefigure midribs; abscission zones at petiole bases drop leaves cleanly in autumn. Phyllodes (Acacia) are flattened petioles replacing fallen leaflets.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Stalks position blades; variations float, store, photosynthesise.
  • Abscission zones at bases drop leaves seasonally.

Chapter 4 · Topic 23

Lamina

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Lamina (blade) maximises light capture: broad thin green surface, midrib plus veins (transport plus support), margins (entire, serrate, lobed) tuning boundary layers, apex shapes dripping rain (drip tips). Mesophyll inside (palisade plus spongy) photosynthesises; stomata below exchange gases; cuticle seals water. Sun leaves thicken small; shade leaves broaden thin - same genome, light-tailored blades.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Expanded photosynthetic surface with veins and stomata.
  • Sun thick-small; shade thin-broad - light tailoring.
Remember
  • Drip tips shed tropical downpours fast.

Photosynthesis in leaves occurs mainly in the

Chapter 4 · Topic 24

Venation

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Venation maps veins: reticulate netted (dicots - pinnate mango, palmate cucumber) versus parallel (monocots - grass lines, banana laterals). Reticulation resists tearing and reroutes around damage; parallel suits strap blades. Veins carry xylem-phloem plus sclerenchyma ribs - transport plus skeleton combined. Venation instantly separates monocot from dicot leaves in field identification.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Reticulate (dicot nets) vs parallel (monocot lines).
  • Veins transport plus stiffen blades.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Parallel venation is characteristic of leaves of

Solution: Monocot veins run parallel; dicot veins net reticulate.

Index / Plant Structure
Chapter 4 · Topic 25

Simple leaf

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Simple leaves carry single undivided blades (mango, banana, Calotropis) - however deeply lobed, one blade on one petiole with axillary bud at its base. Lobing (oak sinuses) increases edge without dividing; dissection never reaches midrib fully. Bud position proves simplicity: one axillary bud per leaf base, never in blade sinuses. Simple versus compound is blade division, not size - huge banana leaves stay simple.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One blade, one petiole, one axillary bud - however lobed.
  • Bud at base proves leaf; buds in sinuses prove leaflets.
Remember
  • No bud in the sinus means leaflet, not leaf.

Compound leaf

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Compound leaves divide blades into leaflets on a rachis: pinnate (feather - unipinnate neem, bipinnate goldmohur, tripinnate Moringa) versus palmate (fingers - silk cotton, chestnut). Leaflets lack axillary buds (only whole-leaf base carries one). Compounding multiplies light capture without huge blades (wind-tolerant, heat-shedding) and enables sleep movements (legume leaflets fold). Neem, tamarind and rain-tree crowns run compound strategies.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Leaflets on rachis; no axillary buds in sinuses.
  • Pinnate feather vs palmate fingers - two compounding plans.

Topic in Depth

Phyllotaxy arranges leaves for light without shading: alternate spiral (mango, one per node), opposite (guava, pairs), whorled (nerium, rings), with divergence angles (golden 137.5 degrees) optimising exposure. Opposite-decussate (mint family, pairs at right angles) aids identification. Arrangement plus venation plus simplicity pin families fast in field keys.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Alternate, opposite, whorled - light-sharing geometries.
  • Golden angle spirals optimise packing mathematically.

Leaf modifications

Topic in Depth

Leaf modifications repurpose blades: tendrils (pea leaflets climb), spines (cactus defence plus dew harvest, Opuntia), pitchers (Nepenthes insect traps supplementing poor soils), bladders (Utricularia underwater suction traps), phyllodes (Acacia petioles photosynthesise), succulence (Aloe water storage), budding plantlets (Bryophyllum notches grow babies). Carnivory supplements nitrogen where soils starve - traps are leaves, not flowers.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Carnivorous leaves mine nitrogen from insects in poor soils.

Racemose

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureD. InflorescenceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Racemose (indefinite) inflorescences grow the main axis indefinitely, flowering youngest near the apex (acropetal: younger above, older below) - raceme (mustard stalked flowers), spike (sesbania sessile), catkin (mulberry drooping unisexual), spadix (banana fleshy spike with spathe), corymb (flat-topped stalked), umbel (flat-topped single-point, carrot family), capitulum/head (sunflower - ray plus disc florets mimicking one flower). Axis never ends in a flower.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Main axis grows on; flowers open bottom-to-top (acropetal).
  • Sunflower head mimics single flower with two floret types.

Cymose

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureD. InflorescenceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cymose (definite) inflorescences terminate the main axis in a flower first, then laterals overtake - flowering oldest at apex (basipetal: older above, younger below). Forms: monochasial (one lateral - helicoid/begonia curls, scorpioid), dichasial (two laterals - jasmine, teak), polychasial (many - Calotropis). Growth stops at each terminal flower; branching overtakes sequentially. Jasmine and teak crowns run cymose programmes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Axis ends in flower first; laterals overtake (basipetal order).
  • Mono-, di-, polychasial by lateral count.
Remember
  • Racemose grows on; cymose ends first - axis fate differs.

Topic in Depth

Special inflorescences bend rules: cyathium (Euphorbia - single female plus male flowers in cup mimicking one bloom), hypanthodium (fig - hollow receptacle lined inside with flowers, wasp-pollinated), verticillaster (mint - condensed dichasial whorls), spikelet (grasses - glume-wrapped florets). Each mimics or miniaturises standard types for specialised pollinators - fig-wasp and grass-wind extremes. Family identification leans heavily on these signatures.

Floral parts

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. FlowerStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Flowers stack four whorls on thalamus: calyx (sepals - bud protection, sometimes petaloid), corolla (petals - pollinator advertisement), androecium (stamens - male), gynoecium (carpels - female) - outer accessory plus inner essential division. Complete flowers carry all four (mustard); incomplete miss any (cucumber unisexual). Thalamus internodes (anthophore, androphore, gynophore - passionflower, Capparis) space whorls in advanced blooms.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Calyx, corolla (accessory) plus androecium, gynoecium (essential).
  • Complete (4 whorls) vs incomplete (missing any).

Topic in Depth

Pedicel is the flower stalk - stalked (pedicellate: mustard, rose) versus sessile (sesbania spike, wheat) attachment deciding inflorescence types. Length positions blooms for pollinators (long-exserted) or wind (nodding grasses); articulation zones shed spent flowers cleanly. Pedicellate versus sessile splits raceme from spike - stalk presence classifies inflorescences.

Topic in Depth

Receptacle (thalamus) is the flower axis tip bearing all whorls - conical (raised centres), flat, or cupped (hypanthium); fleshy expansion makes false fruits (apple, strawberry). Internode elongation between whorls names anthophore (below androecium), androphore (below gynoecium), gynophore (stalked ovary - Capparis, passionflower). Ovary position (hypo-, peri-, epigynous) describes thalamus-ovary geometry.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Axis tip carrying whorls; expanded forms false fruits.
  • Anthophore, androphore, gynophore space advanced flowers.

Topic in Depth

Sepals (calyx) protect buds - usually green, sometimes petaloid (lily tepals), fused (gamosepalous: hibiscus bell) or free (polyphyllous: mustard), persistent (brinjal cap, tomato) or caducous. Epicalyx extra whorls (China rose, strawberry) aid family ID. Aestivation patterns (valvate, twisted, imbricate) describe bud-packing geometry. Sepal number and fusion enter every floral formula.

Topic in Depth

Petals (corolla) advertise to pollinators - colours (bee-blue, bird-red, moth-white-night), nectar guides (UV patterns), scents and shapes filter visitors. Fused (gamopetalous bells/salvers: tobacco, jasmine) versus free (polypetalous: rose, mustard); clawed (Dianthus), spurred (larkspur nectar tubes). Petal number feeds formulas (cruciform 4, rosaceous 5); reduced or absent in wind flowers (grasses use lodicules instead).

Topic in Depth

Stamens (androecium) are microsporophylls - filament stalks plus anther lobes manufacturing pollen. Counts vary (mustard 6 tetradynamous: 4 long + 2 short; China rose many monadelphous; pea 9+1 diadelphous; sunflower 5 syngenesious). Anther lobes (dithecous two, monothecous one) plus dehiscence slits release pollen; sterile staminodes advertise or feed visitors. Stamen number-fusion patterns are prime family characters.

Carpels

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. FlowerStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Carpels (gynoecium) are megasporophylls - ovary (ovules inside) plus style (pollen-tube path) plus stigma (pollen landing receptive surface). Numbers run one (pea) to many (lotus, rose); free (apocarpous: lotus, rose) versus fused (syncarpous: mustard, tomato) decide fruit types. Stigma forms (feathery grass, sticky cousins) match pollination modes. Carpel count and fusion enter formulas and predict fruit architecture.

  • Ovary-style-stigma units; free or fused decide fruits.
  • Feathery stigmas catch wind pollen; sticky ones catch insects.

  • One carpel (pea) to many (lotus) - count predicts fruit.

Actinomorphic

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. FlowerStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Actinomorphic flowers show radial symmetry - divisible into equal halves through any vertical plane (mustard, China rose, lily, brinjal). Ancestral state suiting generalist pollinators approaching from any direction. Formulas mark with circle-plus symbol. Contrast zygomorphic specialists (pea, snapdragon - one plane) and asymmetric oddities (canna). Symmetry reflects pollinator contracts: open-access radial versus exclusive bilateral.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Radial symmetry, any-plane division (mustard, lily).
  • Generalist-pollinator ancestral state.

Chapter 4 · Topic 40

Zygomorphic

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. FlowerStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Zygomorphic flowers show bilateral symmetry - one vertical plane only (pea, snapdragon, orchids, mint). Bilateral architecture forces pollinator orientation, smearing pollen precisely (keel-petal bee mechanics, orchid landing platforms). Derived state from actinomorphic ancestors, repeatedly evolved with bee pollination. Formulas mark with percent-like symbol. Asymmetric flowers (canna, with staminodes) break even bilateral rules.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One-plane symmetry forcing pollinator orientation.
  • Bee-mechanics blooms (pea keel, snapdragon mask) exemplify.
Remember
  • Bilateral blooms aim pollen; radial blooms broadcast it.

Chapter 4 · Topic 41

Bisexual

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. FlowerStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bisexual (perfect, hermaphrodite) flowers carry both stamens and carpels (mustard, rose, pea, lily) - self- or cross-pollination options open. Perfect does not guarantee selfing: dichogamy (timing splits), herkogamy (spatial splits), self-incompatibility (genetic blocks) enforce outcrossing. Breeding programmes emasculate perfect flowers to control crosses - bisexuality aids manipulability.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Both sexes in one bloom; outcrossing devices prevent selfing.
  • Emasculation plus bagging controls perfect-flower crosses.

Unisexual

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. FlowerStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Unisexual (imperfect) flowers carry one sex: staminate (male) or pistillate (female) - monoecious plants bear both (maize, cucumber, coconut), dioecious split sexes across plants (papaya, date palm, mulberry). Unisexuality enforces outcrossing absolutely; dioecy needs pollinator/planting sex ratios managed (date orchards interplant males). Cucumber breeding exploits gynoecious lines for fruit-only crops.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One sex per bloom; monoecious (both sexes, one plant) vs dioecious (separate plants).
  • Unisexuality guarantees cross-pollination.

Complete flowers carry all four whorls (mustard, rose); incomplete miss any - achlamydeous (no perianth: Euphorbia cyathium), monochlamydeous (one perianth whorl: lilies tepals), unisexual (missing a sex). Completeness is structural inventory, not quality judgement - grasses (lodicules, no petals) and Euphorbia cups succeed incompletely. Formulas record presence/absence precisely per whorl.

  • Grasses and spurges thrive structurally incomplete.

Valvate aestivation meets sepal/petal edges edge-to-edge without overlap (mustard calyx, Calotropis) - simplest bud packing, margins just touching. Valvate calyx plus twisted corolla combos (China rose reverses: twisted calyx? no - valvate... check family patterns) mark family signatures.

Twisted (contorted) aestivation overlaps each segment one-margin-in, one-margin-out in rotation (China rose corolla, cotton, ladyfinger) - spiral shingling sealing buds. Twisted corolla plus monadelphous stamens double-mark Malvaceae blooms.

Imbricate aestivation overlaps irregularly - one segment fully outside, one fully inside, rest mixed (Cassia, gulmohur; sepals of many) - shingle packing without rotational order. Ascending imbricate (pea relatives posterior petal inside) versus descending variants fine-tune bud architecture. Cassia yellow blooms demonstrate textbook imbricate corollas. Anthers (usually dithecous two-lobed, four microsporangia; Malvaceae monothecous single) manufacture and release pollen: sporogenous tissue meioses into microspores maturing to 2-3-celled grains, tapetum nurses (plus Ubisch bodies coating exine), dehiscence slits (longitudinal, transverse, porous - Solanaceae pores buzz-pollinated) open at maturity. Dithecous-four-sporangia is the textbook standard; deviations diagnose families.

Topic in Depth

Filaments are stamen stalks - length positions anthers (exserted wind/bee access, included tubular protection), vascular traces supply developing anthers, and fusion patterns (monadelphous tube, diadelphous 9+1, polyadelphous bundles) diagnose families. Hairy or appendaged filaments (spiderwort beards) attract or reward visitors. Filament-free sessile anthers (some Aristolochia) sit directly on perianth - reduction extremes.

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureG. AndroeciumStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pollen grains are male gametophytes in sporopollenin armour - vegetative cell (tube growth) plus generative cell (dividing to two male gametes: 3-celled shed in advanced groups, 2-celled in primitives), sculptured exine (spines, pores, furrows identifying species - palynology), germ pores as tube exits. Viability spans minutes (grasses) to months (stored); allergenic exine proteins trigger hay fever. Pollen banks preserve breeding lines.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Two/three-celled male gametophytes in sporopollenin shells.
  • Exine sculpture identifies species (palynology); germ pores exit tubes.
Remember
  • Sporopollenin resists acids and time - fossils preserve exines.

Topic in Depth

Pollen sacs (microsporangia, usually four per dithecous anther) house sporogenous tissue undergoing meiosis into microspore tetrads maturing to pollen. Wall layers (epidermis, endothecium with fibrous thickenings for dehiscence, middle layers, tapetum) each serve release: endothecium opens slits, tapetum feeds. Archesporial origin and simultaneous/successive cytokinesis patterns classify development microscopically.

  • Endothecium thickenings spring dehiscence slits open.

Parts: ovary (ovule chamber), style (tube path, solid/hollow), stigma (receptive landing - wet sticky or dry feathery). Numbers (one to many) plus fusion (apocarpous free vs syncarpous fused) decide fruit architecture. Carpel theory unifies flower diversity as modified leaves.

Ovaries house ovules and ripen into fruit walls (pericarp): positions superior (hypogynous: mustard, China rose), half-inferior (perigynous: rose, peach), inferior (epigynous: apple, sunflower) - thalamus geometry recorded. Locules (one to many) with placentation patterns (marginal, axile, parietal, free-central, basal) organise ovule attachment. Ovary wall becomes pericarp (exo-meso-endocarp layers); inferior ovaries yield false fruits with thalamus flesh.

Styles are pollen-tube highways - hollow (lily, canal-guided) or solid (transmitting tissue secreting guidance), length matching pollinator placement (long-exserted wind/bee access, short selfing). Style branches multiply stigmas (Hibiscus five, Crocus three saffron strands - costliest spice). Self-incompatibility reactions (S-gene RNases arresting own tubes) execute in styles - outcrossing enforced mid-journey.

  • Saffron is Crocus styles - style product worth more than gold.
Remember
  • Self-incompatibility arrests own pollen tubes inside styles.

Chapter 4 · Topic 56

Stigma

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureH. GynoeciumStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Stigmas are pollen landing pads - wet-sticky (most insect flowers, exudate glues) versus dry-feathery (grasses, huge wind-trapping surface), lobed counts matching carpel numbers (bifid grasses, trifid Crocus). Receptivity windows (mature when anthers shed for selfers, delayed for outcrossers) time fertilisation; incompatible pollen gets rejected at surfaces (sporophytic) or in styles (gametophytic self-incompatibility). Form follows pollination mode precisely.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Wet-sticky (insects) vs dry-feathery (wind) landing surfaces.
  • Lobes count carpels; receptivity times fertilisation.

Solution: Huge dry brush surfaces comb airborne pollen efficiently.

Chapter 4 · Topic 57

Apocarpous

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureH. GynoeciumStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Apocarpous gynoecia keep carpels free (lotus thalamus-top cluster, rose hiplet fruitlets, strawberry achenes on flesh, Michelia) - each carpel ripening its own fruitlet, forming aggregate fruits. Primitive state showing carpel individuality; syncarpy fuses later evolutionarily. Ranunculaceae, Rosaceae, Magnoliaceae showcase apocarpy - aggregate fruits diagnose it at a glance.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Free carpels ripening separate fruitlets (aggregate fruits).
  • Lotus, rose, strawberry demonstrate textbook apocarpy.
Remember
  • Many fruitlets one flower equals apocarpous origin.

Chapter 4 · Topic 58

Syncarpous

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureH. GynoeciumStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Syncarpous gynoecia fuse carpels into compound ovaries (mustard bilocular with replum, tomato multilocular, lily trilocular) - shared styles/stigmas serve all locules, cross-pollination efficiency rises, fruits unify (berries, capsules, drupes). Fusion degree varies (free styles with fused ovaries in Hibiscus); septa may dissolve (free-central Dianthus) or falsely divide (mustard replum). Syncarpy dominates advanced families - fusion is derived, apocarpy ancestral.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fused carpels, compound ovaries, unified fruits.
  • Fusion is evolutionarily derived from free ancestors.

Chapter 4 · Topic 59

Marginal

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureI. PlacentationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Marginal placentation lines ovules along one ridge of a single carpel ovary (pea pod suture) - monocarpellary unilocular standard for legumes. One carpel, one suture, rows of ovules - simplest attachment geometry. Pods split along both sutures at maturity (dehiscent legume) flinging seeds. Marginal plus unicarpellary diagnoses Fabaceae ovaries instantly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Single carpel, ovules on ventral suture (pea).
  • Legume pods split both sutures dispersing seeds.

Chapter 4 · Topic 60

Axile

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureI. PlacentationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Axile placentation radiates ovules from central septa where fused carpel margins meet the axis (China rose, tomato, lemon, cotton) - multilocular compound ovaries with axile columns. Septa count locules; ovules carpet septal faces. Transverse ovary sections show the signature wheel pattern examiners sketch. Syncarpous multilocular ovaries default to axile unless septa dissolve.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fused margins meet centrally; ovules radiate in locules.
  • Wheel-pattern ovary sections diagnose axile.
Remember
  • Tomato, lemon, cotton cross-sections show axile wheels.

Chapter 4 · Topic 61

Parietal

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureI. PlacentationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Parietal placentation pastes ovules on the ovary inner wall (mustard, cucumber, papaya) - unilocular (or falsely bilocular via mustard replum) with peripheral attachment. No central column; walls alone host rows. Mustard replum (false septum between parietal placentae) creates fake bilocular look - the classic syncarpy trap. Cucurbit pepo fruits swell parietal walls into flesh.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Ovules on inner ovary wall; unilocular (replum may fake septa).
  • Mustard replum divides parietal ovary falsely.

Chapter 4 · Topic 62

Free-central

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureI. PlacentationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Free-central placentation mounts ovules on a central column disconnected from walls (Dianthus, Primula) - septa dissolved during development leaving free-standing axis in unilocular ovary. Contrast axile (septa persist) - same central look, different ontogeny (septa lost vs never). Primrose capsules demonstrate textbook free-central columns studded with seeds.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Central column free of walls; septa dissolved away.
  • Dianthus and Primula capsules show free-standing axes.
Remember
  • Axile keeps septa; free-central loses them - development decides.

Chapter 4 · Topic 63

Basal

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureI. PlacentationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Basal placentation seats a single ovule at the ovary floor (sunflower, marigold, wheat - Asteraceae, Poaceae) - unilocular single-ovuled ovaries guaranteeing one seed per flower. Capitulum hundreds of such florets make sunflower heads; spikelets do the same for cereals. Single basal ovules suit wind-pollinated multitudes - minimal investment per bloom, massive bloom counts.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One ovule on ovary floor; one seed per flower.
  • Sunflower heads and cereal spikelets run basal units by hundreds.

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureJ. FruitStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

True fruits ripen from ovary walls alone (mango drupe, pea legume, tomato berry, wheat grain) - pericarp (exo-meso-endocarp) forms flesh, stone or dry coats directly. Ovary position predicts flesh source; locules predict seed counts. True-fruit purity matters in morphology - apple and strawberry fail the test (thalamus flesh), cashew adds hypocotyl swellings. Pericarp layers specialise per dispersal contract.

  • Pericelp layers split flesh, stone and skin duties.
Remember
  • True fruits never include thalamus or receptacle flesh.

False fruit

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureJ. FruitStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

False (accessory) fruits swell accessory parts with or around ovaries: apple and pear (thalamus flesh around core), strawberry (receptacle studded with achenes), cashew (hypocotyl plus nut), pineapple (whole inflorescence plus bracts). Thalamus sugars plus colours recruit dispersers beyond ovary capacity. False-fruit flesh is stem tissue eating like fruit - anatomy versus grocery definitions diverge.

Simple fruit

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureJ. FruitStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Simple fruits come from single ovaries of single flowers - fleshy (berry tomato with many seeds, drupe mango single stone, pome apple) or dry (legume pea splitting, capsule cotton/okra, caryopsis inseparable grain coats, cypsela, samara wings, nut). Pericarp texture (fleshy vs dry) plus dehiscence (splitting vs indehiscent) classifies simply. One ovary, one fruit - however many seeds inside.

  • Berry many-seeded; drupe single-stoned; grain inseparable.

Aggregate fruit

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureJ. FruitStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Aggregate fruits cluster fruitlets from apocarpous (free-carpel) single flowers - raspberry drupelets, strawberry achenes on flesh, lotus nutlets, Michelia follicles. Each carpel ripens independently on shared thalamus. Etaerio naming collects them (etaerio of drupelets, of achenes, of follicles, of berries). Apocarpy visible at flowering predicts aggregation at fruiting - gynoecium reading forecasts harvest.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Many free carpels, one flower - fruitlet clusters.
  • Etaerio terminology collects aggregate types precisely.
Remember
  • Count fruitlets to count original free carpels.

Multiple fruit

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureJ. FruitStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Multiple (composite) fruits fuse whole inflorescences - jackfruit (spadix with fleshy bracts plus perianths), pineapple (spike fused berries plus crown), mulberry (catkin styles), fig syconus (hollow receptacle with internal drupelets). Bracts, perianths and axes join ovaries in the mass. slicing multiples reveals flower boundaries inside flesh - inflorescence architecture preserved in fruit.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Whole inflorescence fused into one mass (jackfruit, pineapple).
  • Bracts plus axes join ovaries - beyond single flowers.

Chapter 4 · Topic 69

Monocot seed

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureK. SeedStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Monocot seeds (maize grain) pack single cotyledon (scutellum) plus endosperm bulk with aleurone protein layer, sheathed plumule (coleoptile) and radicle (coleorhiza), fused pericarp-seed-coat (caryopsis). Endospermic (persistent food) contrasts pea non-endospermic types. Germination pushes coleoptile up, coleorhiza down - sheaths pioneering through soil. Grain structure underlies cereal agriculture.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Single scutellum, endosperm plus aleurone, coleoptile-coleorhiza sheaths.
  • Caryopsis fuses fruit and seed coats inseparably.
Remember
  • Coleoptile up, coleorhiza down - sheathed germination.

Chapter 4 · Topic 70

Dicot seed

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureK. SeedStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dicot seeds (pea, bean) carry two fleshy cotyledons (food-storing, non-endospermic - endosperm consumed) or thin plus persistent endosperm (castor albuminous), with plumule-radicle axis between, all inside testa-tegmen coats with hilum-micropyle scars. Germination lifts cotyledons (epigeal beans) or leaves them buried (hypogeal peas). Cotyledon number plus food location classifies seeds instantly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Two cotyledons; food in cotyledons or persistent endosperm.
  • Epigeal lifts cotyledons; hypogeal leaves them buried.

Chapter 4 · Topic 71

Seed coat

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureK. SeedStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Seed coats (testa outer protective, tegmen inner thin) armour embryos - hard (coconut, beans), papery, winged (Moringa), hairy (cotton lint, Calotropis floss), waterproof (lotus centuries-viable). Hilum scars stalk attachment; micropyle pores admit water and air for germination. Coat-imposed dormancy breaks by scarification (scratching), stratification (chilling) or fire - seed banks exploit coat longevity.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Testa armour plus tegmen lining; hilum scar plus micropyle pore.
  • Coat dormancy breaks by scratch, chill or fire cues.
Remember
  • Cotton lint is seed-coat hair - textile from testa.

Endosperm

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureK. SeedStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Endosperm (triploid, double-fertilisation product) feeds embryos - persistent albuminous (cereals starchy, coconut liquid-plus-solid, castor oily) versus consumed non-endospermic (pea, bean cotyledons take over). Ruminant perisperm (nucellus remnants: beet, pepper) supplements in some. Mosaic endosperm (maize variegation) visualises allele segregation - genetics visible in grains. Food reserves decide seedling independence duration.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Triploid double-fusion food; persistent or consumed by cotyledons.
  • Perisperm (nucellus leftover) supplements in beet-pepper.

Chapter 4 · Topic 73

Embryo

Morphology of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureK. SeedStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Embryos are baby plants in waiting - plumule (shoot tip with leaf primordia), radicle (root tip with cap), cotyledon(s) (food/leaf intermediates), hypocotyl-root axis connecting. Dicot embryos fold two cotyledons laterally; monocot embryos orient scutellum sideways. Polyembryony (citrus adventive embryos) clones mothers via seeds; apomictic embryos skip fertilisation. Embryo axis polarity (shoot up, root down) pre-patterns germination.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Plumule up, radicle down, cotyledons feed - preformed plant.
  • Polyembryony clones mothers; apomixis skips fertilisation.
Remember
  • Tigellum axis (hypocotyl-epicotyl) spans root-shoot junction.

Fabaceae (pea family) runs papilionaceous zygomorphic blooms: vexillary aestivation (standard-wings-keel), diadelphous 9+1 stamens, monocarpellary superior ovary with marginal placentation, legume pods; leaves pinnate with tendrils/stipules; roots nodulate Rhizobium. Pulses (gram, pea, bean), oils (soybean, groundnut), timber (sheesham), dyes (indigo), fibres (sunnhemp) - protein plus nitrogen-fixation family feeding humanity sustainably.

Deep Dive · Inside the plant body

Anatomy reads sections like maps: meristems (apical length, lateral girth) build; simple tissues (parenchyma versatile, collenchyma stretchable, sclerenchyma rigid) bulk; complex tissues (xylem water-team, phloem food-team) pipe; systems (epidermal skin, ground bulk, vascular strands) organise; organs (exarch radial roots, ringed open dicot stems, scattered closed monocot stems, dorsiventral vs isobilateral leaves) assemble; secondary growth (cambium rings, annual records, heartwood-sapwood, bark) archives years. Section patterns diagnose organs and groups instantly.

Chapter 5 · Topic 1

Meristematic tissue

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. Plant TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Meristematic tissues are perpetually young dividing zones - dense protoplasm, no vacuoles, thin walls, prominent nuclei - located at tips (apical), bases (intercalary) and cylinders (lateral). They supply all new cells; their position decides growth direction (length vs girth). Dormancy plus hormones gate their activity seasonally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dense, vacuole-free dividing cells at tips, bases and cylinders.
  • Position decides length growth versus girth growth.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Meristematic cells lack

Solution: Dense protoplasm without storage vacuoles marks dividing cells.

Chapter 5 · Topic 2

Apical meristem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. Plant TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Apical meristems cap root and shoot tips (plus leaf primordia) - root apical protected by root caps with quiescent centres, shoot apical dome sheltered by leaf primordia. They drive primary (length) growth plus organ initiation (leaves, flowers). Auxin from apices suppresses laterals (apical dominance); decapitation releases branching. All length growth traces to apical activity.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Root plus shoot tips drive primary length growth.
  • Apical auxin suppresses lateral buds (dominance).
Remember
  • Quiescent centre resists damage - meristem insurance policy.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Tip-made auxin flowing down inhibits axillary bud outgrowth.

Chapter 5 · Topic 3

Intercalary meristem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. Plant TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Intercalary meristems sit above nodes at leaf bases and grass internodes - regrowing grazed blades and sprinting bamboo (metres daily). Grasses survive grazing because growth zones sit low, not at eaten tips. Dwarf mutants (gibberellin-deficient) plus lodging cereals both involve intercalary activity - the meristem behind lawn mowing tolerance and bamboo records.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Nodal-base meristems regrow grazed grasses and bamboo.
  • Low growth zones survive grazing that destroys tips.

1

Grass leaves regrow after grazing because growth occurs at

Solution: Low intercalary zones push blades up after tip loss.
