Chapter 5 · Topic 4

Lateral meristem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. Plant TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Lateral meristems (vascular cambium plus cork cambium) wrap stems and roots as cylinders adding girth - secondary growth into wood and bark. Fascicular (within bundles) plus interfascicular (between) cambium unite into rings in dicots; monocots lack them (no true wood). Cork cambium (phellogen) makes protective periderm outward, cutting off old cortex. Girth growth heals wounds and thickens trunks yearly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cylindrical side meristems add wood (inside) and bark (outside).
  • Dicots have them; monocots lack them (no true wood).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Vascular cambium produces

Solution: Bidirectional division builds wood inward and bast outward.

Chapter 5 · Topic 5

Permanent tissues

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureA. Plant TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Permanent tissues are matured, specialised, mostly non-dividing cells differentiated from meristems - simple (one cell type: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) or complex (multiple types: xylem, phloem). Differentiation may reverse (dedifferentiation to cork cambium, wound callus) then redifferentiate - plasticity exploited in grafting and tissue culture. Function follows wall and content specialisation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Mature specialised non-dividing cells from meristems.
  • Simple (one type) vs complex (many types cooperating).
Remember
  • Dedifferentiation (cork cambium) proves plant plasticity.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Permanent tissues arise by

Solution: Maturation plus specialisation converts dividing cells to working tissues.

Chapter 5 · Topic 6

Parenchyma

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. Simple Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Parenchyma (thin-walled living packing tissue) fills cortex, pith, mesophyll and flesh - storing starch/water, photosynthesizing (chlorenchyma), floating (aerenchyma with air spaces), secreting. Intercellular spaces connect via plasmodesmata; totipotent parenchyma regenerates whole plants in tissue culture and heals wounds (callus). Most versatile plant tissue - default filler with endless side jobs.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Thin living packing cells: store, photosynthesise, float, heal.
  • Totipotent - tissue culture grows plants from parenchyma.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Aerenchyma (air-space parenchyma) occurs in

Solution: Air channels float water plants and aerate submerged parts.

Chapter 5 · Topic 7

Collenchyma

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. Simple Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Collenchyma (living, unevenly thickened corners - cellulose plus pectin, no lignin) braces growing organs - young stems, petioles, leaf margins - supporting while permitting elongation. Thickening concentrates at corners (angular), plates (lamellar) or spaces (lacunar). Dicot stems show collenchyma ridges; monocots skip it (sclerenchyma instead). Living support for growing parts that lignified dead tissue cannot serve.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living corner-thickened support for growing organs.
  • Pectin-cellulose (stretchable) versus lignin (rigid).
Remember
  • Celery strings are collenchyma strands - chewable support.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Collenchyma differs from sclerenchyma in being

Solution: Living stretchable support suits elongating young organs.

Chapter 5 · Topic 8

Sclerenchyma

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureB. Simple Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sclerenchyma (dead, uniformly lignified thick walls) is plant concrete - fibres (long: jute, flax, hemp textiles; xylem fibres) plus sclereids (stone cells: pear grit, coconut shell, seed coats). Pits (not plasmodesmata) dot walls. Strength without metabolism - dead at functional maturity, persistently strong. Coir, hemp and flax economies run on sclerenchyma fibres.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dead lignified strength tissue: fibres plus stone cells.
  • Pear grit and coconut shells are sclereid clusters.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Pear fruit grit consists of

Solution: Lignified stone-cell clusters crunch in pear flesh.

Chapter 5 · Topic 9

Xylem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Xylem (complex water-conducting tissue) combines tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma - dead conducting plus living storage. Transports water-minerals root-to-shoot via transpiration pull (cohesion-tension), supports mechanically (wood), stores starch. Heartwood (dead, durable, dark) versus sapwood (living outer, conducting) split old stems. Primary (procambium) versus secondary (cambium) origins layer wood history.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Water-mineral highway plus wood support plus starch store.
  • Heartwood dead-durable; sapwood living-conducting.
Xylem team

TracheidsNarrow, tapered, all vascular plants
VesselsWide tubes, angiosperms (plus Gnetum)
FibresStrength
ParenchymaLiving storage

Solution: Dead tracheids and vessels pipe soil water to leaves.

Chapter 5 · Topic 10

Tracheids

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Tracheids are narrow tapered dead cells with bordered pits - overlapping end-to-end (not open tubes), conducting slower but safer (air bubbles block single cells, not columns). All vascular plants use them; ferns and gymnosperms use only them. Pit membranes filter bubbles; torus thickenings seal pits under stress. Safe but slow - vessel evolution traded safety for speed.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Narrow overlapping dead cells with bordered pits.
  • Universal in vascular plants; sole conductors in ferns/gymnosperms.
Remember
  • Pits filter embolisms - tracheid safety design.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Tracheids differ from vessels in

Solution: Tapered overlap with pits replaces open vessel tubes.

Chapter 5 · Topic 11

Vessels

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Vessels are wide open pipelines - stacked dead cells with perforated end walls (dissolved partitions) forming continuous tubes, conducting fast high volumes. Angiosperm (plus Gnetum) innovation enabling rapid growth and big leaves; spring wide vessels plus autumn narrow ones record annual rings. Cavitation risk (air breaks columns) counters speed - drought and frost embolise vessels while tracheids persist.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Open-tube stacked cells for fast bulk water flow.
  • Angiosperm (plus Gnetum) innovation; spring/autumn sizes ring years.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Vessels occur in xylem of

Solution: Open pipelines evolved in flowering plants (plus gnetophytes convergently).

Fig: End walls dissolve between stacked cells forming continuous tubes.

Chapter 5 · Topic 12

Xylem fibres

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Xylem fibres (libriform plus fibre-tracheids) are long lignified dead cells reinforcing wood - timber strength, paper pulp, textile fibres (flax, hemp, jute are extra-xylary phloem/bast fibres, distinct). Shorter than phloem fibres; pitted walls. Wood density and paper quality follow fibre dimensions - forestry selects fibre traits deliberately.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lignified dead strength cells reinforcing wood.
  • Timber, paper and textile strength source.
Remember
  • Jute/hemp are bast (phloem) fibres, not xylem fibres.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Commercial jute fibres are anatomically

Solution: Bast fibres from secondary phloem strip into jute.

Chapter 5 · Topic 13

Xylem parenchyma

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Xylem parenchyma (living thin-walled cells among dead conductors) stores starch and oils, transfers water sideways (ray parenchyma radial shuttles), assists conduction loading, and heals wounds (tyloses balloon into damaged vessels sealing them). Wood rays (radial parenchyma ribbons) store plus transport horizontally - visible grain figures. Living helpers inside dead plumbing.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living storage plus lateral transfer among dead tubes.
  • Rays shuttle horizontally; tyloses plug damaged vessels.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Tyloses plugging injured vessels are outgrowths of

Solution: Neighbouring parenchyma balloons seal embolised vessels.

Chapter 5 · Topic 14

Phloem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phloem (complex food-conducting tissue) runs sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma - living translocation of sugars (source leaves to sink roots/fruits/seeds) by pressure-flow (loading/unloading osmotic gradients). Bidirectional (unlike xylem one-way), seasonal direction shifts (spring up, autumn down to storage). Girdling (bark removal) starves roots proving phloem transport - classic experiment.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living sugar highways, bidirectional, pressure-flow driven.
  • Girdling starves roots - phloem location proof.

Sieve tubesEnucleate conducting cells

Chapter 5 · Topic 15

Sieve tubes

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sieve tube elements are enucleate living conduits stacked end-to-end through sieve plates (perforated walls) - cytoplasm strands stream sugars; P-protein seals wounds. No nucleus or vacuole (companion cells govern); callose plugs plates seasonally (dormancy) and permanently with age. Angiosperm sieve tubes plus companions replace gymnosperm sieve cells plus albuminous cells - partnered evolution.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Enucleate stacked tubes with sieve-plate pores.
  • Companion cells govern each sieve element.
Remember
  • Callose plugs plates in dormancy and old age.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Sieve tube elements lack

Solution: Enucleate conduits depend on adjacent companion-cell nuclei.

Chapter 5 · Topic 16

Companion cells

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Companion cells (nucleated parenchyma sisters of sieve elements, shared mother cell) run phloem metabolism - loading sugars (active transport), signalling, protein supply, wound responses. Dense cytoplasm, many mitochondria fuel loading pumps. Each sieve element pairs its companion for life; death of one kills both. Specialised transfer cells (wall ingrowths) boost loading in some species.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Nucleated life-support partners of enucleate sieve tubes.
  • Loading pumps plus signalling run through companions.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Companion cells are associated with

Solution: Sister-cell partners govern each sieve conduit.

Chapter 5 · Topic 17

Phloem fibres

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phloem (bast) fibres (long lignified dead cells: jute, hemp, flax, ramie) are commercial textiles - longer and softer than xylem fibres, retted (microbial separation) from stems. Primary phloem fibres (protophloem) versus secondary (cambium-made); hemp/flax economies clothe humanity. Ramie (China grass) resists rot for ropes and nets - fibre properties match uses.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Long bast fibres for textiles, ropes and nets.
  • Retting microbes free fibres from stems.
Remember
  • Bast = phloem fibres; xylem fibres differ botanically.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Jute and hemp commercial fibres are

Solution: Secondary-phloem bast strips into textile fibres.

Chapter 5 · Topic 18

Phloem parenchyma

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureC. Complex Permanent TissuesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phloem parenchyma (living thin-walled cells among sieve elements) stores starch, tannins and resins, transfers laterally, and (unlike xylem rays) rarely forms extensive ray systems - scattered helpers. In monocots it may be absent (sieve tubes plus companions suffice). Wound callus and defensive compounds mobilise through parenchyma networks.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living storage plus lateral transfer among sieve elements.
  • Often reduced in monocot phloem.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Phloem parenchyma functions mainly in

Solution: Living helpers store reserves and shuttle sideways.

Chapter 5 · Topic 19

Epidermal tissue system

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureD. Tissue SystemsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Epidermal tissue system (epidermis plus stomata, trichomes, root hairs) skins plants - single parenchyma layer with cuticle waterproofing (thick in xerophytes), stomatal pores with guard cells gating gas exchange, trichomes (hairs/scales deterring herbivores, reflecting light), root hairs absorbing (tubular extensions). Multiple epidermis (banyan, oleander) plus bulliform motor cells (grass rolling) specialise further. First defence plus exchange gate in one layer.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Single skin layer with cuticle, stomata, hairs.
  • Guards gases, blocks germs, absorbs (root hairs).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Root hairs are extensions of

Solution: Tubular epidermal outgrowths multiply absorption area.

Chapter 5 · Topic 20

Ground tissue system

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureD. Tissue SystemsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Ground tissue system (everything between epidermis and vascular strands - cortex, pith, mesophyll, medullary rays) does bulk living work: parenchyma photosynthesis/storage, collenchyma support, sclerenchyma bracing. Cortex stores plus transports radially; pith centres stems; mesophyll specialises leaves. Most plant volume is ground tissue - vascular strands are minority highways through parenchyma countryside.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Bulk living tissue between skin and plumbing.
  • Cortex, pith, mesophyll - storage plus photosynthesis mass.
Remember
  • Most plant volume is ground parenchyma, not vessels.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Ground tissue mainly consists of

Solution: Living packing tissue fills bulk plant volume.

Chapter 5 · Topic 21

Vascular tissue system

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureD. Tissue SystemsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Vascular tissue system (xylem plus phloem in bundles) pipes water up and food around: radial bundles (roots - alternating xylem-phloem poles), conjoint (stems - joint bundles: collateral open with cambium in dicots/gymnosperms, closed without in monocots; bicollateral with phloem both sides in Cucurbita), concentric (amphivasal/amphicribral in ferns). Bundle architecture diagnoses organs and groups instantly in sections.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Xylem-plus-phloem bundles in organ-specific patterns.
  • Radial (roots), conjoint open/closed (stems) patterns.

Chapter 5 · Topic 22

Dicot root

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dicot root anatomy (mango, pea): epiblema with root hairs, parenchymatous cortex, Casparian-strip endodermis, pericycle branching laterals, 2-6-arch radial xylem (tetrarch common) with phloem between, small or absent pith. Protophloem/metaxylem maturation (exarch: protoxylem outward) marks roots versus stems (endarch). Secondary growth later adds cambium wood - taproots thicken into storage.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Epiblema-cortex-endodermis-pericycle-radial bundles-small pith.
  • Exarch xylem (protoxylem outward) diagnoses roots.
Remember
  • Exarch = roots; endarch = stems - maturation direction flips.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Exarch xylem (protoxylem outward) occurs in

Solution: Root maturation runs outside-in, opposite of stems.

Chapter 5 · Topic 23

Monocot root

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Monocot root anatomy (wheat, onion): same epiblema-cortex-endodermis-pericycle plan but polyarch xylem (many arches, 8+) with large central pith - wide stele for fibrous clusters. No secondary growth (no cambium) - roots stay slender, branching profusely instead. Velamen (orchid aerial-root sponge) plus contractile roots (pulling bulbs deeper) specialise further. Pith plus polyarchy instantly separate monocot root sections.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Polyarch xylem plus large pith; no cambium, no thickening.
  • Velamen sponges orchid aerial roots.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Monocot roots show xylem as

Solution: Many xylem poles ring large central pith.

Chapter 5 · Topic 24

Epidermis

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Root epidermis (epiblema/piliferous layer) is thin-walled, cuticle-free (absorption needs permeability) with tubular root hairs extending surface hundreds-fold. Hairs live days, replaced continuously behind growing tips; mycorrhizal fungi extend reach further. No stomata, no trichomes - absorption-only skin. Damage (transplant shock) wilts plants until hairs regrow - handling roots gently matters agriculturally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cuticle-free absorptive skin with tubular hairs.
  • Hairs are temporary; mycorrhiza extends permanent reach.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Root hairs absorb water because epidermis here lacks

Solution: Cuticle-free thin walls let water enter freely.

Chapter 5 · Topic 25

Cortex

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Root cortex (parenchyma layers between epidermis and endodermis) stores starch, transports water radially (apoplast through walls plus symplast through plasmodesmata), and houses mycorrhizal arbuscules plus (in legumes) nodule bacteria. Exodermis (suberised outer cortex in older roots) and passage cells regulate flow. Cortex thickness reflects storage role - fleshy roots expand it massively.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Parenchyma storage plus radial transport zone.
  • Mycorrhiza and nodules colonise cortical cells.
Remember
  • Cortex is the root warehouse and transit hall combined.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Mycorrhizal fungi colonise mainly the

Solution: Arbuscules branch inside cortical cells trading phosphorus for sugars.

Chapter 5 · Topic 26

Endodermis

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Endodermis (single barrel-cell layer with Casparian strips - suberin bands blocking wall flow) forces all water and ions through selective plasma membranes into the stele - the root quality checkpoint. Passage cells (thin-walled, opposite protoxylem) admit flow; suberised cells block back-leak. Endodermis with Casparian strips is THE most-tested anatomy fact - selective gate between cortex freedom and stele control.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Casparian suberin bands force membrane-controlled entry.
  • Root checkpoint deciding what reaches xylem.

Chapter 5 · Topic 27

Pericycle

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pericycle (parenchyma layer just inside endodermis) branches lateral roots endogenously (pushing outward) and contributes vascular cambium plus cork cambium during secondary growth - root meristem reserve. Thick-walled in monocots (supporting fibrous clusters), thin in dicots (branching freely). Pericycle activity plus cambium formation thicken taproots into storage organs.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lateral-root birthplace plus cambium contributor.
  • Endogenous branching bursts from pericycle outward.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Lateral roots arise from the

Solution: Deep pericycle origins push outward through cortex layers.

Chapter 5 · Topic 28

Vascular bundles

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Root vascular bundles are radial - xylem and phloem alternate on different radii (diarch to polyarch by group), connected by conjunctive parenchyma that later forms cambium arcs. Protoxylem faces outward (exarch); metaxylem centres. Arch count diagnoses groups (diarch pea, tetrarch mustard, polyarch monocots). Radial alternation plus exarch maturation is the root-section signature.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Alternate radial poles (not joint bundles).
  • Arch counts diagnose: di-, tetra-, polyarch patterns.
Remember
  • Radial plus exarch equals root - conjoint plus endarch equals stem.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem occur in

Solution: Alternate poles maturing outward mark root sections.

Chapter 5 · Topic 29

Pith

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureE. Anatomy of RootStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pith (central parenchyma, medulla) stores starch and water in stems and monocot roots - large in maize, sunflower and monocot roots; reduced or absent in dicot roots (woody centre instead). Pith rays (medullary rays) shuttle horizontally between xylem and phloem. Pith economy (hollow bamboo, solid maize) tunes stem weight versus storage - grasses hollow for light-speed growth.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Central storage parenchyma; large in monocots, tiny in dicot roots.
  • Rays shuttle radially; hollowing lightens grass stems.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Large well-developed pith occurs in roots of

Solution: Monocot polyarch centres fill with storage pith.

Chapter 5 · Topic 30

Dicot stem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureF. Anatomy of StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dicot stem anatomy (sunflower): epidermis with cuticle plus trichomes, hypodermal collenchyma, cortical parenchyma (plus resin/oil ducts), starch-sheath endodermis, pericycle sclerenchyma caps, ringed conjoint open bundles (xylem inside, phloem outside, cambium between), central pith with rays. Ring arrangement plus cambium enables secondary growth - the woody future built into primary layout.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Epidermis-collenchyma-cortex-ringed open bundles-pith plan.
  • Ring plus cambium prefigures wood and bark.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Conjoint open bundles in a ring occur in stems of

Solution: Ringed open bundles with cambium mark dicot stems.

Chapter 5 · Topic 31

Monocot stem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureF. Anatomy of StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Monocot stem anatomy (maize, bamboo): epidermis with cuticle, sclerenchymatous hypodermis (strength without collenchyma), scattered conjoint closed bundles (no cambium) denser peripherally, ground parenchyma throughout (no cortex-pith distinction), hollow or solid centres. No secondary growth - size fixed at primary growth; palms bulk via diffuse thickening instead. Scattered closed bundles diagnose monocot sections instantly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Scattered closed bundles in ground parenchyma; no ring, no cambium.
  • Sclerenchyma hypodermis replaces collenchyma support.
Remember
  • Scattered bundles scream monocot; rings scream dicot.

1

Scattered conjoint closed bundles occur in stems of

Solution: No ring, no cambium, no pith-cortex split - monocot plan.

Chapter 5 · Topic 32

Vascular bundles

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureF. Anatomy of StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Stem bundles are conjoint (xylem plus phloem together): collateral (phloem outside, xylem inside - standard), bicollateral (phloem outside AND inside xylem - Cucurbita, Solanum), open (cambium between - dicots/gymnosperms) versus closed (none - monocots). Endarch maturation (protoxylem inward) marks stems opposite roots. Bundle caps (sclerenchyma pericycle) armour dicot rings.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Joint xylem-phloem bundles; open/closed decides wood future.
  • Endarch maturation (protoxylem inward) marks stems.

Chapter 5 · Topic 33

Cambium

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureF. Anatomy of StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cambium (lateral meristem) adds girth: vascular cambium (fascicular within bundles plus interfascicular between, uniting into rings) makes secondary xylem inside plus phloem outside; cork cambium (phellogen) makes periderm bark outside. Seasonal activity rings years (spring wide, autumn narrow); dormancy winters temperate trees. Grafting aligns cambia - cambium-to-cambium contact heals unions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Ring meristems build wood inside, bark outside, yearly.
  • Graft success needs cambium-to-cambium contact.
Remember
  • Fascicular plus interfascicular unite into complete cambium rings.

Intrafascicular cambium originates from

Solution: Bundle procambium persists as fascicular cambium strips.

Chapter 5 · Topic 34

Ground tissue

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureF. Anatomy of StemStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Stem ground tissue (cortex plus pith plus rays in dicots; uniform parenchyma in monocots) stores starch, photosynthesises (chlorenchyma), aerates (aerenchyma aquatics) and transports radially via rays. Cortical collenchyma braces young dicot stems; sclerenchyma hypodermis braces monocots. Ground bulk dwarfs vascular strands volumetrically - stems are parenchyma buildings with plumbing installed.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cortex-pith-ray bulk doing storage plus photosynthesis.
  • Dicots zone it; monocots uniform it.

Stem ground tissue mainly consists of

Solution: Living packing bulk fills most stem volume.

Chapter 5 · Topic 35

Dicot leaf

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureG. Anatomy of LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dicot (dorsiventral) leaf anatomy: upper palisade mesophyll (columnar, chloroplast-packed, photosynthesis maximised) plus lower spongy (air spaces for gas diffusion), stomata mainly below (fewer above), midrib bundle with xylem above-phloem below, bundle-sheath extensions, bulliform-free flat blade. Upper-lower asymmetry matches light direction - palisade sun-captures, spongy air-circulates.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Palisade above, spongy below, stomata below - dorsiventral plan.
  • Asymmetry follows light direction precisely.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Palisade mesophyll is positioned toward the

Solution: Columnar sun-capturing cells face incoming light.

Chapter 5 · Topic 36

Monocot leaf

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureG. Anatomy of LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Monocot (isobilateral) leaf anatomy: uniform mesophyll (no palisade-spongy split), stomata both surfaces equally, parallel bundles with bundle-sheath sclerenchyma, bulliform motor cells rolling blades in drought (grass folding). Both sides photosynthesise - vertical/erect blades use light bilaterally. Kranz anatomy (C4 bundle-sheath wreaths) specialises further in maize-sugarcane.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Uniform mesophyll, stomata both sides, parallel bundles.
  • Bulliform cells roll blades against drought.
Remember
  • Isobilateral = both sides equal; dorsiventral = upper-lower split.

Mesophyll

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureG. Anatomy of LeafStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mesophyll is leaf photosynthetic tissue between epidermises: palisade (columnar, perpendicular, chloroplast-dense - light capture) plus spongy (irregular, air-spaced - gas diffusion) in dicots; uniform in monocots; Kranz wreath (bundle-sheath plus mesophyll rings) in C4 plants. Chloroplast arrangement (epistrophe wall appression) plus movement (light avoidance) optimises capture versus damage. Mesophyll does the fixing; epidermis guards; veins supply.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Palisade captures, spongy diffuses, Kranz supercharges C4.
  • Chloroplasts reposition with light intensity.

Stomata

Topic in Depth

Stomata are guard-cell gates (kidney-shaped dicot pair with uneven walls, dumbbell grasses) opening by turgor (K+ influx, malate) and closing by ABA in drought - balancing CO2 entry against water loss. Types: anomocytic (ranunculus, irregular), anisocytic (crucifers, 3 unequal), paracytic (parallel), diacytic (crossed) - subsidiary-cell patterns diagnosing families. Transpiration pull depends on stomatal aperture; closed stomata halt photosynthesis.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Guard-cell turgor opens; ABA drought closes.
  • Subsidiary patterns (anomocytic etc.) diagnose families.

Topic in Depth

Leaf vascular bundles (midrib plus veins) run xylem above-phloem below in a collateral closed plan, sheathed (bundle-sheath parenchyma, sometimes sclerenchyma extensions to epidermis). Midrib dominates (support plus supply); veinlets end freely (open endings visible in cleared leaves). Reticulate dicot nets versus parallel monocot lines branch the same plan differently. Bundle density tracks photosynthetic rate.

  • Vein density matches photosynthetic demand.
Remember

Topic in Depth

Vascular cambium (fascicular within bundles plus interfascicular between, uniting into complete rings) divides bidirectionally - secondary xylem (wood) inside, secondary phloem (bast) outside - thickening dicot and gymnosperm axes yearly. Fusiform initials make conducting cells; ray initials make rays. Seasonal activity (spring wide thin-walled, autumn narrow thick-walled) records annual rings. Grafting aligns cambia for union.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Ring meristem building wood inside, bast outside.
  • Fusiform initials conduct; ray initials shuttle.

Cork cambium (phellogen, arising in cortex or pericycle) builds periderm bark - phellem cork outward (suberised dead cells, waterproof), phelloderm inside, replacing stretched epidermis. Lenticels (loose complementary cells) ventilate through bark. Wound periderm seals injuries; commercial cork (Quercus suber) harvests phellem sustainably. Bark armour plus breathing pores in one meristem.

  • Phellogen makes cork outside, phelloderm inside.
  • Lenticels ventilate bark; cork harvests sustainably.
Remember

Topic in Depth

Secondary xylem (wood) accumulates yearly inside cambium - spring (earlywood wide thin vessels, fast growth) plus autumn (latewood narrow thick, slow) recording rings; porous (ring/diffuse) versus non-porous (tracheids only) woods. Tyloses, resins and tannins age inner wood into durable heartwood. Timber, paper and fuel all harvest secondary xylem - forestry manages cambium output.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Yearly wood inside cambium; spring wide, autumn narrow.
  • Porous hardwoods versus non-porous softwoods.

Secondary phloem

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureH. Secondary GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Secondary phloem (bast outside cambium) translocates sugars in aging stems - sieve tubes crush into non-conducting outer layers yearly (only newest ring functions), while bast fibres (jute, hemp) persist as textiles. Bark includes secondary phloem plus periderm. Girdling removes phloem (roots starve, stem swells above) - transport proof and horticultural technique (air-layering roots girdled branches).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Newest ring conducts; older crushes; fibres persist as textiles.
  • Girdling starves roots - phloem location proof.
Remember

Annual rings

Anatomy of Flowering PlantsPlant StructureH. Secondary GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Annual (growth) rings count years - one spring-plus-autumn wood couplet per growing season (temperate), readable in stumps and cores for age plus climate history (dendrochronology: wide rings wet years, narrow droughts). Tropical evergreens ring faintly (weak seasons); false rings (drought breaks) and missing rings complicate counts. Archaeology dates timber; ecology reconstructs monsoons - wood archives weather.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One spring-autumn couplet per year in temperate wood.
  • Dendrochronology reads climate from ring widths.

Heartwood

Topic in Depth

Heartwood (central old wood) is dead, dark, durable - tannins, resins and oils impregnate vessels (tyloses plug them), resisting rot and termites (teak, sheesham, deodar value). Non-conducting (water runs in outer sapwood), mechanically supreme - timber of choice. Heartwood formation recycles nutrients inward-out (nitrogen, phosphorus salvaged to sapwood) - dying centre feeds living edge.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dead dark durable core; tannins plus tyloses preserve.
  • Teak-sheesham value is heartwood chemistry.
Remember
  • Heartwood no longer conducts - sapwood carries water.

Sapwood

Topic in Depth

Sapwood (outer living wood, alburnum) conducts water-minerals (functional xylem), stores starch (ray parenchyma), and defends actively - lighter, softer, perishable versus heartwood. Sapwood width reflects vigour (wide in fast growers); conversion to heartwood recycles nutrients inward. Timber uses sapwood where toughness matters less; carpenters avoid its perishability for outdoor work.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living outer wood conducting plus storing.
  • Wide sapwood signals vigorous growth.

Bark

Topic in Depth

Bark (everything outside vascular cambium - secondary phloem plus periderm) protects (cork insulation, tannin chemistry), transports sugars (young phloem), breathes (lenticels) and heals (wound periderm). Patterns (smooth birch peeling, fissured oak, papery Melaleuca) identify trees; rhytidome (dead outer layers) sheds. Commercial bark yields cork, quinine (cinchona), cinnamon spice and tannins - protection plus products.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Secondary phloem plus periderm outside cambium.
  • Lenticels breathe; tannins defend; patterns identify.

Cell: The Unit of Life

Cell theory, prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, organelles and plant specialities.

Cell: The Unit of LifeCell and BiomoleculesChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

A. Cell Theory
1. Cell theory2. Scientists associated with cell theory3. Exceptions/limitations
B. Prokaryotic Cell
4. Cell envelope5. Capsule6. Cell wall7. Plasma membrane8. Mesosome9. Ribosomes10. Nucleoid11. Flagella12. Pili
C. Eukaryotic Cell
13. Plasma membrane14. Cell wall15. Cytoplasm16. Nucleus17. Cell organelles

18. Endoplasmic reticulum19. Ribosomes20. Golgi apparatus21. Lysosomes22. Vacuoles23. Mitochondria24. Plastids25. Peroxisomes26. Centrosome

27. Cell wall28. Middle lamella29. Plasmodesmata30. Plastids31. Large central vacuole

Deep Dive · Cells inside out

Cell biology scales organisation: theory (all organisms of cells, new cells from old) frames; prokaryotes (envelope layers, mesosomes, 70S ribosomes, naked nucleoid, flagella-pili) show minimal sufficiency; eukaryotes add membranes around genome (nucleus with pores) and work (organelles); each organelle specialises (ER builds, Golgi ships, lysosomes digest, mitochondria and plastids power via endosymbiotic pasts); plant extras (walls with lamella-plasmodesmata, plastid family, giant vacuole) customise for photosynthesis and turgor. Size (mycoplasma smallest), number and division tie chapters together.
NEET facts:
  • 70S ribosomes mark prokaryotes, mitochondria and plastids; 80S marks eukaryotic cytosol.
  • Lysosomes (suicidal bags), nucleolus (rRNA factory), plasmodesmata (plant cell links) are one-line favourites.
Fig: Naked nucleoid versus membrane-bound nucleus plus organelles - life deepest divide.

Chapter 6 · Topic 1

Cell theory

Cell: The Unit of LifeCell and BiomoleculesA. Cell TheoryStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cell theory (Schleiden 1838 plants, Schwann 1839 animals) states all living things are made of cells and cell products, with Virchow 1855 adding omnis cellulae e cellula - new cells only from pre-existing cells. It unified biology: growth (cell division), heredity (chromosome continuity), disease (cellular pathology, Virchow) all became cell stories. Modern cell biology extends it molecularly without breaking its frame.
NEET Snapshot:
  • All organisms of cells; new cells from old cells.
  • Growth, heredity and disease all reduce to cell events.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Omnis cellulae e cellula (new cells from pre-existing cells) was stated by

Solution: Virchow completed cell theory with cell lineage in 1855.

Fig: All organisms of cells, new cells from old, cells as life units.

Chapter 6 · Topic 2

Scientists associated with cell theory

Cell: The Unit of LifeCell and BiomoleculesA. Cell TheoryStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cell science pioneers: Hooke (1665 cork cells, coined cell), Leeuwenhoek (living bacteria, sperms - first microscopes), Brown (nucleus 1831), Schleiden-Schwann (theory 1838-39), Virchow (lineage 1855), Flemming (mitosis, chromatin naming), Golgi (apparatus), de Duve (lysosomes), Palade (ribosomes, ER). Each tool advance (light to electron microscopy) revealed new organelles - seeing preceded understanding every time.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hooke named, Leeuwenhoek saw living, Brown found nucleus.
  • Flemming (mitosis), Golgi, de Duve, Palade mapped organelles.

Chapter 6 · Topic 3

Exceptions/limitations

Cell: The Unit of LifeCell and BiomoleculesA. Cell TheoryStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cell theory exceptions test its edges: viruses (acellular, no metabolism outside hosts), syncytia and coenocytes (multinucleate single masses - Rhizopus hyphae, skeletal muscle fibres), sieve-tube elements (living but enucleate), mammalian RBCs (anucleate), plus mitochondrial-plastid semi-autonomy (own DNA, double membranes - endosymbiotic guests). Theory bends (units vary) without breaking (cells remain life units) - refinements, not refutations.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Viruses acellular; syncytia multinucleate; RBCs anucleate.
  • Exceptions refine the theory; cells stay life units.
Remember
  • Mitochondria and plastids are former bacteria turned organelles.

Solution: Acellular infectious parcels sit outside cell-theory universality.

Cell envelope

Topic in Depth

Bacterial cell envelope layers three deep: outer capsule/slime (protection, virulence, attachment), middle wall (peptidoglycan shape plus rigidity - Gram-positive thick, Gram-negative thin plus outer membrane), inner plasma membrane (selective transport, respiration enzymes since no mitochondria). Gram staining sorts walls (purple thick vs pink thin) deciding antibiotics. Envelope defends, shapes and feeds simultaneously.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Capsule outside, wall middle, membrane inside - triple armour.
  • Gram sorts wall thickness; antibiotics follow the sort.

Capsules (tight gummy coats) and slime layers (loose) shield bacteria from desiccation, phagocytes and antibiotics - virulence factor in pathogens (pneumococcus capsules defeat immunity; vaccines target them). Sticky capsules build biofilms (dental plaque, catheter slime) resisting treatment collectively. Capsule staining (negative halos) diagnoses virulent strains.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Biofilms are capsule-sharing bacterial cities.

Cell wall

Topic in Depth

Bacterial walls (peptidoglycan mesh: sugars plus amino-acid crosslinks) shape cells (rods, spheres, spirals), resist osmotic bursting, and anchor flagella plus capsules. Gram-positive thick single-layered versus Gram-negative thin plus lipopolysaccharide outer membrane (endotoxin fever source). Penicillin and lysozyme attack wall synthesis/lysis - selective killers sparing wall-less human cells. Wall-less Mycoplasma proves walls optional for life.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Peptidoglycan shape plus burst-proofing; Gram sorts thickness.
  • Penicillin targets walls - human cells escape unharmed.

Topic in Depth

Bacterial plasma membrane (selective phospholipid bilayer) transports nutrients selectively, hosts respiratory enzymes (mesosome folds expand area - mitochondria substitutes), synthesises wall precursors, and anchors DNA during division. Permeases pump specifics; porins (Gram-negative outer) admit small hydrophiles. Antibiotics (polymyxins) punching membranes kill broadly - hence toxicity limits their use.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Mesosomes expand respiratory area without mitochondria.
Remember
  • No mitochondria - membranes respire instead.

Controversy notes some mesosomes are fixation artefacts - yet functional evidence (respiration, segregation roles) keeps them in NCERT. Think bacterial mitochondria-plus-spindle combined in membrane folds.

Bacterial ribosomes (70S = 50S plus 30S subunits) translate mRNA in cytoplasm and on membranes - smaller than eukaryotic 80S, hence antibiotic-selective (streptomycin, tetracycline jam 70S specifically). Polysomes (beaded chains on one message) mass-produce proteins. Mitochondrial and plastid 70S ribosomes betray endosymbiotic bacterial origins - same size, same drug sensitivity.

Nucleoid is naked circular DNA (plus plasmids - bonus resistance/fertility rings) folded by HU proteins in cytoplasm - no membrane, no histones, single chromosome (plus episomes). Supercoiling compacts metres into microns; coupled transcription-translation (no nucleus delay) speeds response. Plasmids (F-factor, R-resistance) transfer horizontally - antibiotic resistance spreads contagiously, not just vertically.

  • No membrane means coupled fast gene expression.

Bacterial flagella (helical filament-hook-basal-body motors, flagellin protein - not tubulin) rotate like propellers (run-and-tumble chemotaxis toward food, away from harm). Arrangements (mono-, lopho-, amphi-, peritrichous) classify species. H-antigen serotyping tracks pathogens (Salmonella). Motors spin 100+ revolutions per second on proton power - the tiniest rotary engines, unrelated to eukaryotic 9+2 whips.

  • Arrangements plus H-antigens classify pathogens.

Pili (short bristles) and fimbriae attach bacteria to surfaces and hosts (pathogenic grip - gonorrhoea, UTIs), build biofilms, and conjugate: sex pili (F-factor tubes) transfer plasmid DNA donor-to-recipient. Twitching motility drags cells via pilus extension-retraction. Anti-adhesion strategies (cranberry UTIs, vaccines) target pili - grip-breaking prevents infection without killing (less resistance pressure).

Plant cell walls (primary extensible cellulose-pectin, secondary lignified in wood, middle lamella gluing neighbours) shape, support and defend - turgor presses protoplasts against walls for rigidity (wilt when lost). Cytoplasm (cytosol plus organelles minus nucleus) is the living medium - watery colloid with enzymes (glycolysis runs here), cytoskeleton tracks (microtubules, actin filaments positioning organelles, driving streaming), inclusions (starch grains, crystals, pigments). Cyclosis (cytoplasmic streaming, visible in Hydrilla/Chara) distributes materials. Cytosol hosts thousands of simultaneous reactions in organised micro-zones.

Nucleus (double membrane with pores, nucleoplasm, chromatin, nucleolus) commands via DNA: chromatin (DNA-histone) condenses to chromosomes in division; nucleolus builds rRNA plus ribosomes; pores traffic RNA out and proteins in. Nucleoplasm suspends the genome; nuclear lamina shapes the envelope. Enucleate sieve elements and RBCs prove cells can run briefly on imported instructions - but command normally stays nuclear.

Organelles divide labour by membranes: endomembrane system (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles - connected traffic), energy converters (mitochondria, plastids - semi-autonomous endosymbionts), cytoskeleton movers, peroxisome detoxifiers, centrosome organisers. Each marks with signature enzymes and pH. Compartmentation lets incompatible chemistries (acid digestion, ATP synthesis) run simultaneously - the eukaryotic efficiency secret.

  • Endomembrane traffics; converters power; skeleton moves.

Endoplasmic reticulum networks protein and lipid synthesis: rough ER (ribosome-studded, secretory/membrane proteins folding with chaperones) versus smooth ER (lipid-steroid synthesis, detoxification, calcium storage - abundant in liver, testes). Sarcoplasmic reticulum (muscle calcium) and transitional ER (Golgi-feeding vesicles) specialise further. ER stress (misfolded overload) triggers responses linked to diabetes and neurodegeneration.

Topic in Depth

Ribosomes translate mRNA to protein: 80S cytosolic (60S+40S - free for intracellular proteins, membrane-bound for secretory), 70S organellar (mitochondria, plastids - bacterial heritage), composed of rRNA plus proteins (ribozymes catalyse peptide bonds). Polysomes (beaded chains) mass-produce; subunits assemble on messages on demand. Antibiotics exploit size differences - translation as drug target.

  • Free ribosomes serve inside; bound serve export.

Golgi apparatus (cisternae stacks with cis-entry, medial-processing, trans-exit faces) glycosylates, sorts and ships: proteins get sugar tags (glycoproteins), lysosomes bud off, secretory vesicles exocytose, plant cell plates form during cytokinesis. Chapter 6 · Topic 21

Lysosomes

Cell: The Unit of LifeCell and BiomoleculesD. Cell OrganellesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Lysosomes (suicidal bags) digest with acid hydrolases at pH around 5 - autophagy (recycling worn organelles), heterophagy (killing engulfed germs), metamorphosis remodelling (tadpole tails), plus pathological rupture (arthritis, silicosis damage). Membrane pumps maintain acidity; leaks digest the cell itself (autolysis). Plant vacuoles double as lysosomes - lytic compartments by another name.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Acid-hydrolase sacs recycling, defending and remodelling.
  • Rupture digests self - suicidal bags literal.

Vacuoles

Cell: The Unit of LifeCell and BiomoleculesD. Cell OrganellesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Vacuoles (tonoplast-bound sacs) store water, salts, pigments (anthocyanins colour petals), toxins and wastes; maintain turgor pressing protoplasts to walls (rigidity, growth drive); and run lytic digestion (plant lysosome equivalents). Contractile vacuoles pump water in freshwater protists; food vacuoles digest prey. Central vacuole (up to 90 percent plant cell volume) dominates plant physiology - growth by inflation, not just division.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Store, pressurise (turgor), digest - plant triple duty.
  • Central vacuole fills most mature plant cells.
Remember
  • Turgor loss wilts; contractile vacuoles pump protist water out.

Mitochondria (double membrane: outer porous, inner cristae-folded with F0-F1 ATP synthase, matrix with circular DNA plus 70S ribosomes) run aerobic respiration - Krebs plus electron transport yielding energy-rich ATP per glucose. Semi-autonomous (own genome, maternal inheritance, endosymbiotic bacterial past); maternal DNA traces lineages. Numbers match energy demand (muscle thousands, resting few); exercise builds more.

  • Cristae expand respiratory area; matrix runs Krebs cycle.

Deep Dive · Molecules of life

Biomolecules layer chemistry into biology: carbohydrates (mono-di-poly sugars fuelling and building), proteins (20 amino acids folding primary to quaternary into workers), lipids (dense energy plus membranes plus signals), nucleic acids (DNA archives, RNA acts, nucleotides double as currency), enzymes (protein catalysts with active-site precision gated by temperature, pH, substrate and inhibitors). Tests (Benedict, iodine, Biuret, Sudan) diagnose each class practically.
NEET facts:
  • Benedict reduces sugars; iodine blues starch; Biuret violets proteins; Sudan oranges fats.
  • Alpha-links digest (starch); beta-links resist (cellulose); peptide bonds chain amino acids.
Fig: Four molecule classes plus enzyme catalysts - chemistry feeding biology.

Topic in Depth

Carbohydrates (hydrates of carbon, Cn(H2O)n) are instant energy plus structure: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose - single units), disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose - pairs), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose - storage versus structure). Benedict test detects reducing sugars (free aldehyde/ketone groups); iodine turns starch blue-black. Plants transport sucrose, store starch, build cellulose - one chemistry, three careers.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Mono (single), di (pair), poly (chains) - size defines class.
  • Benedict reduces sugars; iodine blues starch.

Topic in Depth

Monosaccharides are single sugar units - trioses to heptoses by carbon count, aldoses (glucose, aldehyde) versus ketoses (fructose, ketone) by group. Glucose (blood sugar, instant fuel, respiratory substrate), fructose (fruit sugar, sweetest), galactose (milk part), ribose-deoxyribose (nucleic backbones). Ring forms (pyranose six, furanose five) dominate in solution; reducing ends react in tests.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Glucose (aldohexose), fructose (ketohexose) head the list.
  • Ribose and deoxyribose build nucleic acids.
Remember
  • Glucose is blood sugar; fructose is fruit sugar (sweetest).

Disaccharides pair monosaccharides with water loss (glycosidic bonds): sucrose (glucose plus fructose - table sugar, transport sugar), maltose (glucose plus glucose - germinating grain), lactose (glucose plus galactose - milk sugar). Hydrolysis (maltase, sucrase, lactase) splits them back at brush borders. Lactose intolerance (lost lactase) troubles most adults worldwide - persistence is the mutant exception.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sucrose (transport), maltose (germination), lactose (milk).
  • Glycosidic bonds form by dehydration, break by hydrolysis.

Topic in Depth

Polysaccharides chain sugars into storage (starch: amylose unbranched plus amylopectin branched in plants; glycogen hyper-branched in animals/fungi) or structure (cellulose beta-linked straight ribbons hydrogen-bonding into fibres; chitin in fungi/insects). Iodine blues starch (amylose helices trap iodine), not cellulose or glycogen (reddish). Branching decides mobilization speed - glycogen branches most for fastest release.

  • Storage branched (starch, glycogen) vs structure straight (cellulose, chitin).
  • Iodine blue-black diagnoses starch specifically.

Glucose

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesCarbohydratesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Glucose (dextrose, blood sugar, aldohexose C6H12O6) is life central fuel - respiratory substrate yielding ~36 ATP aerobically, photosynthesis product, blood homeostasis target (insulin/glucagon push-pull around 100 mg/dL), brain near-exclusive food. Ring alpha/beta anomers polymerise differently (starch alpha-links digestible; cellulose beta-links indigestible). Diabetes is glucose regulation failure - too much blood sugar, too little control.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Universal respiratory fuel; blood homeostasis target.
  • Alpha-links digest (starch); beta-links resist (cellulose).
Remember
  • Brain runs almost purely on glucose - supply never stops.

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesCarbohydratesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fructose (fruit sugar, ketohexose) is the sweetest natural sugar - free in honey and fruits, half of sucrose, converted to glucose in liver for use. Excessive high-fructose intake bypasses insulin regulation (fructose metabolism skips key checkpoints), linking sodas to fatty liver and metabolic syndrome. Ketose structure (ketone group) distinguishes it from glucose (aldehyde) in tests.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sweetest sugar; fruit and honey source; half of sucrose.
  • Liver converts fructose to glucose for use.

Topic in Depth

Sucrose (table sugar, glucose plus fructose) is the plant transport sugar - soluble, non-reducing (no free reactive groups, stable in transit), loaded into phloem at sources and unloaded at sinks. Sugarcane and beet store it massively; refining strips molasses nutrients leaving empty calories. Invert sugar (hydrolysed glucose-fructose mix) sweetens and preserves (jams) - hydrolysis inverts optical rotation, naming it.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Non-reducing transport sugar; sugarcane/beet store it.
  • Stable in transit; hydrolysed at sinks for use.

Starch (amylose straight chains plus amylopectin branched, alpha-linked glucose) stores plant energy in grains, tubers and seeds - iodine blue-black diagnosis, amylase digestion to maltose. Cooking gelatinises granules (digestible softening); retrogradation (staling) recrystallises them. Resistant starch (cooled potatoes, green bananas) feeds gut flora like fibre - storage with prebiotic bonus.

Cellulose (beta-1,4 glucose ribbons hydrogen-bonding into microfibrils plus fibres) builds plant walls - most abundant organic molecule on Earth. Humans lack cellulase (fibre passes as roughage feeding gut flora); ruminants host microbes that digest it; termites farm protozoa for the same. Cotton (pure cellulose), paper, timber and rayon all process wall cellulose - structure chemistry running economies.

Proteins (amino-acid polymers) do everything - enzymes catalyse, haemoglobin carries, antibodies defend, actin-myosin move, keratin-collagen build, hormones signal, channels gate. Twenty amino-acid types combine into endless sequences; shape (primary to quaternary) decides function; denaturation (heat, pH) destroys shape and function together. Amino acids (amino plus carboxyl plus R-group on alpha carbon) link into proteins: 20 types (essential 9 from diet - histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine; rest synthesised), classified polar/nonpolar, acidic/basic/aromatic. Glycine simplest (H side chain); cysteine bridges disulphides; proline kinks helices. Zwitterion form (both charges) buffers pH; ninhydrin stains them purple.

Peptide bonds (C-N links between carboxyl and amino groups, water lost) chain amino acids - dipeptides, oligopeptides, polypeptides to proteins. Ribosomes form them (peptidyl transferase rRNA catalyses); proteases break them. Bond rigidity (partial double-bond character) constrains rotation, shaping backbones; disulphide, hydrogen, ionic and hydrophobic side-bonds fold chains further. Every protein is a peptide-bonded sentence spelled in 20 letters.
NEET Snapshot:
  • C-N links chaining amino acids with water loss.
  • Ribosomes make them; proteases break them.

Primary structure is amino-acid sequence (insulin 51 residues in A-B chains was first sequenced, Sanger Nobel) - dictating all higher folding: sickle-cell single swap (Glu to Val) proves one residue changes fate. Gene codons encode sequence directly (colinearity); mutation edits sequence first, function follows. Sequencing (Edman, mass-spec) reads order; synthesisers build to order - primary structure is protein source code.

Remember

Secondary structure

Topic in Depth

Secondary structure folds backbones locally: alpha-helices (keratin hair, coiled coils stabilised by hydrogen bonds every fourth residue) and beta-pleated sheets (silk fibroin stacked plates, antibody domains). Proline kinks helices; glycine flexes sheets. Pauling predicted both from X-ray patterns before seeing them - hydrogen-bond geometry constrains backbones to these motifs. Secondary motifs assemble into domains, domains into proteins.

  • Alpha-helices (coils) plus beta-sheets (plates) from H-bonds.
  • Keratin coils; silk stacks - motif matches material.

Tertiary structure

Topic in Depth

Tertiary structure folds whole polypeptides into 3D functional shapes - hydrophobic cores burying water-fearing residues, disulphide bridges locking (insulin interchain), ionic plus hydrogen bonds bracing, active sites sculpted as pockets. Myoglobin (oxygen store) and enzymes show single-chain tertiary function. Denaturation unravels tertiary first (function dies before sequence breaks); chaperones assist folding; misfolding aggregates cause Alzheimer and prion diseases.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Whole-chain 3D shape with active-site pockets.
  • Disulphides lock; hydrophobic cores pack; chaperones assist.
Remember
  • Denaturation kills shape first, sequence never - function needs folding.

Quaternary structure assembles multiple polypeptides: haemoglobin (2 alpha plus 2 beta chains cooperating - oxygen loading eases further loading), antibodies (2 heavy plus 2 light), many enzymes (subunits regulating each other allosterically). Subunit cooperation (cooperativity) and assembly regulation add control layers single chains lack. Not all proteins reach quaternary - myoglobin works solo; haemoglobin teamwork carries oxygen efficiently.

Lipids (water-insoluble, energy-dense) span storage (triglycerides - concentrated fuel, insulation, organ padding), membranes (phospholipid bilayers), signals (steroid hormones, prostaglandins), and vitamins (A, D, E, K fat-soluble). Gram-for-gram lipids store double carbohydrate energy (9 vs 4 kcal) - migration and hibernation run on fat. Sudan test stains them orange-red; rancidity (oxidation) spoils oils.

Fatty acids (carboxyl heads plus hydrocarbon tails) split saturated (no double bonds - straight, solid fats: butter, ghee) versus unsaturated (one/mono, many/poly double bonds - kinked, liquid oils; essential omega-3/6 from diet). Saturation decides melting (kinks prevent packing) and health effects (excess saturates raise LDL). Soaps saponify fatty acids with alkali - cleaning chemistry from lipid tails.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Saturated straight solids vs unsaturated kinked liquids.
  • Omega-3/6 essential - diet must supply them.
Remember
  • Kinks melt: unsaturated oils flow, saturated fats sit solid.

Fats

Topic in Depth

Fats (triglycerides - glycerol plus three fatty acids) store concentrated energy in adipose, insulate against cold, pad organs against shocks, and supply essential acids plus fat-soluble vitamins. Saturated animal fats (butter, ghee) stay solid; plant oils stay liquid (mustard, groundnut). Excess storage drives obesity, atherosclerosis and metabolic syndrome - energy savings overflowing. Hibernators and migrants live off fat banks seasonally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Triglyceride energy banks plus insulation plus padding.
  • Animal saturated solids vs plant unsaturated oils.

Oils

Topic in Depth

Oils are liquid triglycerides (unsaturated - mustard, groundnut, sunflower, olive) plus essential oils (volatile aromatic terpenes - eucalyptus, clove, rose perfumes and medicines). Cooking mediums, salad dressings, biodiesel feedstocks and massage bases all run plant oils. Hydrogenation hardens oils to vanaspati (trans-fat caution); rancidity (oxidation) turns them foul - antioxidants preserve. Volatile oils scent; fixed oils feed and fuel.

  • Cooking, fuel, perfume and medicine from pressed plants.

Topic in Depth

Phospholipids (glycerol plus two fatty acids plus phosphate head) build membranes - hydrophilic heads face water, hydrophobic tails hide inside, self-assembling bilayers with embedded proteins (fluid mosaic). Lecithin (egg yolk, soy) emulsifies foods and supplements; lung surfactant (dipalmitoyl lecithin) keeps alveoli open. Phospholipid asymmetry (different leaflets) signals apoptosis when scrambled - membrane chemistry as cell fate code.

  • Lecithin emulsifies; surfactant keeps alveoli open.

DNA

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesNucleic AcidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA (deoxyribose, A-T-G-C, double helix, usually double-stranded) stores heredity stably - antiparallel strands, complementary pairing, semiconservative replication, mutation-readable sequence. Nuclear chromosomes plus mitochondrial-plastid circles plus plasmids distribute genomes. Hershey-Chase proved DNA (not protein) carries genes; Watson-Crick modelled the helix; sequencing reads it fully. Stability plus copyability makes DNA the archive molecule.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Hershey-Chase proved DNA heredity; Watson-Crick modelled it.
Remember

RNA

Topic in Depth

RNA (ribose, A-U-G-C, usually single-stranded) acts where DNA archives: mRNA messages, tRNA adaptors, rRNA machines, plus regulatory microRNAs and catalytic ribozymes. Uracil replaces thymine; folding creates function (tRNA cloverleaf, ribosome core). Retroviruses store genomes as RNA (reverse transcriptase copies back); RNA-world hypotheses cast RNA as life first molecule (information plus catalysis combined). Versatile, degradable, hardworking.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Single-stranded actor: message, adaptor, machine, regulator.
  • Uracil for thymine; folding for function.

Nucleotides

Topic in Depth

Nucleotides (nitrogenous base plus pentose sugar plus phosphate) are nucleic monomers plus energy currency: ATP (energy coin), cAMP (second messenger), NAD/FAD (redox carriers), CoA (acyl carrier). DNA nucleotides (dAMP, dTMP, dGMP, dCMP) versus RNA (AMP, UMP, GMP, CMP) differ in sugar and uracil. Phosphodiester bonds chain them 5-to-3; triphosphate hydrolysis powers polymerisation - monomers that double as fuel.

  • ATP, NAD, cAMP are nucleotide side careers.

Nucleosides

Topic in Depth

Nucleosides (base plus sugar, no phosphate) are nucleotide precursors: adenosine, thymidine, guanosine, cytidine, uridine - named by base plus ribose/deoxyribose. Phosphorylation upgrades them to nucleotides (mono-, di-, triphosphates); deoxy- prefix marks DNA versions. Antiviral and anticancer nucleoside analogues (AZT, Ara-C) sabotage replication by mimicking building blocks - medicine exploiting monomer chemistry.

  • Analogues (AZT) sabotage viral and cancer replication.

Chapter 7 · Topic 26

Enzymes

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesEnzymesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Enzymes are biocatalysts (mostly proteins, some ribozymes) accelerating reactions millions-fold without being consumed - lowering activation energy via precise active-site fits. Turnover numbers (catalase millions per second) stun; specificity (one substrate, one reaction) organizes metabolism. Named -ase (maltase, polymerase) with EC numbers classifying six reaction classes. Life chemistry runs at body temperature because enzymes cheat energy barriers.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Protein catalysts lowering activation energy, unconsumed.
  • Specificity plus speed plus mild conditions - enzyme triple.

Chapter 7 · Topic 27

Nature of enzymes

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesEnzymesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Enzyme nature: globular proteins (mostly) with precise 3D active sites - heat, pH extremes and heavy metals denature them (shape loss kills function); ribozymes (catalytic RNA - intron splicing, ribosome peptide bonds) prove proteins lack monopoly. Cofactors assist: prosthetic groups (tightly bound - haem, FAD), coenzymes (loose carriers - NAD, CoA), metal activators (Zn, Mg). Apoenzyme plus cofactor equals holoenzyme (complete worker).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Mostly protein, some RNA; cofactors complete the worker.
  • Denaturation kills shape first, function with it.
Remember
  • Apoenzyme (protein) plus cofactor equals holoenzyme (worker).

Chapter 7 · Topic 28

Active site

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesEnzymesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Active sites are sculpted pockets binding substrates by shape plus chemistry (lock-key rigid fits versus induced-fit moulding) - catalytic residues (acid-base, covalent, metal-assisted) transform bound molecules. Specificity pockets exclude wrong molecules; allosteric sites elsewhere modulate remotely. Competitive inhibitors mimic substrates (succinate vs malonate); irreversible poisons (cyanide, nerve gases) kill sites permanently. Pockets plus chemistry equal catalysis.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Shaped pockets binding substrates, excluding others.
  • Lock-key versus induced-fit describe fit dynamics.

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesEnzymesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Enzyme-substrate complexes (ES) form, react, release: binding (induced fit moulds), catalysis (transition-state stabilisation via proximity, strain, acid-base, covalent routes), product release freeing enzyme. Michaelis-Menten kinetics quantifies it - Km (substrate affinity measure: low Km means tight binding), Vmax (saturation speed). Catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) ranks enzymes; diffusion sets the speed ceiling.

  • Km measures affinity; Vmax measures saturated speed.
Remember
  • Low Km means tight binding - affinity inverse.

Enzyme activity answers to conditions: temperature (rises to optimum ~37C human, then denaturation crashes), pH (pepsin acid ~2, trypsin alkaline ~8, most neutral ~7 - ionisation shapes sites), substrate concentration (Michaelis-Menten saturation to Vmax), enzyme concentration (linear at excess substrate), plus inhibitors and activators. Each factor shifts rates predictably - lab assays control all five to measure true activity.

  • Temperature, pH, substrate, enzyme levels plus effectors.
  • Optima reflect working environments (stomach acid vs blood neutral).

Temperature

Topic in Depth

Temperature speeds enzymes (Q10 roughly doubles per 10C rise) until optimum, then denaturation unravels them - human enzymes peak near 37C, thermophile enzymes near boiling (Taq polymerase runs PCR), psychrophile enzymes work near freezing. Fever boosts immunity but extreme heat kills enzymes irreversibly - proteins cook. Cold preserves (refrigeration slows spoilage enzymes); freezing may still damage structures.

pH

Topic in Depth

pH shapes enzyme sites by ionising acidic-basic residues: pepsin pH ~2 (stomach), salivary amylase ~6.8 (mouth), trypsin ~8 (intestine), most intracellular ~7.4 (blood-buffered). Wrong pH mischarges sites (activity falls) then denatures (shape lost). Buffers (bicarbonate blood, phosphate cells) hold working pH; acidosis-alkalosis emergencies reflect enzyme-wide pH sensitivity.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Each enzyme peaks at its working pH; extremes denature.
  • Buffers defend optima against metabolic acids.

Substrate concentration

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesEnzymesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Substrate concentration drives rates Michaelis-Menten style: low substrate (first-order, rate climbs linearly), rising saturation (mixed-order), excess (zero-order plateau at Vmax - all sites busy). More enzyme raises Vmax without changing Km; more substrate overcomes competitive inhibition but not non-competitive. Industrial reactors feed substrate to hold Vmax - saturation economics.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Linear rise, then saturation plateau at Vmax.
  • Competitive inhibition yields to extra substrate; non-competitive never.
Remember
  • Vmax needs saturated sites; Km needs half-saturated measure.

1

Solution: Every active site occupied - adding substrate changes nothing.

Enzyme inhibition

BiomoleculesCell and BiomoleculesEnzymesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Enzyme inhibition regulates and poisons: competitive (mimic substrates - malonate vs succinate; overcome by substrate), non-competitive (allosteric binders - cyanide metals; never overcome), irreversible (nerve-gas covalent killers), feedback (end-product allosterically brakes its pathway - threonine deaminase classic). Drugs exploit inhibition (statins block cholesterol synthesis, penicillin blocks wall building); poisons prove sites matter lethally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Competitive (beat by substrate) vs non-competitive (never beaten).
  • Feedback inhibition auto-regulates pathways.

Chapter 8 · Step-by-step

Cell Cycle and Cell Division

Interphase, mitosis, meiosis and why each division matters.

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

Cell Cycle
1. Cell Cycle2. G1 phase3. S phase4. G2 phase5. M phase6. Interphase
Mitosis
7. Mitosis8. Prophase9. Metaphase10. Anaphase11. Telophase12. Cytokinesis
Meiosis
13. Meiosis14. Meiosis I15. Meiosis II16. Prophase I17. Leptotene18. Zygotene19. Pachytene20. Diplotene21. Diakinesis22. Crossing over23. Metaphase I24. Anaphase I25. Telophase I
Importance
26. Importance27. Growth28. Repair29. Asexual reproduction30. Genetic variation31. Chromosome number maintenance

Deep Dive · Copy then divide, halve then fuse

Cell cycle runs growth plus copying (G1 monitor, S duplicate 2C-4C, G2 stock, M divide) under checkpoint guards; mitosis copies identically (PMAT plus cytokinesis - furrow vs cell plate) for growth, repair and cloning; meiosis halves across two divisions (prophase I five-stage recombination theatre, metaphase I assortment, anaphase I disjunction) for gametes plus variation; importance spans growth to constancy (meiosis-fertilisation cycle stabilising ploidy). Colchicine arrests metaphase; chiasmata map crossovers; checkpoints (p53, spindle) prevent cancer and aneuploidy.
NEET facts:
  • DNA replicates in S (2C to 4C); best chromosome counts at metaphase; crossing over at pachytene.
  • Anaphase I separates homologues; anaphase II (and mitosis) separates sisters.
Fig: Mitosis copies identically; meiosis halves homologues then sisters into four haploids.

Chapter 8 · Topic 1

Cell Cycle

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesCell CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cell cycle (G1-S-G2-M) orders growth plus division: G1 grows and monitors, S replicates DNA (2C to 4C, chromosomes same count), G2 builds division machinery, M divides (mitosis plus cytokinesis). Checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M, spindle assembly) halt faults - p53 guards G1; failures seed cancer. Duration varies (yeast 90 minutes, human ~24 hours, G1 most variable); neurons exit to G0 permanently.
NEET Snapshot:
  • G1 grows, S copies DNA, G2 prepares, M divides.
  • Checkpoints guard each transition; G1/S uses p53.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

DNA replication occurs in cell-cycle phase

Solution: S synthesises DNA (2C to 4C); chromosome number stays same.

Chapter 8 · Topic 2

G1 phase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesCell CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

G1 (first gap) grows cells, makes organelles and proteins, and passes the restriction checkpoint (nutrients, size, DNA integrity, growth signals) - committing to division or withdrawing to quiescent G0 (neurons, muscle). Cyclin D-CDK4/6 drives G1; p53 arrests damaged cells here. Longest most-variable phase; starvation stalls cells in G1/G0 until conditions improve.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Growth plus monitoring; restriction point commits or exits.
  • Cyclin D-CDK4/6 drives; p53 guards the gate.
Remember
  • G0 is exited cycle - neurons and muscle rest there permanently.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Cells withdraw to quiescent G0 from

Solution: Pre-replication G1 exit avoids half-copied genomes.

Chapter 8 · Topic 3

S phase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesCell CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

S (synthesis) replicates every chromosome (DNA 2C to 4C) via helicase-polymerase-ligase forks plus histone doubling - each chromatid needs packaging proteins too. Centrosomes duplicate alongside. Replication errors proofread (mismatch repair); damage stalls forks (ATR checkpoint). Duration fairly constant (~8 hours human); no growth monitoring - pure copying shift. End result: identical sister chromatids ready for segregation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • DNA doubles (2C to 4C); chromatids pair identically.
  • Histones double too; errors proofread immediately.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

After S phase, DNA content per cell is

Solution: Replication doubles 2C diploid content to 4C pre-division.

Chapter 8 · Topic 4

G2 phase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesCell CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

G2 (second gap) stockpiles division machinery - tubulin for spindles, condensins for chromosomes, kinases (cyclin B-CDK1 maturing), plus final damage checks (G2/M checkpoint arrests broken genomes). Organelles (mitochondria, plastids) divide independently here. Short phase (~4 hours); caffeine overrides G2 arrest (premature mitosis experiments prove checkpoint reality). Cells enter M only fully stocked and verified.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Stockpiles spindle plus condensation machinery; final checks.
  • Cyclin B-CDK1 triggers mitotic entry.
Remember
  • G2/M checkpoint blocks damaged genomes from dividing.

1

Maturation promoting factor (cyclin B-CDK1) triggers

Solution: MPF activity spikes push cells past G2 into M.

Index / Cell and Biomolecules
Chapter 8 · Topic 5

M phase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesCell CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

M (mitotic/meiotic division) segregates genomes: prophase condensation, metaphase alignment, anaphase separation, telophase reformation, plus cytokinesis splitting cytoplasm. Shortest yet most visible phase (~1 hour mitosis); colchicine arrests metaphase (spindle poison) for karyotyping. M-phase kinase cascades phosphorylate hundreds of targets - histones, lamins, microtubules - remodelling cells for division.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Prophase to telophase plus cytokinesis - visible division hour.
  • Colchicine arrests metaphase for chromosome counts.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Colchicine arrests mitosis at

Solution: Microtubule inhibition freezes aligned chromosomes for karyotypes.

Index / Cell and Biomolecules
Chapter 8 · Topic 6

Interphase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesCell CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Interphase (G1+S+G2, ~95 percent of cycle) is the working life - growth, DNA copying, preparation - misnamed resting because nuclei look quiet while busiest. Chromatin decondensed for transcription; nucleolus prominent (rRNA production); cells perform tissue functions between divisions. Rapid embryos shorten G1/G2 (syncytial cycles skip cytokinesis); neurons extend G1 into permanent G0. Interphase activity decides division quality.
NEET Snapshot:
  • 95 percent of cycle; growth plus copying plus preparation.
  • Decondensed working chromatin; prominent nucleolus.
Remember
  • Interphase is busiest phase despite quiet looks.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Interphase occupies about what fraction of cell cycle?

Solution: Growth plus copying dwarf the brief visible division.

Chapter 8 · Topic 7

Mitosis

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMitosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mitosis (equational division) copies one diploid nucleus into two identical diploids - growth, repair, asexual reproduction running it. Stages flow PMAT (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) plus cytokinesis; checkpoints (spindle assembly) guard alignment. Open mitosis (plants, animals - envelope breaks) versus closed (fungi - envelope persists) vary packaging. Errors (nondisjunction) make aneuploid cells - mosaicism or death.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One diploid to two identical diploids - equational copying.
  • PMAT plus cytokinesis; checkpoints guard alignment.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Mitosis is called equational division because

Solution: Daughter nuclei match parent ploidy exactly.

Chapter 8 · Topic 8

Prophase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMitosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Prophase condenses chromatin (coiling, shortening, thickening visible), dissolves nucleolus, duplicates centrosomes migrating to poles (asters in animals), and breaks nuclear envelope (open mitosis) - spindle microtubules invading. Longest mitotic stage; chromosome counting impossible yet (overlapping). Phosphorylated histones plus condensins drive compaction - packaging metres into microns for safe moving.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Chromatin condenses; nucleolus vanishes; envelope breaks; spindle forms.
  • Longest stage; chromosomes still overlapping.
Remember
  • Condensation plus envelope breakdown define prophase.

Metaphase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMitosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Metaphase aligns condensed chromosomes on equatorial plates (congression via kinetochore microtubule tug-of-war), spindle fully formed pole-to-pole, spindle-assembly checkpoint verifying every kinetochore attached - best stage to count chromosomes and photograph karyotypes (colchicine-arrested spreads). Sister chromatids face opposite poles, poised for separation. Alignment errors trigger aneuploidy if checkpoint fails.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Equatorial alignment; checkpoint verifies; best counting stage.
  • Kinetochore tug-of-war centres chromosomes.

Chapter 8 · Topic 10

Anaphase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMitosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Anaphase separates sisters (cohesin cleaved, chromatids now chromosomes) pulled poleward (kinetochore microtubule shortening plus polar elongation) - V/J/I shapes by centromere position. Shortest stage; segregation errors here (nondisjunction) cause trisomies. Anaphase A (chromosome-to-pole) plus B (pole-to-pole elongation) combine; separase enzyme triggers the split. Equal partition is mitosis entire point.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sisters split and move poleward; shapes mark centromeres.
  • Nondisjunction here causes aneuploid daughters.
Remember
  • Anaphase A moves chromosomes; B stretches poles apart.

1

Sister chromatids separate during

Solution: Separase cuts cohesin; spindle pulls chromatids poleward.

Chapter 8 · Topic 11

Telophase

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMitosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Telophase reverses prophase: chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes reform (vesicle fusion), nucleoli reappear, spindle disassembles - two daughter nuclei in one cytoplasm awaiting cytokinesis. Karyokinesis ends here; cytokinesis divides the rest. Telophase plus cytokinesis overlap (furrowing/phragmoplast starts late anaphase). Two identical nuclei ready for independent cytoplasms.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Decondense, re-envelope, nucleolus returns, spindle dismantles.
  • Karyokinesis ends; cytokinesis completes division.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Nuclear envelope reforms during

Solution: Vesicles fuse around decondensing daughter genomes.

Chapter 8 · Topic 12

Cytokinesis

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMitosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cytokinesis splits cytoplasm: animal contractile-ring furrowing (actin-myosin pinch from outside) versus plant phragmoplast cell-plate (Golgi vesicles fusing outward, pectin middle lamella first). Symmetric (equal daughters) versus asymmetric (stem-cell divisions) outcomes. Failures make binucleate cells (liver, heart polyploidy normal) or syncytia (Drosophila embryos, muscle fibres) - division without splitting has uses.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Animals furrow in; plants plate out - opposite cytokinesis.
  • Phragmoplast Golgi vesicles build plant walls outward.
Remember
  • Cell plate grows centrifugally; furrow pinches centripetally.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Plant cytokinesis occurs by

Solution: Golgi vesicles fuse outward into dividing walls.

Chapter 8 · Topic 13

Meiosis

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Meiosis (reductional division) halves diploid to haploid across two divisions (meiosis I separates homologues, meiosis II separates sisters like mitosis) - one 2n cell yields four n cells, fuelling sexual life cycles. Crossing over plus independent assortment shuffle combinations; errors cause aneuploid gametes (Down syndrome). Germ cells only (somatic cells never reduce); timing varies (human oocytes pause decades in prophase I).
NEET Snapshot:
  • 2n to n across two divisions; four haploid products.
  • Homologues separate first, sisters second.

Meiosis I

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Meiosis I (heterotypic, reductional) separates homologous chromosomes - prophase I (leptotene to diakinesis with synapsis plus crossing over), metaphase I (homologue pairs align), anaphase I (homologues part, sisters stay), telophase I (two haploid cells, chromosomes still double-chromatid). Recombination plus independent assortment happen here - variation manufactured in one division. Nondisjunction here causes whole-chromosome trisomies.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Homologues part; sisters stay together; ploidy halves.
  • Variation manufactured via crossing over plus assortment.
Remember
  • Anaphase I separates homologues (mitosis never does this).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Homologue separation halves ploidy in first division.

Chapter 8 · Topic 15

Meiosis II

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Meiosis II (homotypic, equational) splits sister chromatids in both haploid cells - prophase II (brief), metaphase II (equatorial alignment), anaphase II (sister separation), telophase II (four haploid nuclei) - mitosis-like mechanics without preceding S phase. No DNA copying between divisions (interkinesis brief rest only). Errors cause chromatid-level aneuploidies. Products mature into gametes or spores by lineage.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Mitosis-like sister split without DNA copying between.
  • Two haploid cells become four haploid nuclei.
Remember
  • No S phase between I and II - copying happens once only.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

DNA replication before meiosis II

Solution: Single S phase serves both divisions - hence halving.
Back to Index
