Chapter 8 · Topic 16

Prophase I

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Prophase I (longest meiotic stage) runs five substages: leptotene (chromosomes appear thin), zygotene (homologues synapse via synaptonemal complex), pachytene (crossing over at recombination nodules, tetrads visible), diplotene (homologues repel except chiasmata), diakinesis (terminalisation, envelope breaks, spindles form). Recombination nodules plus chiasmata physically exchange segments - variation engineered deliberately. Oocytes may pause in diplotene (dictyotene) for decades.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Leptotene-Zygotene-Pachytene-Diplotene-Diakinesis sequence.
  • Synapsis plus crossing over happen here only.

Leptotene

Topic in Depth

Leptotene opens prophase I: chromosomes condense into thin visible threads (lepto = thin), chromomeres (beaded thickenings) dot lengths, bouquet arrangement (telomeres clustering at envelope) aids homologue finding. Transcription continues; axial elements assemble precursors of synaptonemal complexes. Chromosome individuality becomes microscopically visible first here - condensation journey begins.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Thin-thread chromosomes with chromomere beads appear.
  • Bouquet telomere clustering aids pairing search.
Remember
  • Lepto-thin threads start the prophase parade.

Chapter 8 · Topic 18

Zygotene

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Zygotene zips homologues via synaptonemal complexes (protein ladders between aligned axes) - pairing (synapsis) exact gene-to-gene, starting at telomeres inward. Pairing enables crossing-over machinery loading; asynaptic mutants (no zipper) segregate randomly causing sterility. Bivalents (paired homologues) form here; each bivalent holds four chromatids (tetrad) ready for exchange next stage.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Synaptonemal zippers pair homologues gene-to-gene.
  • Bivalents (tetrads) assemble for crossing over.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Synaptonemal complex forms during

Chapter 8 · Topic 19

Pachytene

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pachytene (thick stage) crosses over: fully synapsed tetrads exchange segments at recombination nodules (enzyme complexes cutting-rejoining non-sister chromatids), visible as chiasmata later. Multiple crossovers per bivalent shuffle allele combinations - variation manufactured deliberately. Recombination-defective mutants (no nodules) segregate homologues randomly, spiking aneuploidy - crossing over mechanically aids segregation too, not just variation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Recombination nodules exchange non-sister segments.
  • Crossing over shuffles alleles plus aids segregation.
Remember
  • Pachytene thick tetrads trade segments at nodules.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Tetrad non-sisters exchange at recombination nodules in pachytene.

Chapter 8 · Topic 20

Diplotene

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Diplotene dissolves synaptonemal complexes - homologues repel except where crossovers (chiasmata) hold them, X-shaped junctions sliding toward ends (terminalisation beginning). Lampbrush chromosomes (amphibian oocytes) transcribe massively here; human oocytes arrest in diplotene dictyotene stage from foetal life till puberty (decades-long pause). Chiasma counts map crossover frequency - one chiasma minimum per bivalent for proper segregation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Complex dissolves; chiasmata hold repelling homologues.
  • Oocytes pause here (dictyotene) till puberty.
Remember
  • Chiasmata are crossover scars holding pairs together.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Chiasmata are first visible in

Solution: Repelling homologues stay linked at crossover points.

Chapter 8 · Topic 21

Diakinesis

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Diakinesis finalises prophase I: terminalisation completes (chiasmata slide to ends), chromosomes maximally condense, nucleolus vanishes, nuclear envelope breaks, spindles assemble - bivalents ready for metaphase plates. Short transitional stage; counts (bivalent numbers) confirm ploidy. After this point homologues commit to opposite poles - segregation machinery takes over from pairing machinery.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Terminalisation completes; envelope breaks; spindles form.
  • Bivalents poised for metaphase alignment.
Remember
  • Dia = across - chiasmata move to chromosome ends.

1

Chapter 8 · Topic 22

Crossing over

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Crossing over exchanges non-sister chromatid segments at pachytene recombination nodules - breaking and rejoining DNA (Spo11 cuts, repair synthesis), creating recombinant chromatids mixing parental alleles. Frequency maps gene distance (1 percent recombination = 1 map unit/centimorgan - Sturtevant maps); interference suppresses nearby second crossovers; hotspots cluster exchanges. Minimum one crossover per bivalent ensures proper disjunction - variation plus mechanics in one act.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Segment exchange shuffles alleles; frequency maps distance.
  • 1 percent recombination equals 1 map unit.

Chapter 8 · Topic 23

Metaphase I

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Metaphase I aligns homologous pairs (not single chromosomes) on equatorial plates - maternal-paternal orientation random per pair (independent assortment: 2^n combinations for n pairs; humans 2^23 ≈ 8 million gamete types). Kinetochores face opposite poles per homologue (sisters co-oriented, unlike mitosis). Spindle checkpoint verifies tension. Orientation randomness manufactures variation equal to crossing over - two shuffling engines in one division.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Homologue pairs align; orientation random per pair.
  • Independent assortment yields 2^n gamete combinations.
Remember
  • Sisters co-orient in meiosis I (versus opposite in mitosis).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Random pair orientation shuffles parental chromosomes freely.

Chapter 8 · Topic 24

Anaphase I

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Anaphase I parts homologues (disjunction) - entire doubled chromosomes (two chromatids each) move poleward, sisters staying together (cohesin persists at centromeres, lost on arms). Reduction happens here: 2n bivalents become n doubled-chromosomes per pole. Nondisjunction (both homologues same pole) causes trisomic-monosomic gametes (Down syndrome). Anaphase bridges (dicentric chromatids) signal crossover errors.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Homologues (not sisters) separate; ploidy halves.
  • Nondisjunction here causes whole-chromosome trisomies.
Remember
  • Centromere cohesin survives anaphase I, dies in anaphase II.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Homologous chromosomes separate during

Solution: Disjunction halves ploidy in first meiotic division.

Chapter 8 · Topic 25

Telophase I

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesMeiosisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Telophase I reforms nuclei around haploid doubled-chromosome sets (chromosomes still two-chromatid), nucleoli return, spindles dissolve - two cells via cytokinesis (or shared cytoplasm in plants). Interkinesis follows (brief rest, NO DNA replication) before meiosis II. Chromosome counts halved but chromatids doubled - half the journey (reduction done, sister-splitting pending). Some species skip telophase I envelopes entirely (rushing to division II).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Two haploid nuclei with doubled chromosomes; no S phase follows.
  • Interkinesis rests without copying before division II.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

After telophase I, each daughter cell is

Solution: Halved counts but doubled chromatids await meiosis II splitting.

Chapter 8 · Topic 26

Importance

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesImportanceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cell division matters at every scale: growth (mitotic mass increase), repair (wound healing, skin-gut-blood turnover), asexual reproduction (mitotic clones: cuttings, budding, fragmentation), gametes (meiotic halving enabling fertilisation constancy), variation (crossing over plus assortment fuelling evolution), chromosome constancy (meiosis-fertilisation cycle stabilising ploidy). Uncontrolled division is cancer; failed halving is aneuploidy - division precision underwrites life continuity.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Growth, repair, cloning, gametes, variation, constancy - six roles.
  • Precision failures cause cancer (mitosis) or trisomies (meiosis).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Meiosis maintains chromosome constancy across generations by

Solution: Halving-then-fusing cycle stabilises ploidy sexually.

Chapter 8 · Topic 27

Growth

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesImportanceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Growth by mitosis adds cells (hyperplasia) plus enlarges them (hypertrophy): plant meristems divide lifelong (indeterminate), animals grow to adult size then maintain (determinate, stem-cell pockets excepted). Allometric scaling (brain vs body rates differ) shapes forms; determinate organs (leaves, flowers) stop on schedule. Unchecked mitosis is neoplasia - growth control (contact inhibition, checkpoints, apoptosis) separates development from tumours.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Mitosis adds cells; enlargement plus differentiation follow.
  • Determinate organs stop; meristems persist; checkpoints gate.
Remember
  • Contact inhibition stops normal cells crowding - cancer ignores it.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Plant growth continues lifelong mainly due to

Solution: Apical plus lateral meristems divide indeterminately.

Chapter 8 · Topic 28

Repair

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesImportanceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Repair replaces lost cells mitotically: skin (weeks turnover), gut lining (days), blood (marrow millions per second), liver (regenerates lobes), bone (callus remodelling), plants (wound callus plus graft unions). Stem-cell pools (basal skin, crypts, marrow, cambium) fuel turnover; scarring (fibrosis) patches where regeneration fails (heart, CNS). Salamander limbs regrow fully (dedifferentiation blastemas) - mammals mostly scar instead.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Skin, gut, blood, liver, bone all turn over mitotically.
  • Stem pools fuel repair; scars patch failures.

Chapter 8 · Topic 29

Asexual reproduction

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesImportanceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Asexual reproduction clones via mitosis: binary fission (Amoeba, Paramecium), budding (yeast, Hydra), fragmentation (Spirogyra, Planaria), spores (fungi millions, fern meiospores), vegetative propagation (runners, tubers, bulbs, cuttings, grafting, tissue culture). Speed plus uniformity suit stable habitats; no variation risks total vulnerability (Irish potato famine cloned disaster). Agriculture clones elites (banana, sugarcane, potato) while breeding adds variation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Mitosis clones: fission, budding, fragmentation, spores, cuttings.
  • Fast uniform crops risk uniform vulnerability.

Chapter 8 · Topic 30

Genetic variation

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesImportanceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Meiotic variation fuels evolution: crossing over (allele shuffling within chromosomes), independent assortment (chromosome shuffling, 2^23 human combos), random fertilisation (gamete lottery multiplies combos), plus mutation (new alleles). Siblings differ (except identical twins) because each gamete samples uniquely. Selection acts on this variation; conservation (captive breeding) maximises it deliberately. Sex costs double (males) but variation pays survival dividends.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Crossing over plus assortment plus random fusion manufacture uniqueness.
  • Variation feeds selection; cloning starves it.
Remember
  • Siblings differ because gametes sample independently twice over.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Maximum genetic variation in sexual reproduction comes from combined

Solution: Three shuffling engines stack multiplicatively per zygote.

Chapter 8 · Topic 31

Chromosome number maintenance

Cell Cycle and Cell DivisionCell and BiomoleculesImportanceStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Chromosome constancy runs the meiosis-fertilisation cycle: meiosis halves (2n to n), fertilisation restores (n plus n to 2n) - stable counts generation after generation (human 46). Nondisjunction breaks constancy (trisomy 21 Down, XO Turner, XXY Klinefelter); polyploidy (whole-set multiples - triploid seedless watermelon, hexaploid wheat) reroutes it agriculturally. Colchicine-doubled crops exploit constancy-breaking deliberately.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Halve (meiosis) then restore (fertilisation) - counts hold steady.
  • Nondisjunction breaks it; polyploidy reroutes it usefully.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Chromosome number stays constant across sexual generations because

Solution: Reduction then restoration closes the ploidy loop.

Chapter 9 · Step-by-step

Transport in Plants

Diffusion to transpiration pull - how water and food move through plants.

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

A. Transport Mechanisms
1. Diffusion2. Facilitated diffusion3. Active transport4. Membrane transport5. Passive transport
B. Water Relations
6. Water Relations7. Osmosis8. Osmotic pressure9. Water potential10. Solute potential11. Pressure potential12. Plasmolysis13. Deplasmolysis14. Imbibition
C. Water Absorption
15. Root hairs16. Apoplast pathway17. Symplast pathway18. Transmembrane pathway
D. Long-Distance Water Transport
19. Xylem20. Root pressure21. Capillarity22. Cohesion-tension theory23. Transpiration pull
E. Transpiration
24. Stomatal transpiration25. Cuticular transpiration26. Factors affecting transpiration27. Significance of transpiration
F. Phloem Transport
28. Translocation29. Source30. Sink31. Pressure-flow hypothesis32. Loading33. Unloading

Deep Dive · Water up, food around

Plant transport runs two one-and-two-way systems: water relations (diffusion, osmosis, water potential equals solute plus pressure potentials, plasmolysis) govern entry; root hairs absorb via apoplast-symplast-transmembrane routes; xylem lifts by root pressure plus capillarity but mainly cohesion-tension transpiration pull; transpiration (stomatal bulk, cuticular minor) costs water for CO2 and cooling; phloem pressure-flow ships sugars source-to-sink (loading-unloading osmotic gradients). Potential gradients drive everything - water to lower potential, sugar to lower pressure.
NEET facts:
  • Water moves to lower (more negative) water potential; plasmolysis reverses in hypotonic solutions.
  • Cohesion-tension-transpiration pull lifts columns; pressure-flow pushes sugars source to sink.
Fig: Roots absorb, cohesion chains columns, leaves evaporate the pull - ascent without pumps.

Diffusion

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyA. Transport MechanismsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Diffusion (molecules spreading down concentration gradients) needs no energy - gases entering leaves, scents spreading. Rate rises with steep gradients, temperature and small size; membranes gate by permeability. Short hops diffuse; long hauls need bulk flow (xylem pull, phloem push) because diffusion crawls over centimetres.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Down-gradient passive spread; steeper, warmer, smaller moves faster.
  • Short hops diffuse; long hauls need bulk flow.

Facilitated diffusion

Topic in Depth

Facilitated diffusion ferries polar cargo (glucose, ions, water via aquaporins) through membrane proteins downhill without ATP - channels (gated pores) plus carriers (conformation-flipping transporters). Specific, saturable and blockable (toxins prove protein mediation). Faster than simple diffusion for reluctants, capped at transporter maximum.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Protein-aided downhill transport without ATP.
  • Aquaporins channel water; carriers flip cargo across.
Remember
  • Blockers stopping flow prove protein routes.

Active transport

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyA. Transport MechanismsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Active transport pumps against gradients spending ATP - root minerals concentrated hundred-fold from dilute soil, gut glucose absorbed, nerve Na+-K+ gradients built (3 out, 2 in). Pump ATPases couple hydrolysis to uphill moves; cotransport piggybacks second cargo. Poison ATP and uptake halts - energy dependence proved. Uphill accumulation defines the process.
NEET Snapshot:
  • ATP-spent uphill pumping against gradients.
  • Root minerals, gut glucose, nerve ions all pump actively.

Membrane transport sorts by cargo and cost: simple diffusion (small nonpolar gases), facilitated diffusion (polar via proteins, downhill), active transport (ATP uphill), bulk vesicles (endo/exocytosis for macromolecules). Selectively permeable membranes decide routes; patch-clamp recordings watch single channels flicker visibly.

  • Diffuse, facilitate, pump, vesicle - four routes.
  • Membrane selectivity plus gradients route all traffic.

Passive transport (no metabolic energy) covers diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis - downhill to equilibrium, gradient-driven. Rates follow gradient, area, thinness and temperature; membranes filter by size-charge-solubility. Dialysis, breathing gases and initial water uptake run passive - free physics before costly pumps engage.

Water Relations

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyB. Water RelationsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Water relations quantify plant water status: water potential (total, pure water zero, plant cells negative) equals solute potential (dissolved pull, negative) plus pressure potential (turgor positive, xylem tension negative) - water always flows to more negative potential. Wilting, plasmolysis and guttation all read as potential stories replacing vague wet-dry intuition.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Water flows to more negative potential always.
  • Solute lowers, pressure raises; sum decides direction.

Osmosis

Topic in Depth

Osmosis (water across selective membranes to lower-potential sides) powers roots absorbing, turgor stiffening, stomata opening (guard-cell turgor), seeds germinating. Thistle-funnel demos visualise it; reverse osmosis (pressure-driven) desalinates industrially. Animal cells burst or shrivel without walls - plant walls convert osmosis into safe turgor pressure.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Turgor, stomata, germination all run on osmosis.
Remember
  • Walls convert bursting osmosis into useful turgor.

Osmotic potential (solute pull, negative) and osmotic pressure (counter-pressure to stop entry, positive) describe one attraction dually. Seawater (very negative) versus freshwater roots explains mangrove salt exclusion; pickling and sugaring preserve food by osmotically dehydrating microbes. Fertilisers over-applied reverse gradients burning roots - osmotic scorch, not chemical poison.

  • Pickling preserves by microbe dehydration.

Topic in Depth

Water potential (megapascals, pure water zero) sums solute (negative) plus pressure (turgor positive, xylem tension negative) potentials. Leaves (very negative, transpiring) pull from roots (less negative) from soil (near zero); drought steepens gradients. Pressure-chamber readings diagnose crop stress before wilting shows - potential meters beat eyeballing.

  • Solute plus pressure potentials sum to water status.
  • Leaves most negative pull; soil near zero supplies.

Solute potential drops with dissolved particle count (identity-independent) - more moles, more negative. Salty soils starve plants osmotically despite wetness (physiological drought); halophytes accumulate compatible solutes (proline, glycine-betaine) balancing without toxicity. Fertilisers over-applied reverse gradients burning roots.

Pressure potential

Topic in Depth

Pressure potential is turgor (positive wall-pressed protoplasts stiffening herbs, opening stomata, driving growth) or xylem tension (negative stretched columns lifting sap). Wilting (turgor lost, walls contacted) differs from plasmolysis (membranes detached). Growth expansion, seedling emergence and stomatal movement all spend turgor pressure mechanically.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Positive turgor stiffens; negative tension lifts columns.
  • Wilting keeps contact; plasmolysis detaches membranes.

Plasmolysis

Topic in Depth

Plasmolysis (protoplast shrinking from walls in hypertonic baths) stages incipient to evident to final - reversible early in hypotonic solutions (deplasmolysis), lethal if prolonged (death point). Onion-peel demos visualise osmosis live. Only living walled cells plasmolyse; animal cells crenate instead - walls make detachment visible.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hypertonic shrinkage from walls; reversible if brief.
  • Living walled cells only; animals crenate instead.
Remember
  • Deplasmolysis rescues early; death-point kills.

Deplasmolysis

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyB. Water RelationsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Deplasmolysis (hypotonic rescue re-inflating protoplasts to walls) reverses early plasmolysis - water re-enters, turgor rebuilds, streaming resumes. Failed recovery marks membrane death (proteins denatured). Irrigating wilted crops is mass deplasmolysis - timely watering rescues turgor before permanent injury sets in.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hypotonic rescue re-inflating protoplasts to walls.
  • Failed recovery diagnoses membrane death.
Remember
  • Irrigation rescues wilt by field-scale deplasmolysis.

Imbibition (dry solids drinking water: swelling seeds, warping doors, jelling agar) runs on matric adhesion plus osmosis - generating splitting pressures (seeds lift pavements). Dry seeds (8-10 percent water) imbibe past 60 percent waking metabolism - water entry precedes life restart.

Root hairs

Root hairs (tubular epidermal extensions, cuticle-free thin walls) absorb water-minerals at maturation zones - living days, replaced as tips advance. Mycorrhizal fungi extend reach hundred-fold; rhizosphere microbes trade nutrients. Transplant shock (hair damage) wilts until regrowth - nursery handling protects hairs; hydroponics bathes them directly.

Apoplast pathway

Topic in Depth

Apoplast (connected walls plus intercellular spaces, dead continuum) carries water-minerals rapidly without membrane crossings - until Casparian strips bar wall flow at endodermis, forcing symplast entry. Fast but unselective; cortex transit runs apoplastic; stele entry demands symplastic selection. Dyes trace apoplast visibly in experiments.

  • Casparian strips end apoplast at endodermis.

Symplast pathway

Topic in Depth

Symplast (connected cytoplasms via plasmodesmata) carries selected molecules cell-to-cell through living continuum - slower than apoplast but controllable via callose gating and carriers. Casparian-forced entry routes all stele traffic symplastically. Sugars, signals and ions travel symplastically; bulk water shortcuts apoplastically - dual routes balance speed against selection.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cytoplasm continuum via plasmodesmata; regulated living route.
  • Stele entry forces symplastic selection.

Transmembrane pathway

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyC. Water AbsorptionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Transmembrane (vacuolar) pathway crosses membranes plus vacuoles cell-by-cell - slowest, most selective route, serving storage tissues and glands. Aquaporins gate water; ion channels select minerals; tonoplast transporters load vacuoles. Energy-costly precision for special deliveries - bulk flows use faster routes; valuable cargo uses membrane control.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Membrane-by-membrane crossings; slowest, most selective.
  • Aquaporins and channels gate each crossing.

  • Fast walls, living cytoplasm, gated membranes - three root routes.

Xylem

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyD. Long-Distance Water TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Xylem lifts water-minerals root-to-shoot through dead tracheids plus vessels - one-way upward bulk flow driven by transpiration pull (main engine), root pressure (night supplement) and capillarity (assist). Heartwood retires to support; sapwood pipes actively. Dead tubes plus living pull move tonnes of water daily in big trees.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dead-tube upward bulk flow; transpiration pull engine.
  • Sapwood pipes; heartwood retired to support.

Root pressure

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyD. Long-Distance Water TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Root pressure (night osmotic push from stele ion loading, up to ~2 bars) pushes sap upward when transpiration rests - causing guttation droplets at hydathodes and refilling dawn embolisms. Insufficient for tall trees (needs tens of bars) but vital for seedlings, herbs and spring vine bleeding (maple syrup taps). Exuding cut stumps demonstrate it (bleeding experiments).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Night osmotic push causing guttation; refills embolisms.
  • Bars of push versus tens needed - supplement, not engine.
Remember
  • Guttation droplets prove night root pressure visibly.

Capillarity

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyD. Long-Distance Water TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Capillarity (narrow-tube rise from adhesion-cohesion) lifts water centimetres in xylem micro-tubes and soil pores - assisting (never driving) tall ascent; menisci curve visibly in cut stems. Soil capillarity wicks moisture to roots; blotting demos model it. Height limits prove trees need transpiration pull beyond capillary aid - helper, not hero.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Narrow-tube wicking assists ascent by centimetres.
  • Soil capillarity supplies roots; xylem capillarity aids columns.
Remember
  • Capillarity helps centimetres; trees need pull for metres.

Cohesion-tension theory

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyD. Long-Distance Water TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Cohesion-tension theory explains ascent: water cohesion (hydrogen bonding) plus wall adhesion form unbroken columns; leaf evaporation creates tension (negative pressure) transmitted down, pulling columns up; roots refill. Needs continuity (embolism breaks), lignin strength (walls resist collapse) and massive evaporation (pull engine). Unbeaten after a century - physics lifting forests.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cohesive columns plus evaporative tension pull water skyward.
  • Needs continuity, lignin strength and transpiration engine.

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyD. Long-Distance Water TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Transpiration pull (tension from leaf evaporation transmitted down cohesive columns) is ascent main engine - tens of bars suction lifting redwoods, powered free by sun-driven evaporation. Stomata throttle it (ABA drought closure slows ascent); cut shoots keep absorbing while transpiring (pull independent of roots); embolism snaps columns (tyloses seal, nights refill). Pull follows vapour-pressure deficits daily.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Evaporative tension transmitted down cohesive water.
  • Stomata throttle; embolisms snap; nights refill.

Topic in Depth

Stomatal transpiration (~90-95 percent of loss) exits guard-cell pores - K+-driven turgor opens days (CO2 entry), ABA closes droughts (water saving). Uneven guard walls bow with turgor; subsidiary patterns diagnose families. Potometers measure uptake approximating loss; antitranspirants (films, ABA mimics) cut losses agriculturally. Gas exchange versus water loss trades at every pore.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Guard-cell pores lose ~95 percent transpired water.
  • Turgor opens (K+ in); ABA closes (drought).
Remember
  • Stomata trade CO2 entry against water exit constantly.

Cuticular transpiration

Topic in Depth

Cuticular transpiration (~5-10 percent) seeps through leaf cuticle - thick wax (xerophytes) cuts it; thin shade cuticles leak more. Antitranspirant sprays supplement wax artificially. Lenticular plus peridermal losses add woody totals. Evergreens invest wax heavily; deciduous drop leaves instead - seal versus shed strategies.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Wax-seepage minority loss; thick cuticles minimise.
  • Xerophytes wax heavily; deciduous shed instead.
Remember
  • Cuticle thickness inversely tracks water loss.

Chapter 9 · Topic 26

Factors affecting transpiration

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyE. TranspirationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Transpiration factors split external (temperature up, humidity down, wind up, light opens stomata raise loss; still humid high-CO2 air lowers it) versus internal (leaf area, cuticle thickness, stomatal density, sunken pits, hairiness). Desert adaptations stack reductions; rainforest leaves maximise exchange. Potometer plus cobalt-chloride paper quantify experimentally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hot, dry, windy, bright loses most; humid, still, high-CO2 loses least.
  • Wax, hairs, pits, rolling are plant-side brakes.

Chapter 9 · Topic 27

Significance of transpiration

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyE. TranspirationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Transpiration significance outweighs water cost: cooling leaves (evaporative air-conditioning), ascent engine (pull lifting minerals), mineral distribution (mass flow delivery), turgor maintenance (growth expansion), salt flushing. Necessary-evil framing captures cost-benefit - plants pay water for CO2 access plus cooling plus transport. Antitranspirants must preserve benefits while trimming waste.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cools, lifts, distributes, inflates - paid in water.
  • Necessary evil: costs water, buys CO2 plus cooling plus flow.

Chapter 9 · Topic 28

Translocation

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyF. Phloem TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Translocation (phloem sugar transport source-to-sink) runs pressure-flow: loading drops source potential (water enters, pressure rises), flow pushes bulk sap through sieve tubes, unloading drops sink pressure (water exits). Bidirectional (unlike xylem), seasonally rerouted (spring stores-to-shoots, summer leaves-to-fruits/roots). Tracers plus aphid stylets map flows live.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Pressure-driven sugar flow from producing sources to needy sinks.
  • Bidirectional, rerouted seasonally by need.
Remember
  • Aphid stylets tap sieve tubes - natural pressure gauges.

Chapter 9 · Topic 29

Source

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyF. Phloem TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sources (net sugar producers: mature photosynthesizing leaves, germinating reserves mobilising) load phloem actively (proton-sucrose cotransport) dropping water potential, drawing water in, building export pressure. Source strength (rate times area) limits yield - defoliation starves sinks; shading cuts export. Storage-to-shoot spring reversal makes tubers temporary sources - source status follows surplus, not identity.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Net producers loading phloem by active transport.
  • Leaves normally; storage organs seasonally (spring mobilisation).

Chapter 9 · Topic 30

Sink

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyF. Phloem TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sinks (net importers: roots, fruits, seeds, growing tips, filling stores) unload sugars, dropping pressure to sustain inflow; sink strength (size times activity) pulls yield (more grains, bigger tubers). Pruning balances source-sink ratios (thinning sizes survivors); harvest index measures capture efficiency. Storage sinks reverse to sources each spring (sprouting tubers feed shoots).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Net importers unloading sugars; strength pulls yield.
  • Fruits, roots, tips, filling stores - all sink by deficit.

1

Developing fruits act as phloem

Pressure-flow hypothesis

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyF. Phloem TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pressure-flow (mass-flow) hypothesis: osmotic gradients (loaded source high, unloaded sink low) push bulk sap through sieve tubes - water follows sugars in at sources, exits at sinks, xylem recycles water back. Supported by bidirectional flow, speed measurements and stylet pressures; debated details refine without refuting. Bulk flow, not diffusion, moves tonnes of sugar.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Osmotic gradients push bulk sap source-to-sink.
  • Water cycles phloem-to-xylem completing loops.

Chapter 9 · Topic 32

Loading

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyF. Phloem TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phloem loading (source sieve entry) runs active proton-sucrose symport concentrating sugars 2-3 fold - apoplastic (via walls, most crops) or symplastic (through plasmodesmata, some trees) routes. Loading drops source water potential, drawing xylem water in, building export pressure. Virus yellows plus herbicides blocking loading starve plants despite green leaves - transport failure mimics deficiency.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Active sugar pumping into sieve tubes builds export pressure.
  • Apoplastic (pumped) versus symplastic (diffused) routes.
Remember
  • Loading failure starves plants with green leaves intact.

Chapter 9 · Topic 33

Unloading

Transport in PlantsPlant PhysiologyF. Phloem TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phloem unloading (sink sieve exit) runs symplastic diffusion (growing tips) or apoplastic pumping (storage organs, seeds) - sugars exit, water returns to xylem, pressure drops sustaining inflow. Transfer cells (wall ingrowths amplifying membrane area) boost unloading in seeds and nodes. Cold-blocked stems or boron lack starve sinks despite loaded sources - delivery, not supply, limits yield.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sieve exit to sink cells; pressure drops sustain inflow.
  • Transfer-cell ingrowths amplify seed/node delivery.

Criteria for essentiality

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyA. Essential ElementsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Arnon-Stout essentiality criteria: element required to complete life cycle (no seeds without it), irreplaceable by another (specific function), directly involved in metabolism (not merely corrective). Hydroponics (soilless culture in defined solutions) proves essentiality by omission - 17 elements qualify. Aeration plus pH plus light controlled; deficiency symptoms diagnose field shortages.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Required for life cycle, irreplaceable, directly metabolic.
  • Hydroponic omission cultures prove essentiality.

Macronutrients

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyA. Essential ElementsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Macronutrients (needed over 10 mmol/kg dry matter): N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S - plus C, H, O from air-water. Nitrogen builds proteins-nucleic acids; phosphorus builds ATP-membranes; potassium gates stomata plus enzymes; calcium walls plus signals; magnesium centres chlorophyll; sulphur bridges proteins (cysteine, vitamins). Bulk roles in structure and energy define macro status.
NEET Snapshot:
  • N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S (plus C, H, O) needed in bulk.
  • Structure plus energy roles define macro need.
Remember
  • Macro mnemonic: NP K Ca Mg S - fertiliser bag trio plus trio.

Chapter 10 · Topic 3

Micronutrients

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyA. Essential ElementsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Micronutrients (trace needs under 10 mmol/kg): Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl, Ni - enzyme cofactors and redox players in tiny doses. Iron (cytochromes, chlorophyll synthesis), manganese (water-splitting), zinc (auxin synthesis), copper (redox enzymes), boron (sugar transport, pollen), molybdenum (nitrogenase, nitrate reductase), chlorine (water-splitting), nickel (urease). Toxic in excess - narrow sufficiency windows.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl, Ni in traces.
  • Cofactor roles; toxic beyond narrow windows.

1

Chapter 10 · Topic 4

Nitrogen

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyB. MacronutrientsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nitrogen (proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll, hormones) is the growth-limiting macro - deficiency yellows old leaves first (mobile element translocated to young growth), stunting overall. Sources: soil nitrates (nitrification), ammonium fertilisers, symbiotic fixation (Rhizobium nodules), urea sprays. Excess delays flowering (vegetative luxury) and pollutes waterways (eutrophication) - dose discipline matters.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Proteins plus nucleic acids plus chlorophyll - growth element.
  • Mobile: old leaves yellow first in deficiency.
Remember
  • Nitrogen moves to young growth - old leaves signal first.

Phosphorus

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyB. MacronutrientsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phosphorus (ATP, nucleic acids, membranes, root growth) energises metabolism - deficiency purples leaves (anthocyanin), stunts roots, delays maturity. Rock-phosphate fertilisers plus mycorrhizal delivery supply it; fixation in acidic/alkaline soils locks it (pH management unlocks). Seedlings need phosphorus most (root establishment) - starter fertilisers target early growth.
NEET Snapshot:
  • ATP plus nucleic acids plus membranes - energy element.
  • Purple leaves plus poor roots signal lack.

Potassium

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyB. MacronutrientsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Potassium (stomatal regulation, enzyme activation, osmoregulation - never built into structures) deficiency scorches leaf margins (marginal necrosis) plus weak stems. Muriate of potash fertilises; luxury consumption stores surplus harmlessly. Stomatal K+ fluxes (in opens, out closes) link potassium directly to transpiration control - drought tolerance follows potassium status.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Stomatal plus enzyme plus osmotic roles; never structural.
  • Margin scorch plus weak stems signal lack.
Remember
  • Potassium gates stomata - drought tolerance follows K status.

Calcium

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyB. MacronutrientsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Calcium (middle-lamella pectin bridges, membrane stability, second-messenger signalling, spindle function) is immobile - deficiency hits growing tips (necrosis, blossom-end rot tomatoes) since old tissues hoard it. Gypsum/lime supplies; excess raises pH locking other nutrients. Signalling spikes (cytosolic Ca2+ waves) translate stimuli to responses - wall glue plus messenger dual role.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Walls plus membranes plus signals; immobile so tips suffer first.
  • Blossom-end rot is calcium-deficiency lamella failure.

Mineral NutritionPlant PhysiologyB. MacronutrientsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Magnesium centres chlorophyll (one Mg per molecule - no magnesium, no green) plus activates Rubisco and ATPases; deficiency yellows between veins (interveinal chlorosis) of old leaves (mobile). Epsom-salt sprays correct fast; dolomite limes supply plus pH. Photosynthesis literally runs on magnesium-centred pigments - the green atom.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Chlorophyll centre plus enzyme activator; mobile element.
  • Interveinal chlorosis of old leaves signals lack.
Remember
  • One Mg per chlorophyll - green depends on magnesium.

Sulphur

Topic in Depth

Sulphur (cysteine-methionine amino acids, vitamins biotin-thiamine, coenzyme A, disulphide bridges) builds proteins plus active compounds - deficiency mimics nitrogen (pale young leaves, since sulphur is immobile unlike N). Mustard oils (pungency), garlic allicin and onion tears are sulphur chemistry. Gypsum and sulphate fertilisers supply; elemental sulphur acidifies alkaline soils usefully.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Amino acids, vitamins, CoA, disulphide bridges.
  • Immobile: young leaves pale first (unlike nitrogen).

Iron

Topic in Depth

Iron (cytochromes, ferredoxin, chlorophyll synthesis enzymes - not in chlorophyll itself) shuttles electrons in photosynthesis plus respiration; deficiency bleaches young leaves (interveinal chlorosis, immobile) since chlorophyll cannot assemble. Foliar Fe sprays bypass alkaline-soil lockup; chelated forms stay available. Chlorosis with green veins is the iron signature.

  • Young-leaf interveinal chlorosis signals lack.
Remember
  • Iron builds chlorophyll machinery but sits outside the pigment.

Topic in Depth

Manganese splits water in photosystem II (oxygen-evolving complex) plus activates decarboxylases - deficiency causes grey speck (oats), interveinal chlorosis with tiny necrotic spots. Needed in traces; excess toxic (brown spots, stunting) especially in acidic soils. Mn-Fe antagonism complicates diagnosis (excess either induces other deficiency) - balanced fertilisation matters.

  • Grey speck oats; Mn-Fe balance complicates diagnosis.

Zinc

Topic in Depth

Zinc builds auxin (tryptophan synthesis needs Zn - deficiency dwarfs via little-leaf, shortened internodes) plus stabilises ribosomes and enzymes (carbonic anhydrase). Khaira disease of rice (dusty brown spots) is classic zinc lack. Foliar zinc sulphate corrects; excess induces iron chlorosis (antagonism). Little-leaf plus rosetting diagnose field zinc shortage.

Copper

Nitrogen cycle circulates N2 (78 percent air, unusable directly) through fixation (N2 to ammonia: lightning, industry, bacteria), nitrification (ammonia to nitrite to nitrate: Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), assimilation (plants absorb nitrate/ammonium building proteins), ammonification (decomposers return organic N to ammonia), denitrification (Pseudomonas returns N2 to air, anaerobic). Biological fixation (symbiotic plus free-living) fixes comparably without fossil cost - nature Haber-Bosch at room temperature.

  • Biological fixation matches industry without fossil cost.

Deep Dive · Light to sugar in two acts

Photosynthesis splits into photochemical (photosystems II-plus-I, water photolysis, electron transport making ATP plus NADPH via cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation) and biosynthetic (Calvin C3 fixation-reduction-regeneration via RuBisCO; C4 Kranz pump concentrating CO2 via PEP carboxylase; photorespiration wasting when RuBisCO oxygenates) phases, gated by light, CO2, temperature, water and chlorophyll factors. Z-scheme electron flow plus Calvin stoichiometry plus C3-C4 comparison answer most numerical and reasoning questions.

Photosynthesis equation (6CO2 + 12H2O capturing light gives C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O) summarises water-splitting oxygenic photosynthesis - oxygen comes from water (proved by 18O labelling), not CO2. Van Niel generalised it from sulphur bacteria; Hill proved isolated chloroplasts evolve oxygen with artificial acceptors. One equation encodes energy capture, water oxidation and carbon reduction together.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Oxygen comes from water photolysis, not CO2.
  • Light energy plus water plus CO2 yield sugar plus oxygen.

Photophosphorylative ATP forms as protons rush through CF0-CF1 ATP synthase (thylakoid-embedded rotary motor) - chemiosmotic coupling. Respiration in Plants

Glycolysis, fermentation, Krebs cycle, electron transport and RQ.

Respiration in PlantsPlant PhysiologyChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

A. Glycolysis
1. Glucose breakdown2. Investment phase3. Payoff phase4. ATP5. NADH6. Pyruvate
B. Fermentation
7. Alcoholic fermentation8. Lactic acid fermentation9. ATP yield
C. Krebs Cycle
10. Acetyl-CoA11. Citrate12. Isocitrate13. Alpha-ketoglutarate14. Succinyl-CoA15. Succinate16. Fumarate17. Malate18. Oxaloacetate

Deep Dive · Glucose to ATP in stages

Respiration stages energy release: glycolysis (cytosol glucose to pyruvate, net 2 ATP plus 2 NADH; fermentation variants when oxygen absent), Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix acetyl-CoA oxidised, CO2 plus NADH/FADH2 banked, substrate-level ATP), electron transport (inner-membrane carriers pumping protons, ATP synthase cashing gradients - ~34 ATP), with RQ values (carbohydrate 1, fats below 1, proteins ~0.9, organic acids above 1) diagnosing fuel. Total aerobic yield ~36-38 ATP per glucose versus 2 in fermentation.
NEET facts:
  • Glycolysis nets 2 ATP; Krebs banks carriers; ETS pays ~34 ATP via ATP synthase.
  • RQ equals CO2 out over O2 in - fuel fingerprint (1 carbs, <1 fats).

Lactic acid fermentation (muscle sprints, Lactobacillus curd: pyruvate directly to lactate oxidising NADH, no CO2) sustains ATP bursts without oxygen - oxygen debt repaid post-exercise converting lactate back (liver Cori cycle). Curd, yoghurt, cheese, pickles, silage all run lactic bacteria; muscle burn signals lactate plus acidity. Less efficient than aerobic (2 vs ~36 ATP) but instant and oxygen-free.

ATP yield

Respiration in PlantsPlant PhysiologyB. FermentationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fermentation ATP yield (2 per glucose, glycolysis only) versus aerobic (~36-38 via Krebs plus ETS) explains oxygen payoff - 18-fold energy multiplication for breathing. Pasteur effect (oxygen suppressing fermentation) shows cells prefer efficient routes; Crabtree effect (sugar excess fermenting despite oxygen - yeast, tumours) shows overflow exceptions. Yield gaps drive ecology (aerobes dominate energy-rich niches) and industry (aeration boosts yeast biomass, stillness brews alcohol).
NEET Snapshot:
  • 2 (fermentation) versus ~36 (aerobic) - oxygen multiplies 18-fold.
  • Pasteur suppresses fermentation; Crabtree overflows despite oxygen.

Acetyl-CoA

Acetyl-CoA (2C activated acetate on coenzyme A) is Krebs entry ticket - made from pyruvate (dehydrogenase complex, CO2 plus NADH released), fatty beta-oxidation, and amino-acid breakdown - converging all fuels into one cycle. Thiamine (B1) plus lipoate cofactors run the complex; arsenic poisons lipoate (toxic mechanism). Acetyl-CoA also builds fatty acids and steroids when energy suffices - hub between burning and building.

  • Thiamine-dependent gateway; arsenic poisons it.

Respiration in PlantsPlant PhysiologyC. Krebs CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Citrate (6C first Krebs product: acetyl-CoA plus oxaloacetate via citrate synthase) starts cycle turns - exported for fatty synthesis when abundant (ATP-citrate lyase), chelating metal ions, flavouring foods (citrus sour). Aconitase rearranges it to isocitrate (via cis-aconitate) for oxidation. Fluoroacetate poison (1080) jams aconitase making fluorocitrate - Krebs-blocking pesticide mechanism.
NEET Snapshot:
  • 6C cycle entry; exported for fat synthesis when abundant.
  • Fluoroacetate jams aconitase lethally.

Isocitrate (6C rearranged citrate) undergoes first oxidative decarboxylation (isocitrate dehydrogenase: CO2 out, NADH banked, alpha-ketoglutarate formed) - rate-limiting, ADP-activated (energy need accelerates), NADH-inhibited. First CO2 exhaled per turn; first NADH earned. Bacterial isocitrate lyase shortcuts to glyoxylate cycle (seeds converting fats to sugars) - plants and microbes bypass decarboxylations when building from fat.
NEET Snapshot:
  • First decarboxylation: CO2 out, NADH banked, rate-limiting.
  • Glyoxylate shortcut bypasses in fat-to-sugar seeds.
Remember
  • ADP activates, NADH inhibits - energy-state throttle.

Also transamination hub (glutamate family amino acids) linking carbon-nitrogen metabolism. Second CO2 exit; second NADH deposit - cycle progressively oxidises acetyl carbons to air.

  • Second decarboxylation; transamination hub to amino acids.
  • Thiamine-dependent; arsenic blocks it.

Succinyl-CoA (4C high-energy thioester) drives substrate-level phosphorylation (succinyl-CoA synthetase making GTP/ATP - Krebs only direct ATP) while becoming succinate. Heme synthesis starts here too (succinyl-CoA plus glycine). Energy captured without gradients - single GTP per turn (~2 per glucose). Thioester bond energy pays directly - rare direct ATP in oxidative stages.

Malonate (competitive inhibitor) blocks it (classic inhibition demo); TTFA and carboxin (fungicides) target Complex II. Membrane-embedded step links cycle to chain physically.

Hydration readies the final oxidation regenerating oxaloacetate - cycle nearly closed.

Malate (4C) oxidises to oxaloacetate via malate dehydrogenase (NADH banked - final carrier deposit) regenerating the acceptor for next acetyl-CoA - cycle closes. Cytosolic malate shuttles (malate-aspartate) carry glycolytic NADH into mitochondria (bonus ATP accounting). C4 plants decarboxylate malate in bundle sheaths (pump mechanism); CAM plants store it nightly (acid taste dawn). Malate multitasks across pathways.

Oxaloacetate

Respiration in PlantsPlant PhysiologyC. Krebs CycleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Oxaloacetate (4C acceptor) condenses with incoming acetyl-CoA restarting cycles - catalytic (regenerated, never consumed net) yet rate-setting (availability gates Krebs speed). Also transaminates to aspartate (amino-acid family), feeds gluconeogenesis (PEP carboxykinase exit), and accepts glycolytic overflow. Low oxaloacetate stalls acetyl entry (ketogenesis shunts excess acetyl to ketones in starvation/diabetes) - acceptor shortage reroutes metabolism.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Catalytic acceptor regenerated each turn; gates cycle speed.
  • Shortage shunts acetyl to ketone bodies.
Remember
  • Oxaloacetate never consumed net - true catalyst of Krebs.

Electron carriers

Respiration in PlantsPlant PhysiologyD. Electron TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Electron carriers (NADH, FADH2 from Krebs plus glycolysis) donate to inner-membrane complexes I (NADH dehydrogenase), II (succinate dehydrogenase), III (cytochrome bc1), IV (cytochrome oxidase to oxygen) - energy dropping stepwise pumped as protons (I, III, IV pump; II bypasses). Ubiquinone shuttles (mobile), cytochrome c ferries (peripheral) connect fixed complexes. Poisons target precisely: rotenone (I), cyanide/CO (IV) - murder by carrier blockade.

  • NADH/FADH2 donate to complexes I-IV ending at oxygen.
  • I, III, IV pump protons; II feeds quinones pumpless.

Proton gradient

Respiration in PlantsPlant PhysiologyD. Electron TransportStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Proton gradient (intermembrane H+ high from complexes I, III, IV pumping; matrix low) stores electron energy as electrochemical potential (~200 mV) - Mitchell chemiosmotic theory (Nobel) replacing chemical-intermediate hypotheses. Uncouplers (DNP, thermogenin brown fat) leak protons making heat instead of ATP (hibernators, newborns warm this way). Gradient, not electron flow itself, is the conserved currency - flow without pumping wastes as heat.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Pumped protons store electron energy as gradient.
  • Uncouplers leak heat instead of ATP (brown fat).
Remember
  • Gradient is currency; flow is income - store before spending.

Topic in Depth

ATP synthase (F0 proton channel plus F1 catalytic head, rotary motor) makes ~3 ATP per NADH-worth of protons (P/O ratio ~2.5 NADH, ~1.5 FADH2) - Boyer binding-change mechanism (rotation drives conformational synthesis) plus Walker crystallography (Nobel pair). Oligomycin plugs F0 stopping ATP (respiration continues idling); IF1 inhibits reverse hydrolysis. Nanomotor spinning hundreds of revolutions per second powers life.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Rotary motor cashing proton gradients into ATP.
  • P/O ~2.5 (NADH), ~1.5 (FADH2) set yields.

Oxidative phosphorylation couples electron flow to ATP synthesis via gradients - ~34 ATP per glucose (NADH shuttles plus FADH2 plus Krebs GTP tally to ~36-38 total with glycolysis) versus 2 fermentative. Efficiency ~40 percent (rest heat); P/O ratios quantify (mitochondrial poisons, uncouplers, ADP availability regulate). Chemiosmosis unifies photosynthesis (thylakoid) and respiration (mitochondrial) ATP making - one principle, two organelles.

  • Chemiosmosis unifies chloroplast and mitochondrial synthesis.

Germinating starchy seeds read 1; succulents at night read 0 (acid making without gas exchange). RQ 1 diagnoses carbohydrate burning.

Germinating oily seeds (groundnut, mustard) read ~0.7; hibernators meter fat RQ through winter. High ATP per gram reflects same reduced chemistry - oxygen debt repaid on burning.

Plant Growth and Development

Growth phases, five hormone classes, photoperiodism and vernalisation.

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

A. Growth
1. Growth definition2. Growth phases3. Meristematic phase4. Elongation phase5. Maturation phase6. Arithmetic growth7. Geometric growth
B. Differentiation
8. Differentiation9. Dedifferentiation10. Redifferentiation
C. Plant Growth Regulators
11. Auxin12. Cell elongation13. Apical dominance14. Root initiation15. Tropisms16. Gibberellins17. Stem elongation18. Bolting19. Seed germination20. Breaking dormancy21. Cytokinins22. Cell division23. Shoot formation24. Delay of senescence25. Ethylene26. Fruit ripening27. Abscission28. Senescence29. ABA30. Dormancy31. Stomatal closure32. Stress response
D. Photoperiodism
33. Short-day plants34. Long-day plants35. Day-neutral plants36. Critical photoperiod
E. Vernalisation
37. Low-temperature treatment38. Flowering response

Deep Dive · Hormones run plant lives

Growth runs phases (meristematic division, elongation expansion, maturation differentiation; arithmetic linear versus geometric S-curves) plus plasticity (differentiation-dedifferentiation-redifferentiation) under five hormone classes - auxin (elongation, dominance, rooting, tropisms), gibberellins (stem growth, bolting, germination), cytokinins (division, shoots, youth), ethylene (ripening, abscission, senescence), ABA (dormancy, stomatal closure, stress) - timed by photoperiod (short/long/neutral days measuring nights via phytochrome-florigen) and vernalisation (winter cold licensing spring blooms).
NEET facts:
  • Auxin-cytokinin ratios programme tissue culture (high auxin roots, high cytokinin shoots).
  • Short-day plants measure long nights; vernalisation is winter-cold flowering license.
Fig: Five hormones: auxin elongates, GA stretches, cytokinin divides, ethylene ripens, ABA rests.

Chapter 13 · Topic 1

Growth definition

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyA. GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Growth (irreversible mass increase by cell division plus enlargement) differs from mere swelling - plants grow indeterminately lifelong via meristems (open growth), animals determinately to maturity. Measured as length, area, volume, weight or cell counts; auxanometers track stem elongation live. Growth needs water (turgor expansion), oxygen (respiration energy), nutrients, optimal temperature and light - all five limiting jointly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Irreversible division-plus-enlargement increase.
  • Plants indeterminate; animals determinate.

Chapter 13 · Topic 2

Growth phases

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyA. GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Growth phases sequence meristematic (dividing, dense protoplasm), elongation (vacuolation plus wall loosening expanding hundreds-fold), maturation (differentiation into tissues, growth stopping) - root-tip zones display all three linearly. Sigmoid (lag-log-stationary) whole-organ curves sum countless cells passing phases asynchronously. Phase-specific hormones (auxin elongates, ABA matures) gate transitions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Divide, elongate, differentiate - three zones in order.
  • Root tips show all phases spatially separated.
Remember
  • Sigmoid growth curves sum asynchronous cellular phases.

Meristematic phase

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyA. GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Meristematic phase packs dense dividing cells (apical tips, cambium rings, intercalary bases) - thin walls, big nuclei, no vacuoles, high respiration. Cell number multiplies exponentially here; all later growth builds on these divisions. Cancer-like uncontrolled plant tumours (crown gall, Agrobacterium T-DNA) hijack meristematic programmes - division without differentiation plans.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dense dividing cells with big nuclei, no vacuoles.
  • Exponential number multiplication at tips and cambia.

Elongation phase

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyA. GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Elongation phase expands new cells hundreds-fold via vacuolation (water influx) plus wall loosening (expansins, acid growth - auxin acidifies walls activating loosening) - root hairs zone and shoot stretches demonstrate. Turgor pressure drives expansion against yielding walls; cellulose microfibril orientation decides direction (transverse hoops elongate lengthwise). Gibberellins stretch stems; dwarf mutants fail elongation, not division.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Vacuolation plus wall loosening expand cells massively.
  • Auxin acid-growth loosens; turgor pushes outward.
Remember
  • Expansins loosen walls; turgor inflates cells directionally.

Chapter 13 · Topic 5

Maturation phase

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyA. GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Maturation phase differentiates expanded cells (walls thicken, plastids develop, hairs emerge, vessels lignify) ending growth permanently - root-hair zone, xylem vessels, cork layers all mature here. ABA promotes maturation-dormancy programmes; differentiation follows position, not lineage (regeneration reprogrammes). Mature tissues rarely divide (cambium and wound callus excepted) - growth story concludes in specialisation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Differentiation ends growth; walls thicken, functions fix.
  • Position, not lineage, decides mature fate.

Arithmetic growth

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyA. GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Arithmetic growth adds constant cells per time (one daughter divides, one differentiates - root elongation at constant rate) graphing linear length-versus-time lines. Rate (dL/dt) stays constant; size accumulates steadily. Root tips and early embryos approximate arithmetic phases before switching geometric. Linear growth suits steady extension organs - predictable millimetres per day regardless of size.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Constant cells per time; linear growth curve.
  • One divides, one differentiates - steady addition.
Remember

Geometric growth

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyA. GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Geometric (exponential) growth multiplies (both daughters divide - early embryos, microbes, unchecked tumours) graphing J-curves then S-curves as resources cap (logistic: lag, log, stationary phases). Grand period of growth (total time to mature size) sums exponential phases. Crop modelling (logistic yield curves) and bacterial counts use geometric maths - doubling populations outrun arithmetic additions explosively.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Both daughters divide; J then S curves; resources cap.
  • Embryos, microbes and tumours grow geometrically.

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyB. DifferentiationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Differentiation specialises cells structurally-functionally (tracheids lignify dead tubes, sieve elements lose nuclei, guard cells shape pores) via selective gene expression - same genome, different active sets. Position signals (auxin gradients, mechanical stress) assign fates, not lineage clocks. Totipotent parenchyma retains full programmes (tissue culture regenerates whole plants); animal cells mostly lock fates permanently.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Position signals assign fates; totipotency preserves options.
Remember
  • Differentiation is selective gene expression, not gene loss.

Dedifferentiation

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyB. DifferentiationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dedifferentiation reverts mature cells to dividing state - cork cambium from cortex/parenchyma, wound callus from surrounding tissues, graft unions bridging stocks and scions. Auxin plus wound signals (oligosaccharins) unlock division programmes; Agrobacterium hijacks it into crown galls. Plants dedifferentiate routinely (regeneration superpower); animals rarely (salamander limbs excepted) - plasticity kingdom gap.

  • Wound plus auxin signals unlock division programmes.
Remember
  • Grafting succeeds on dedifferentiating wound callus.

Redifferentiation commits dedifferentiated cells to new fates - callus to tracheids/vessels (xylem), to roots/shoots in culture (auxin-cytokinin ratios decide: high auxin roots, high cytokinin shoots, balanced callus), wound periderm sealing injuries. Skoog-Miller hormone ratios programme tissue-culture morphogenesis commercially (micropropagation clones elites). Dedifferentiation unlocks, redifferentiation reassigns - plasticity round trip.

Auxin (IAA - indole acetic acid, first discovered hormone: Darwin phototropism, Boysen-Jensen, Went oat-curvature experiments) is the growth master - cell elongation (acid growth), apical dominance, root initiation (cuttings), tropisms (phototropism, geotropism via lateral redistribution), parthenocarpy, abscission prevention. Auxin elongates via acid growth: proton pumps acidify walls (expansins loosen cellulose networks), potassium plus water enter, turgor expands cells directionally (transverse microfibrils channel lengthwise growth). Apical dominance (terminal bud suppressing laterals via downward auxin) shapes trees (excurrent pines) versus bushes; decapitation (pruning, hedging, tea plucking) releases laterals into bushy growth. Cytokinins oppose (promote laterals); strigolactones reinforce suppression (branching mutants reveal). Orchardists balance dominance (leader protection) against branching (fruiting wood) - hormone management sculpts canopies.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Cytokinins oppose; strigolactones reinforce suppression.
Remember

Tropisms

Plant Growth and DevelopmentPlant PhysiologyC. Plant Growth RegulatorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Tropisms are directional growth responses: phototropism (shoots to light, roots away - auxin redistribution), geotropism (roots down positive, shoots up negative - statolith gravity sensing, auxin-cytokinin mediation), hydrotropism (roots to water), thigmotropism (tendrils coil on touch), chemotropism (pollen tubes to ovules). Nastic movements (Mimosa fold, stomatal) ignore direction - tropic grows toward/away, nastic merely reacts.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Directional growth toward/away stimuli (tropic) vs direction-free (nastic).
  • Auxin redistribution mediates most tropisms.

Anther to embryo sac, pollination, double fertilisation and special concepts.

Deep Dive · Flower to fruit in double fusion

Sexual reproduction runs anther (microsporangia, sporogenous tissue, microsporogenesis to 2-3-celled pollen with exine-intine walls plus germ pores) and ovule (megasporangium nucellus, integuments, funicle-chalaza-micropyle orientation, megasporogenesis to 7-celled 8-nucleate monosporic embryo sac with egg apparatus, central cell and antipodals) tracks; pollination modes (autogamy, geitonogamy, xenogamy; wind, water, insect vectors) deliver; double fertilisation (syngamy plus triple fusion) launches endosperm, embryogenesis, seeds and fruits; apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy bend rules agriculturally.
NEET facts:
  • Typical embryo sac: 7 cells, 8 nuclei, monosporic (Polygonum type).
  • Double fertilisation (syngamy plus triple fusion) is angiosperm-exclusive.
Fig: Seven cells, eight nuclei: egg apparatus micropylar, antipodals chalazal, central cell between.

Topic in Depth

Flowers are compressed reproductive shoots - pedicel stalk, thalamus base, four whorls (calyx protection, corolla advertisement, androecium male, gynoecium female). Complete (all whorls) versus incomplete; bisexual versus unisexual; actinomorphic versus zygomorphic - combinations classify every bloom. Thalamus internodes (anthophore, androphore, gynophore) space advanced flowers. Angiosperm dominance rides flower-pollinator coevolution.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Four whorls on thalamus; completeness, sexuality, symmetry classify.
  • Flowers are shoots specialised for sex.

Topic in Depth

Reproductive organs divide labour: androecium (stamens manufacturing pollen - filament positions, anthers produce) and gynoecium (carpels housing ovules - stigma receives, style conducts, ovary protects). Unisexual flowers split them across blooms/plants (maize monoecious, papaya dioecious); bisexual combines. Position (hypo-, peri-, epigynous ovaries) records thalamus evolution. Organ number-fusion predicts fruit architecture.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Androecium makes pollen; gynoecium houses ovules.
  • Ovary position (superior to inferior) tracks floral evolution.
Remember

Stamens (microsporophylls) contain filament stalks positioning anthers plus anther lobes manufacturing pollen. Counts vary (mustard 6 tetradynamous, pea 9+1 diadelphous, sunflower syngenesious) diagnosing families; attachment (basifixed, dorsifixed, versatile grasses) tunes dispersal; sterile staminodes advertise. Filament vascular traces feed developing pollen; dehiscence slits release at maturity.

  • Versatile anthers dangle for wind pollination.

Topic in Depth

Carpels (megasporophylls) contain ovary (ovule chamber) plus style (tube path) plus stigma (receptive landing). Numbers one (pea) to many (lotus); free apocarpous (aggregate fruits) versus fused syncarpous (compound ovaries, unified fruits). Stigma forms match pollination (feathery wind, sticky insect). Carpel theory (folded-leaf homologues) unifies flower diversity - pea pod suture shows folding visibly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Ovary-style-stigma units; free or fused decide fruits.
  • Feathery stigmas catch wind; sticky catch insects.
Remember

Topic in Depth

Anthers (usually dithecous two-lobed, four microsporangia; Malvaceae monothecous) manufacture pollen: sporogenous tissue meioses to microspores maturing to 2-3-celled grains; tapetum nurses plus coats exine; dehiscence slits (longitudinal, transverse, porous Solanaceae buzz-pollinated) release at maturity. Dithecous-four-sporangia is textbook standard; deviations diagnose families.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dithecous lobes, four sporangia, tapetum nurses, slits release.
  • Dehiscence mode matches pollinator mechanics.

Topic in Depth

Microsporangia (pollen sacs, four per dithecous anther) house sporogenous cells undergoing meiosis into microspore tetrads. Wall layers (epidermis, endothecium with fibrous thickenings springing dehiscence, middle layers, tapetum) each serve release. Archesporial origin plus simultaneous/successive cytokinesis patterns classify development microscopically. Sac number (four standard) plus wall behaviour define anther function.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Four sacs per anther; wall layers feed then open.
  • Endothecium thickenings spring dehiscence slits.

Topic in Depth

Sporogenous tissue (archesporial derivatives) divides into pollen mother cells undergoing meiosis - each yielding tetrad microspores. Dense cytoplasm, large nuclei mark sporogenous cells; tapetal neighbours nurse them. Quantity (massive anthers) ensures pollen surplus for wasteful pollination odds. All male gametophytes trace to sporogenous founders.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Meiocyte founders yielding tetrad microspores.
  • Dense active cells surrounded by nursing tapetum.

Microsporogenesis

Topic in Depth

Microsporogenesis (microspore formation via meiosis in anthers) runs simultaneous cytokinesis (furrows after both divisions - most dicots) or successive (walls after each - monocots); tetrad arrangements (tetrahedral, isobilateral, decussate, linear) classify groups. Callose walls isolate meiocytes then dissolve releasing microspores. Each microspore mitoses into 2-3-celled pollen - gametophyte generation begins.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Meiotic tetrad formation; simultaneous or successive walls.
  • Callose isolates meiocytes then frees microspores.
Remember
  • Tetrad geometry (tetrahedral etc.) classifies groups.

Topic in Depth

Pollen grains are male gametophytes in sporopollenin armour - vegetative cell (tube growth) plus generative cell (dividing to two male gametes: 3-celled shed advanced, 2-celled primitive), sculptured exine (spines, pores identifying species - palynology), germ pores as tube exits. Viability spans minutes (grasses) to months (stored); allergenic proteins trigger hay fever. Pollen banks preserve breeding lines; bee bread feeds hives.

  • Exine sculpture identifies species; pores exit tubes.
Remember
  • Sporopollenin resists acids and time - fossils preserve exines.

Topic in Depth

Pollen walls layer exine (outer sporopollenin - sculptured, decay-proof, allergenic proteins) over intine (inner pectin-cellulose, thin). Exine patterns (spines, reticulations, pores/furrows) identify taxa palynologically and filter compatible stigmas; intine grows tubes through germ pores. Fossil exines date strata; forensic pollen traces locations. Wall chemistry (toughest organic) outlasts parent plants millennia.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Exine armour (sporopollenin) over intine (pectin-cellulose).
  • Sculpture identifies; pores exit tubes; fossils persist.

Exine

Topic in Depth

Exine (outer pollen wall of sporopollenin) sculpts species signatures - spines (sunflower), reticulations, wings (pine sacci floating), pores and furrows (germination exits plus harmomegathy volume regulation). Intine (inner pectin-cellulose) grows tubes. Exine resists acids, heat and time (fossil pollen dates rocks; allergies persist in dust). Palynology reads exines like fingerprints.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sculptured sporopollenin armour with pores/furrows.
  • Fossil exines date strata; airborne exines trigger allergies.
Remember
  • Pine sacci wings float pollen on wind.

Topic in Depth

Intine (inner pollen wall of pectin-cellulose) grows pollen tubes through germ pores - thin, extensible, enzymatically active (cutinases digest stigmas). Thicker under pores (tube exit ramps); continuous with tube walls during growth. While exine protects outside, intine works inside - division of wall labour. Compatible pollination hydrates intine first (stigma signals prime tubes).

  • Hydration activates intine for tube emergence.
Remember
  • Intine grows; exine guards - wall labour divided.

Topic in Depth

Germ pores (thin exine gaps: porate round, colpate furrowed, colporate combined) exit pollen tubes - numbers/positions classify (monocot single pore, dicot three furrows, grass single annular). Harmomegathy (volume folding at pores) survives desiccation. Incompatible stigmas reject at pores (sporophytic self-incompatibility acts here). Pore patterns identify taxa palynologically.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Thin exine gaps exiting tubes; numbers classify groups.
  • Monocot one pore; dicot three furrows typically.

Topic in Depth

Pollen viability (germination capacity) spans minutes (grasses, cereals - sow fresh), hours-days (most), months (stored dry-cold; banked lines last years). Temperature, humidity and UV kill; desiccation plus cold preserve (pollen banks at -20C). Breeding schedules morning anthesis collections; allergy seasons follow viability plus wind - counts forecast sneezing.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Dry-cold banks preserve breeding lines for years.

Ovules (megasporangia wrapped in integuments on funiculus stalks) house embryo sacs - anatropous (inverted, micropyle facing placenta - commonest), orthotropous (straight), campylotropous (curved), hemianatropous types orient micropyle-chalaza axes. Topic in Depth

Nucellus (megasporangial tissue surrounding embryo sacs) nourishes developing female gametophytes - consumed during growth (thin tenuinucellate) or persisting as perisperm food (beet, pepper, water lily). Adventive embryos sprout from nucellus in polyembryonic citrus/mango (maternal clones via seeds). Endosperm plus perisperm dual foods occur where nucellus persists - double provisioning.

Integuments (ovule coats: two unitegmic? no - bitegmic two in dicots, unitegmic one in many monocots/sympetalous) become seed coats (testa outer protective, tegmen inner thin) after fertilisation - micropyle left open. Arils (litchi flesh, mace spice) and caruncles (castor) are integument outgrowths (dispersal bribes). Coats armour embryos; micropyles manage water.

Length and curvature orient ovules (anatropous bending pivots on funicles); funicular outgrowths (arils) bribe dispersers. Seed-stalk detachment scars (hilum) identify seed orientation permanently - bean-eye marks funicle history.

Chalaza (ovule base opposite micropyle, where integuments plus nucellus join) anchors vascular entry and orients embryo-sac polarity (antipodals cluster chalazally, egg apparatus micropylarly). Chalazogamy (tube entry via chalaza - Casuarina) bypasses micropyles exceptionally. Chalazal end marks food-supply pole; micropylar end marks tube-entry pole - ovule geography in two poles.

Micropyle

Topic in Depth

Micropyle (integument gap at ovule tip) admits pollen tubes to embryo sacs (porogamy usual; chalazogamy/mesogamy exceptions), later admitting germination water and seedling radicles. Persistent micropyles (pea water entry) versus sealed ones time germination. Tube guidance (synergid attractants) targets micropyles precisely - millimetre accuracy over centimetre journeys.

Functional megaspore mitoses into embryo sacs - female gametophyte generation begins with survivor selection.

Functional megaspore (surviving chalazal cell) enlarges, vacuolates and mitoses thrice into 8-nucleate embryo sacs (Polygonum) - free-nuclear divisions then walling into 7 cells. Degenerate sisters nourish nothing (programmed death); survivor monopolises nucellar support. Megaspore mitoses (not meiosis - already haploid) build female gametophytes - mitotic expansion of meiotic products.

Monosporic embryo sacs (Polygonum type - single functional megaspore) dominate angiosperms: 3 mitoses yield 8 nuclei walled into 7 cells (egg apparatus 3, central 1 binucleate, antipodals 3). Bisporic/tetrasporic types (Allium, Fritillaria, Adoxa, Plumbago variations) distribute nuclei differently with fewer mitoses. Monosporic standard simplifies teaching; variants test advanced understanding - count survivors to classify types.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Single-spore origin; 3 mitoses; 7 cells 8 nuclei standard.
  • Bi/tetrasporic variants use more survivors, fewer mitoses.

Synergids (paired micropylar helpers flanking eggs) attract tubes (calcium-peptide signals), receive discharge (one degenerates), and nourish early embryos - hooked filiform thickenings maximise exchange. Persistent synergids (many) versus ephemeral (grasses) vary lifespan. Attractant mutants miss tubes proving chemical guidance - helpers, not bystanders, in fertilisation logistics.

Egg cell (female gamete in apparatus centre, wall thinned toward synergids for fusion) fuses with one male gamete (syngamy) forming diploid zygote - first cell of sporophyte generation. Haploid maternal genome plus haploid paternal make diploid offspring; cytoplasm mostly maternal (paternal mitochondria excluded - maternal inheritance of organelle DNA). Egg quiescence (metabolic quiet) awaits fertilisation wake-up.

Remember

Central cell (large binucleate sac centre: 2 polar nuclei pre-fused to secondary nucleus) receives second male gamete (triple fusion) forming triploid primary endosperm nucleus - food tissue founder. Vacuolated, metabolically primed (starch, enzymes ready); fertilisation triggers endosperm proliferation outpacing embryos initially. Central-cell fate (endosperm vs perisperm supplements) decides seed food architecture.

Polar nuclei (two central-cell nuclei, upper plus lower, fusing pre- or post-fertilisation into secondary nucleus) contribute double maternal genomes to triploid endosperm (2 maternal + 1 paternal ratio drives imprinting - maternal excess genes express). Fusion timing varies (before tubes arrive in most; during in some). Endosperm balance number (EBN) mismatches cause seed failure in wide crosses - polar dosage matters agriculturally.

  • 2:1 maternal-paternal ratio imprints endosperm genes.
Remember

Topic in Depth

Antipodals (3 chalazal cells, sometimes multiplying to dozens in cereals) nourish early embryo sacs (transfer-cell activity) then degenerate - ephemeral helpers like synergids at opposite ends. Grass antipodals proliferate massively (wheat 20+ cells) feeding endosperm initiation. Persistent antipodals (some Ranunculaceae) photosynthesise briefly. Bottom-end support crew degenerating after service.

Autogamy

Sexual Reproduction in Flowering PlantsReproductionE. PollinationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Autogamy (self-pollination within one flower: same anther to same stigma) guarantees seed set (wheat, rice, pea - cleistogamous buds never open, chasmogamous open first) but forfeits variation (homozygosity rises, vigour falls - inbreeding depression). Devices ensuring it: homogamy (maturity together), cleistogamy (closed buds), bisexuality plus proximity. Breeders enforce selfing (bagging) purifying lines; nature mostly avoids it.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Same-flower selfing; guaranteed seeds, no variation.
  • Cleistogamy (closed buds) enforces obligate selfing.
Remember
  • Cleistogamous buds never open - forced selfing.

Sexual Reproduction in Flowering PlantsReproductionE. PollinationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Geitonogamy (pollen between flowers of one plant - functionally selfing genetically, ecologically cross-pollinating mechanically) needs vectors (bees commuting within crowns) yet yields inbred seed like autogamy. Monoecious plants (maize, cucumber) routinely geitonogamise; dichogamy/herkogamy blocks reduce it. Genetic selfing with pollinator costs - worst of both worlds unless outcrossing fails (reproductive assurance).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Genetically selfing, mechanically outcrossing - inbred yet vectored.
  • Monoecious crowns geitonogamise routinely.
Remember
  • Geitonogamy: self genes, foreign delivery.

Topic in Depth

Xenogamy (cross-pollination between different plants) maximises variation (heterozygosity, hybrid vigour) at pollination cost and uncertainty - devices promoting it: unisexuality (papaya dioecy), dichogamy (timing splits), herkogamy (spatial splits), self-incompatibility (genetic rejection), male sterility (hybrid seed industry). Breeders force xenogamy (emasculation plus bagging) crafting hybrids.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Different-plant crossing; maximum variation, maximum uncertainty.
  • Unisexuality, dichogamy, incompatibility enforce it.

Enormous pollen waste (allergies prove volumes) versus zero pollinator dependence - economy of abundance.

Pollen waterproofed (mucilage coats); stigmas unwettable; densities matched to water. Aquatic ancestry constrains few lineages to true hydrophily - most water plants keep insect pollination aerially.

Buzz pollination (Solanaceae poricidal anthers vibrated by bees), trap mechanisms (Aristolochia), lever systems (Salvia) engineer fidelity. Colour/scent/landing guides filter visitors.

Growth rates (maize centimetres per hour) rank fastest plant cell elongation. Tube bursts release two gametes plus tube nucleus into degenerating synergid - delivery complete.

Syngamy

Sexual Reproduction in Flowering PlantsReproductionF. FertilisationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Syngamy (one male gamete fusing egg into diploid zygote) restores sporophyte ploidy - plasmogamy (cytoplasm fusion) then karyogamy (nuclear fusion) sequence; maternal cytoplasm dominates (paternal mitochondria excluded - organelle maternal inheritance). Zygote sleeps briefly (suspensor pushes embryo into endosperm food) then embryogenesis patterns body axes. Syngamy plus triple fusion together constitute angiosperm double fertilisation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Gamete-plus-egg fusion restoring diploid zygote.
  • Maternal cytoplasm dominates; paternal organelles excluded.
Remember
  • Zygote sleeps while endosperm stocks food first.

Topic in Depth

Triple fusion (second male gamete fusing binucleate central cell into triploid primary endosperm nucleus) builds food tissue matched to embryos - 2 maternal plus 1 paternal genomes imprinting growth (maternal excess restrains, paternal promotes). Endosperm balance number mismatches abort wide crosses. Triple fusion is angiosperm-exclusive - gymnosperms feed from haploid gametophyte instead.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Gamete plus two polars triples into 3n food founder.
  • Imprinted 2:1 maternal-paternal ratio tunes growth.
Remember
  • Endosperm balance numbers gate wide-hybrid seeds.
