Double fertilisation

Sexual Reproduction in Flowering PlantsReproductionF. FertilisationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Double fertilisation (syngamy plus triple fusion together) is angiosperm-defining - embryo plus matched food forming only when fertilisation succeeds (no wasted provisioning of unfertilised ovules, unlike gymnosperm stockpiling). Discovered by Nawaschin (1898, lilies); confirmed across angiosperms with variations. Apomixis bypasses it (seeds without fusion); parthenocarpy skips seeds entirely - exceptions proving the double rule.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Twin fusions (embryo plus food) only on fertilisation.
  • Nawaschin 1898 discovery defines flowering plants.

Perisperm supplements in beet-pepper. Mosaic endosperm (maize variegation) visualises allele segregation - genetics visible in grains.

Embryogenesis patterns plant bodies: zygote divides transversely (apical embryo-forming cell plus basal suspensor pushing into endosperm), globular proembryo, heart stage (cotyledon bulges), torpedo (axis elongating), mature embryo (plumule-radicle-cotyledons). Suspensor funnels nutrients then dies; protoderm-ground-procambium differentiate; monocots (single cotyledon sideways) versus dicots (paired) diverge early. Polyembryony (citrus adventive) clones alongside zygotic embryos.

Seed development matures ovules: integuments harden to testa-tegmen coats, endosperm fills or yields to cotyledons, embryo matures then desiccates (water below 15 percent, metabolism suspends), dormancy programmes arm (coat, embryo, inhibitor types), dispersal structures equip (wings, hairs, flesh, hooks). Orthodox seeds dry-store decades (banks); recalcitrant seeds (cacao, oak) die drying - conservation strategies split accordingly.

Fruit signals seed maturity to dispersers - ripeness advertises readiness.

Genetics and Inheritance

Mendel laws, extensions, chromosomal basis, sex linkage and disorders.

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

Mendelian Genetics
1. Mendel experiments2. Characters3. Traits4. Dominant/recessive5. Monohybrid cross6. Dihybrid cross7. Test cross8. Back cross9. Law of dominance10. Law of segregation11. Independent assortment
Extensions of Mendelism
12. Incomplete dominance13. Codominance14. Multiple alleles15. Pleiotropy

16. Chromosome17. Gene18. Allele19. Homologous chromosomes20. Linkage21. Crossing over22. Recombination23. Sex Determination

Deep Dive · Mendel to syndromes

Genetics runs Mendel experiments (seven traits, counting ratios) through laws (dominance uniformity, segregation 3:1, assortment 9:3:3:1) and crosses (test, back) into extensions (incomplete, codominance, multiple alleles, pleiotropy) on chromosomal basis (genes on chromosomes, linkage-crossing-recombination mapping) with sex systems (XX-XY, XO, ZW-ZZ, haplodiploidy) channelling sex-linked patterns (criss-cross haemophilia, holandric Y) into disorders (Mendelian single-gene plus chromosomal Down-Turner-Klinefelter syndromes). Ratios prove laws; pedigrees diagnose modes; karyotypes confirm syndromes.
NEET facts:
  • 9:3:3:1 proves assortment; 1:2:1 (incomplete) mirrors genotypes; criss-cross proves X-linkage.
  • Down (21), Turner (XO), Klinefelter (XXY) - nondisjunction numbers to memorise.
Fig: Gametes on margins, zygotes inside - three boxes carry T, only tt stays dwarf.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio proves law of

Solution: Recombinant classes prove free shuffling of gene pairs.

Subtopics in this Chapter

Deep Dive · Every ratio and criss-cross inheritance

Ratio table - the most scoring page of genetics
CrossPhenotypic ratioMeaning
Monohybrid F2 (Tt x Tt)3 : 1 (genotypic 1:2:1)Law of segregation
Dihybrid F29 : 3 : 3 : 1Independent assortment; deviation signals linkage
Test cross (unknown x tt)1 : 1 means heterozygous; all dominant means homozygousReveals hidden genotype
Incomplete dominance (Rr pink)1 : 2 : 1 (same as genotypic)Dog flower, Mirabilis
CodominanceBoth traits visibleAB blood group, sickle-cell carriers
Linkage breaks Mendel's third law: genes on the same chromosome travel together (Morgan's Drosophila), so parental combinations exceed 50% and the 9:3:3:1 collapses. Crossing over in pachytene rescues variation by swapping segments; recombination frequency maps distance (1% = 1 map unit/centimorgan). Sex determination: XX-XY (humans - male heterogametic), ZZ-ZW (birds - female heterogametic), XX-XO (grasshopper), haplodiploidy (honeybees - males haploid from unfertilised eggs, so a drone has a grandfather but no father).
Fig: Gametes along the margins, zygotes inside - three boxes carry T (tall), only tt is dwarf.
Disorders cheat-sheet
  • Autosomal recessive: sickle-cell anaemia (GAG to GUG point mutation), thalassemia, cystic fibrosis, PKU, albinism.
  • Autosomal dominant: myotonic dystrophy. X-linked recessive: haemophilia, colour blindness (criss-cross: father to daughter to grandson).
  • Chromosomal: Down (trisomy 21), Turner (XO female), Klinefelter (XXY male).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

In a dihybrid cross the F2 phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1 is obtained because of

Solution: Mendel's law of independent assortment shuffles the two gene pairs freely; tight linkage would destroy the 9:3:3:1 pattern.

Chapter 15 · Topic 1

Mendel experiments

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mendel (1860s monastery garden, pea Pisum sativum) tracked seven contrasting traits across thousands of plants: self-pollination gave true lines, emasculation plus dusting made exact crosses, short generations plus big progeny revealed ratios. Three laws emerged purely from counting - dominance, segregation, independent assortment. Ignored till 1900 rediscovery (de Vries, Correns, Tschermak), then chromosomes supplied mechanism.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Pea advantages: selfing, easy crosses, binary traits, big families.
  • Counting thousands revealed ratios; mechanism came 35 years later.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Mendel experiments used pea because it

Solution: True lines, controlled crosses and binary traits made ratios visible.

Chapter 15 · Topic 2

Characters

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Characters are heritable features (plant height, flower colour, seed shape); Mendel tracked seven contrasting pairs. Characters transmit as factors (genes) with alternative forms (alleles); genotype (allele set) produces phenotype (observable trait) via dominance interactions. Character (height) versus trait (tall/dwarf) distinction structures every genetics problem - factor, allele and trait vocabulary must stay precise.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Character (height) versus trait (tall) - feature versus form.
  • Genotype (alleles) produces phenotype (appearance) via dominance.
Remember
  • Seven pea characters, each with two contrasting traits.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

In genetics, character versus trait means

Solution: Characters are features; traits are their alternative expressions.

Index / Genetics, Evolution and Biotech
Chapter 15 · Topic 3

Traits

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Traits are alternative character forms: tall/dwarf stems, violet/white flowers, axial/terminal positions, inflated/constricted pods, green/yellow pods, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds - Mendel seven pairs. Dominant traits appear in heterozygotes (F1 all dominant); recessive reappear in F2 (3:1). Contrasting binary traits enabled clean counting - continuous traits (height in humans) need polygenic statistics instead.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Seven contrasting pairs; dominant shows in F1, recessive returns in F2.
  • Binary traits count cleanly; continuous need statistics.

1

Solution: Unchanged segregation preserves recessives for reappearance.

Chapter 15 · Topic 4

Dominant/recessive

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dominant alleles express in heterozygotes (Tt tall), recessive only in homozygotes (tt dwarf) - dominance is expression relationship, not strength or frequency (recessive albinism persists widely; dominant Huntington stays rare). Complete dominance (pea), incomplete (pink dog-flowers), codominance (AB blood) grade expression. Dominance describes heterozygote appearance only - homozygotes show whatever they carry.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dominant shows in heterozygotes; recessive needs homozygosity.
  • Dominance is expression, not frequency or fitness.
Remember
  • Rare dominants (Huntington) vs common recessives - frequency independent.

Solution: Masked in heterozygotes, visible when paired with itself.

Chapter 15 · Topic 5

Monohybrid cross

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Monohybrid cross (Tt x Tt): F1 all tall (dominance masks t), F2 phenotypic 3:1 with genotypic 1:2:1 (TT:Tt:tt) - the hidden recessive reappears, proving alleles separate unchanged (law of segregation: gametes carry one allele each). Punnett squares place gametes on margins and read zygotes inside; three of four boxes carry T, only tt is dwarf. Every ratio question starts here.

Topic in Depth · Monohybrid cross

Monohybrid Tt x Tt delivers the founding ratio: F1 all tall (dominance masks t), F2 three tall to one dwarf phenotypically with 1:2:1 TT:Tt:tt genotypically (segregation preserves alleles unchanged through gametes). Punnett squares place parental gametes on margins and read zygotes inside - three of four boxes carry T, only tt shows dwarf. Every ratio problem reduces to this template; dihybrid is just two monohybrids running simultaneously.
NEET Snapshot:
  • F2 3:1 phenotype, 1:2:1 genotype - segregation made visible.
  • Hidden recessive reappears unchanged - alleles do not blend.
Remember
  • Punnett margins are gametes; interiors are zygotes - read accordingly.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Genotypic ratio of monohybrid F2 is

Solution: TT:Tt:tt = 1:2:1 underlies the 3:1 dominant appearance.

Chapter 15 · Topic 6

Dihybrid cross

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dihybrid cross (YyRr x YyRr): F2 phenotypic 9:3:3:1 - 9 round-yellow (both dominant), 3 round-green, 3 wrinkled-yellow, 1 wrinkled-green - proving genes on different chromosomes assort independently (law of independent assortment). New combinations (round-green, wrinkled-yellow) appear that neither parent showed. Tight linkage collapses this ratio toward parental types - the standard signal that assortment failed.

Linkage and crossing over

Sutton–Boveri chromosomal theory: genes sit on chromosomes, explaining Mendel. Linkage (Morgan, Drosophila): genes on the same chromosome travel together; strength falls as distance rises. 1% recombination = 1 map unit (centimorgan) — the basis of genetic maps. Crossing over (pachytene) breaks linkage and creates new combinations.
Morgan student Sturtevant built the first genetic map as an undergraduate: recombination percentages between Drosophila genes became map distances (1% = 1 map unit). Double crossovers underestimate long distances, so far-apart genes can appear unlinked (>50% recombination looks like independent assortment). Cytological proof came from maize (Creighton and McClintock) showing physical exchange of chromosome segments exactly where crossing over was predicted - genetics met microscopy.

Topic in Depth · Dihybrid cross

Dihybrid YyRr x YyRr yields 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green - two parental plus two recombinant classes proving genes on different chromosomes assort independently into gametes (YR, Yr, yR, yr equally). New combinations neither parent showed are the recombination signature. Tight linkage collapses the ratio toward parental types; crossing over partially restores recombinants - the bridge from Mendel to Morgan mapping.
NEET Snapshot:
  • 9:3:3:1 with two new recombinant classes = independent assortment.
  • Linkage destroys the ratio; crossing over partly rescues it.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

New phenotypic combinations in dihybrid F2 arise due to

Solution: Free shuffling of two gene pairs manufactures round-green and wrinkled-yellow classes.

Chapter 15 · Topic 7

Test cross

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Test cross (unknown dominant phenotype x homozygous recessive): all dominant offspring means the parent was homozygous; a 1:1 mix means it was heterozygous. Breeders use it to purify lines; examiners use it to test whether you can work ratios backwards. A back cross is any cross back to a parent - test cross is the special back cross to the recessive parent.

Related Diagram · Test cross reading

Fig: Cross to recessive and read the children: uniform means pure, half-half means hybrid.

Topic in Depth · Test cross

Test cross (unknown dominant phenotype crossed to homozygous recessive) reads hidden genotype from children: all dominant means parent was homozygous; 1:1 dominant-to-recessive means heterozygous. Breeders purify lines this way; examiners test reverse-ratio thinking the same way. It is the special back cross to the recessive parent - the only cross where offspring phenotypes directly spell parental genotype.
NEET Snapshot:
  • All dominant children = homozygous parent. 1:1 = heterozygous parent.
  • Test cross is back cross to the recessive parent specifically.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

A tall plant crossed to dwarf gives 1:1 tall:dwarf. Its genotype is

Solution: Equal segregation to recessive reveals heterozygosity - the test-cross verdict.

Chapter 15 · Topic 8

Back cross

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Back cross means crossing F1 (or any progeny) back to either parent: to the dominant parent it hides genotypes (all dominant phenotypes), to the recessive parent it becomes a test cross revealing them (1:1 if heterozygous). Plant breeders backcross repeatedly to transfer one desired gene (e.g. disease resistance) into an elite variety while recovering its genome - each generation halves the donor remainder.

Topic in Depth · Back cross

Back cross means progeny crossed back to either parent: to the dominant parent all children look dominant (genotypes hidden); to the recessive parent it becomes a test cross (genotypes revealed 1:1 if heterozygous). Breeders backcross repeatedly to transfer one desired gene (disease resistance) into elite varieties - each generation halves donor genome remainder while keeping the target gene. After 6-7 backcrosses the line is ~99 percent elite plus the new trait.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Back to dominant hides; back to recessive reveals (test cross).
  • Repeated backcrossing moves one gene into elite backgrounds.
Remember
  • Test cross is a back cross; not every back cross is a test cross.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Repeated backcrossing in plant breeding is used to

Solution: Each backcross halves unwanted donor genome while retaining the target gene.

Law of dominance

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Law of dominance: of two contrasting alleles, only dominant expresses in heterozygotes (F1 uniformity - all Tt tall); recessive hidden yet transmitted. Exceptions (incomplete, codominance) refine expression without breaking segregation underneath. Dominance operates per gene pair independently - dihybrid F1 shows both dominants simultaneously. F1 uniformity is dominance proof; F2 3:1 reappearance proves segregation behind it.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Heterozygotes show dominant trait only (F1 uniformity).
  • Hidden recessives transmit silently to reappear in F2.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Law of dominance is proven by

Solution: Heterozygote uniformity shows dominant masking directly.

Chapter 15 · Topic 10

Law of segregation

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mendel (pea, 7 contrasting traits): law of dominance, law of segregation (alleles separate in gametes) and law of independent assortment (dihybrid). Monohybrid F₂: phenotypic 3:1, genotypic 1:2:1; dihybrid F₂ phenotypic 9:3:3:1. Test cross (unknown × homozygous recessive) reveals genotype: 1:1 means heterozygous.
NEET facts:
  • Pea is ideal: self-pollinating, short life cycle, clear contrasting traits.
  • Failure of 9:3:3:1 signals linkage between the gene pairs.

Deeper Understanding · Mendel seven traits decoded

Mendel tracked exactly seven pea traits: stem height (tall/dwarf), flower colour (violet/white) and position (axial/terminal), pod shape (inflated/constricted) and colour (green/yellow), seed shape (round/wrinkled) and colour (yellow/green). Pea suited him perfectly: self-pollinating (true lines), easy emasculation + dusting for crosses, short generation, and large progeny for ratios. His laws waited 35 years because chromosomes and meiosis were unknown - Sutton and Boveri later supplied the physical basis (chromosomal theory).

Topic in Depth · Laws of inheritance

Three laws ladder complexity: dominance (F1 shows dominant allele only), segregation (allele pairs separate into gametes unchanged - proven by 3:1 F2 reappearance), independent assortment (different gene pairs shuffle freely - proven by 9:3:3:1 recombinants). Dominance describes expression, segregation describes transmission, assortment describes multi-gene shuffling. Exceptions refine rather than refute - incomplete dominance, codominance, linkage each reveal the law operating underneath modified expression.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dominance (show), segregation (separate), assortment (shuffle).
  • Exceptions reveal mechanisms; laws still anchor every problem.
Law proofs
PointDetail
DominanceF1 uniformity
Segregation3:1 F2 with 1:2:1 genotypes
Independent assortment9:3:3:1 with recombinants

Law of segregation is proven by

Solution: Recessive reappearance proves alleles separate unchanged into gametes.

Chapter 15 · Topic 11

Independent assortment

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMendelian GeneticsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Law of independent assortment: different gene pairs shuffle freely into gametes (YyRr makes YR, Yr, yR, yr equally) - proven by dihybrid 9:3:3:1 with recombinant classes neither parent showed. Holds for genes on different chromosomes (or far apart); tight linkage violates it (parental excess). Assortment multiplies variation combinatorially (2^n gamete types for n pairs) - 8 million human combinations.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Gene pairs shuffle independently (different chromosomes).
  • Linkage violates; distance restores via crossing over.
Remember
  • 2^n gamete types for n heterozygous pairs.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Independent assortment holds for genes on

Solution: Free metaphase orientation shuffles unlinked pairs only.

Chapter 15 · Topic 12

Incomplete dominance

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechExtensions of MendelismStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Complete dominance: heterozygote shows the dominant trait (Tt = tall). Incomplete dominance (dog flower/Mirabilis): F₂ 1:2:1 pink — phenotype blends. Codominance: both alleles fully expressed — AB blood group, sickle-cell heterozygotes. Multiple alleles: ABO system (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) — 6 genotypes, 4 phenotypes; IᴬIᴮ = codominant.

A red (RR) and white (rr) dog flower cross gives all pink (Rr); selfing gives red:pink:white in what ratio?

Answer: 1:2:1 — incomplete dominance makes the genotypic and phenotypic ratios identical.

Deeper Understanding · ABO genotypes fully listed

Three alleles (IA, IB, i) make six genotypes: IAIA + IAi = A, IBIB + IBi = B, IAIB = AB (codominant), ii = O. A cross of AxB parents can yield all four groups in children - classic pedigree puzzle. Sickle-cell heterozygotes (HbA/HbS) show codominance at molecular level (both haemoglobins made) but the trait protects against malaria - balanced polymorphism keeping a lethal allele alive. Rh blood group is independently inherited (D/d alleles), so ABO x Rh problems multiply: 4 x 2 = 8 possible phenotypes.

Topic in Depth · Incomplete dominance

Incomplete dominance blends heterozygotes between parents: dog-flower red x white gives all pink F1, and F2 runs 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white - phenotypic ratio identical to genotypic (1:2:1) because no allele fully masks. Snapdragons (Mirabilis) are the textbook; Andalusian fowl and Tay-Sachs carriers show similar intermediacy. It refines dominance (expression blends) without touching segregation (alleles still separate) - laws intact, appearances intermediate.
NEET Snapshot:
  • F2 1:2:1 both ways - phenotype mirrors genotype.
  • Blending is expression-level; alleles stay discrete underneath.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Pink F1 from red x white dog-flower selfed gives F2 ratio

Solution: Incomplete dominance makes phenotypic and genotypic ratios identical at 1:2:1.

Related Diagram · Pink middle

Fig: Heterozygote blends between parents - 1:2:1 mirrors genotypes.

Chapter 15 · Topic 13

Codominance

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechExtensions of MendelismStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Codominance expresses both alleles fully in the heterozygote: AB blood group (IAIB makes both antigens), sickle-cell carriers (both HbA and HbS haemoglobins detectable), roan cattle (red + white hairs intermingled). Unlike incomplete dominance there is no blending - both products sit side by side. At molecular level most heterozygotes are codominant (both proteins made); dominance is often just the visible-trait description.

Topic in Depth · Codominance

Codominance expresses both alleles fully side by side: AB blood (both antigens on RBCs), sickle-cell carriers (both HbA and HbS haemoglobins detectable), roan cattle (red plus white hairs intermingled, not blended pink). Unlike incomplete dominance there is no intermediate - both products sit visibly together. Molecularly most heterozygotes are codominant (both proteins made); dominance versus codominance often just describes which level examiners inspect.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Both alleles fully visible - AB blood, sickle carriers, roan coat.
  • No blending: products coexist, not merge.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

AB blood group illustrates

Solution: IAIB red cells carry both A and B antigens simultaneously and fully.

Chapter 15 · Topic 14

Multiple alleles

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechExtensions of MendelismStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Multiple alleles means 3+ alleles of one gene in the population (though each individual carries two): ABO has IA, IB, i giving 6 genotypes and 4 phenotypes. Hierarchy: IA and IB dominate i, and codominate each other. Rabbit coat colour (C, cch, ch, c) and Drosophila eye colours extend the pattern - dominance series with stepwise expression. Population genetics counts allele frequencies, not just individual pairs.

Topic in Depth · Multiple alleles

Multiple alleles mean 3+ gene versions population-wide (each individual still carries two): ABO (IA, IB, i), rabbit coat series (C > cch > ch > c dominance hierarchy), Drosophila eye colours. Hierarchies stack - IA and IB dominate i but tie each other. Population genetics then counts allele frequencies (p, q, r) rather than individual pairs, extending Hardy-Weinberg to three alleles. More alleles mean more genotypes combinatorially but unchanged meiotic rules per individual.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Population carries many; individual carries two.
  • Dominance hierarchies stack (rabbit C series classic).
Remember
  • Count genotypes combinatorially; apply dominance pairwise.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

ABO system has how many alleles and genotypes?

Solution: IA, IB, i combine into six genotypes collapsing to four phenotypes.

Pleiotropy

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechExtensions of MendelismStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pleiotropy (one gene, many effects: sickle-cell anaemia - blood plus organs; phenylketonuria - brain plus skin/hair; white-eyed Drosophila males - blind plus sterile) contrasts polygenic inheritance (many genes, one trait: human height, skin colour, wheat kernels). Pleiotropy complicates pedigrees (one mutation, syndrome); polygeny creates continuous bell-curve variation. Starch-branching peas (wrinkled plus sweet) show plant pleiotropy.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One gene many effects (pleiotropy) vs many genes one trait (polygenic).
  • Sickle-cell and PKU are human pleiotropy classics.

Chromosome

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChromosomal BasisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Chromosomes (DNA-histone packages: chromatin condensing in division) carry genes linearly - number constant per species (human 46, pea 14, fruitfly 8), structure (metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric, telocentric by centromere) identified in karyotypes. Homologues pair in meiosis; sister chromatids split in mitosis. Sutton-Boveri theory (genes on chromosomes explain Mendel) founded cytogenetics - behaviour parallels proved location.
NEET Snapshot:
  • DNA-histone packages; number constant per species.
  • Centromere position names metacentric to telocentric types.
Remember
  • Karyotypes arrange chromosomes by size and centromere.

Gene

Topic in Depth

Genes (hereditary units, DNA segments coding proteins/RNAs) sit at loci on chromosomes - cistron (coding unit), recon (recombination unit), muton (mutation unit) subdivide classically. One gene-one enzyme (Beadle-Tatum Neurospora) grew to one gene-one polypeptide (many proteins multi-subunit). Gene number (~30,000 human) underwhelms versus complexity - regulation and splicing multiply outputs. Alleles are gene versions differing by mutation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • DNA segments at loci coding products; alleles are versions.
  • Cistron-recon-muton subdivide gene functionally.
Remember
  • Locus is address; allele is version; gene is instruction.

Allele

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChromosomal BasisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alleles (alternative gene forms: IA, IB, i for ABO; T/t for height) arise by mutation, occupy same loci on homologues, and interact by dominance patterns (complete, incomplete, codominant). Homozygous (same pair) breeds true; heterozygous (mixed) shows dominance relations; hemizygous (single X in males) exposes recessives. Multiple alleles (ABO trio) expand population variety while individuals carry two. New alleles fuel evolution; old ones record history.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Same-locus variants interacting by dominance.
  • Homozygous true-breeds; heterozygous shows dominance.

Chapter 15 · Topic 19

Homologous chromosomes

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChromosomal BasisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Homologous chromosomes (one maternal, one paternal per pair - same genes, possibly different alleles, same length-centromere pattern) synapse and cross over in meiosis, then segregate - basis of segregation and assortment. Non-homologous pairs assort independently. Sister chromatids (identical copies) differ from homologues (similar but variant) - confusing them breaks meiosis understanding. Karyotypes pair homologues visually.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Maternal-plus-paternal pairs; same genes, variant alleles.
  • Synapse, cross over, segregate - homologue duties.
Remember
  • Sisters identical copies; homologues variant pairs - never swap.

Linkage

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChromosomal BasisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Linkage (genes on same chromosome travelling together - Morgan Drosophila white-eye plus miniature wings) breaks independent assortment (parental combinations exceed 50 percent); strength falls with distance (crossing over separates). Complete linkage (no crossing over - male Drosophila) versus incomplete (some recombinants). 1 percent recombination equals 1 map unit (centimorgan) - Sturtevant mapped genes by linkage percentages.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Same-chromosome genes travel together; distance weakens linkage.
  • Recombination percent measures map distance.
Remember
  • Linkage violates 9:3:3:1 toward parental types.

Chapter 15 · Topic 21

Crossing over

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChromosomal BasisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Crossing over (pachytene exchange between non-sister chromatids at recombination nodules, visible as chiasmata) shuffles alleles, maps genes (frequency equals distance), and aids disjunction (minimum one chiasma per bivalent). Double crossovers underestimate long distances; interference suppresses nearby seconds; hotspots cluster exchanges. Cytological proof (Creighton-McClintock maize segment swaps) matched genetics to microscopy.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Non-sister exchange shuffling alleles plus aiding segregation.
  • Frequency maps distance; chiasmata mark spots.

Recombination

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChromosomal BasisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Recombination (new allele combinations via crossing over plus independent assortment) manufactures variation - parental types reshuffled into recombinants (dihybrid 9:3:3:1 holds 6/16 recombinants). Recombination frequency (recombinants over total) maps loci; 50 percent maximum (unlinked genes). Recombinant DNA technology borrows the name for engineered combinations - natural shuffling inspires artificial splicing.
NEET Snapshot:
  • New combinations via crossover plus assortment.
  • Frequency (recombinants/total) measures locus distance.
Remember
  • Recombinant classes are dihybrid new combinations.

Sex Determination

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechChromosomal BasisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Chromosomal sex determination assigns heterogamety: XX-XY (mammals, Drosophila - Y/male decides), ZZ-ZW (birds, butterflies - female decides), XX-XO (grasshoppers - male single X), haplodiploidy (bees - fertilisation decides females, unfertilised makes drone males). Y carries SRY testis switch (mammals); X carries housekeeping genes (explaining X-linked disease patterns). Environment decides some reptiles (temperature-dependent) - chromosomes rule most, heat rules some.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Heterogametic sex decides offspring sex.
  • SRY (mammals) switches maleness on.
Remember
  • Turtles use temperature; mammals use Y - two determination logics.

Topic in Depth

XX-XY system (humans, Drosophila, mammals generally): females homogametic XX, males heterogametic XY - father sperm (X or Y) decides offspring sex (50-50 chance). Y chromosome carries SRY triggering testis development; X carries vital genes (X-linked disorders strike males). Drosophila adds X:autosome ratio refinement. Paternal decision with equal odds is the mammalian norm.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Father decides (X or Y sperm); 50-50 odds.
  • SRY on Y triggers maleness.

XO system (grasshoppers, cockroaches - male heterogametic with single X, no Y): females XX, males XO - sperm with or without X decides daughters versus sons. Demonstrates Y dispensability (maleness needs X-dosage difference, not Y genes). Squash bugs and some nematodes run XO variants. Simpler than XY - presence/absence deciding instead of X/Y competition.

  • No Y needed - dosage difference suffices.

ZW-ZZ system

Topic in Depth

ZW-ZZ system (birds, butterflies, some fishes/reptiles): females heterogametic ZW, males homogametic ZZ - mothers decide offspring sex (reversed mammalian logic). W chromosome (like Y, gene-poor) carries female determinants in birds. Poultry sexing (vent/feather-sexing day-olds) exploits ZW genetics commercially. Female heterogamety flips criss-cross patterns (mothers to sons) versus X-linked mammalian ones.

  • Poultry sexing exploits ZW inheritance.
Remember
  • ZW reverses mammalian decision logic to mothers.

Haplodiploidy (honeybees, ants, wasps): fertilised diploid eggs become females (queens/workers by feeding), unfertilised haploid eggs become drone males - males have grandfathers but no father, mothers but no sons-to-fathers logic twists pedigrees. Sisters share 75 percent genes (supersisters) explaining eusocial altruism (kin selection). Arrhenotoky (unmated females make males only) proves the system experimentally.

X-linked inheritance (genes on X: haemophilia, colour blindness, DMD, G6PD) strikes males harder (hemizygous exposure) with criss-cross patterns (father to daughter carrier to grandson; never father to son). X-linked dominant (fragile X, vitamin-D rickets) hits heterozygous females too. Barr-body inactivation equalises female dosage (calico mosaicism proves). Pedigrees diagnose by male excess plus criss-cross flow.

  • Barr inactivation balances female double dose.
Remember
  • Father-to-son transmission rules out X-linkage instantly.

Y-linked (holandric) genes (hypertrichosis ear hair, some spermatogenesis factors/AZF regions) pass father-to-son only, never to daughters - straight male lines in pedigrees. Y gene-poverty (SRY plus few spermatogenesis genes, mostly heterochromatin) limits holandric traits. Male infertility (AZF microdeletions) is the medical face of Y-linkage. All sons of affected fathers inherit - 100 percent male transmission.

  • Y gene-poverty limits holandric trait counts.

  • Daughter inheritance rules out Y-linkage instantly.

Topic in Depth

Haemophilia (X-linked recessive clotting-factor VIII/IX lack - A and B types) bleeds into joints and muscles from minor injuries; royal families spread it through carrier queens (Victoria to Russian-Spanish lines). Treatment replaces factors (plasma-derived, recombinant); gene therapy trials advance. Female haemophiliacs need affected father plus carrier mother (rare). Criss-cross pedigrees diagnose textbook cases.

Colour blindness (X-linked recessive red-green defects: protanopia red-blind, deuteranopia green-blind - Ishihara dotted-number plates diagnose) affects ~8 percent males versus ~0.5 percent females. Female carriers pass to half their sons; colour-blind fathers make all daughters carriers (normal mates). Driving and pilot careers screen it; enrichment proves X-linkage arithmetic publicly.

Chapter 15 · Topic 32

Mendelian disorders

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGenetic DisordersStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mendelian disorders: autosomal recessive - sickle-cell anaemia (GAG to GUG point mutation, Glu to Val), thalassemia (reduced globin synthesis), cystic fibrosis, PKU, albinism, Tay-Sachs; autosomal dominant - myotonic dystrophy, Huntington (late onset), achondroplasia; X-linked recessive - haemophilia, colour blindness, DMD. Recessive disorders need carrier parents; dominant ones need just one affected parent (usually heterozygous, as homozygous is often lethal).

Topic in Depth · Genetic disorders

Mendelian disorders follow single-gene logic: autosomal recessive (sickle-cell GAG-to-GUG point mutation, thalassemia reduced synthesis, cystic fibrosis, PKU, albinism, Tay-Sachs - carrier parents, 25 percent risk), autosomal dominant (myotonic dystrophy, Huntington late-onset, achondroplasia - one affected parent suffices, homozygous often lethal), X-linked recessive (haemophilia, colour blindness, DMD - male excess). Counselling multiplies probabilities per pregnancy independently - each child rolls fresh odds.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Recessive needs two carriers; dominant needs one affected parent.
  • Sickle-cell: GAG to GUG, Glu to Val - the famous point mutation.

Chromosomal disorders

Genetics and InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGenetic DisordersStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Chromosomal disorders come from nondisjunction: Down syndrome (trisomy 21 - mongoloid slant, simian crease, mental retardation; risk rises with maternal age), Turner (XO female - sterile, webbed neck, shield chest, no Barr body), Klinefelter (XXY male - tall, gynaecomastia, sterile, one Barr body). Autosomal monosomies are lethal (missing essential genes); sex-chromosome variants survive because X-inactivation and Y gene-poverty cushion the imbalance.

Topic in Depth · Chromosomal disorders

Chromosomal disorders come from nondisjunction numbers, not gene spellings: Down (trisomy 21 - slant eyes, simian crease, intellectual disability; risk rises with maternal age), Turner (XO female - sterile, webbed neck, shield chest, no Barr body), Klinefelter (XXY male - tall, gynaecomastia, sterile, one Barr body). Autosomal monosomies die (missing essential genes); sex-chromosome variants survive via X-inactivation cushioning and Y gene-poverty. Karyotype (arranged chromosome portrait) diagnoses all three.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Down 47 (21), Turner 45 (X0), Klinefelter 47 (XXY).
  • Maternal age raises Down risk; Barr bodies count extra Xs.

Deep Dive · DNA to proteins to identity

Molecular biology flows DNA structure (helix, pairing, Chargaff) through replication (semi-conservative forks, polymerases, Okazaki-ligase patchwork) into transcription (polymerase, promoters, template-coding strands, processed mRNA) read by the code (triplet, degenerate, start-stop) on ribosomes (translation initiation-elongation-termination with tRNA adaptors) under regulation (lac operon logic) - with mutations (point, frameshift, mutagens) editing text and fingerprinting (VNTR profiling) identifying individuals. Dogma DNA-RNA-protein organises everything.
NEET facts:
  • Semi-conservative replication; AUG starts; UAA/UAG/UGA stop; lac operon combines negative plus positive control.
  • VNTR profiling identifies; child bands must trace to parents.
Fig: Antiparallel backbones with complementary rungs - A=T double, G triple C.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Operon model (lac) was proposed by

Solution: Jacob-Monod operon logic revealed gene regulation principles.

Subtopics in this Chapter

Deep Dive · Experiments and enzymes of molecular biology

Three experiments prove DNA is genetic material: Griffith (1928) showed harmless R-strain bacteria transformed into deadly S-strain inside mice; Avery-MacLeod-McCarty proved the transforming substance was DNA (destroyed by DNase, not protease); Hershey-Chase (1952) blended bacteriophages off bacteria and found only 32P-labelled DNA entered cells while 35S protein stayed outside. Meselson-Stahl then proved replication is semi-conservative using heavy 15N DNA across generations.

TranscriptionRNA polymerase + sigma / rho factorsCopy template 3' to 5' into mRNA; start and stop signals
RNA processingSpliceosome machineryCapping, tailing, splicing out introns - exons joined
TranslationRibosomes, tRNA, aminoacyl synthetaseRead codons; charge tRNAs; start at AUG, stop at UAA/UAG/UGA
Fig: tRNA cloverleaf - anticodon reads mRNA below, amino acid rides on top; charging by aminoacyl synthetase.
HGP + fingerprinting numbers
  • Human genome: ~3 billion bp, ~30,000 genes, under 2% coding; chromosome 1 most genes, Y fewest; 99.9% bases identical in all humans.
  • DNA fingerprinting (Alec Jeffreys) compares VNTR/minisatellite patterns by Southern blotting.

Nuclear chromosomes plus organelle circles plus plasmids distribute genomes. Hershey-Chase proved DNA (not protein) carries genes; Watson-Crick modelled structure; sequencing reads it fully.

Chapter 16 · Topic 2

DNA structure

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNAStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA: deoxyribose sugar, bases A/T/G/C, usually double-stranded, stable — the genetic material (proven by Hershey–Chase blender experiment on bacteriophages; Griffith's transformation + Avery–MacLeod–McCarty pointed the way). RNA: ribose sugar, uracil instead of thymine, usually single-stranded; types — mRNA (message), tRNA (adaptor with anticodon + CCA amino-acid arm), rRNA (ribosome machine). Some viruses use RNA as genetic material (retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase).
Fig: DNA double helix — antiparallel strands, A=T (2 bonds), G≡C (3 bonds), following Chargaff's rules.

Deeper Understanding · Chargaff mathematics

Chargaff rules let you compute any base: if A = 30%, then T = 30% (pairing), leaving G + C = 40%, so G = C = 20% each. The ratio (A+T)/(G+C) is species-specific (low in humans, high in some bacteria) because G-C pairs carry 3 hydrogen bonds vs 2 for A-T - GC-rich DNA melts at higher temperature, which PCR exploits. RNA replaces thymine with uracil and usually stays single-stranded, folding into functional shapes (tRNA cloverleaf, ribozymes) - a few viruses even use RNA as genetic material, with reverse transcriptase copying it back to DNA.

Related Diagram · Three RNA workers

Fig: Messenger copies, transfer carries, ribosomal assembles - translation needs all three.

Topic in Depth · RNA

RNA trades thymine for uracil, ribose for deoxyribose, and usually runs single-stranded - folding into functional shapes instead of duplexes. Three workers divide translation: mRNA (message copy with UTR regulators), tRNA (cloverleaf adaptor with anticodon plus CCA amino-acid arm), rRNA (ribosome catalytic core - the ribosome is a ribozyme). Some viruses store genomes as RNA, copying via reverse transcriptase - the retroviral exception proving DNA usual rule. RNA world hypotheses even cast RNA as life first molecule (information plus catalysis combined).
NEET Snapshot:
  • mRNA message, tRNA adaptor, rRNA machine.
  • Uracil replaces thymine; usually single-stranded and folded.
Remember
  • Ribosome peptide-bond formation is RNA-catalysed - protein machine with RNA engine.

Double helix

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNAStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Double helix (Watson-Crick: antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones outside, bases inside - A=T double bonds, G triple C) coils right-handed at 10 bp per 3.4 nm turn. Major-minor grooves expose bases to proteins; supercoiling compacts chromosomes; denaturation (melting) separates strands reversibly (PCR cycles exploit). X-ray diffraction plus model-building converged on the helix in 1953.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Antiparallel backbones; complementary bases; 10 bp per turn.
  • Grooves expose bases; supercoiling compacts chromosomes.
Remember
  • Major groove reads sequences; minor groove stabilises.

Nucleotides (base plus pentose sugar plus phosphate) are nucleic monomers plus energy currency: ATP (energy coin), cAMP (messenger), NAD/FAD (redox carriers), CoA (acyl carrier). DNA uses dAMP, dTMP, dGMP, dCMP; RNA uses AMP, UMP, GMP, CMP. Phosphodiester bonds chain 5-to-3; triphosphate hydrolysis powers polymerisation - monomers doubling as fuel.

  • ATP, NAD, cAMP are nucleotide side careers.

Chargaff rules (A=T, G=C in any duplex; (A+T)/(G+C) species-specific) revealed pairing before the helix - ratios varying from AT-rich Plasmodium to GC-rich Mycobacterium identify species molecularly. Second parity rules extend to single strands statistically. Chargaff plus Franklin X-ray plus model-building converged on Watson-Crick structure - quantitative clue cracking the code.

DNA Replication

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNA ReplicationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA replication copies genomes semiconservatively (Meselson-Stahl 15N proof) via helicase unzipping, primase priming, polymerase extending 5-to-3 (leading smooth, lagging Okazaki patches sealed by ligase), proofreading to one error per billion. Origins fire bidirectionally; telomerase maintains ends in germ/stem cells. Speed plus accuracy plus coordination make replication the cell most regulated synthesis.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Semi-conservative; leading smooth, lagging patchwork plus ligase.
  • Proofreading plus telomeres guard ends and fidelity.

Semiconservative replication

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNA ReplicationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Semiconservative replication keeps one parental strand per daughter duplex - proved by 15N-labelled DNA banding intermediate after one generation (neither fully heavy-conservative nor fully mixed-dispersive). Each strand templates its complement; helicase unzips, polymerase copies. Dispersive and conservative models died on density-gradient evidence - textbooks still test all three predictions comparatively.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Each daughter keeps one parental strand.
  • Density gradients killed conservative and dispersive models.
Remember
  • Intermediate first-generation band proves semi-conservative.

Replication fork

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNA ReplicationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Replication forks (Y-junctions where helicase unzips ahead, primase primes, polymerases extend both arms) move bidirectionally from origins (oriC bacteria single, eukaryotic many per chromosome). Leading strand synthesises continuously toward forks; lagging synthesises backward Okazaki patches. Fork stalling (damage, secondary structures) recruits repair; collapsed forks break chromosomes - replication stress drives genome instability and cancer.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Y-junctions unzipping ahead, synthesising both arms.
  • Bidirectional from origins; stalling recruits repair.
Remember
  • Leading smooth toward fork; lagging patchy away from it.

DNA polymerase

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNA ReplicationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA polymerases extend 5-to-3 only (needs RNA primers - no de novo starts), proofread via 3-to-5 exonuclease (mismatch removal), and specialise: Pol III (bacterial chromosome), Pol I (primer removal, repair), eukaryotic alpha (priming), delta/epsilon (leading/lagging), Taq (PCR heat-stable). Fidelity (one error per 10^9 with repair) plus speed (1000 bases/second bacterial) balance accuracy against pace.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Extend 5-to-3 only; need primers; proofread mismatches.
  • Specialised Pols divide labour across tasks.
Remember
  • No primer, no start - polymerases extend only.

Leading strand

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNA ReplicationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Leading strand synthesises continuously 5-to-3 toward the moving fork (same direction as unwinding) - single primer suffices, polymerase runs uninterrupted, fastest synthesis. Helicase ahead, primase once, ligase uninvolved. Continuous simplicity contrasts lagging patchwork - direction relative to fork decides smoothness. Eukaryotic leading uses Pol epsilon; bacterial Pol III both strands.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Continuous synthesis toward fork direction.
  • One primer suffices; no ligase needed.
Remember
  • Toward fork equals smooth; away equals patchy.

Lagging strand

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDNA ReplicationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Lagging strand synthesises discontinuously away from forks - repeated priming, short Okazaki patches (1000-2000 bases bacteria, 100-200 eukaryotes), primer removal plus ligase sealing. Slower, costlier, but unavoidable (polymerase one direction only). Telomere end-replication problem (terminal primers unreplaceable) shortens chromosomes each division - telomerase (germ, stem, cancer) rebuilds ends.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Discontinuous patches away from fork direction.
  • Priming plus sealing overhead per patch.
Remember
  • Telomeres pay the lagging-strand end price.

Okazaki fragments (short lagging-strand patches: ~1000-2000 bases bacteria, ~100-200 eukaryotes) prime, extend, then join - primers removed (Pol I/RNase H), gaps filled, ligase seals nicks into continuity. Discovered in phage-infected bacteria (Reiji Okazaki pulse-labelling). Fragment size reflects priming frequency; joining efficiency decides lagging speed. Every lagging base travels via Okazaki intermediates.

  • Bacteria long patches; eukaryotes short frequent ones.

  • Pulse-labelling revealed patchwork lagging synthesis.

DNA ligase seals nicks (3-OH to 5-phosphate phosphodiester bonds, ATP/NAD+ powered) joining Okazaki patches, repair patches and recombinant ends - molecular glue of replication, repair and cloning (recombinant DNA ligates inserts into vectors). Ligase failure breaks chromosomes (LIG4 syndrome immunodeficiency); inhibitors probe repair pathways. Sealing completes every patchwork synthesis.

  • ATP-powered phosphodiester bond formation.

Chapter 16 · Topic 15

Transcription

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechTranscriptionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Watson–Crick model: antiparallel strands coiled right-handed around a common axis. DNA wraps on histone octamers (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) forming nucleosomes ("beads on a string") that coil into chromatin. Replication is semi-conservative (Meselson–Stahl ¹⁵N experiment): helicase unwinds, DNA polymerase III extends the leading strand continuously and the lagging strand as Okazaki fragments joined by ligase.
NEET facts:
  • Chargaff: A = T, G = C; (A+T)/(G+C) varies between species.
  • Replication proceeds 5′ → 3′ only; the template is read 3′ → 5′.

Deeper Understanding · Chromatin packing levels

Two metres of human DNA fit in a micrometre nucleus through layered packing: DNA wraps histone octamers (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) into nucleosomes (beads on a string, ~200 bp each), coiling into 30-nm fibres, looped domains and finally metaphase chromosomes (~10,000-fold compaction). Euchromatin is loose and transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is dense and silent (centromeres, Barr body). Histone acetylation loosens packing (genes on), methylation tightens it - the epigenetic layer above the sequence itself.

Topic in Depth · DNA replication

Replication copies semi-conservatively (Meselson-Stahl 15N proof): helicase unzips, single-strand proteins stabilise, primase lays RNA primers, DNA polymerase III extends 5 to 3 only - continuous leading strand, patchwork lagging Okazaki fragments sealed by ligase - with proofreading exonuclease correcting errors to one per billion bases. Origins fire bidirectionally; telomerase maintains chromosome ends in germ and stem cells. Speed plus accuracy plus coordination makes replication the cell most regulated synthesis.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Semi-conservative; leading smooth, lagging patchwork plus ligase.
  • Polymerase extends 5 to 3 only; helicase unzips ahead.

Rifampicin blocks bacterial polymerase (TB drug); alpha-amanitin kills eukaryotic Pol II (death-cap poison). One bacterial enzyme versus three eukaryotic specialists.

Promoters (DNA sequences upstream: bacterial -10 Pribnow plus -35 boxes; eukaryotic TATA box plus enhancers) recruit polymerase via sigma/transcription factors - strength (consensus match) sets expression level. Inducible promoters (lac) switch on demand; constitutive run always; tissue-specific enhancers restrict expression spatially. Promoter engineering drives biotechnology (strong promoters overexpress insulin, vaccines in microbes).

Template strand

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechTranscriptionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Template (antisense, 3-to-5) strand is copied into RNA - polymerase reads it building complementary message; coding (sense, 5-to-3) strand matches RNA sequence (T for U) but is never copied. Gene direction defines which strand templates (opposite strands serve different genes). Confusing template with coding inverts sequences - polarity discipline (read 3-to-5, build 5-to-3) prevents errors.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Copied 3-to-5 strand; coding strand matches RNA instead.
  • Different genes use opposite strands as templates.
Remember
  • Template copied; coding matches RNA (T for U).

Translation begins where scanning stops - initiation defines reading frame for everything downstream.

Codon usage bias (preferred synonyms per species) tunes translation speed and accuracy - transgenes recoded (codon optimisation) express better. Degeneracy is evolution error-tolerance built into the code.

Universality (near-identical code across life - bacteria to humans translate same codons similarly) proves common ancestry; mitochondrial tweaks (UGA-Trp, AUA-Met) and ciliate reassignments are rare dialects. Universality enables transgenesis (human insulin in E. coli reads identically) and horizontal transfer interpretation. Chapter 16 · Topic 27

Translation

Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechTranslationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

mRNA is copied by RNA polymerase from the template (3′→5′) strand; promoter (with sigma factor in bacteria) starts it, terminator (rho factor) ends it. Eukaryotic genes are split — coding exons interrupted by non-coding introns; hnRNA is capped, tailed and spliced into mature mRNA. Only one strand (with polarity 3′→5′) acts as template.

Deeper Understanding · Split genes surprise

Until 1977 everyone assumed genes were continuous; Roberts and Sharp (Nobel) showed eukaryotic genes are split - coding exons interrupted by non-coding introns removed by splicing. One gene can therefore yield several proteins via alternative splicing (human ~30,000 genes make ~100,000+ proteins). Only the template strand (3' to 5') is copied; the coding strand matches mRNA sequence (with T instead of U). Bacterial genes lack introns, so their transcription needs no processing - mRNA is translation-ready instantly.

Topic in Depth · Transcription

Transcription copies the template (3 to 5) strand into mRNA: RNA polymerase plus sigma factor recognise promoters, unwind a bubble, extend RNA 5 to 3, and rho factor terminates - no primers needed (unlike replication). Bacterial mRNA translates instantly; eukaryotic hnRNA needs capping, poly-A tailing and spliceosome intron removal first. Only one strand per gene serves as template, though different genes use opposite strands - transcription is local, not genome-wide.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Template read 3 to 5; RNA built 5 to 3; no primer needed.
  • Eukaryotes process hnRNA (cap, tail, splice) before export.
Remember
  • Promoter starts (sigma), terminator ends (rho) - bacterial signals.

Lac operon

Topic in Depth

The code is triplet, degenerate, unambiguous, universal (nearly): 61 sense codons for 20 amino acids, start AUG (methionine), stops UAA, UAG, UGA. Read 5' to 3' without overlap or punctuation; a frameshift garbles everything downstream while a nonsense mutation truncates early. Mitochondria slightly rewrite it (UGA = Trp).

Topic in Depth · Genetic code

The code maps 64 triplets to 20 amino acids plus stops: triplet reading, degenerate synonyms (wobble third base), unambiguous assignment (one codon, one meaning), near-universal dialect (mitochondria tweak UGA to Trp). Start AUG doubles as methionine; stops UAA, UAG, UGA end chains via release factors. Degeneracy buffers mutations (third-base changes often silent); frameshifts garble everything downstream while nonsense truncates early - mutation severity follows code position.

Point mutations swap single bases: silent (synonymous, no amino-acid change - wobble saves), missense (different residue - sickle-cell GAG-GUG, function alters), nonsense (early stop - truncated dead proteins: thalassemia, DMD). Transitions (purine-purine) outnumber transversions; spontaneous deamination plus replication slips cause them; mutagens (radiation, chemicals, base analogues) multiply rates. Molecular Basis of InheritanceGenetics, Evolution and BiotechMutationsStep-by-step Topic

Frameshift mutations (insertions/deletions not multiple of three) garble all downstream codons - usually worst mutation class (thalassemia frameshifts, Tay-Sachs 4-base loss). In-frame indels (multiples of three) merely add/remove residues mildly. Acridine intercalators cause frameshifts experimentally; Seymour Benzer mapped genes with phage frameshifts. Downstream garbling exceeds point-change damage almost always.

  • Worst class; in-frame multiples merely add/remove.

Repair (photolyase, excision, mismatch, SOS) counters constantly - mutation-repair balance sets observed rates.

Deep Dive · From molecules to humans

Evolution runs origin chemistry (reducing air, Miller sparks) through evidence quartets (fossils, homology-analogy, embryos, molecules) into Darwin selection (variation, struggle, fittest survival) modernised by synthesis (mutation, recombination, drift, flow, isolation) with Hardy-Weinberg maths (p2+2pq+q2 equilibrium, disturber signatures) patterning radiations (finches, marsupials) convergences and divergences toward humans (australopiths striding, habilis tooling, erectus firing, Neanderthals burying, sapiens symbolising). Molecules to humans in one connected ascent.
NEET facts:
  • Miller sparks made amino acids; Hardy-Weinberg 16 percent recessive means 48 percent carriers.
  • Archaeopteryx bridges reptiles-birds; Neanderthal DNA persists 1-2 percent in non-Africans.
Fig: Stride, tools, fire, burials, symbols - brain and culture compounding along the walk.

Solution: Handy Man Oldowan tools plus meat mark genus Homo start.

Subtopics in this Chapter

Deep Dive · Theories, Hardy-Weinberg and human journey

Theories of evolution compared
TheoryCore ideaStatus
LamarckUse and disuse; inheritance of acquired characters (long giraffe necks)Rejected - acquired traits are not inherited
DarwinBranching descent + natural selection; survival of the fittestFoundation; lacked genetics
de Vries (mutation theory)Sudden large mutations drive evolutionPartially absorbed into modern synthesis
Modern synthetic theoryGene frequency change via mutation, recombination, gene flow, drift, selectionAccepted
Hardy-Weinberg worked example (exact NEET pattern): if 16% of a population shows a recessive trait, q2 = 0.16 so q = 0.4, p = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6, and carriers 2pq = 2 x 0.6 x 0.4 = 48%. Equilibrium holds only with random mating and no selection, mutation, migration or drift - any disturbance means evolution is occurring. Genetic drift (bottleneck + founder effects) bites hardest in small populations. Living proofs of selection: industrial melanism (soot-darkened moths), DDT-resistant mosquitoes, antibiotic-resistant bacteria appearing within months.
Fig: Brain capacity climbs 650 to 900 to 1400 cc along the human journey; agriculture began ~10,000 years ago.

Solution: q2 = 0.16 gives q = 0.4 and p = 0.6; carriers = 2pq = 2 x 0.6 x 0.4 = 48%.

Chapter 17 · Topic 1

Chemical evolution

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechOrigin of LifeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Chemical evolution (Oparin-Haldane) proposes lifeless chemistry becoming biology: simple gases to organic monomers (amino acids, sugars, bases) to polymers (proteins, nucleic acids) to replicating systems - each step driven by lightning, UV and heat energy. Coacervates and microspheres (proteinoid droplets) model protocells concentrating reactions. Panspermia relocates origin off-Earth but still needs first chemistry somewhere.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Gases to monomers to polymers to replicators - stepwise chemistry.
  • Energy from lightning, UV and volcanic heat drove synthesis.

Solution: Oparin-Haldane placed life origin in ancient reducing-atmosphere chemistry.

Chapter 17 · Topic 2

Primitive Earth

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechOrigin of LifeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Primitive Earth differed totally: hot volcanic surface, reducing atmosphere (CH4, NH3, H2, water vapour - no free oxygen), intense UV (no ozone shield), lightning storms and asteroid impacts. Absent oxygen allowed organics accumulating instead of burning; absent ozone let UV power reactions; hot pools concentrated solutes by evaporation. Modern oxidising, ozonised Earth cannot repeat the experiment - origin chemistry needs its ancient kitchen.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hot, reducing, UV-baked, lightning-struck, oxygen-free.
  • No O2 meant organics accumulated instead of burning.
Remember
  • Oxygen absence was essential - modern air prevents repeat origin.

Miller experiment

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechOrigin of LifeStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Miller-Urey experiment (1953, electric discharge through CH4-NH3-H2 plus water vapour) produced amino acids within a week - proving ancient-atmosphere chemistry creates life monomers spontaneously. Later variants (volcanic gases, hydrothermal chemistry, extraterrestrial delivery via meteorites carrying organics) extend sources. Critics note atmosphere uncertainties, but core result stands: non-living chemistry yields biomolecules under plausible early conditions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sparks through reducing gases yielded amino acids in days.
  • Proof-of-principle for chemical evolution, not full recipe.

Chapter 17 · Topic 4

Fossils

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechEvidencesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fossils (preserved remains/impressions in dated strata) document evolution directly: geological succession (simple deep, complex shallow), transitional forms (Archaeopteryx reptile-bird, Tiktaalik fish-tetrapod, Ambulocetus walking whale), extinction chronicles (dinosaurs vanishing at K-Pg boundary), and radiometric dating (U-Pb, K-Ar clocks) timing splits. Fossil gaps reflect preservation bias (hard parts fossilise, soft rot) - incompleteness expected, not disproof.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Strata succession plus transitional forms plus radiometric dates.
  • Gaps reflect preservation bias toward hard parts.
Remember
  • Tiktaalik (fishapod) bridges water-to-land transition.

Topic in Depth

Homologous organs (same origin, different functions - human arm, whale flipper, bat wing, cheetah leg; vertebrate hearts, brains) prove divergent evolution from common ancestors - structure conserved, function remodelled by selection. Thorn-tendril (Bougainvillea-Cucurbita), potato-sweet-potato storage roots, and molecular homologies (cytochrome c sequences grading with relatedness) extend homology from anatomy to molecules.

  • Molecular homologies (cytochrome c) grade with kinship.
Remember
  • Homology is origin-based; analogy is function-based.

Topic in Depth

Analogous organs (different origins, same function - butterfly vs bird wings, sweet-potato root vs potato stem, cactus spines vs rose prickles) prove convergent evolution under similar pressures - natural selection sculpting similar solutions from different starting materials. Eyeestin? no - octopus vs human camera eyes (separate inventions) stun most. Analogy warns against grouping by looks; homology groups by ancestry correctly.

  • Looks deceive; ancestry classifies correctly.
Remember
  • Sweet potato (root) vs potato (stem) is textbook analogy.

Vestigial organs (reduced functionless remnants - human appendix, coccyx, wisdom teeth, ear muscles; whale hip bones; flightless-bird wings; python limb spurs) testify ancestry - structures useful to ancestors, shrunk by disuse/selection shifts. Atavisms (rare reappearances: human tails, extra nipples) confirm dormant genetic programmes. Vestiges are evolution leftovers, not design flaws - history written in shrinking anatomy.

  • Atavistic reappearances confirm dormant programmes.
Remember
  • Whale hips and human tails betray ancestry.

Embryological evidence: vertebrate embryos pass gill-slit, tail and similar heart stages (Haeckel drawings overstated but pattern holds) - ontogeny echoes phylogeny because developmental programmes inherit conservatively. Temporary embryonic structures (human lanugo hair, yolk sac, pronephric kidneys) replay ancestry. Evo-devo (Hox gene colinearity across phyla) now explains why embryos resemble - shared toolkit genes pattern all bodies.

Topic in Depth

Molecular evidence grades kinship precisely: cytochrome c sequences (human-chimp identical, human-yeast differ), haemoglobin chains, rRNA clocks timing splits (molecular-clock mutation rates date divergences), DNA hybridisation melting points, chromosome banding parallels. Universal code plus ATP plus left-handed amino acids prove single origin; sequence distances measure relatedness quantitatively - molecules turned evolution-measurement science.

  • Universal code plus ATP prove single origin.

Natural selection filters heritable variation: overproduction (more offspring than survive), competition (struggle for resources), survival of best-adapted variants, inheritance of winning traits - antibiotic resistance (months), industrial melanism (decades), beak shifts (years, measured live) demonstrate live. Selection acts on phenotypes, preserves genotypes - differential reproductive success, not strength, decides fitness.

  • Vary, compete, survive best-adapted, inherit winners.
  • Fitness means reproductive success, not muscle.
Remember
  • Selection edits phenotypes; genotypes ride along.

Topic in Depth

Survival of the fittest (Spencer phrase Darwin adopted) means fittest-to-environment leave most offspring - camouflaged moths survive soot, resistant bacteria survive drugs, drought-beaked finches survive famines. Fitness is contextual (peppered moth colours flipped with clean air) and reproductive (sterile strength is evolutionary zero). Tautology charges misunderstand - fitness predicts via testable trait advantages, not circular survival definitions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fittest means best-reproducing in current conditions.
  • Contextual and reproductive, not muscular or moral.
Remember

Chapter 17 · Topic 12

Struggle for existence

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechDarwinismStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Struggle for existence (Malthus-inspired) runs three competitions: intraspecific (same species, severest - identical needs), interspecific (different species, predators-prey-parasites), extraspecific (environmental odds - drought, cold, catastrophe). Overproduction guarantees struggle (single oyster millions of eggs, most eaten); struggle guarantees selection (only adapted persist). Darwin saw fecundity-versus-scarcity tension everywhere.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Same-species, cross-species and environmental competitions.
  • Overproduction guarantees struggle; struggle filters winners.
Remember
  • Intraspecific struggle cuts deepest (identical needs).

Chapter 17 · Topic 13

Mutation

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechModern Evolutionary TheoryStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Evolutionarily, mutation is the only ultimate allele source: recombination reshuffles existing cards, mutation prints new ones (de Vries sports). Rates (~10^-8 per base per generation) seem tiny until multiplied by billions of individuals over millions of generations - inevitability through numbers. Most mutations neutral (molecular clocks tick), many harmful (purged), few beneficial (swept) - and beneficial ones drive every adaptation story.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Only mutation creates alleles; all else reshuffles.
  • Neutral majority clocks time; beneficial minority drives change.
Remember
  • De Vries rediscovered Mendel plus proposed mutation theory.
NEET Practice MCQ

Solution: All other forces rearrange existing variation; mutation alone invents.

Recombination

Topic in Depth

Recombination (crossing over plus independent assortment) shuffles parental alleles into novel gamete combinations every meiosis - human 8 million gamete types per person before fertilisation multiplies further. Recombination hotspots cluster exchanges; interference spaces them; map distances measure frequencies. Shuffling existing variation (not creating) feeds selection endless novelty from finite alleles.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Meiotic shuffling (crossover plus assortment) makes novelty.
  • Finite alleles, endless combinations via reshuffling.
Remember
  • Recombination shuffles dealt cards; mutation prints new ones.

Topic in Depth

Natural selection as modern force acts on phenotypes preserving genotypes differentially - directional (antibiotic resistance shifts traits), stabilising (birth-weight middle wins), disruptive (finch beak splits) modes reshape bell curves; artificial selection (dairy, broilers) applies human goals; sexual selection (peacock tails) trades survival for mating. Selection edits variation recombination supplies - two-step evolutionary engine.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Directional shifts, stabilising centres, disruptive splits traits.
  • Artificial plus sexual selection extend natural modes.
Remember
  • Selection needs variation first - recombination supplies it.

Chapter 17 · Topic 16

Genetic drift

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechModern Evolutionary TheoryStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Genetic drift is sampling-error wandering - powerful in small populations (founder colonies, crash survivors), negligible in large ones. Bottleneck effect (cheetah near-zero diversity after ancient crash) and founder effect (island species, Amish disorders from few settlers) fix alleles by accident, even harmful ones - chance, not merit. Conservation breeding maximises effective population size precisely to outrun drift.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Small populations wander; large ones hold steady.
  • Bottleneck (crash) and founder (colony) slash diversity.
Remember
  • Drift fixes by accident; selection fixes by merit.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Sampling error swings frequencies wildly when headcounts are low.

Gene flow

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechModern Evolutionary TheoryStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gene flow (migration) moves alleles between populations - wind-blown pollen fields over, dispersing animals, travelling humans - homogenising gene pools and opposing speciation. Enough flow merges diverging groups; barriers (rivers, mountains, behaviour, chromosomes, timing) cut flow letting differences accumulate toward new species. Hybrid zones (narrow interbreeding borders) visualise flow-versus-selection balance; wildlife corridors preserve flow for fragmented endangered populations.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Migration homogenises; barriers isolate toward speciation.
  • Flow opposes divergence; isolation enables it.
Remember
  • Speciation needs isolation; flow is its enemy.

Solution: Migrant alleles blend populations; barriers let divergence accumulate.

Chapter 17 · Topic 18

Isolation

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechModern Evolutionary TheoryStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Isolation (reproductive barriers) splits gene pools toward speciation: geographic (rivers, mountains - allopatric), ecological (habitat, timing - sympatric beginnings), behavioural (mating rituals), mechanical (genital mismatch), gametic (fertilisation failure), hybrid inviability/sterility (mule dead-ends). Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibilities accumulate separately then clash on contact. Barriers sequence from pre-mating (cheap) to post-zygotic (costly) - reinforcement strengthens early blocks.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Barriers split pools; incompatibilities accumulate separately.
  • Pre-mating blocks cheap; hybrid failures costly.

Allele frequency (gene frequency: proportion of an allele among all copies at a locus) quantifies evolution - p plus q equal 1 for two alleles; counting (allele copies over total) from genotype censuses. Selection, drift, migration, mutation shift frequencies; equilibrium freezes them. Fingerprinting, conservation (rare-allele retention) and breeding (desired-allele enrichment) all manage frequencies deliberately.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Allele proportion at a locus; p+q=1 for two alleles.
  • Frequency shifts define evolution quantitatively.
Remember
  • Count alleles, not individuals, for frequencies.

Gene frequency (usually synonymous with allele frequency; sometimes genotype frequencies p2, 2pq, q2) tracks population genetic composition - Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p2+2pq+q2=1) predicts genotype frequencies from allele frequencies under no evolution. Shifts diagnose forces (selection directional, drift random, migration blending, mutation introducing). Gene banks conserve frequencies; breeders shift them toward desired traits deliberately.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Shifts diagnose operating evolutionary forces.
Remember
  • p2+2pq+q2=1 translates alleles to genotypes.

Chapter 17 · Topic 21

Equilibrium

EvolutionGenetics, Evolution and BiotechHardy-Weinberg PrincipleStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (allele plus genotype frequencies constant across generations given random mating with no selection, mutation, migration or drift) provides the null model - evolution defined as any disturbance. Large panmictic populations approximate it; chi-square tests compare observed versus expected counts detecting forces. Equilibrium assumptions (infinite size, random mating) never fully hold - real populations always evolve slightly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Constant frequencies under no evolutionary forces - null model.
  • Deviations diagnose selection, drift, migration or mutation.
Remember
  • Equilibrium is the no-evolution baseline for comparison.

Factors disturbing equilibrium

Topic in Depth

Equilibrium disturbers (selection directional shifts, mutation introduces, migration blends, drift wanders randomly, non-random mating reshuffles genotypes) each leave signatures - directional allele climbs, bottlenecks crash diversity, migrants converge populations, inbreeding raises homozygosity without changing allele frequencies. Conservation fights drift (corridors, breeding), agriculture exploits selection, medicine tracks migrating resistance - disturbing forces managed deliberately.

  • Inbreeding reshuffles genotypes without shifting alleles.

Convergent evolution sculpts similar solutions from different origins under similar pressures - wings (insects, birds, bats), fins (fish, whales, penguins), succulence (cactus-Euphorbia deserts), eyes (octopus-human cameras). Divergent evolution splits one ancestor into varied descendants (Darwin finches from one founder, mammals from shrew-like ancestor into whales-bats-humans, homologous limbs remodelled per lifestyle). Adaptive radiation is rapid divergent burst; background divergence accumulates steadily. Homologous structures (same bones, different jobs) diagnose divergence; DNA distances measure its depth. One origin, many destinies - divergence is evolution creative mode.

Homo habilis (handy man, ~2 mya, 650-800 cc) first made stone tools systematically (Oldowan choppers - butchery unlocking marrow), ate meat plus plants omnivorously, and sheltered socially - brain expansion tracking tool dependence. Homo erectus (upright man, ~1.9 mya-100kya, ~900-1100 cc, Java-Man, Peking-Man) mastered fire (cooking, warmth, protection), crafted Acheulean handaxes, migrated out of Africa first (Dmanisi, Java), and hunted big game cooperatively. Modern body proportions (long legs, narrow hips) plus controlled fire (hearths, burnt bones) mark full human ecology without modern brains. Erectus world spanned continents for a million years.

Neanderthals

Neanderthals (~400-40kya, Europe-West Asia, ~1400-1600 cc - larger than modern) were stocky cold-adapted hunters burying dead (Shanidar flowers), caring for injured (elderly healed), wearing hides, using Mousterian tools and fire - culture without full symbolism. 1-2 percent DNA persists in non-Africans (interbreeding, not just replacement). Disappearance (competition, climate, assimilation) remains debated - cousins, not ancestors.

Homo sapiens

Homo sapiens (anatomically ~300kya Africa, behaviourally modern ~50kya: Cro-Magnon art, language, agriculture 10kya) combined gracile bodies, globular brains (~1350 cc), symbolic culture (cave paintings, burials with goods, music), and cumulative technology (microliths to spacecraft). Out-of-Africa waves (60kya) populated continents, outcompeting Neanderthals-Denisovans (partly absorbing them). Agriculture (Neolithic) exploded populations plus diseases - civilisation trade-off starting history.

Topic in Depth

Recombinant DNA (engineered DNA combining foreign genes with host vectors) rewrites organisms: cut (restriction enzymes), paste (ligase), deliver (transformation), select (markers), express (host machinery makes insulin, Bt toxin, vaccines). Cohen-Boyer 1973 frog-to-bacteria plasmid proved concept; Genentech insulin (1982) proved commerce.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Foreign gene plus vector, delivered and expressed in hosts.
  • Cohen-Boyer 1973 proved; Genentech 1982 commercialised.

Gene cloning

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGenetic EngineeringStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gene cloning amplifies single genes into millions of copies: insert into plasmid vectors, transform bacteria, select carriers (antibiotic markers), culture bulk (fermenters scale to tonnes). Genomic libraries (whole-genome fragments) versus cDNA libraries (expressed genes only) archive species molecularly. Cloning multiplies DNA; expression harvests proteins.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Insert, transform, select, culture - single gene to millions.
  • Libraries archive genomes (genomic) or transcriptomes (cDNA).
Remember
  • Clone copies DNA; express harvests protein - two-stage payoff.

Solution: Bacterial division copies inserted genes exponentially.

Foreign DNA

Topic in Depth

Foreign DNA (donor genes: human insulin, Bt cry) must suit hosts - codon optimisation (matching host preferences), promoter compatibility, intron removal (bacteria cannot splice eukaryotic introns - cDNA used instead). Gene guns, Agrobacterium, microinjection and electroporation deliver across walls. Donor-host compatibility decides expression success.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Donor genes need codon, promoter and intron compatibility.
  • cDNA (intron-free) suits bacterial hosts.
Remember
  • Bacteria cannot splice - eukaryotic genes enter as cDNA.

Solution: Spliced cDNA bypasses bacterial inability to remove introns.

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGenetic EngineeringStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Host organisms express foreign genes: E. coli (fast, cheap, no glycosylation - insulin pioneer), yeast (eukaryotic processing plus secretion), plant cells (Agrobacterium Ti-plasmid, biolistics - GM crops), animal cells (complex proteins needing human-like modifications - costly bioreactors). Host choice balances speed, cost, fidelity and scale.
NEET Snapshot:
  • E. coli fast-cheap; yeast processing; mammalian faithful-costly.
  • Host matches product complexity and scale needs.

Restriction enzymes

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechToolsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Restriction enzymes (molecular scissors: EcoRI GAATTC, HindIII, BamHI - bacterial defence against phages) cut palindromic sequences leaving sticky (overhanging, ligation-ready) or blunt ends. Type II enzymes (precise, commercial) versus I/III (complex, research); methylation protects host DNA. Nomenclature (EcoRI equals E. coli RY13 first enzyme) encodes source. Star activity (relaxed specificity) troubles digestions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Palindromic cutters leaving sticky or blunt ends.
  • Bacterial phage defence turned cloning scissors.
Remember
  • Sticky ends ligate directionally; blunt ends join bluntly.

Solution: Six-base palindrome recognition with sticky-end cuts.

Chapter 18 · Topic 6

DNA ligase

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechToolsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA ligase (molecular glue: T4 phage enzyme standard) seals nicks forming phosphodiester bonds (ATP powered) - joining inserts to vectors, Okazaki patches, repair patches. Sticky-end ligation (complementary overhangs, efficient) versus blunt-end (any ends, inefficient). Ligase failure breaks genomes; inhibitors probe repair. Sealing completes every recombinant build.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Nick-sealing glue for cloning, replication and repair.
  • Sticky ends ligate efficiently; blunt ends need help.
Remember
  • Ligase seals; polymerase extends; nucleases cut - tool trio.

1
