Chapter 18 · Topic 7

DNA polymerase

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechToolsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA polymerases extend primers 5-to-3 (Taq heat-stable for PCR cycling; Pfu proofreading-high-fidelity; reverse transcriptase RNA-to-DNA for cDNA libraries). No de novo starts (primers mandatory); proofreading varies by enzyme. PCR cycles Taq through denaturation-annealing-extension tirelessly; sequencing reads via polymerase stops.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Primer-extending synthesizers with varying fidelity.
  • Taq cycles PCR; RT makes cDNA; Sanger reads via stops.
Remember
  • No primer, no start - polymerases extend only.

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechToolsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Vectors (DNA vehicles: plasmids, phages, cosmids, BACs/YACs for big inserts, Ti-plasmid plants, retroviral animal vectors) carry foreign genes into hosts - needing origin of replication, selectable markers, cloning sites (polylinker insertion), plus promoters for expression vectors. Capacity scales (plasmid ~10 kb, BAC ~300 kb, YAC megabases); host range restricts choices.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Origin plus marker plus cloning site (plus promoter if expressing).
  • Capacity scales plasmid to YAC by insert size.

Plasmids

Topic in Depth

Plasmids (small circular extra-chromosomal DNA: F-factor fertility, R-resistance, Ti-tumor, pBR322/pUC lab workhorses) replicate independently at high copy numbers - ideal cloning vehicles (cut, paste, transform, select via markers, blue-white screening via lacZ). Copy number and incompatibility groups manage lab stocks. Natural plasmid traffic spreads antibiotic resistance - cloning exploits bacterial sex machinery.

  • Independent high-copy circles with markers for selection.
  • pBR322/pUC workhorses; blue-white screens carriers.
Remember
  • Antibiotic markers plus colour screens find carriers.

Selectable markers

Topic in Depth

Selectable markers (antibiotic-resistance genes: ampicillin, tetracycline, kanamycin; herbicide resistance in plants) identify transformed carriers - only insert-bearing cells survive selection plates. Reporter genes (GFP glowing, GUS blue staining, luciferase) visualise expression; auxotrophic markers select metabolically. Marker-free technologies answer biosafety concerns about resistance spread.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Antibiotic/herbicide resistance flags carriers.
  • Reporters (GFP, GUS) visualise expression live.
Remember
  • Markers find carriers; reporters show expression.

Chapter 18 · Topic 11

Denaturation

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechPCRStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

PCR denaturation (~94C, 30 seconds) melts double-stranded templates into single strands breaking hydrogen bonds - heat separates without chemicals each cycle. Initial extended denaturation opens genomic complexity; incomplete melting (GC-rich) stalls amplification - additives ease tough templates. Reversible melting underlies all thermal cycling.
NEET Snapshot:
  • 94C melting separates template strands each cycle.
  • GC-rich templates need hotter/longer melting.
Remember
  • Melt apart to copy each strand separately.

1

PCR denaturation step (~94C) functions to

Solution: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds opening templates for priming.

Chapter 18 · Topic 12

Annealing

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechPCRStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

PCR annealing (~54-60C, primer-melting dependent) binds forward-reverse primers to complementary template sites flanking targets - temperature set below primer Tm (too hot misses, too cold misprimes). Primer design (18-25 bases, 40-60 percent GC, no dimers/hairpins) decides specificity; touchdown protocols maximise fidelity. Annealing selects WHAT amplifies - design precision equals product purity.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Primers bind flanking sites at Tm-minus degrees.
  • Design (length, GC, dimers) decides specificity.
Remember
  • Too hot misses targets; too cold misprimes elsewhere.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

PCR annealing temperature is set based on primer

Solution: Near-Tm binding balances specificity against yield.

Chapter 18 · Topic 13

Extension

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechPCRStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

PCR extension (~72C, Taq optimum) synthesises new strands 5-to-3 from annealed primers - time scaled to length (~1 kb per minute), final extended hold finishes partials. Proofreading Pols (Pfu) trade speed for fidelity. Extension completes doubling; 25-35 cycles exponentiate (2^n theory, plateau reality as reagents exhaust).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Taq extends primers at 72C optimum.
  • Time scales with target length (~1 kb/minute).
Remember
  • Final hold finishes partial extensions completely.

Taq polymerase

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechPCRStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Taq polymerase (Thermus aquaticus hot-spring enzyme) survives PCR 94C denaturation repeatedly - processive, fast, error-prone (no proofreading) yet revolutionary for diagnostics, forensics, cloning. Pfu (proofreading archaeal) clones accurately slower; reverse transcriptase prefaces RNA targets. Hot-stable enzymes turned thermal cycling from dream to bench routine.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Heat-stable extender surviving denaturation cycles.
  • Fast error-prone Taq vs slow accurate Pfu trade-off.
Remember
  • PCR Nobel rode Taq heat stability.

Solution: Boiling-proof enzyme cycles PCR tirelessly.

Amplification

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechPCRStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

PCR amplification exponentiates targets (2^n theory: 30 cycles toward billion-fold) through denaturation-annealing-extension cycling - plateauing as primers/dNTPs exhaust and polymerase tires. Real-time qPCR (fluorescent probes measuring per-cycle) quantifies starting copies (viral loads, gene expression); nested PCR boosts specificity; multiplex runs parallel targets. Contamination (aerosol amplicons) is the constant enemy.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cycling doubles targets toward billion-fold yields.
  • qPCR quantifies; nested specifies; multiplex parallels.

DNA separation

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGel ElectrophoresisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gel electrophoresis separates DNA by size (phosphate-backbone uniform negative charge means length alone decides mobility) - small fragments sprint, large crawl through agarose pores under voltage. Southern blotting transfers bands to membranes for probing; pulsed-field resolves megabase chromosomes; capillary systems automate sequencing. Separation precedes probing, cutting and cloning.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Uniform charge makes length decide mobility.
  • Small sprint, large crawl through pores.
Remember
  • Charge equalises; size separates - electrophoresis logic.

Agarose gel

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGel ElectrophoresisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Agarose gels (seaweed polysaccharide matrices: low percent large pores for big fragments, high percent tight for small) cast with comb wells, run in buffer tanks, sized against ladders. Concentration tunes resolution (0.7 percent genomic chunks to 2 percent tiny PCRs). Non-toxic, meltable (band recovery), cheap - routine lab workhorse.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Seaweed gels; concentration tunes pore resolution.
  • Low percent big fragments; high percent small ones.
Remember
  • Ladders calibrate; concentration resolves - gel logic.

Solution: Tight matrices sieve tiny differences finely.

DNA bands

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGel ElectrophoresisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA bands (stained fluorescent lines under UV) mark fragment sizes against ladders - intensity quantifies mass (brighter equals more DNA); single crisp bands prove pure PCR, smears diagnose degradation, primer-dimers crowd bottoms. Gel documentation photographs evidence; band cutting (clean blades, minimal UV nicking) recovers inserts for cloning. Bands are data made visible.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fluorescent lines sized against ladders; intensity measures mass.
  • Crisp bands pass; smears fail; dimers crowd bottoms.
Remember
  • Cut bands cleanly with minimal UV damage for cloning.

Visualization

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechGel ElectrophoresisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Visualization (ethidium bromide UV fluorescence - mutagenic, careful handling; safer SYBR Green; silver staining sensitivity) reveals separated DNA - transilluminators excite, cameras document, software quantifies. Blue-light plus safe dyes modernise teaching labs away from UV-ethidium hazards. Seeing bands confirms everything upstream (extraction, PCR, digestion) worked.
NEET Snapshot:
  • UV-ethidium classic; SYBR-safe modern alternatives.
  • Document bands to validate upstream steps.
Remember
  • Ethidium is mutagenic - gloves plus safe dyes modernise.

Isolation of DNA

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechRecombinant DNA ProcessStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA isolation (lysis: grind plus detergent bursting cells, RNase/protease clearing RNA-proteins, phenol-chloroform or spin-column purifying, ethanol precipitating spoolable DNA) must yield pure high-molecular-weight templates - A260/280 ratios (~1.8 pure) check quality. Plant polysaccharides (CTAB protocols), blood heme (inhibitors), ancient samples (degraded traces) each need tweaks. Pure template decides every downstream success.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lyse, clear, purify, precipitate spoolable DNA.
  • A260/280 ~1.8 proves purity for downstream steps.
Remember
  • CTAB handles plant polysaccharides; spin columns speed preps.

Restriction digestion

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechRecombinant DNA ProcessStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Restriction digestion (purified DNA plus chosen enzymes plus buffers, 37C incubations) cuts at specific sites - complete digestion (all sites cut, clean bands) versus partial (missed sites, extra bands); double digests (two enzymes, compatible buffers) tailor ends; dephosphorylation blocks vector self-ligation. Time, enzyme units and DNA purity decide completeness - star activity (relaxed specificity) overdigests.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Enzyme-buffer-temperature cutting at cognate sites.
  • Complete digests clean; partials confuse patterns.
Remember
  • Star activity (overdigestion) relaxes specificity harmfully.

Chapter 18 · Topic 22

Ligation

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechRecombinant DNA ProcessStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Ligation (insert plus vector compatible ends joined by T4 ligase, ATP-powered) seals recombinant molecules - insert:vector molar ratios (3:1 typical) optimise single-insert clones; dephosphorylated vectors resist self-closure; controls (vector-only ligation) measure background. Transformation follows with ligation mixes; colony PCR screens inserts.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Compatible ends sealed at optimised molar ratios.
  • Dephosphorylation blocks vector self-closure background.
Remember
  • 3:1 insert-vector ratios favour single inserts.

Topic in Depth

Transformation (competent cells taking up DNA: CaCl2 heat-shock E. coli, electroporation zaps, Agrobacterium plant co-cultivation, biolistic gene guns, microinjection) delivers constructs - efficiency (colonies per microgram) measures competence; recovery broth revives shocked cells before selection plating. Natural competence plus artificial protocols span bacteria to mammals.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Competent cells internalise DNA by shock, zap or biology.
  • Efficiency (colonies/microgram) gauges competence.

Selection

Selection (antibiotic/herbicide plates killing non-carriers) plus screening (blue-white lacZ, GFP glow, colony PCR, replica plating) isolates correct clones - markers flag carriers, reporters confirm expression, sequencing verifies inserts base-perfect. Marker-free strategies answer biosafety resistance-spread worries. Select carriers, screen correct, sequence confirm - triple gate before expression scale-up.

  • Marker-free designs ease biosafety resistance fears.

  • Select (survive), screen (verify), sequence (confirm) - triple gate.

Expression

Biotechnology: Principles and ProcessesGenetics, Evolution and BiotechRecombinant DNA ProcessStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Expression (host machinery transcribing-translating inserts into proteins) needs promoters (strong, inducible - lac, T7), codon optimisation (host preferences), folding chaperones, plus purification tags (His-tag nickel columns). Inclusion bodies (bacterial misfolded aggregates) refold painfully; yeast/mammalian systems glycosylate properly. Fermenters scale microlitres to kilolitres - insulin, growth hormone, vaccines flow from expressed clones commercially.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Promoters drive, codons match, tags purify, fermenters scale.
  • Inclusion bodies refold; glycosylation needs eukaryotes.
Remember
  • His-tags nickel-purify recombinant proteins routinely.

Trait benefits versus ecological caution frame every deployment decision.
NEET facts:
  • 1982 Humulin first rDNA drug; Bt cotton stacks cry genes; TKDL defeats biopiracy.

Yield plus nutrition plus pesticide savings argue for; gene flow, resistance evolution and corporate control argue caution.

Bt crops

Topic in Depth

Bt crops (cry-gene cotton, brinjal, maize - Bacillus thuringiensis delta-endotoxin expressed in tissues) kill chewing caterpillars specifically (alkaline guts activate protoxin, pores lyse midguts) sparing beneficials, humans and livestock (acid guts, no receptors). Refuge (non-Bt strips) slows resistance evolution; secondary pests sometimes surge. Pesticide sprays drop dramatically where Bt succeeds.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Bacterial cry toxin in tissues kills caterpillars specifically.
  • Refuge strips delay resistance evolution.
Remember
  • Alkaline insect guts activate protoxin; human guts ignore it.

Bt cotton

Topic in Depth

Bt cotton (cryIAc/cryIIAb against bollworms) cut insecticide sprays, raised yields and farmer incomes where pink bollworm dominated - resistance management (refuge compliance) decides durability (resistance emerged where refuges lapsed). Second-generation Bollgard-II stacks two cry genes delaying resistance. Socioeconomics (seed costs, spurious seeds, credit) matter as much as molecular biology in field outcomes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cry cotton versus bollworms - spray cuts plus yield gains.
  • Refuge compliance decides resistance durability.
Remember
  • Two stacked cry genes (Bollgard-II) delay resistance longer.

Chapter 19 · Topic 4

Pest resistance

Biotechnology and Its ApplicationsGenetics, Evolution and BiotechAgricultural BiotechnologyStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pest resistance engineering stacks tactics: Bt toxins (chewing caterpillars), protease inhibitors (cowpea trypsin inhibitor starving guts), lectins (sap-sucker deterrents), RNAi (silencing pest essential genes - host-induced gene silencing), plus refuge and rotation delaying counter-evolution. Integrated pest management (resistant varieties plus biocontrol plus judicious sprays) outlasts single-tactic reliance.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Toxins plus inhibitors plus RNAi plus refuges stack durably.
  • IPM integrates resistant varieties with biocontrol.
Remember
  • Pyramided traits outlast solo toxins against evolution.

Fermenters now supply global diabetics; pumps plus pens deliver precisely.

Edible vaccines (banana-expressed antigens - cold-chain-free dreams) plus DNA vaccines extend platforms. Subunit precision trades some potency for major safety gains.

  • No live pathogen means no reversion risk.

Gene therapy (correcting defective genes: SCID-X1 retroviral cure proof, retinal gene replacement, CAR-T cancer cell engineering, CRISPR trials editing sickle-cell genes) delivers functional copies via viral/non-viral vectors ex vivo (cells out, fixed, returned) or in vivo (vectors injected). Safety (insertional risks), efficacy durability and pricing gate access - cures exist unequally. Germline editing (heritable) stays banned ethically almost everywhere.

  • SCID, retinal replacement, CAR-T prove; pricing gates access.

Sensitivity (few molecules) plus specificity (sequence-exact) beats culture delays - treatment starts on molecular evidence.

Contamination controls (no-template blanks) guard false positives.

Pharming grows drugs in plants (antibodies in tobacco, vaccines in banana dreams); phytoremediation cleans soils (hyperaccumulators mining metals). Trait speed is transgenic advantage; ecology needs watching.

Field trials phase (contained to open) plus monitoring plus labelling manage deployment. Precaution scales with novelty.

Bioprospecting (legal search with consent plus royalties) contrasts piracy (taking without credit). Traditional knowledge plus modern patents need fair contracts.

TRIPS sets global minimums; compulsory licences for health emergencies balance. Patent thickets (overlapping CRISPR claims) complicate research freedom - ownership shapes who benefits from biology.

Coexistence (buffer zones, refuge, identity preservation) manages GM with conventional/organic neighbours. Evidence-based case-by-case verdicts beat blanket bans or blank cheques.

Deep Dive · Environment meets populations

Populations live inside abiotic frames (temperature, water, light, soil selecting adaptations morphological-physiological-behavioural) counted as densities (quadrats, mark-recapture) changing via natality-mortality-migration plus age structures, growing exponentially until logistic carrying-capacity caps, and interacting (predation, competition, parasitism, commensalism, mutualism, amensalism) in webs. Density, growth and interaction lenses together read any wild population story - from tiger censuses to algal blooms.
NEET facts:
  • Lincoln mark-recapture estimates mobiles; age pyramids forecast (expanding, stable, declining).
  • Gause exclusion, 10 percent energy transfer and mutualism networks organise communities.

Chapter 20 · Topic 1

Temperature

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentAbiotic FactorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Temperature (thermal regimes: stenothermal narrow-tolerance polar/tropical specialists versus eurythermal wide-tolerance temperate generalists) controls enzyme kinetics, membrane fluidity and metabolic rates (Q10 doubling per 10C to optima). Bergmann (bigger bodies cold), Allen (smaller extremities cold) and Gloger (darker humid tropics) rules map body responses. Hibernation, aestivation and migration escape extremes temporally or spatially.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Stenothermal narrow versus eurythermal wide tolerance.
  • Bergmann, Allen and Gloger rules map thermal responses.

Water

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentAbiotic FactorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Water (solvent, reactant, habitat) limits life by availability: aquatic (problems of salt balance, not supply), xeric (drought adaptations: deep roots, succulence, CAM, ephemeral life), mesic (moderate sufficiency). Stenohaline versus euryhaline tolerance splits aquatic osmoregulators. Productivity tracks rainfall (deserts barren, rainforests exuberant) - water is the master ecological variable on land.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Availability, not presence, limits terrestrial life.
  • Productivity tracks rainfall globally.
Remember
  • Deserts lack water; oceans lack balance - different scarcities.

Solution: Xeric strategies hoard every drop plus minimise loss.

Topic in Depth

Light (energy plus signal: intensity, quality, duration) drives photosynthesis (saturation curves), photoperiodism (flowering by night length), phototropism (growth steering) and vision. Shade tolerance (sciophytes) versus sun demand (heliophytes) stratifies forests vertically; phytoplankton zonation follows light penetration; UV selects pigments and repair. Daylength cues time reproduction across kingdoms.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Energy, signal and timer - light triple role.
  • Sciophytes tolerate shade; heliophytes demand sun.

Topic in Depth

Soil (weathered rock plus humus plus air-water pores) varies by texture (sand-silt-clay settling rates), pH (acidic leached versus alkaline calcareous), nutrients (N-P-K plus micros), and water-holding (field capacity). Edaphic factors select communities (laterite scrub, alluvial farmland, saline marshes); earthworms engineer structure; mycorrhizae extend roots. Soil profiles (O-A-B-C horizons) record formation history.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Texture, pH, nutrients and water-holding select communities.
  • Topsoil fertility decides agricultural fate.
Remember
  • Loam (balanced sand-silt-clay) suits most crops.

Topic in Depth

Adaptations (heritable fitness traits: morphological structures, physiological processes, behavioural patterns) evolve by selection for habitat demands - desert succulence, Arctic fur, deep-sea enzymes, mimicry disguises. Acclimatisation (lifetime reversible adjustment) differs fundamentally (non-heritable). Convergent adaptations (cactus-Euphorbia) solve same problems separately; divergent radiations split one stock many ways.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Heritable fitness traits shaped by selection.
  • Adaptation evolves; acclimatisation adjusts temporarily.

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentAbiotic FactorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Morphological adaptations reshape bodies: desert (reduced spiny leaves, succulent stems, deep roots), aquatic (aerenchyma floats, dissected leaves reduce drag, waxy coats repel), Arctic (dense fur, blubber, small extremities per Allen rule), climbing (tendrils, hooks, thorns), parasitic (haustoria, scale leaves). Form follows habitat pressure visibly - cactus versus water-lily contrasts teach adaptation at a glance.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Desert succulence, aquatic airiness, Arctic insulation.
  • Form visibly follows habitat pressure.
Remember
  • Spines defend plus save water; aerenchyma floats plus aerates.

Chapter 20 · Topic 7

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentAbiotic FactorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Physiological adaptations rewire chemistry: CAM photosynthesis (night CO2 fixation, desert water saving), C4 pumps (hot efficiency), antifreeze glycoproteins (Antarctic fish), salt glands (mangrove excretion), aestivation enzymes (desert dormancy),Altitude haemoglobin (high dwellers). Invisible but decisive - physiology extends tolerance beyond morphology. Crop breeding borrows wild physiological traits (drought genes into wheat).
NEET Snapshot:
  • CAM, C4, antifreeze, salt glands - chemical tolerance tricks.
  • Invisible physiology extends ranges morphology cannot.
Remember
  • CAM trades time (night gas exchange) for water.

Behavioural adaptations

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentAbiotic FactorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Behavioural adaptations move animals to better conditions: migration (Arctic terns pole-to-pole, wildebeest rains-chasing, salmon homing), hibernation (ground-squirrel torpor), aestivation (desert frog dormancy), nocturnality (desert heat avoidance), courtship rituals (mate choice), sociality (herd defence, hive labour). Behaviour evolves fastest (learning supplements genes) - first response to change before bodies follow.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Migration, dormancy, nocturnality, rituals, sociality evade pressures.
  • Behaviour evolves fastest - genes follow later.
Remember
  • Arctic terns migrate pole to pole chasing summer.

Population density (individuals per area/volume) measures crowding - quadrat counts (plants), mark-recapture (Lincoln index: marked-recaptured ratios estimate mobiles), faecal/trap indices approximate shy species. Density drives competition, disease, predation and dispersal pressures (density-dependent regulation); human densities reshape landscapes absolutely. Sampling design (random quadrats, unbiased traps) decides estimate quality.

Remember

Natality

Topic in Depth

Natality (birth rate per 1000 per year) adds individuals - crude birth rate counts all births; age-specific fertility pinpoints reproductive cohorts. High natality (developing nations, r-strategists spawning millions) versus low (developed, K-strategists investing few) shapes age pyramids. Family planning lowers natality deliberately; conservation boosts endangered births (captive breeding). Births minus deaths sets natural increase.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Births per thousand per year add population.
  • r-strategists mass-produce; K-strategists invest few.
Remember
  • Crude rates count all; specific rates target cohorts.

Mortality

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mortality (death rate per 1000 per year) subtracts individuals - crude plus age-specific plus infant (IMR: deaths under one per 1000 births - development indicator) rates. High mortality (predation, disease, famine) versus low (medicine, sanitation) shapes pyramids inversely to natality. Survivorship curves trace cohort deaths: Type I (humans, low early loss), II (birds, constant), III (oysters, massive early loss).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Deaths per thousand per year subtract population.
  • IMR (infant deaths) gauges development level.

Immigration

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Immigration (individuals entering populations) adds like births - seeds blowing in, animals dispersing, humans migrating for jobs. Island colonisation, range expansions (cane toads Australia) and urban influxes demonstrate immigration power. Gene flow accompanies migrants (new alleles enter pools); invasive immigrants (water hyacinth, Lantana) disrupt natives without enemies. Borders (mountains, oceans) gate immigration naturally.

  • Entries add like births; genes flow with migrants.
  • Colonisation plus invasions demonstrate immigration force.
Remember
  • Immigrants bring alleles - gene flow follows movement.

Emigration

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Emigration (individuals leaving populations) subtracts like deaths - seeds dispersing outward, juveniles expelled at maturity (territorial species), humans emigrating for opportunity. Crowding triggers emigration (locust swarms, lemming myths); corridors enable it (wildlife linkages); barriers trap (island endemics cannot leave). Net migration (immigration minus emigration) plus natural increase sets growth.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Exits subtract like deaths; crowding triggers departures.
  • Corridors enable; barriers trap emigrants.
Remember
  • Net migration plus natural increase equals total growth.

Topic in Depth

Age distribution (pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive proportions) forecasts futures: expanding pyramids (broad bases - developing nations), stable bell shapes (replacement fertility), declining urns (narrow bases - ageing Japan/Europe). Working-age dependency ratios plan economies (schools versus pensions). Conservation (tiger cub ratios) and fisheries (juvenile protection) manage age structures deliberately.

  • Pre/reproductive/post proportions forecast growth.
  • Pyramids expand, bells stabilise, urns decline.

Exponential growth

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Exponential (J-curve) growth multiplies unchecked (dN/dt = rN - bacteria, locusts, introduced species pre-limits) - doubling populations outrun arithmetic additions explosively. Resources seem infinite initially; overshoot then crashes follow (reindeer islands, algal blooms). r-selected species (many offspring, little care) specialise in exponential bursts. Human history tracked exponential until demographic transitions bent curves.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Unchecked multiplication; J-curve to overshoot-crash.
  • r-strategists burst; resources eventually cap.
Remember
  • J-curves ignore limits until crashes teach them.

Solution: Constant-rate multiplication compounds without ceiling.

Chapter 20 · Topic 16

Logistic growth

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Logistic (S-curve) growth caps exponentially at carrying capacity K (dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K - lag, log, deceleration, stationary phases) - resources, waste, predators and disease brake expansion realistically. K varies (drought lowers, irrigation raises); overshoot oscillates around K; humans raise K technologically (fertilisers, medicine) postponing limits. Most natural populations follow logistic, not exponential, trajectories.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Exponential take-off capped at carrying capacity.
  • Lag-log-deceleration-stationary phases sequence.
Fig: Lag, log, slowdown, plateau at K - realistic capped growth.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Logistic growth caps populations at

Solution: Resource-limited plateau replaces exponential fantasy.

Carrying capacity

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation GrowthStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Carrying capacity (K: maximum sustainable population given resources) varies by environment (drought lowers, irrigation raises), technology (fertilisers lift human K), and consumption (affluent footprints shrink effective K). Overshoot (exceeding K) degrades capacity itself (overgrazing deserts); undershoot wastes potential. Ecological footprints (hectares per person) measure K-shares - sustainability means living within K income, not capital.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Maximum sustainable population given resources.
  • Overshoot degrades K itself; technology lifts K temporarily.
Remember
  • Footprints measure K-shares per lifestyle.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Exceeding carrying capacity (overshoot) causes

Solution: Overuse damages capacity itself - boom then bust.

Chapter 20 · Topic 18

Predation

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation InteractionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Predation (one eats another: lions-deer, owls-mice, pitcher plants-insects, sparrow-seeds debated) transfers energy up trophic levels with ~10 percent efficiency, regulates prey (preventing overgrazing), and drives defences (camouflage, mimicry, spines, toxins) plus counter-adaptations (speed, senses, herd vigilance) in arms races. Prudent predators (parasitoids sparing hosts till larvae mature) optimise harvests. Keystone predators (sea otters protecting kelp from urchins) structure whole communities.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Eating transfers energy (~10 percent) and regulates prey.
  • Defences versus counter-adaptations race endlessly.
Remember
  • Keystone predators structure communities disproportionately.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Predation transfers energy between trophic levels at about

Solution: Metabolic costs dissipate most energy as heat.

Related Diagram · Predator-prey cycle

Fig: Prey peaks feed predator peaks that crash prey - coupled oscillations.

Related Diagram · Teeth and claws

Fig: Defences versus counter-weapons race endlessly.

Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 20 · Topic 19

Competition

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation InteractionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Competition (same-resource rivalry: intraspecific severest - identical needs; interspecific - Gause exclusion principle: complete competitors cannot coexist, one excludes) drives niche partitioning (warbler zones, root depths), character displacement (Galapagos finch beaks diverge where coexisting), and succession (weeds yield to trees). Interference (allelopathy, aggression) versus exploitation (faster uptake) modes differ. Competition organises communities by exclusion and partitioning.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Same needs compete; exclusion or partitioning resolves.
  • Gause: complete competitors cannot coexist stably.
Competition outcomes
PointDetail
ExclusionOne ousts other (Gause)
PartitioningDivide resources (warbler zones)
DisplacementTraits diverge where coexisting

1

Gause competitive exclusion principle states complete competitors

Solution: Identical niches resolve by exclusion, not sharing.

Chapter 20 · Topic 20

Parasitism

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation InteractionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Parasitism (one benefits, host harmed: ticks, lice, tapeworms, Cuscuta haustoria, Plasmodium) ranges ecto (surface) to endo (internal), with complex life cycles (liver fluke snails-sheep, malaria mosquito-human) frustrating control. Brood parasitism (cuckoo eggs in crow nests) outsources parenting; social parasitism (slave ants) steals labour. Host-parasite coevolution (resistance versus virulence) runs Red-Queen races - running to stay in place.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Benefits at host expense; complex cycles frustrate control.
  • Cuckoo brood parasitism outsources parenting entirely.
Remember
  • Red Queen races: hosts resist, parasites counter endlessly.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Cuckoo laying eggs in crow nests shows

Solution: Hosts rear foreign chicks at own chicks expense.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 20 · Topic 21

Commensalism

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation InteractionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected: orchids on trees, barnacles on whales, cattle egrets following grazers eating flushed insects, clownfish-anemone? debated mutual) costs hosts nothing measurable. Epiphytes use trees as stands (light access without parasitism); phoronts hitchhike (mites on beetles). Proving zero effect is hard - many commensalisms hide subtle mutualisms or parasitisms on closer study (egret-tick removal benefits grazers).
NEET Snapshot:
  • One gains, other unaffected (measurably).
  • Orchids, barnacles, egrets exemplify harmless hitchhiking.
Remember
  • Zero-effect proof is hard - commensalism often hides mutualism.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Orchids growing on tree branches show

Solution: Epiphytes gain stands; trees lose nothing measurable.

Fig: Shelter for food - both partners profit.

Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 20 · Topic 22

Mutualism

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation InteractionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mutualism (both benefit: lichens alga-fungus, mycorrhiza phosphorus-sugars, Rhizobium-ammonia for plant sugars, fig-wasp nursery-pollination, cleaner fish-client health) ranges facultative (loose, replaceable partners) to obligate (yucca-moth exclusive interdependence). Coevolution tightens partnerships (flower-tube lengths matching moth tongues); cheating (nectar robbers) tests stability. Mutualism networks underpin ecosystems - pollination plus seed dispersal run on reciprocal deals.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Both partners gain; loose to obligate interdependence.
  • Fig-wasp and yucca-moth are obligate extremes.
Mutualism deals

LichenShelter for food
MycorrhizaPhosphorus for sugars
RhizobiumAmmonia for sugars
Fig-waspNursery for pollination

Chapter 20 · Topic 23

Amensalism

Organisms and PopulationsEcology and EnvironmentPopulation InteractionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Amensalism (one harmed, other unaffected: black-walnut juglone poisoning neighbours, Penicillium antibiotics killing bacteria, tall trees shading seedlings) is competition chemical warfare (allelopathy) or incidental damage. Antibiosis (microbial chemical inhibition) founds antibiotic medicine - soil microbes seasoned amensalists. Distinguishing amensalism (0/-) from competition (-/-) needs benefit audits - walnuts gain nothing from killed neighbours, competitors both lose.
NEET Snapshot:
  • One harmed, other unaffected (chemical or incidental).
  • Allelopathy (juglone) plus antibiosis (penicillin) exemplify.
Remember
  • Amensalism harms one-sidedly; competition harms mutually.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Penicillium killing nearby bacteria shows

Solution: Antibiotic inhibition harms bacteria benefiting fungus negligibly.

Deep Dive · Systems cycling energy and matter

Ecosystems organise components (abiotic stage plus biotic producers-consumers-decomposers) into productivity accounts (GPP income, NPP surplus, secondary trickle), decomposition sequences (fragment-leach-catabolise-humify-mineralise), energy flows (grazing plus detritus chains into webs, trophic levels taxed 10 percent, pyramids of number-biomass-energy with energy never inverting), nutrient cycles (gaseous carbon versus sedimentary phosphorus) and successions (primary rock-to-forest, secondary fast return, xerarch wettening, hydrarch filling, pioneers engineering, climax stabilising). Energy flows one-way; matter cycles round.
NEET facts:
  • Energy pyramids never invert; biomass/number may (oceans, trees).
  • Xerarch starts dry rock; hydrarch starts open water - mirror trajectories.
Fig: Energy narrows upward always - thermodynamics guarantees upright pyramids.

Chapter 21 · Topic 1

Abiotic components

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentComponentsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Abiotic components (light, temperature, water, air, soil minerals, pH, topography, fire) set ecosystem stages - energy input (solar), matter pools (soil, water, air reservoirs), and climatic regimes filtering which biota persist. Abiotic-biotic feedbacks rule (vegetation cools climate, beavers flood valleys). Monitoring abiotics (rain gauges, soil tests) predicts productivity - environment first, organisms second.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Light, heat, water, air, minerals, pH, fire set stages.
  • Feedbacks run both ways (forests make rain).
NEET Practice MCQ

Abiotic components of ecosystems exclude

Solution: Decomposers are living biotic members, not physical factors.

Chapter 21 · Topic 2

Biotic components

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentComponentsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Biotic components organise by feeding: producers (photo/chemoautotrophs fixing energy), consumers (primary herbivores, secondary small carnivores, tertiary top carnivores, omnivores mixing, detritivores eating dead), decomposers (bacteria-fungi mineralising). Standing crop (biomass present) versus production rate (energy fixed per time) measure differently. Removing any tier cascades (wolf removal explodes elk, starving aspens) - trophic downgrading proof.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Producers fix; consumers eat levels up; decomposers mineralise.
  • Standing crop stocks; production flows - different metrics.
Remember
  • Trophic cascades prove every tier matters structurally.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Decomposers in ecosystems mainly

Solution: Bacteria-fungi return locked nutrients to circulation.

Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 3

Producers

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentComponentsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Producers (photoautotrophs: plants, algae, cyanobacteria; chemoautotrophs: nitrifiers, sulphur bacteria) fix inorganic carbon into organic energy - entry gate for all ecosystem energy (deep-vent chemosynthetic oases excepted from sunlight). Gross production minus respiration equals net available upward. Phytoplankton (oceanic half of global production) plus forests (terrestrial bulk) lead planetary fixing.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Autotrophs fixing energy entry for all food webs.
  • Phytoplankton plus forests split global production.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Primary producers in deep-sea vent ecosystems are

Solution: Sunless vents run on chemical-energy fixation instead.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 4

Consumers

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentComponentsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Consumers eat producers or each other: primary (herbivores: deer, grasshoppers, zooplankton), secondary (small carnivores: frogs, spiders), tertiary (top carnivores: tigers, eagles, sharks), omnivores (humans, bears mixing levels), detritivores (earthworms, detritus feeders). Trophic position decides toxin load (biomagnification climbs) and energy share (10 percent rule shrinks upward). Food chains simplify; webs interconnect reality.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Herbivores to top carnivores plus omnivores and detritivores.
  • Position decides energy share and toxin burden.
Remember
  • Omnivores feed across levels frustrating neat chains.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Secondary consumers eat

Solution: Small carnivores prey on herbivore trophic level.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 5

Decomposers

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentComponentsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Decomposers (saprotrophic bacteria-fungi plus detritivores: earthworms fragmenting, termites chewing wood) mineralise dead matter - fragmentation, leaching, catabolism (enzymatic), humification (humus forming), mineralisation (inorganic release) sequence recycling. Without them nutrients lock in corpses and life starves amid plenty. Antibiotics (slow decay) and cold (tundra peat) stall decomposition visibly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Mineralise dead matter recycling locked nutrients.
  • Fragmentation to mineralisation five-step sequence.
Remember
  • Decomposers close nutrient loops producers open.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Decomposition rate is slowest in

Solution: Cold plus dryness freeze microbial recycling.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 6

Primary productivity

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentProductivityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Primary productivity (producer biomass/energy accumulation rate: g/m2/yr or kcal/m2/yr) varies ocean-desert low to rainforest-coral-reef high - light, water, nutrients plus temperature gate it. Most productive systems (tropical forests, estuaries, reefs, sugarcane fields) combine all inputs; deserts and deep oceans starve one. Satellite NDVI maps global productivity live - greeness quantifies fixing.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Producer accumulation rate; varies light-water-nutrient gated.
  • Rainforests, reefs, estuaries, cane fields top charts.
Remember
  • NDVI satellite greenness maps productivity globally.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most productive natural ecosystems include

Solution: Year-round light plus water plus nutrients maximise fixing.

Fig: Total fixing minus plant breathing equals web-feeding surplus.

Chapter 21 · Topic 7

Gross primary productivity

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentProductivityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Gross primary productivity (total organic matter/energy fixed by photosynthesis including respiration costs) is ecosystem income before expenses - measured by oxygen evolution, CO2 uptake or biomass harvest plus respiration estimates. Tropical forests (~2000 g/m2/yr) dwarf deserts (~200); oceans moderate per area but vast in total. GPP minus autotrophic respiration equals NPP available upward - income statement top line.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Total fixed including respiration costs (income before expenses).
  • GPP minus plant respiration equals NPP upward.
Remember
  • Harvest plus respiration estimates reconstruct GPP.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

GPP minus autotrophic respiration equals

Solution: Net producer surplus feeds all higher trophic levels.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 8

Net primary productivity

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentProductivityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Net primary productivity (GPP minus plant respiration - actually available to heterotrophs) feeds every food web; agricultural NPP harvested as yield (harvest index: grain over total biomass). Human appropriation (~25-40 percent terrestrial NPP) starves wild webs - HANPP footprint. Oceans: high total NPP from vast areas despite low per-area rates; coastal upwellings spike locally. NPP is ecology spendable income.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Producer surplus feeding heterotrophs (yield basis).
  • Humans appropriate a quarter-plus of terrestrial NPP.
Remember
  • Harvest index (grain/total) measures NPP capture efficiency.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Agricultural yield relates most directly to

Solution: Harvestable surplus is net production after plant costs.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 9

Secondary productivity

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentProductivityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Secondary productivity (consumer biomass formation rate - growth plus reproduction minus respiration) runs an order below primary (10 percent transfer efficiency); P/B ratios (production per biomass: bacteria high, whales low) compare turnover. Fisheries MSY (maximum sustainable yield) harvests secondary production sustainably - overfishing exceeds it collapsing stocks. Pastures convert primary to meat/milk at ~10 percent efficiency - trophic tax visible.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Consumer biomass formation (~10 percent of primary).
  • MSY harvests secondary sustainably; excess collapses stocks.
Remember
  • P/B ratios compare turnover across life histories.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Secondary productivity is formation rate of biomass by

Solution: Heterotroph growth plus reproduction minus respiration defines it.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 10

Fragmentation

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentDecompositionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fragmentation (detritivores: earthworms, termites, millipedes pulverising litter) opens surface area for microbes - first decomposition step accelerating everything downstream. Shredders plus macerators fragment; microbivores graze microbe blooms in turn. Leaf-litter bags (mesh excluding macrofauna) quantify fragmentation contribution experimentally - coarse-mesh loss exceeds fine-mesh visibly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Detritivores pulverise litter multiplying microbial area.
  • First step accelerating all downstream decay.
Remember
  • Litter-bag mesh sizes isolate fragmentation roles.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Leaf litter fragmentation is done mainly by

Solution: Macro-shredders open area microbes then colonise.

Chapter 21 · Topic 11

Leaching

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentDecompositionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Leaching (water percolating soluble nutrients downward out of litter into soil) follows fragmentation - sugars, amino acids and minerals wash to microbes and roots below. Heavy rains leach fastest (tropical downpours strip litter quickly); waterlogging slows (anaerobic stalling). Throughfall (canopy drip enriched) plus stemflow deliver leachates continuously. Leaching moves nutrients vertically toward uptake zones.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Water washing solubles downward from litter to soil.
  • Rains accelerate; waterlogging stalls leaching flows.
Remember
  • Throughfall enriches rain passing canopies.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Leaching during decomposition moves nutrients

Solution: Percolating water carries solubles to soil layers.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 12

Catabolism

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentDecompositionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Catabolism (microbial enzymatic breakdown: cellulases, ligninases, proteases cleaving polymers to monomers) is decomposition chemical core - bacteria plus fungi secreting exoenzymes digesting dead matter externally then absorbing products. Lignin resists most (white-rot fungi uniquely crack it); simple sugars vanish first. Enzyme cocktails (industrial biomass fuels mimic them) unlock plant matter - decay chemistry powering recycling plus biofuels.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Microbial exoenzymes cleaving polymers to absorbable monomers.
  • Lignin resists most; white-rot fungi crack it.
Remember
  • Biofuel pretreatments mimic microbial enzyme cocktails.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Lignin in dead wood is decomposed mainly by

Solution: Specialised fungal enzymes uniquely crack lignin polymers.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 13

Humification

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentDecompositionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Humification (humus formation: dark amorphous colloid of partially decayed organics) builds soil fertility - water-nutrient holding, structure, microbial habitat. Slow (years-centuries); peat bogs accumulate undecayed humus carbon stores. Humus C:N ratios (~10:1) stabilise; fulvic (soluble) plus humic (insoluble) fractions differ. composting accelerates humification deliberately - humus is decay paused usefully.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Partial decay forming dark fertile colloid.
  • Peat bogs bank undecayed humus carbon.
Remember
  • Composting speeds humification deliberately.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Humus is

Solution: Stabilised decay products hold water and nutrients.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 14

Mineralisation

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentDecompositionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Mineralisation (humus microbes releasing inorganic nutrients: ammonium, phosphate, sulphate) completes recycling - dead organics back to plant-usable ions. Warm-moist conditions accelerate (tropical soils cycle fast, poor in humus); cold/acidic stalls (peat accumulates). Mineralisation-immobilisation balance (microbes release vs re-absorb) decides plant availability - C:N ratios predict net release (low) or lockup (high).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Humus to inorganic ions - recycling completion.
  • Warm-moist accelerates; cold-acid stalls into peat.
Remember
  • Low C:N releases nutrients; high C:N locks them.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Mineralisation releases nutrients from humus as

Solution: Microbes convert organic stores to plant-usable ions.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 15

Food chain

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEnergy FlowStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Food chains (linear feeding links: grass-deer-tiger; phytoplankton-zooplankton-fish) trace energy paths simply - single routes through trophic levels. Length limited (~4-5 levels by 10 percent losses); keystone links disproportionately matter. Chains teach direction (producers up to top carnivores) but oversimplify (omnivores, loops, detours) - webs correct the picture while chains introduce it.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Linear feeding links tracing energy upward.
  • Length capped ~4-5 levels by compounding losses.
Remember
  • Chains introduce; webs correct - teaching progression.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels because

Solution: Exponential energy decay starves higher levels.

Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 16

Grazing food chain

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEnergy FlowStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Grazing food chains (living producers to herbivores to carnivores: grass-deer-tiger, phytoplankton-zooplankton-fish) move most ecosystem energy visibly - green-world pathway supporting charismatic megafauna. Herbivore pressure shapes vegetation (grazing lawns, thorn defences); predator removal explodes herbivores (trophic cascades denuding flora). Rangeland carrying capacities manage grazing chains sustainably.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Living-producer chains feeding visible megafauna.
  • Herbivore pressure shapes vegetation; predators check it.
Remember
  • Wolf reintroduction revived Yellowstone aspens via cascades.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Grazing food chain starts with

Solution: Green-plant energy enters herbivores first.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 17

Detritus food chain

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEnergy FlowStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Detritus chains (dead matter to detritivores to predators: leaf litter-earthworms-birds; mangrove detritus-crabs-fish) move most ecosystem energy invisibly - forest floors and ocean depths run detrital. Detritus (dead organics plus microbes) feeds specialised fauna; energy recycles continuously rather than dissipating upward only. Mangrove fisheries depend on detrital chains - fallen leaves feed commercial fish via detritus routes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dead-matter chains feeding forest floors and ocean depths.
  • Most ecosystem energy flows detritally, invisibly.
Remember
  • Mangrove fish eat leaves via detritus middlemen.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Detritus food chain starts with

Solution: Dead-matter energy enters detritivores first.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 18

Food web

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEnergy FlowStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Food webs (interconnected chains with omnivores, loops, detrital links) model real feeding - stability rises with connectance (many weak links buffer shocks); keystone removals cascade disproportionately (otters-urchins-kelp, wolves-elk-aspen). Web complexity resists perturbation (diversity-stability debate nuances) while simplifying under stress. Conservation protects web architecture, not just species lists.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Interlinked chains with omnivores and loops - real feeding.
  • Connectance buffers; keystones structure disproportionately.
Remember
  • Remove keystones and webs unravel from within.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Food webs are more stable than single chains due to

Solution: Multiple pathways reroute around broken links.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 19

Trophic levels

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEnergy FlowStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Trophic levels (feeding positions: 1 producers, 2 herbivores, 3 small carnivores, 4+ top carnivores, decomposers across) organise energy flow - each level keeps ~10 percent, passes upward, respires rest. Omnivores straddle levels; parasites invert pyramids occasionally; humans span levels 2-4 flexibly. Level number caps food-chain length; biomagnification climbs levels concentrating toxins upward.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Feeding positions 1-4+ with ~10 percent transfer each.
  • Omnivores straddle; toxins climb levels.
Remember
  • Level determines energy share and toxin load.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Humans eating both plants and meat occupy trophic levels

Solution: Omnivory straddles producer-to-carnivore positions.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 20

10% law

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEnergy FlowStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

10 percent law (Lindeman: ~10 percent energy transfers between trophic levels, 90 percent lost to respiration, heat, waste) caps chain length (~4-5 levels), explains vegetarian efficiency (eating lower wastes less), and predicts top-predator rarity (tigers need vast deer bases). Ecological efficiency varies (5-20 percent) but order-of-magnitude holds. Biomass pyramids usually follow energy losses - except inverted aquatic ones (fast-turnover phytoplankton supporting heavier zooplankton).
NEET Snapshot:
  • ~10 percent passes up; ~90 percent dissipates as heat/waste.
  • Caps levels, favours vegetarian efficiency, rarifies top predators.
10 percent consequences
PointDetail
Chain lengthCapped ~4-5 levels
Diet efficiencyLower levels waste less
Top predatorsRare (need huge bases)
Aquatic exceptionInverted biomass pyramids

1

10 percent law of energy transfer was proposed by

Solution: Lindeman trophic-dynamic aspect quantified ecosystem energetics.

Chapter 21 · Topic 21

Pyramid of number

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological PyramidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pyramid of number (individual counts per level) is usually upright (grass hundreds to deer tens to tiger one) but inverts with single trees hosting hundreds of birds/insects (tree-birds-parasites spindle). Shape follows size-number trade-offs, not energy rules - number pyramids can mislead (one tree outweighs thousand insects). Students must separate number (countable, invertible) from biomass/energy (usually upright).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Counts per level; upright usually, tree-based inverted.
  • Size-number trade-offs shape number pyramids.
Remember
  • Tree-birds-parasites spindle inverts number pyramids.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Inverted pyramid of number occurs in systems like

Solution: One massive producer hosts hundreds of consumers.

Fig: Number and biomass may flip; energy never does - entropy guarantees upright.

Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 22

Pyramid of biomass

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological PyramidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pyramid of biomass (dry weight per level) is usually upright (forest tonnes to herbivore kilos) but inverts in oceans (tiny fast-breeding phytoplankton supporting heavier zooplankton-fish standing crops) - turnover rate, not standing stock, sustains marine webs. Biomass snapshots mislead where turnover differs; production-rate pyramids correct the view. Standing crop versus production rate distinction resolves the inversion paradox.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dry weight per level; ocean inverts via fast turnover.
  • Standing stock snapshots mislead where turnover differs.
Remember
  • Phytoplankton reproduce daily supporting heavier grazers.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Inverted biomass pyramid occurs in

Solution: Rapid phytoplankton turnover sustains heavier standing consumers.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 23

Pyramid of energy

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological PyramidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pyramid of energy (kcal flow per level per time) is always upright - thermodynamics forbids inversion (energy dissipates irreversibly upward, 10 percent passes). Most accurate trophic picture (rates, not stocks); production-rate pyramids never invert. Exam trap: number and biomass pyramids may invert, energy never does - entropy guarantees upright energy flow.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Energy flow per level; always upright (thermodynamics).
  • Never inverts - entropy forbids upward energy gain.
Remember
  • Energy pyramids cannot invert - exam trap certainty.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Which ecological pyramid is always upright?

Solution: Thermodynamic losses guarantee upright energy flow.
Back to Index
Index / Ecology and Environment
Chapter 21 · Topic 24

Carbon cycle

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentNutrient CyclesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Carbon cycle circulates CO2 (atmosphere 0.04 percent) through photosynthesis (fixation into biomass), respiration/combustion (return), ocean exchange (dissolution, largest sink), fossilisation (coal-oil over eons) and industry (fossil burning adding ~10 Gt yearly). Fossil disruption (burning ancient carbon) drives warming; forests-oceans-soils buffer (sinks saturating). Paris targets stabilise atmospheric stocks by balancing flows.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Photosynthesis in, respiration-combustion out, oceans buffer.
  • Fossil burning disrupts balance driving warming.
Fig: Fixation draws down; respiration and burning return - fossil burning overloads.

Chapter 21 · Topic 25

Phosphorus cycle

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentNutrient CyclesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phosphorus cycle runs sedimentary (no atmospheric gas phase): rock weathering releases phosphate, plants absorb, animals eat, decomposers return, runoff carries to oceans (sedimentation locking for eons), uplift returns rocks - one-way geological loop. Guano/mined phosphates fertilise; runoff eutrophies waters (algal blooms). Unlike carbon/nitrogen, no gaseous shortcut - phosphorus limits productivity where scarce, mined where concentrated.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Rock to life to sediment to rock - sedimentary one-way loop.
  • No atmospheric phase; mining plus runoff move stocks.
Remember
  • Phosphorus limits growth where scarce; eutrophies where excess.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Phosphorus cycle differs from carbon/nitrogen in lacking

Solution: Sedimentary cycling runs rock-life-sediment without air transit.

Chapter 21 · Topic 26

Primary succession

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological SuccessionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Primary succession colonises lifeless substrates (bare rock, lava, new islands): lichens-mosses pioneer (etching, soil-building), annuals follow, shrubs then forests mature over centuries - facilitation (early species improving conditions) drives forward. Surtsey island (1963 volcanic birth) documents primary succession live. Slow (centuries) because soil builds from zero - every stage engineers the next.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lifeless substrate colonised from zero (lichens first).
  • Centuries-long; pioneers engineer soil for successors.
Remember
  • Surtsey island watches primary succession live since 1963.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: No soil or legacy life - pioneers build from stone.

Fig: Pioneers engineer soil successors inherit toward climax.

Chapter 21 · Topic 27

Secondary succession

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological SuccessionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Secondary succession recolonises disturbed vegetated areas (abandoned farms, burnt forests, logged lands) from soil banks plus survivors - faster than primary (soil, seeds, roots persist), grasses-weeds first, shrubs then forest return in decades. Old-field succession (US farm studies) and shifting-cultivation fallows demonstrate cycles. Disturbance regimes (fire frequencies) maintain mosaic landscapes - climax interrupted sustainably.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Disturbed vegetated areas recover fast from banks plus survivors.
  • Decades, not centuries - legacy accelerates return.
Remember
  • Shifting-cultivation fallows are managed secondary succession.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Legacy life and soil shortcut pioneer stages.

Chapter 21 · Topic 28

Xerarch succession

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological SuccessionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Xerarch succession (dry bare rock to forest: lichens-mosses etch, annuals root cracks, shrubs shade, forest closes) builds water-holding soil grain by grain - each stage wetter than last. Lichen acids dissolve minerals; moss mats trap dust; humus accumulates; shade-tolerant trees finish. Rajasthan rock outcrops to scrub demonstrate truncated xerarch where rain limits climax - succession stalls at water ceiling.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dry rock to forest via wettening stages.
  • Each stage engineers moister conditions for next.
Remember
  • Xerarch starts dry; hydrarch starts wet - opposite origins.

Solution: Dry-stone pioneers wetten habitats toward forest.

Chapter 21 · Topic 29

Hydrarch succession

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological SuccessionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hydrarch succession (pond to forest: phytoplankton-submerged (Hydrilla) to floating (Nymphaea) to reed-swamp (Typha) to sedge-meadow to woodland) fills water bodies with peat and silt - each stage shallower than last. Siltation plus organic accumulation terrestrialise lakes (oxbow succession visible); drainage accelerates artificially. Wetland conservation fights hydrarch completion (dredging resets stages) - succession versus preservation tension.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Open water to woodland via filling stages.
  • Silt plus peat terrestrialise lakes progressively.
Remember
  • Hydrarch fills wet; xerarch wets dry - mirror trajectories.

Solution: Aquatic pioneers fill basins toward terrestrial climax.

Pioneer species

EcosystemEcology and EnvironmentEcological SuccessionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Pioneer species (lichens, mosses, hardy grasses) colonise bare/disturbed ground first - tolerating extremes, reproducing prolifically, engineering conditions (soil-building, nitrogen-fixing Alnus-Casuarina, shade-casting) for successors while dooming themselves (shaded out later). R-strategist traits (many offspring, fast growth) suit colonisation. Restoration plants pioneers deliberately (mine-spoil greening starts with hardy grasses-legumes).
NEET Snapshot:
  • First colonists tolerating extremes, engineering succession.
  • R-strategist traits suit colonisation roles.
Remember
  • Pioneers prepare habitats successors inherit.

Topic in Depth

Climax community (stable self-perpetuating endpoint: oak forest, sal forest) maintains via gap-phase regeneration (fallen trees release saplings) resisting invasion - Clements monoclimax (one climate endpoint) versus polyclimax (soil-fire-topography multiples) debate structure. Disclimax (grazing/fire-maintained grasslands) persists under disturbance; catastrophe resets to pioneers. Climax stability is dynamic equilibrium, not frozen stasis.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Stable self-replacing endpoint resisting invasion.
  • Gap dynamics renew climax continuously.
Remember
  • Disclimax persists under maintained disturbance.

Hotspots prioritise; Red Lists grade; zonation coexists - variety mapped, mourned and managed.

Chapter 22 · Topic 1

Genetic diversity

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Genetic diversity (gene variants within species: basmati versus IR36 rice, dog breeds, human blood groups) fuels adaptation and breeding - uniform clones (tissue-cultured banana, Cavendish) risk wipeout (Panama disease threatens monocultures). Conservation samples widely (seed banks capture landrace alleles); inbreeding depression warns when diversity crashes. Diversity within species is evolution raw material.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Gene variants within species fuel adaptation and breeding.
  • Uniform clones risk wipeout; banks preserve alleles.

Solution: Diverse gene pools adapt and breed; uniformity risks collapse.

Chapter 22 · Topic 2

Species diversity

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Species diversity (counts plus evenness per area: Western Ghats thousands, deserts hundreds) measures community richness - alpha (local), beta (turnover between habitats), gamma (regional total) scales. India mega-diverse (~8 percent global species); tropics richest (stable climate plus area plus time). Hotspots (high endemism plus high threat) prioritise protection globally - 36 hotspots cover 2.4 percent land holding 60 percent species.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Counts plus evenness; alpha-beta-gamma scales.
  • Tropics richest; hotspots prioritise protection.
Remember
  • Western Ghats plus Himalaya are Indian hotspots.

Solution: Stable warm-wet conditions plus time accumulate species.

Ecosystem diversity

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Ecosystem diversity (habitat variety: forests, grasslands, wetlands, reefs, deserts) supports species diversity - heterogeneous landscapes hold more niches (mountain gradients stack zones). India spans alpine to marine ecosystems; each harbours unique assemblages. Ecosystem loss (wetland drainage, reef bleaching) erases whole communities at once - protecting variety protects residents collectively.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Habitat variety supporting species variety.
  • Mountains stack ecosystems vertically.

Solution: Himalayan-to-ocean gradients stack habitats nationally.

Chapter 22 · Topic 4

Patterns

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Biodiversity patterns repeat globally: latitudinal gradient (richness rises toward equator), altitudinal decline (peaks thin with height), species-area curves (bigger areas hold more, Arrhenius S=cA^z), productivity correlation (energy-rich rains support more). Peninsular India (ancient Gondwana stability) out-diversifies young Himalaya per area. Patterns guide reserve design (bigger, connected, tropical prioritised).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Equator-rich, altitude-poor, area-scaled, energy-fed patterns.
  • Stable time plus area plus energy build richness.
Remember
  • Tropics, big areas and old landscapes hold most species.

Solution: Stable warm-wet tropics accumulate species over time.

Chapter 22 · Topic 5

Latitudinal gradient

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Latitudinal gradient (diversity peaking at equator, thinning toward poles) reflects stable warm-wet time (tropics suffered no ice ages), higher productivity (year-round growing), larger areas (tropical belt widest), plus faster speciation (short generations, intense interactions). Temperate zones impoverished by glaciations; poles extreme-filter survivors. Gradient steepness varies by taxon (mammals gentle, insects steep).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Equator richest; poles poorest - stability plus energy plus time.
  • Glaciations impoverished temperate zones recently.
Remember
  • Tropics escaped ice ages; temperates restarted recently.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Latitudinal diversity gradient shows richness

Solution: Equatorial stability, energy and time accumulate species.

Chapter 22 · Topic 6

Species-area relationship

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversityStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Species-area relationship (Arrhenius S=cA^z: log-log straight line, z ~0.1-0.2 continents, ~0.6 islands) means bigger areas hold disproportionately more species - reserve design doubles areas for outsized gains; habitat fragmentation shrinks effective areas crashing diversity. Island biogeography (immigration-extinction equilibrium) extends area logic with isolation. SLOSS debate (single large versus several small reserves) applies area science to protection.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Bigger areas hold more species (log-log law).
  • Fragmentation shrinks effective areas crashing diversity.

ArrheniusS=cA^z log-log straight

Habitat loss

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversity LossStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Habitat loss (deforestation, wetland drainage, reef destruction, urbanisation - top biodiversity threat) shrinks, fragments and degrades living space - Amazon clearance, Southeast Asian palm-oil conversion, Indian wetland reclamation exemplify. Fragmentation isolates (edge effects penetrate, interiors vanish); degradation poisons remnants. Corridors reconnect; restoration rebuilds; protection prevents - hierarchy of responses matching damage stages.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Top threat: shrink, fragment and degrade living space.
  • Corridors reconnect; restoration rebuilds; reserves prevent.
Remember
  • Habitat loss outranks all other threats combined.

Overexploitation

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversity LossStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Overexploitation (harvesting beyond renewal: whaling, overfishing cod/tuna collapse, poaching rhino-tiger-elephant for horn-bone-ivory, medicinal plant stripping) empties populations commercially then biologically - tragedy of open-access commons. Quotas (fisheries MSY), bans (CITES trade controls), farming (crocodile ranching) and certification (MSC seafood) manage harvests sustainably. Passenger pigeon (billions to zero in decades) warns unrestrained take.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Harvest beyond renewal empties populations then species.
  • Quotas, bans, farming and certification manage takes.
Remember
  • Steller sea cow to passenger pigeon: overkill extinctions.
NEET Practice MCQ

Solution: Sailors ate flightless birds; rats ate their eggs.

Chapter 22 · Topic 9

Alien species invasion

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversity LossStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alien species invasion (water hyacinth choking Indian waters, Lantana smothering forests, Parthenium Congress grass allergenic, Nile perch emptying cichlids, cane toads poisoning Australia) outcompetes, preys on or diseases natives lacking defences - islands worst hit (evolved isolation). Ballast water, horticulture and pets import invaders; quarantine plus early eradication (cheapest at arrival) manage. Invasion is globalisation ecological cost.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Introduced species outcompeting defenceless natives.
  • Islands suffer worst (naive biota, no enemies).
Remember
  • Water hyacinth terror of Bengal waters exemplifies invasion.

Co-extinction

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentBiodiversity LossStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Co-extinction (dependents dying with hosts: host-specific parasites, pollinator-dependent figs/wasps, monophagous insects on vanishing plants) multiplies losses beyond counted species - every extinction cascades unseen partners. Fig-wasp obligate pairs risk double loss; gut-microbiome partners vanish unrecorded. Conservation must protect interactions, not just species lists - networks die together.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Dependents vanish with hosts (parasites, pollinators).
  • Fig-wasp pairs risk double extinction.
Remember
  • Saving hosts saves unseen dependent partners.

Endangered species (very high extinction risk: tiger, Asiatic lion, snow leopard, one-horned rhino, Great Indian Bustard) face habitat loss, poaching and fragmentation - Red List criteria (population size, decline rate, range shrink) classify risk scientifically. Project Tiger/Elephant/Rhino plus protected areas pulled several back from brinks. Captive breeding (vulture centres) plus corridors plus community guards combine recovery.
NEET Snapshot:

  • Projects plus parks plus breeding pull species back.

Threatened species

Topic in Depth

Threatened species (Vulnerable plus Endangered plus Critically Endangered IUCN tiers) face escalating risk - criteria combine small numbers, fast declines, tiny ranges and fragmentation. Near-Threatened (watchlisted) plus Data-Deficient (unknown) flank the list. uplisting (worsening) versus downlisting (recovering: rhino successes) track conservation performance. Legal schedules (Wildlife Protection Act I-VI) enforce protection nationally.

  • Schedules plus Red List drive legal protection.
Remember
  • Downlisting (rhino) proves conservation works.

Extinct species

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentExtinctionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Extinct species (no living individuals: dodo, passenger pigeon, Tasmanian tiger, dinosaurs; Indian cheetah, pink-headed duck) ended via overkill, habitat loss, invasives or catastrophes - five mass extinctions (end-Ordovician to K-Pg asteroid) reset life repeatedly; sixth (human-driven) unfolds now. De-extinction (mammoth gene-editing dreams) cannot restore ecosystems - prevention beats resurrection fantasies.
NEET Snapshot:
  • No living members; overkill, habitat, invasives, catastrophes caused.
  • Fifth K-Pg asteroid reset; sixth human-driven unfolds.
Remember
  • De-extinction cannot resurrect lost ecosystems.

Chapter 22 · Topic 14

In-situ conservation

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentConservationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

In-situ conservation (protecting in natural habitats: biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries, sacred groves, Ramsar wetlands) preserves species plus interactions plus evolution (wild relatives keep adapting). Cheaper per species at scale, needs vast areas and guards against encroachment-poaching-conflict. Community reserves (local stewardship) plus eco-development (livelihood alternatives) sustain protection socially - parks need people buy-in.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Protect in wild habitats with interactions evolving.
  • Needs areas plus guards plus community support.
Remember
  • In-situ preserves evolution itself, not just specimens.

Chapter 22 · Topic 15

Ex-situ conservation

Biodiversity and ConservationEcology and EnvironmentConservationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Ex-situ conservation (outside habitats: zoos breeding, botanical gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation, tissue culture, pollen banks) backs wild protection - captive breeding (vultures, rhinos), seed vaults (Svalbard global backup, NBPGR Indian), botanical garden rarities. Limitations (small gene pools, no evolution, reintroduction challenges) make it supplement, never substitute. Integrated conservation blends both strategies per species needs.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Zoos, gardens, banks, cryo backup wild protection.
  • Supplement, never substitute, in-situ conservation.

Zonation (strict core, experimental buffer, lived-in transition) models coexistence; ecosystem services (water, tourism, research) fund acceptance. Reserves are living laboratories of sustainability.

Reintroduction (gharial restocking, red panda releases) returns captives wild-side with mixed success. Parks as arks plus hospitals plus classrooms triple role.

Deep Dive · Pollution to management

Environmental issues run air pollution (particulates, SO2, NOx, CO, smogs, acid rain) through water pollution (sewage BOD, industrial effluents, eutrophication, waterborne diseases) and soil pollution (pesticides, chemicals, heavy metals with Minamata-itai-itai-Bengal warnings) into biological effects (biomagnification up chains, bioaccumulation within bodies) and global problems (greenhouse warming, ozone holes healing under Montreal, acid rain borders) ending in waste management (segregate, treat sewage, recycle, compost, biodegrade versus persistent plastics). Monitor, prevent, treat, recycle - response hierarchy.
NEET facts:
  • Montreal Protocol heals ozone; Paris guards 2C; GEAC clears GMOs; TKDL defeats biopiracy.
  • Biomagnification rises per level (DDT eagles); BOD fall proves sewage cleaning.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Biomagnification means pollutant concentration

Solution: Fat-stored persistent toxins concentrate as biomass shrinks upward.

Chapter 23 · Topic 1

Particulate matter

Environmental IssuesEcology and EnvironmentAir PollutionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Particulate matter (PM10 coarse, PM2.5 fine - dust, smoke, soot, fly ash) lodges in lungs (fine penetrates alveoli-bloodstream: asthma, bronchitis, heart disease, cancer) - Delhi winter smog exemplifies seasonal spikes (stubble burning plus inversion trapping). Graded Response Action Plans (construction halts, odd-even traffic) emergency-respond; BS-VI fuels plus dust control prevent chronically. Masks filter coarsely; policy must clean sources.
NEET Snapshot:
  • PM2.5 fines penetrate lungs to bloodstream.
  • Stubble plus inversion plus traffic spike Delhi winters.
Remember
  • PM2.5 crosses into blood; PM10 stops in airways.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most hazardous air particulate size is

Solution: Fine particles bypass airway defences into circulation.

Fig: Coarse dust stops in airways; fines cross into blood.

Chapter 23 · Topic 2

SO2

Environmental IssuesEcology and EnvironmentAir PollutionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sulphur dioxide (coal-plant, smelter emissions) chokes lungs (bronchoconstriction), kills lichens first (bioindicator wipeout mapping pollution), acidifies rain (sulphuric acid damaging marble-Taj, crops, lakes), and seeds smog particles. Scrubbers (flue-gas desulphurisation) plus low-sulphur fuels cut emissions; Taj Trapezium Zone restricts industries around the monument. Lichen return signals cleanup success visibly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lung irritant, lichen killer, acid-rain source.
  • Scrubbers plus low-sulphur fuels cut emissions.
Remember
  • Lichens vanish first where SO2 rises.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Solution: Sulphuric precipitation dissolves marble surfaces.

Chapter 23 · Topic 3

NOx

Environmental IssuesEcology and EnvironmentAir PollutionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nitrogen oxides (vehicle exhaust, thermal plants: NO plus NO2) brown-haze cities, irritate airways (asthma trigger), seed photochemical smog (sunlight cooking NOx plus VOCs into ozone-PAN), acidify rain (nitric acid), and fertilise waters (nitrogen deposition eutrophying). Catalytic converters (vehicles), low-NOx burners (plants) and BS-VI norms cut emissions. NOx plus VOC plus sun equals smog recipe.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Brown haze, airway irritant, smog seed, acid source.
  • Converters plus low-NOx burners cut vehicle-plant emissions.
Remember
  • Sunlight cooks NOx plus VOCs into smog ozone.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Photochemical smog forms when sunlight acts on

Solution: Sun-baked nitrogen oxides plus organics brew ozone-PAN smog.
